title: A Stochastic Gradient Method with an Exponential Convergence Rate for Finite Training Sets
authors: Nicolas Le Roux, Mark Schmidt, Francis Bach
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 25 (NIPS 2012)
summary: First linearly convergent stochastic method for strongly convex finite sums g = (1/n) sum_i f_i: SAG keeps a memory y_i of the last gradient of each f_i and moves along the average of the memory (a randomized version of the IAG method of Blatt et al.). Two propositions give a linear rate with a tiny step 1/(2nL) and a condition-number-free per-pass rate in the big-data regime n >= 8L/mu. Experiments on logistic regression show SAG beating FG, accelerated FG, SGD, Pegasos and L-BFGS in later passes.
main_result: Assumptions: each f_i' is L-Lipschitz (L = L_max), g mu-strongly convex, y_i^0 = 0, sigma^2 = (1/n) sum_i ||f_i'(x*)||^2. Proposition 1 (constant step alpha_k = 1/(2nL)): for k >= 1, E||x^k - x*||^2 <= (1 - mu/(8Ln))^k [3||x^0 - x*||^2 + 9 sigma^2/(4L^2)]; the text adds that an exponential rate holds for any constant step smaller than 1/(2nL). Proposition 2 (if n >= 8L/mu, step alpha_k = 1/(2 n mu); stated for k >= n because the first n iterations are assumed to use an SG-type step): E[g(x^k) - g(x*)] <= C (1 - 1/(8n))^k with C = (16L/(3n))||x^0 - x*||^2 + (4 sigma^2/(3 n mu)) (8 log(1 + mu n/(4L)) + 1), i.e. a per-pass contraction exp(-1/8) independent of kappa; the paper notes Prop. 2 allows alpha_k <= 1/(16L). Proofs: Lyapunov functions on (x^k, {y_i^k}). Documented gap (section 'Large step sizes', verified verbatim): 'In practice we observed better performance using step sizes of alpha_k = 1/L and alpha_k = 2/(L + n mu)', which the theory does not cover; a doubling line search estimating L is proposed without proof.
relevance: A1/A4: the first SAG rate already has the min(1/n, mu/L)-type contraction refined by all later papers; its kappa-independent per-pass rate under n >= 8 kappa is the big-data regime of the lower bound. B3: earliest explicit statement of the step-size gap (1/(2nL) in theory vs 1/L in practice), a target for the tightness-ratio experiments. Pipeline: baseline SAG implementation details (y_i^0 = 0, sigma^2 at optimum).

title: Minimizing Finite Sums with the Stochastic Average Gradient
authors: Mark Schmidt, Nicolas Le Roux, Francis Bach
venue: Mathematical Programming 162(1-2):83-112 (online June 2016)
summary: Journal version of SAG with a unified Lyapunov proof covering both convex (O(n/k)) and strongly convex (linear) cases under a single step size 1/(16L), and a long section on implementation (line search, re-weighting, mini-batches, non-uniform sampling). The proof uses a more general Lyapunov function whose polynomial positivity conditions are checked by computer; code is released. It explicitly catalogs which practical choices lack theory.
main_result: Theorem 1 (verified verbatim; each f_i' L-Lipschitz, L = L_max; constant step alpha_k = 1/(16L)): for k >= 1, E[g(xbar^k)] - g(x*) <= (32n/k) C_0, where C_0 = g(x^0) - g(x*) + (4L/n)||x^0 - x*||^2 + sigma^2/(16L) if y_i^0 = 0, and C_0 = (3/2)[g(x^0) - g(x*)] + (4L/n)||x^0 - x*||^2 if y_i^0 = f_i'(x^0) - g'(x^0); further, if g is mu-strongly convex, E[g(x^k)] - g(x*) <= (1 - min{mu/(16L), 1/(8n)})^k C_0. The bound is valid for any L above the true constant, hence for any step <= 1/(16L), and the method adapts to unknown mu. Proof: Lyapunov function of the nonlinear stochastic system (x^k, y^k), with computer-aided verification of positivity of certain polynomials (Appendix B). Documented gaps (verified): Sec. 4.5 'always converged and often performed better than the step size of 1/16L suggested by our analysis. Thus, in our experiments we used alpha_k = 1/L even though we do not have a formal analysis of the method under this step size'; stochastic line search without theory (Sec. 4.6); non-uniform sampling: 'we do not yet have any theoretical proof', and sampling proportional to L_i with step n/sum_i L_i 'does not seem to converge in general' (later resolved by Xiao-Zhang 2014, Schmidt et al. 2015, Gower et al. 2021).
relevance: A1/A4: SAG rate 1 - min{mu/(16L), 1/(8n)} to compare with SAGA/Bach's 1 - min{1/(3n), 3mu/(16R^2)}; its comparison of SAG over n iterations with FG (1 - mu/L) and AFG (1 - sqrt(mu/L)) frames the kappa vs sqrt(kappa) question of A1/A4. B3: clearest catalogue of practical choices (1/L step, line search, non-uniform sampling) without theory, i.e. the gap the tightness ratios should explain. Pipeline: implementation tricks (storing scalars for linear models, exact regularization, mini-batches). | A4/B3: canonical documented 16x step-size gap for a SAG(A)-type method and identification of 'cocoercivity/variance' steps as the source of the conservative constant; B2: explicit statement that the effective (local) mu governs the observed rate. | Pipeline/(A4): the de-facto protocol (lambda = 1/n, effective passes, seeds, line-searched L) that the project's experiments should mirror or deliberately deviate from (lambda << 1/n to reach kappa >> n). (B3): the gap between the analytic constant 0.25 max ||a_i||^2 and the line-search estimate is a first 'tightness ratio' of the smoothness inequality; L_max vs mean L_i quantifies anisotropy of sample norms.

title: Accelerating Stochastic Gradient Descent using Predictive Variance Reduction
authors: Rie Johnson, Tong Zhang
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 26 (NIPS 2013), pp. 315-323
summary: Introduces SVRG: an outer loop computes the full gradient at a snapshot w~ and an inner loop of m steps uses the control variate v_t = grad psi_i(w_{t-1}) - grad psi_i(w~) + grad P(w~). Linear convergence is proved with an explicit variance-reduction argument and no gradient storage, so the method applies to structured prediction and neural networks. Experiments compare SVRG with SGD and SDCA on convex losses and with SGD on neural nets.
main_result: Theorem 1 (verified verbatim; Option II: w~_s drawn uniformly from the inner iterates; each psi_i convex and L-smooth, L = L_max; P gamma-strongly convex): if m is large enough that alpha = 1/(gamma eta (1 - 2 L eta) m) + 2 L eta/(1 - 2 L eta) < 1, then E P(w~_s) - P(w*) <= alpha^s [P(w~_0) - P(w*)]. The paper's own example: in the case L/gamma = n one may take eta = 0.1/L and m = O(n) to get alpha = 1/2 (equivalently m = 50 L/gamma), hence O((n + L/gamma) log(1/eps)) gradient evaluations (each stage costs 2m + n). Key inequality (verified): E||v_t||^2 <= 4L[P(w_{t-1}) - P(w*) + P(w~) - P(w*)], obtained from ||a+b||^2 <= 2||a||^2 + 2||b||^2 and cocoercivity; no Lyapunov function, the proof telescopes over an epoch and uses strong convexity of P. Documented gaps (verified verbatim): 'In practical implementations, it is natural to choose option I, or take w~_s to be the average of the past t iterates. However, our analysis depends on option II'; experiments use Option I with m = 2n (convex) and 5n (nonconvex) although the theory needs m of order kappa; the analysis forces eta < 1/(4L) (as noted by Nguyen et al. 2017). Acknowledgment: 'We thank Leon Bottou and Alekh Agarwal for spotting a mistake in the original theorem.'
relevance: A2: SVRG is the estimator plugged into Nesterov's method in the naive acceleration and the base of loopless methods and L-Katyusha (A3); its 4L[...] variance bound is the inequality that must become 'absorbable' in A3. B3: the Option I vs Option II and m = 2n vs m ~ kappa discrepancies are canonical theory-practice gaps to instrument. Pipeline: reference two-loop implementation. | A2/A3: defines the estimator that is plugged into Nesterov's algorithm (A2) and into L-Katyusha (A3); its classical variance bound 4L(f(w) - f* + f(wtilde) - f*) is exactly the 'loose' bound that Allen-Zhu says cannot give acceleration, versus the tight bound 2L(f(wtilde) - f(x) - <grad f(x), wtilde - x>) whose inner-product term the negative momentum cancels. Bridge to Bach's Section 5.4.4: SVRG is the snapshot-based sibling of SAGA (Bach's Prop. 5.9), and L-SVRG's coin-flip reference point is its loopless form. | (A2): the estimator plugged into Nesterov's scheme in the naive-acceleration hypothesis. (B3): the update-variance plot is precisely the instrumented quantity (variance <= second-moment step) that the project's tightness ratios need. Pipeline: the historical lambda convention (lambda n of order 1-10 on these datasets, i.e. kappa of order n or below).

title: SAGA: A Fast Incremental Gradient Method With Support for Non-Strongly Convex Composite Objectives
authors: Aaron Defazio, Francis Bach, Simon Lacoste-Julien
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 27 (NIPS 2014)
summary: SAGA stores one past gradient per component and uses the unbiased estimator f_j'(x^k) - f_j'(phi_j^k) + (1/n) sum_i f_i'(phi_i^k), with a proximal step for composite objectives. It sits between SAG (biased, lower variance) and SVRG (unbiased, no memory), is the first such method with linear rates that also adapts automatically to unknown strong convexity, and handles non-strongly convex composite objectives at rate O(n/k). This is the algorithm analyzed in Bach's Proposition 5.9.
main_result: Assumptions: each f_i convex with L-Lipschitz gradient (L = L_max), h convex with cheap prox. Theorem 1 (verified; each f_i mu-strongly convex, step gamma = 1/(2(mu n + L))): with the Lyapunov function T^k = (1/n) sum_i f_i(phi_i^k) - f(x*) - (1/n) sum_i <f_i'(x*), phi_i^k - x*> + c||x^k - x*||^2, c = 1/(2 gamma (1 - gamma mu) n), one has E[T^{k+1}] <= (1 - 1/kappa) T^k with 1/kappa = gamma mu = mu/(2(mu n + L)), hence E||x^k - x*||^2 <= (1 - mu/(2(mu n + L)))^k [||x^0 - x*||^2 + (n/(mu n + L)) (f(x^0) - <f'(x*), x^0 - x*> - f(x*))]. Verified in the text: if strong convexity holds only on average (f, not each f_i) the rate degrades to 1 - mu/(6(mu n + L)) with gamma = 1/(3(mu n + L)). mu-free step gamma = 1/(3L): E||x^k - x*||^2 <= (1 - min{1/(4n), mu/(3L)})^k [||x^0 - x*||^2 + (2n/(3L))(f(x^0) - <f'(x*), x^0 - x*> - f(x*))] (automatic adaptivity to mu). Non-strongly convex, gamma = 1/(3L): E[F(xbar^k) - F(x*)] <= (4n/k)[(2L/n)||x^0 - x*||^2 + f(x^0) - <f'(x*), x^0 - x*> - f(x*)] for the average iterate. Theory-practice (verified verbatim): 'Each method had its step size parameter chosen so as to give the fastest convergence', and SVRG is run with the recalibration pass every n iterations. Contrast with Bach's Prop. 5.9: same algorithm, but Bach uses gamma = 1/(4R^2), the gradient-difference Lyapunov ||theta - eta*||^2 + 3 gamma^2 sum_i ||z_i - f_i'(eta*)||^2 (instead of Bregman terms), assumes only F strongly convex, and gets 1 - min{1/(3n), 3mu/(16R^2)}.
relevance: Core of every hypothesis: A1 (the n + kappa_max complexity whose sqrt(n kappa) improvement is the subject), A3/A4 (baseline whose exponent kappa^1 is measured), B1 (Theorem 1's proof steps are the ones to re-derive with P^{-1}), B2/B3 (each inequality of Theorem 1 - Bregman Lyapunov vs Bach's gradient-norm Lyapunov, cocoercivity, variance <= second moment - is instrumented). Pipeline: SAGA reference step sizes 1/(3L) and 1/(2(mu n + L)). | A1/A4/B3 baseline: the two SAGA Lyapunov structures (function-value based here, gradient-norm based in Bach's notes) have different tight constants; PEPit shows this one is tight per step. Documents that tuned step sizes beat theoretical ones (theory-practice gap of B2/B3). | (A1)/(B3): comparison point for Bach's constants (gamma = 1/(4R^2), rate min{1/(3n), 3mu/(16R^2)}) against the original (gamma = 1/(3L), rate min{1/(4n), mu/(3L)}) and against the Bregman Lyapunov function, which is tighter than the squared-gradient one when the f_i are far from quadratic (logistic); the instrumented proof of (B3) can test both. Pipeline: datasets and the 'tuned step size' convention.

title: Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent Methods for Regularized Loss Minimization
authors: Shai Shalev-Shwartz, Tong Zhang
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 14:567-599
summary: Analyzes stochastic dual coordinate ascent for regularized loss minimization P(w) = (1/n) sum_i phi_i(w^T x_i) + (lambda/2)||w||^2: at each step one dual coordinate is maximized exactly (or approximately). It proves the first linear rate for smooth losses and O(1/eps) for Lipschitz losses, measured by the duality gap, which also gives a practical stopping criterion. SVRG and SAGA were designed to match this rate without the dual.
main_result: Assumptions: ||x_i|| <= 1, phi_i convex, phi_i(0) <= 1 and phi_i >= 0 for the Lipschitz part, alpha^(0) = 0. Theorem 2 (verified; (1/gamma)-smooth losses, i.e. an L_max-type constant 1/gamma with mu = lambda): T >= (n + 1/(lambda gamma)) log((n + 1/(lambda gamma)) / eps_P) iterations give E[P(w^(T)) - D(alpha^(T))] <= eps_P, i.e. O~((n + kappa) log(1/eps)) with kappa = 1/(lambda gamma); a variant with averaging after T_0 is also stated. Theorem 1 (verified; L-Lipschitz losses): T >= T_0 + n + 4L^2/(lambda eps_P) with T_0 >= max(0, ceil(n log(0.5 lambda n L^{-2}))) + n + 20 L^2/(lambda eps_P), i.e. O~(n + L^2/(lambda eps)); Remark 2: for the hinge loss the constant 4 can be replaced by 1. Proof: the dual objective is the potential: E[D(alpha^(t)) - D(alpha^(t-1))] >= (s/n)[P(w^(t-1)) - D(alpha^(t-1))] - (s/n)^2 G^(t)/(2 lambda) for s in [0,1], where G^(t) collects ||u_i - alpha_i||^2 ||x_i||^2 terms (the only place smoothness enters); no step size is needed. Practice notes: experiments also run SDCA-Perm (random permutation per epoch) while the analysis assumes i.i.d. sampling; the averaging/random-stopping variants need T, T_0 only in theory; SDCA ties the strong convexity to lambda (documented disadvantage when mu > lambda, see Gower et al. 2020).
relevance: A1: SDCA is the dual member of the lower-bound class (span-based, i.i.d. uniform sampling) and the O~((n + kappa) log(1/eps)) benchmark; the Lipschitz-loss O(1/eps) regime shows what is lost without smoothness. B2: SDCA's rate uses mu = lambda only, so the trajectory-dependent mu_eff(t) of B2 is exactly the curvature SDCA cannot exploit. B3: duality gap as an exact computable progress measure for the logistic-regression instrumentation.

title: Finito: A Faster, Permutable Incremental Gradient Method for Big Data Problems
authors: Aaron J. Defazio, Tiberio S. Caetano, Justin Domke
venue: Proceedings of the 31st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2014), PMLR 32(2):1125-1133
summary: Finito keeps a table of points phi_i and gradients f_i'(phi_i) and iterates w = phibar - (1/(alpha s n)) sum_i f_i'(phi_i), then overwrites one phi_j by w. Under the 'big data condition' n >= 2L/s it converges at a per-epoch rate exp(-1/2) with a fixed, tuning-free step size, described in the abstract as 'a theoretical convergence rate four times faster than existing methods, for sums with sufficiently many terms'. The method supports sampling without replacement (permutations), which is faster empirically but unproven; it is essentially MISO with step sizes n times larger.
main_result: Assumptions: each f_i L-smooth (L = L_max) and s-strongly convex; big data condition n >= beta L/s. Theorem 1 (verified verbatim; beta = 2, alpha = 2, all phi_i^(0) equal): E f(phibar^(k)) - f(w*) <= (3/(4s)) (1 - 1/(2n))^k ||f'(phibar^(0))||^2; the text contrasts this with SAG's 1 - 1/(8n) rate when beta = 2 and notes that per epoch the Finito rate is (1 - 1/(2n))^n ~ exp(-1/2) = 0.606, independent of kappa as long as n >= 2 kappa. Proof: Lyapunov function T = T_1 + T_2 + T_3 + T_4 built from f(phibar), -(1/n) sum_i [f_i(phi_i) + <f_i'(phi_i), w - phi_i>], (s/(2n))||w - phibar||^2 and -(s/(2n^2)) sum_i ||phibar - phi_i||^2, shown to decrease geometrically in expectation and to dominate f(phibar) - f(w*). Documented gaps (verified): 'In cases where the big data condition does not hold, we conjecture that the step size must be reduced proportionally to the violation of the big data condition. In practice, the most effective step size can be found by testing a number of step sizes'; permutation sampling gives further speed-ups in practice with no theory; the related-work section recalls that the best step size for SAG is usually not the theoretical one (1/L instead of 1/16L) and that MISO is essentially Finito 'but with step sizes n times smaller'.
relevance: A1: a span-based method with the kappa-free big-data rate, illustrating the regime kappa << n of the lower bound where only n log(1/eps) matters. B2: its rate uses the individual strong convexity s of each f_i, a local curvature quantity, motivating the mu_eff(t) diagnostic. B3: documented without-replacement and step-size gaps.

title: Incremental Majorization-Minimization Optimization with Application to Large-Scale Machine Learning
authors: Julien Mairal
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization 25(2):829-855
summary: Journal version of MISO (first presented at ICML 2013): an incremental majorization-minimization scheme that keeps one surrogate per component and minimizes their average at each step. With majorizing proximal-gradient surrogates it yields a linearly convergent incremental proximal gradient method; with strongly convex lower-bound surrogates (MISOmu) it attains the SAG/SDCA-type rate under n >= 2L/mu. The paper also covers non-convex objectives (asymptotic stationarity) and gives practical heuristics for choosing the step size.
main_result: f = (1/T) sum_t f^t. Proposition 3.3 (verified; majorizing surrogates in S_{L,rho}(f^t, .) with rho >= L... stated for strongly convex surrogate functions): convex case E[f(thetabar_n) - f*] <= L T ||theta* - theta_0||^2/(2n) (eq. 3.2); if f is mu-strongly convex, E[f(theta_n) - f*] <= (1 - 2mu/(T(L + mu)))^{n-1} (L/2)||theta* - theta_0||^2 (eq. 3.3), a per-iteration rate 1 - 2/(T kappa)-type, i.e. O(T kappa log(1/eps)) (the original MISO rate). Proposition 3.4 (verified verbatim; MISO for strongly convex unconstrained smooth problems: each f^t mu-strongly convex, L-smooth and bounded below, lower-bound quadratic surrogates g_n^t of eq. (3.8), requires T >= 2L/mu): E[f(theta_n) - f*] <= (1 - 1/(3T))^n (2T/mu) ||f'(theta_0)||^2 (eq. 3.9), i.e. O(T log(1/eps)) in the big-data regime; the potential is the gap between f* and the average lower-bound surrogate ('inspired by the convergence proof of SDCA'); the text notes (verified) that the same result 'was independently obtained by Defazio et al. [18], where a refined analysis provides a slightly better rate, namely the constant 1/3 in (3.9) may be replaced by 1/2'. L is the smoothness of each component (L_max). Documented gaps (verified, Secs. 3.3-3.4): 'using a smaller value for L than the theoretical one could work well in practice'; heuristics MISO1/MISO2 choose L by a one-pass search on 5% of the data, inspired by Leon Bottou's sgd toolbox, and the text 'suggest[s] using larger step sizes than 1/L in practice', without theory.
relevance: A1: MISOmu is another span-based method with a kappa-free rate under n >= 2 kappa. B2/B3: the two MISO rates (1 - 2/(T kappa) vs 1 - 1/(3T)) show how strongly a proof's constants depend on the surrogate (upper vs lower bound), a concrete example of 'which inequality is loose'; the step-size heuristic is a documented practice-theory gap.

title: Semi-Stochastic Gradient Descent Methods
authors: Jakub Konecny, Peter Richtarik
venue: Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics 3:9 (published 23 May 2017; first version arXiv:1312.1666, December 2013)
summary: S2GD generalizes SVRG: each epoch computes one full gradient and then a random number of stochastic steps drawn from a geometric-like distribution that depends on a known lower bound nu on the strong convexity. The analysis contains SVRG (nu = 0) as a special case with slightly better constants, gives a closed-form choice of step size and epoch length minimizing total work, and obtains O((n + kappa) log(1/eps)) gradient evaluations. A practical variant S2GD+ is proposed without analysis.
main_result: Assumptions: f_i convex and L-smooth (L = L_max), f mu-strongly convex, 0 <= nu <= mu. Theorem 4 (verified): for step 0 < h < 1/(2L) and m such that c := (1 - nu h)^m/(beta h (1 - 2Lh)) + 2(L - mu)h/(1 - 2Lh) < 1, with beta = sum_{t=1}^m (1 - nu h)^{m-t} (eq. 4), E[f(x_j) - f*] <= c^j (f(x_0) - f*). For nu = 0 this is c = 1/(mu h (1 - 2Lh) m) + 2(L - mu)h/(1 - 2Lh) (Johnson-Zhang's constant with L replaced by L - mu in the second term); for nu = mu, c = (1 - mu h)^m/((1 - (1 - mu h)^m)(1 - 2Lh)) + 2(L - mu)h/(1 - 2Lh). Theorem 6 (verified, 'Choice of parameters'): fix j >= 1 epochs and eps, put Delta = eps^{1/j}; with h = h(j) = 1/(4(L - mu)/Delta + 2L) (eq. 24) and m(j) as in eq. (25), E(f(x_j) - f*) <= eps (f(x_0) - f*); with j = ceil(log(1/eps)), Delta >= exp(-1), m(j) = O(kappa), and the total work is W = log(1/eps)(n + O(kappa)) = O((n + kappa) log(1/eps)) (eq. 26). Proof ingredients: cocoercivity and the SVRG variance bound; no Lyapunov function. Example (verified): S2GD only needs the workload equivalent to about 2.1 full-gradient evaluations for n = 1e9, kappa = 1e3, eps = 1e-6. Gap (verified): S2GD+ 'exhibits superior performance in practice' but is not analyzed.
relevance: A1: explicit O((n + kappa) log(1/eps)) work bound with constants and a comparison table (SAG, SDCA, SVRG, EMGD); shows the n vs kappa trade-off through the epoch length. A3: the random epoch length is the mechanism that loopless methods (Kovalev et al.) push to the limit. B3: the closed-form optimal (h, m) is a theory-driven parameter choice that can be checked against practice on the logistic-regression instances.

title: SARAH: A Novel Method for Machine Learning Problems Using Stochastic Recursive Gradient
authors: Lam M. Nguyen, Jie Liu, Katya Scheinberg, Martin Takac
venue: Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2017), PMLR 70:2613-2621
summary: SARAH replaces the SVRG control variate by the recursive, biased estimator v_t = grad f_i(w_t) - grad f_i(w_{t-1}) + v_{t-1} (v_0 = full gradient), which needs no gradient storage. It proves linear convergence for strongly convex finite sums with the same O((n + kappa) log(1/eps)) complexity as SVRG but with step sizes up to 1/L instead of 1/(4L), and, unlike SVRG, linear convergence of a single inner loop. A practical variant SARAH+ with adaptive inner-loop length is proposed.
main_result: Assumptions: each f_i convex and L-smooth (L = L_max), P mu-strongly convex; w~_s drawn uniformly from the inner iterates. Theorem 4 (verified): if sigma_m := 1/(mu eta (m + 1)) + eta L/(2 - eta L) < 1 then E||grad P(w~_s)||^2 <= sigma_m^s ||grad P(w~_0)||^2 (any eta < 1/L works, versus SVRG's alpha_m which forces eta < 1/(4L)). Corollary 3 (verified): eta = 1/(2L), m = 4.5 kappa, T = log(||grad P(w~_0)||^2/eps)/log(9/7) outer iterations (sigma_m = 7/9) give total complexity O((n + kappa) log(1/eps)); Lemma 6 gives the optimal m for eta = 1/(alpha L). Theorem 1a (eta < 2/L, each f_i strongly convex) and Theorem 1b (verified; P mu-strongly convex and L-smooth, eta <= 2/(mu + L)): within one inner loop E||v_t||^2 <= (1 - 2 eta mu L/(mu + L))^t ||grad P(w_0)||^2, i.e. the SARAH inner loop itself converges linearly (rate 1 - 1/kappa for eta = O(1/L)), whereas the SVRG inner loop does not. Theorem 2 (verified; convex, eta < 1/L): E||grad P(w~_s)||^2 <= (2/(eta(m+1))) E[P(w~_{s-1}) - P*] + (eta L/(2 - eta L)) E||grad P(w~_{s-1})||^2, giving O((n + 1/eps) log(1/eps)). Key identity (Lemma 2): E||grad P(w_t) - v_t||^2 = sum_{j<=t} E||v_j - v_{j-1}||^2 - sum_{j<=t} E||grad P(w_j) - grad P(w_{j-1})||^2, bounded by (eta L/(2 - eta L)) E||v_0||^2. Convergence is measured in gradient norm; no Lyapunov function. Gap (verified): SARAH+ (Algorithm 2, stop the inner loop when ||v_t||^2 <= gamma ||v_0||^2) is practical but unanalyzed.
relevance: A1: SARAH is the other 'hybrid' (non-span) method that Hannah et al. 2018 show can beat the n log(1/eps) barrier - the second half of A1. A3: its biased recursive estimator is an alternative to negative momentum for making variance absorbable. B3: the bias-variance identity of Lemma 2 is a different inequality chain to instrument; the eta < 1/L vs eta < 1/(4L) comparison is a concrete constant-tightness question.

title: Variance Reduced Stochastic Gradient Descent with Neighbors
authors: Thomas Hofmann, Aurelien Lucchi, Simon Lacoste-Julien, Brian McWilliams
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28 (NIPS 2015), pp. 2305-2313
summary: Defines 'uniform q-memorization algorithms', iterations w+ = w - gamma(f_i'(w) - alpha_i + alphabar) in which each stored gradient alpha_j is refreshed with probability q/n, covering SAGA (q = 1), q-SAGA, and an SVRG variant that refreshes all alpha_j with probability q/n at every step, i.e. the first loopless SVRG. A single Lyapunov analysis gives geometric rates for every step size below 1/(4L), including a mu-independent universal step, and is extended to N-SAGA, which shares gradient memory between neighboring data points at the price of converging to a neighborhood. The paper explicitly sacrifices tightness in one inequality for simplicity.
main_result: Assumptions: f_i convex and L-smooth (L = L_max), f mu-strongly convex, unconstrained (grad f(w*) = 0). Lyapunov family (eq. 13, verified): L(w, H) = ||w - w*||^2 + S Hbar, Hbar = (1/n) sum_i H_i where H_i >= ||alpha_i - f_i'(w*)||^2 is refreshed to 2L h_i(w), h_i(w) = f_i(w) - f_i(w*) - <w - w*, f_i'(w*)>, and S := sigma gamma n/(L q) with 0 <= sigma <= 1 (described as a simplified version of the SAGA Lyapunov function of Defazio et al.); Lemma 2 (verified): E Hbar+ = ((n - q)/n) Hbar + (2Lq/n) f(w) (with f normalized so that f(w*) = 0). Theorem 1 (verified): for any step gamma = a/(4L) with a < 1 the algorithm converges at a geometric rate at least 1 - rho(a), with rho(a) = ((1 - a)/(1 - a/2)) q/n if a <= a(K) and rho(a) = a mu/(4L) otherwise, K := 4qL/(n mu), a(K) = 2K/(1 + K + sqrt(1 + K^2)); Corollary 1: rho is maximized at a = a(K); Corollary 2 (verified): the mu-free step gamma = (2 - sqrt 2)/(4L) (a = 2 - sqrt 2 ~ 0.5858) is within a factor 2 of the optimal rate for every K (first mu-adaptive proof for SVRG-type methods); Corollary 3 (verified): gamma = a/(4L) yields rho = min{((1 - a)/(1 - a/2)) q/n, a mu/(4L)}, e.g. gamma = 1/(5L) gives rho = min{q/(3n), mu/(5L)} ('roughly matching the rate given in [4] for q = 1', i.e. SAGA). Theorem 2: with epsilon-accurate (neighbor) corrections, geometric convergence up to a neighborhood of size 4 gamma delta-bar/mu-type. On tightness, verbatim (verified): 'for the sake of simplicity, we sacrifice tightness and choose beta = 1' in the generalized square-norm inequality ||x + y||^2 <= (1 + beta)||x||^2 + (1 + beta^{-1})||y||^2 - the same 2||a||^2 + 2||b||^2 step as in Bach's proof. Experiments use the step suggested by the analysis; 'using a step size of 1/L for SAGA as suggested in previous work did not appear to give better results' (verified).
relevance: A3: precursor of loopless SVRG (probability-q/n refresh) that Kovalev et al. turn into L-SVRG/L-Katyusha (acknowledged in their footnote 1). B3: Hofmann's Lyapunov is Bach's V_t with H_i in place of ||z_i - f_i'(eta*)||^2, and the paper names the exact inequality (beta = 1 in the square-norm step) where tightness is given up - a prime candidate for the tightness-ratio bottleneck. B1: the analysis is written for any memory update with uniform refresh probability, a template for the preconditioned variant. | B3 (central): the same Lyapunov as Prop. 5.9 with explicit optimal weight sigma and the exact 'min of two rates' trade-off rho*(K) parametrized by K = 4 kappa q/n, so the bottleneck step can be predicted per (n, kappa) regime (A4: kappa >> n vs kappa << n). B2: transient-phase discussion as a trajectory effect.

title: Don't Jump Through Hoops and Remove Those Loops: SVRG and Katyusha are Better Without the Outer Loop
authors: Dmitry Kovalev, Samuel Horvath, Peter Richtarik
venue: Proceedings of the 31st International Conference on Algorithmic Learning Theory (ALT 2020), PMLR 117:451-467
summary: Removes the outer loop of SVRG and Katyusha: at each step the reference point w^k is reset to x^k with probability p (a coin flip), otherwise kept. L-SVRG with eta = 1/(6L) and p = 1/n is analyzed with a four-lemma, one-page Lyapunov proof on ||x^k - x*||^2 plus the memory-gradient discrepancy, closing the open question of SVRG with an outer loop of length n (independent of kappa). L-Katyusha achieves the accelerated O((n + sqrt(n kappa)) log(1/eps)) rate with a step that does not depend on mu; experiments show gains over the loopy versions.
main_result: Assumptions: f_i convex and L-smooth (L = L_max), f mu-strongly convex. L-SVRG: g^k = grad f_i(x^k) - grad f_i(w^k) + grad f(w^k), x^{k+1} = x^k - eta g^k, w^{k+1} = x^k with probability p, else w^k. Lyapunov Phi^k = ||x^k - x*||^2 + D^k with D^k = (4 eta^2/(p n)) sum_i ||grad f_i(w^k) - grad f_i(x*)||^2 (for p = 1/n: 4 eta^2 sum_i ||.||^2, cf. Bach's 3 gamma^2 sum_i ||z_i - f_i'(eta*)||^2). Numbering of the ALT/PMLR version (verified; arXiv version: Lemmas 3.1-3.4, Theorem 3.5, Theorem 4.6): Lemma 1 (eq. 9): E||x^{k+1} - x*||^2 <= (1 - eta mu)||x^k - x*||^2 - 2 eta (f(x^k) - f*) + eta^2 E||g^k||^2; Lemma 2 (eq. 10): E||g^k||^2 <= 4L(f(x^k) - f*) + (p/(2 eta^2)) D^k; Lemma 3 (eq. 11): E D^{k+1} <= (1 - p) D^k + 8 L eta^2 (f(x^k) - f*); Lemma 4 (eq. 12): for eta <= 1/(6L), E Phi^{k+1} <= (1 - eta mu)||x^k - x*||^2 + (1 - p/2) D^k. Theorem 5: eta = 1/(6L), p = 1/n gives E Phi^k <= max{1 - mu/(6L), 1 - 1/(2n)}^k Phi^0, i.e. O((n + L/mu) log(1/eps)); the discussion shows total complexity O((1/p + n + L/mu + L p n/mu) log(1/eps)), optimal for any p in [min{c/n, c mu/L}, max{c/n, c mu/L}]; 'the step size does not depend on the strong convexity parameter mu and yet the resulting complexity adapts to it'. L-Katyusha (Lemma 10 and Theorem 11, verified): sigma = mu/L, theta_1 = min{sqrt(2 sigma n/3), 1/2}, theta_2 = 1/2, p = 1/n, eta = theta_2/((1 + theta_2) theta_1): E Psi^{k+1} <= (1 - theta) E Psi^k with theta = min{sigma/(6 theta_1), 1/(2n)}, hence k = O((n + sqrt(n L/mu)) log(1/eps)), with Lyapunov Psi = Z + Y + W (distance term in z, function gaps at y and at the reference point w). Footnote 1 (verified): the loopless idea 'was independently explored in Hofmann et al. (2015)'.
relevance: A3: this is the loopless Katyusha whose proof the project reproduces in Bach's Lyapunov style; the L-SVRG Lyapunov Phi^k is structurally identical to Bach's V_t (distance + gamma^2 times sum of stored-gradient errors), so Lemmas 1-4 map one-to-one onto the inequality chain of Prop. 5.9 with explicit constants (1/(6L), 4 eta^2, 1 - p/2) to compare with (1/(4R^2), 3 gamma^2, 1 - 1/(3n)). A4: the methods whose kappa^(1/2) exponent is measured. B3: the lemma-by-lemma structure is the natural unit for tightness ratios. | A3 (core reference): gives exactly the parameters theta_1, theta_2, p, eta, the Lyapunov function and the final O((n + sqrt(n kappa)) log(1/eps)) rate asked in key question (iii); the theta_2 w^k term is the loopless negative momentum, and the lemma with the -(theta_2/(2L theta_1))||g^k - grad f(x^k)||^2 term shows how the variance is paid by the reference-point term and absorbed via the function-value bound at w^k (ii). The W-recursion E[W^{k+1}] = (1 - p)W^k + theta_2(1 + theta_1)Y^k is the loopless analogue of the (1 - 1/n) table-update step in Bach's SAGA Lyapunov (Prop. 5.9), which makes this the natural template for reproducing the proof in Bach's style; L-SVRG's Lyapunov Phi^k is literally Bach's V_t with a coin-flip table. A4/B3: experiments use l2-regularized logistic regression with mu swept ('different regularizer weights, thus different condition numbers'), parameters set exactly as the theory prescribes; they deliberately do not compare with SAGA (memory argument), so the SAGA-vs-L-Katyusha kappa-scaling must be produced by the project (iv). | (A3): the method and Lyapunov style the project reproduces. (A4)/pipeline: protocol (distance to x* vs epochs, mu sweep, p = 1/n); the GD-computed reference optimum is a weak point the project can improve with Newton-based optima; the p-sweep is a cheap sanity check on the kappa-dependence.

title: A Simple Practical Accelerated Method for Finite Sums
authors: Aaron Defazio
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (NIPS 2016)
summary: Point-SAGA replaces the gradient step of SAGA by a proximal step on the sampled component, z = x^k + gamma(g_j^k - gbar^k), x^{k+1} = prox_{gamma f_j}(z), g_j^{k+1} = (z - x^{k+1})/gamma, so the gradient is implicitly evaluated at the new point. With a single step-size parameter it attains the accelerated O((n + sqrt(n kappa)) log(1/eps)) rate for smooth strongly convex sums, and fixed-step convergence for non-smooth f_i. The proof is a one-step Lyapunov contraction with the same Lyapunov function as Hofmann et al. (2015).
main_result: Assumptions: each f_i L-smooth and mu-strongly convex (individual strong convexity), 0 < mu < L; prox oracle for each f_i; L = L_max. Theorem 5 (verified verbatim, 'single step Lyapunov descent'): with T^k = (c/n) sum_i ||g_i^k - f_i'(x*)||^2 + ||x^k - x*||^2, c = 1/(mu L), and step gamma = sqrt((n - 1)^2 + 4 n L/mu)/(2 L n) - (1 - 1/n)/(2L), E[T^{k+1}] <= (1 - kappa') T^k with kappa' = mu gamma/(1 + mu gamma); the paper states this 'is the same Lyapunov function as used by Hofmann et al. [2015]'. Corollary 6 (verified): E||x^k - x*||^2 <= (1 - kappa')^k ((mu + L)/mu) ||x^0 - x*||^2, i.e. k = O((sqrt(n L/mu) + n) log(1/eps)) steps, matching the Lan-Zhou lower bound for gradient oracles ('We conjecture that this rate is optimal under the proximal operator oracle as well', verified). Theorem 7 (verified; non-smooth, mu-strongly convex f_i, ||g_i^0 - g_i^*|| <= B, ||x^0 - x*|| <= R): with gamma = R/(B sqrt n), E||xbar^k - x*||^2 <= 2 sqrt(n)(1 + mu R/(B sqrt n)) R B/(mu k). Proof tools: strengthened firm non-expansiveness of the prox under strong convexity (Prop. 1) and the Moreau decomposition (Prop. 2). Practice (verified): in the experiments the step size of every method is chosen using a grid search of powers of 2.
relevance: A3: an accelerated rate without momentum, obtained purely through where the gradient is evaluated (implicit/prox step), a contrast with the negative-momentum mechanism of L-Katyusha; its Lyapunov T^k is Bach's V_t with c = 1/(mu L) in place of 3 gamma^2. A4: a second accelerated baseline for the kappa^(1/2) exponent. B1: the implicit per-component step is a form of preconditioning, relevant to the P^{-1} modification. | A3 and B1: Lyapunov function identical in structure to Bach's V_t (Prop. 5.9) - table term with weight c = 1/(mu L) instead of Bach's Delta = 3 gamma^2 - so it shows precisely which step of Bach's proof must change (the cocoercivity step is applied to the proximal operator, i.e. an implicit/preconditioned-type update) to gain the sqrt(n kappa) rate without momentum; a natural reference for the project's P^{-1}-preconditioned SAGA modification and for the reproduction of accelerated proofs in Bach's style. | A3/B3: an accelerated finite-sum method whose Lyapunov is almost exactly Bach's V_t, with a quantified (small) tightness gap; a useful second 'tightness ratio' benchmark next to SAGA.

title: SAGA with Arbitrary Sampling
authors: Xun Qian, Zheng Qu, Peter Richtarik
venue: Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2019), PMLR 97:5190-5199
summary: SAGA-AS: a SAGA variant in which the set of updated components S_k is drawn from an arbitrary proper sampling (importance sampling, mini-batches, independent or partition samplings) with a bias-correcting random vector theta^S. Linear rates are proved with a new stochastic Lyapunov function (one that depends on the sampled set), for strongly convex f and under a quadratic functional growth condition without strong convexity, matching the primal-dual method Quartz. For serial sampling it recovers O((n + L_max/mu) log(1/eps)) (uniform) and O((n + Lbar/mu) log(1/eps)) (importance), with minibatch speed-ups and the first linear rate for a SAGA variant without strong convexity.
main_result: Assumptions: f mu-strongly convex, f_i convex and L_i-smooth, S proper (p_i = P(i in S) > 0), theta^S bias-correcting (E[theta_i^S 1_{i in S}] = 1, eq. 5/7). Theorem 3.1 (structure verified from the PDF): with the stochastic Lyapunov function Psi_S^k = ||x^k - x*||^2 + 2 alpha |S| sum_{i in S} sigma_i theta_i^S ||J_{:i}^k - grad f_i(x*)||^2, where sigma_i = 1/(4 L_i v_i p_i) and v_i := sum_{C ni i} p_C |C| (theta_i^C)^2 (eq. 8), if alpha satisfies the sampling-dependent bound (9) (of the form alpha <= min_i p_i/(mu + 4 L_i v_i p_i ...); the exact placement of the sampling constants could not be read reliably from the PDF text), then E[Psi_S^k] <= (1 - alpha mu)^k E[Psi_S^0]; with the largest admissible alpha the iteration complexity is max_i (1/p_i + 4 L_i v_i/(... mu)) log(1/eps) (eq. 10), and with theta_i^S = 1/p_i it becomes max_i (1/p_i + 4 L_i E_i[|S|]/(p_i mu)... ) log(1/eps) (eq. 11). Special cases stated explicitly in the paper's text (verified): serial uniform sampling O((n + L_max/mu) log(1/eps)) (Defazio et al.), serial importance sampling O((n + Lbar/mu) log(1/eps)) with Lbar = (1/n) sum_i L_i, and minibatch rates 'essentially the same as that of Quartz', including on sparse data (Sec. 3.4). Theorem 4.4 (verified): under the quadratic functional growth condition (Assumption 4.2, no strong convexity) linear convergence with the same Lyapunov structure, with Remark 4.5 giving a step alpha = min{(1/12) min_i p_i/(v_i ...), ...} that keeps the same order of complexity without knowing the growth constant; Theorem 4.6 (mu-strongly convex regularizer): the same complexity as Quartz. Constants: per-component L_i, so L_max or Lbar depending on p.
relevance: A1: shows how the n + kappa term depends on the sampling distribution (uniform vs importance vs minibatch), the sampling assumption in the lower bound. B1/B3: the stochastic Lyapunov with per-component weights sigma_i is the natural generalization when the step is preconditioned (P^{-1}) or when feature-covariance anisotropy makes the L_i heterogeneous; the L_max vs Lbar dichotomy is a measurable constant in the diagnosis. | B2: SAGA converges linearly with a growth-type (effective) constant instead of global strong convexity, supporting mu_eff-based explanations of fast practical rates; B3: same expected-smoothness constants as the project's data-dependent diagnosis.

title: Non-Uniform Stochastic Average Gradient Method for Training Conditional Random Fields
authors: Mark Schmidt, Reza Babanezhad, Mohamed Osama Ahmed, Aaron Defazio, Ann Clifton, Anoop Sarkar
venue: Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2015), PMLR 38:819-828
summary: Applies SAG to conditional random fields with a memory-efficient implementation and a non-uniform sampling (NUS) scheme that samples examples proportionally to adaptive estimates of their Lipschitz constants L_i. The appendix analyzes two NUS variants of SAGA and shows that sampling proportional to L_i with the memory updated uniformly gives a rate depending on the mean Lbar = (1/n) sum_i L_i instead of L_max. The practical scheme (mixture of uniform and Lipschitz sampling, step (1/2)(1/L + 1/Lbar), L_i estimates decreased by 0.9 after each visit) outperforms tuned SGD but has no theory.
main_result: Assumptions: f_i convex with L_i-Lipschitz gradients, f mu-strongly convex, L = max_i L_i, Lbar = (1/n) sum_i L_i. Proposition 1 (verified; sample j_t ~ p, estimator (1/(n p_j))(f_j'(w_t) - s_j) + (1/n) sum_i s_i, memory index r_t). (a) r_t = j_t: with alpha = n p_min/(4L + n mu), E||w_t - w*||^2 <= (1 - mu alpha)^t [||x_0 - x*||^2 + C_a], C_a = (2 p_min/(4L + n mu)^2) sum_i (1/p_i)||f_i'(x_0) - f_i'(x*)||^2 (for uniform p: step 1/(4L + n mu) and rate 1 - mu/(n mu + 4L) = 1 - 1/(n + 4 kappa_max)); proved (Appendix A) with a gradient-difference Lyapunov function. (b) p_j = L_j/sum_i L_i and r_t uniform: with alpha = 1/(4 Lbar), E||w_t - w*||^2 <= (1 - min{1/(3n), mu/(8 Lbar)})^t [||x_0 - x*||^2 + C_b], C_b of order n (f(x_0) - f*)/Lbar (Appendix B, SAGA Bregman Lyapunov). The text notes (verified) that (a) achieves its fastest rate at p_i = 1/n while (b) requires two samples per iteration, and 'We were not able to show a faster rate using only one sample on each iteration as used in our implementation.' Gap: the method actually used (mixture of uniform and L_i-proportional sampling, step (1/2)(1/L + 1/Lbar), adaptive L_i multiplied by 0.9 at each visit, verified) has no convergence proof; the conjecture that a suitable NUS gives O((n + Lbar/mu) log(1/eps)) was resolved by Gower et al. (2021).
relevance: B3: the only early paper with a gradient-norm Lyapunov identical in form to Bach's V_t (Prop. 1(a)), giving a second set of constants (1/(4L + n mu), 1 - 1/(n + 4 kappa)) for the tightness comparison; the L_max vs Lbar distinction and heterogeneous L_i are exactly the geometry knobs of B3. A1: shows which part of n + kappa is sampling-dependent.

title: Stochastic Quasi-Gradient Methods: Variance Reduction via Jacobian Sketching
authors: Robert M. Gower, Peter Richtarik, Francis Bach
venue: Mathematical Programming 188(1):135-192 (online May 2020)
summary: JacSketch maintains a sketch-and-project estimate J^k of the Jacobian of (f_1,...,f_n), updated by a random linear measurement at each step, and uses it as a control variate; SAGA, minibatch SAGA, reduced-memory and importance-sampling variants are special cases of the choice of sketch. Two theorems are proved: a general one with a deterministic Lyapunov function and two 'expected smoothness' constants, and a refined one with a stochastic Lyapunov function for partition samplings that yields the conjectured O((n + 4 Lbar/mu) log(1/eps)) rate for SAGA with importance sampling. It also gives the first minibatch SAGA complexities precise enough to define an optimal minibatch size.
main_result: Assumptions: f mu-strongly convex, f_i convex, sketch S unbiased with bias-correcting variable theta_S, and two expected smoothness constants (verified): Assumption 3.1 E_D||grad f_S(x) - grad f_S(x*)||^2 <= 2 L_1 (f(x) - f(x*)) and Assumption 3.2 E_D||(grad F(x) - grad F(x*)) Pi_S||^2_{W^{-1}} <= 2 L_2 (f(x) - f(x*)). Theorem 3.6 (verified): with Lyapunov Psi^k = ||x^k - x*||^2 + (alpha/(2 L_2)) ||J^k - grad F(x*)||^2_{W^{-1}} and step 0 < alpha <= min{1/(4 L_1), kappa/(4 L_2 rho/n^2 + mu kappa)} (kappa the stochastic condition number of the sketch, rho the sketch residual, eq. 51), E Psi^k <= (1 - alpha mu)^k Psi^0, hence iteration complexity max{4 L_1/mu, 1/kappa + 4 L_2 rho/(mu n^2 kappa)} log(1/eps). Table 1 (verified): gradient descent 4L/mu; SAGA with uniform sampling (n + 4 L_max/mu) log(1/eps) (step alpha = 1/(4 L_max + n mu)); tau-nice minibatch SAGA max{4 L_max^G/mu, n + ((n - tau)/(tau(n - 1))) 4 L_max/mu} log(1/eps), interpolating between SAGA and GD and giving an optimal minibatch size; Theorem 4.16 gives closed forms for L_1 and L_2 for minibatch sketches (specializing for tau-nice sampling to L_1 = L_max^G := max_i (1/C(n-1,tau-1)) sum_{C ni i} L_C and L_2 = max_i L_i/w_i). Theorem 5.2 (verified; stochastic Lyapunov, tau-partition samplings, W = I): step alpha <= min_C p_C/(mu + 4 L_C/n ...)-type and complexity max_C (1/p_C + 4 L_C/(n p_C mu)) log(1/eps); with singletons and p_i = (mu n + 4 L_i)/sum_j (mu n + 4 L_j) this gives (n + 4 Lbar/mu) log(1/eps) for SAGA with importance sampling, 'resolving a conjecture by Schmidt et al (2015)' (abstract, verified). The constants are expected-smoothness constants (L_max for serial uniform sampling, Lbar for importance sampling, between L and L_max for minibatches).
relevance: B1: JacSketch is literally the framework for a modified SAGA - a preconditioner P changes the metric W and the sketch, and Theorem 3.6 tells which constants (L_1, L_2, kappa, rho) absorb it; the Lyapunov Psi^k is Bach's V_t with Delta = alpha/(2 L_2) instead of 3 gamma^2. B3: expected smoothness is the constant that depends on feature-covariance anisotropy and sampling, a measurable quantity for the geometry-dependent bottleneck analysis. A1: sharpest non-accelerated constants (n + 4 kappa_max vs n + 4 kappa_bar) against which the sqrt(n kappa) rate is compared. | B3: replaces the uniform bound R^2 of the cocoercivity step by data-dependent expected-smoothness constants (L_max vs L_bar vs L(F)), the first candidate explanation of the gap on anisotropic feature covariances; B1: the sketch/weight matrix W is a form of preconditioning of the gradient memory, with proof steps spelled out in the W-norm.

title: A Unified Theory of SGD: Variance Reduction, Sampling, Quantization and Coordinate Descent
authors: Eduard Gorbunov, Filip Hanzely, Peter Richtarik
venue: Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2020), PMLR 108:680-690
summary: A single parametric assumption on the stochastic gradient g^k and a sequence sigma_k^2 - E||g^k - grad f(x*)||^2 <= 2A D_f(x^k, x*) + B sigma_k^2 + D_1 and E sigma_{k+1}^2 <= (1 - rho) sigma_k^2 + 2C D_f(x^k, x*) + D_2 - together with one Lyapunov theorem recovers the best known linear rates of SGD, SAGA, L-SVRG, SEGA, JacSketch, quantized and coordinate-descent variants (proximal setting), and generates five new methods. Variance-reduced methods are exactly those with D_1 = D_2 = 0.
main_result: Assumption 4.1 (verified, eqs. 7-9): E[g^k | x^k] = grad f(x^k); E[||g^k - grad f(x*)||^2 | x^k] <= 2A D_f(x^k, x*) + B sigma_k^2 + D_1; E[sigma_{k+1}^2 | sigma_k^2] <= (1 - rho) sigma_k^2 + 2C D_f(x^k, x*) + D_2. Theorem 4.1 (verified; f mu-strongly quasi-convex, Assumption 4.2): choose M > B/rho and a step 0 < gamma <= min{1/mu, 1/(A + C M)} (eq. 13); then with V^k = ||x^k - x*||^2 + M gamma^2 sigma_k^2, E V^k <= max{(1 - gamma mu)^k, (1 + B/M - rho)^k} V^0 + gamma^2 (D_1 + M D_2)/min{gamma mu, rho - B/M}. SAGA (Lemma A.6, verified, arXiv numbering): E||g^k - grad f(x*)||^2 <= 4L D_f(x^k, x*) + 2 sigma_k^2 and E sigma_{k+1}^2 <= (1 - 1/n) sigma_k^2 + (2L/n) D_f(x^k, x*), with sigma_k^2 = (1/n) sum_i ||grad f_i(phi_i^k) - grad f_i(x*)||^2, i.e. A = 2L, B = 2, rho = 1/n, C = L/n, D_1 = D_2 = 0; Corollary A.5 (verified): SAGA with gamma = 1/(6L) satisfies E V^k <= (1 - min{mu/(6L), 1/(2n)})^k V^0 (M = 4n, so V^k = ||x^k - x*||^2 + 4 gamma^2 sum_i ||grad f_i(phi_i^k) - grad f_i(x*)||^2). L-SVRG (Lemma A.11, Corollary A.10, verified): A = 2L, B = 2, rho = p, C = Lp, M = 4/p, gamma = 1/(6L): E V^k <= (1 - min{mu/(6L), p/2})^k V^0. Here L = L_max (each f_i convex and L-smooth); for SGD-SR and JacSketch the A parameter is an expected smoothness constant. Non-VR methods have D_1 or D_2 > 0 and converge only to an oscillation region of size O(gamma (D_1 + M D_2)).
relevance: B1: the cleanest template for 'which proof steps become loose under a modification': a preconditioned step only changes the constants (A, B, C, rho) of the two inequalities, which the project can recompute for P^{-1}. B3: the two parametric inequalities are exactly the two inequalities of Bach's proof (variance bound and memory recursion), with Bach's constants (R^2 from cocoercivity, 1/n refresh) as a special case: tightness ratios can be defined directly on A, B, C, rho. A3: the same framework is extended to loopless/accelerated variants in follow-up work. | B3 (central): the generic form of Bach's V_t = ||theta - eta*||^2 + Delta sum ||z_i - f_i'(eta*)||^2 with the 'min of two rates' made explicit through (A, B, C, rho); the parametric constants are exactly what the instrumented inequalities (cocoercivity -> A, memory contraction -> rho, C) measure; B1: a preconditioned variant only changes the constants of Assumption 4.1, so which step loosens with P can be read off directly.

title: Variance-Reduced Methods for Machine Learning
authors: Robert M. Gower, Mark Schmidt, Francis Bach, Peter Richtarik
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE 108(11):1968-1983
summary: Tutorial survey of variance-reduced methods for finite sums written for non-experts: the control-variate view of SAG/SAGA/SVRG/SDCA, their O((kappa_max + n) log(1/eps)) complexity versus O(kappa log(1/eps)) for GD at cost n per iteration, a 'Practical Considerations' section (step size, termination, memory, sparse gradients) and a survey of extensions (non-uniform sampling with kappa_mean, mini-batching, acceleration to O((sqrt(n kappa_max) + n) log(1/eps)), proximal and non-convex settings). It states clearly which practical settings lack theory.
main_result: Table 1: GD O(kappa log(1/eps)) iterations at cost O(n), VR methods O((kappa_max + n) log(1/eps)) at cost O(1), with kappa_max = L_max/mu, the basic inequality E_i||grad f_i(x) - grad f_i(x*)||^2 <= 2 L_max (f(x) - f(x*)) (Lemma A.1, verified) and the SVRG variance bound E||grad f_i(x~) - grad f_i(x^k)||^2 <= 4 L_max (f(x^k) - f* + f(x~) - f*). Statements of the theory-practice gap (verified in the PDF): SAG and SAGA have complexity O((kappa_max + n) log(1/eps)) using a stepsize gamma = O(1/L_max); 'In practice, SVRG tends to work well by using gamma = O(1/L_max)' and inner loop length t = n, whereas the original theory needs a complex dependency between L_max, mu, the stepsize gamma, and t, with later variants allowing O(1/L_max) steps (Hofmann et al. 2015; Kulunchakov and Mairal 2019; Kovalev et al. 2020); the theory for the primal VR methods relies on stepsizes of the form gamma = O(1/L_max), yet in practice one may not know L_max; the stochastic Armijo line search of the SAG implementation ('no theory exists for the method') and the 'Bottou trick' of Mairal (2015) ('tends to work well in practice but no theory is known'); SDCA needs no step size but 'implicitly assumes that the strong convexity constant mu is equal to lambda'. Non-uniform sampling gives O((kappa_mean + n) log(1/eps)) with kappa_mean = ((1/n) sum_i L_i)/mu; accelerated VR methods O((sqrt(n kappa_max) + n) log(1/eps)), matching the Woodworth-Srebro (2016) lower bound.
relevance: Pipeline and all hypotheses: the authoritative summary of rates and step sizes and of what is unproven in practice, to cite in the introduction and when designing the B3 experiments; A1 for the lower-bound statement and the kappa_max vs kappa_mean distinction; B2 because it singles out mu = lambda vs true curvature as a documented loss. | A1/A2/A3 framing: states in one place the gap between the naive hope (sqrt(kappa)) and the true optimal rate (sqrt(n kappa) + n), and the regime where acceleration pays off; the 'naive' sentence is the survey-level formulation of hypothesis A2. Bridge to Bach's notes (same authors' style, SAGA proof with the same Lyapunov function). | Pipeline/B3: the survey cited by the course notes; gives the accepted practical settings (step sizes, inner-loop conventions) for the SAGA/SVRG baselines of A4 and lists the known extensions (acceleration, memory-free variants) whose Lyapunov proofs share the structure of Prop. 5.9.

title: Learning Theory from First Principles
authors: Francis Bach
venue: MIT Press, Adaptive Computation and Machine Learning series, ISBN 978-0-262-04944-3 (released December 2024); Chapter 5 'Optimization for Machine Learning', Section 5.4.4 'Variance Reduction' (printed pp. 146-150 in the author's online PDF dated May 26, 2025)
summary: Textbook whose Chapter 5 treats optimization for machine learning; Section 5.4.4 presents SAGA for finite sums F = (1/n) sum_i f_i with each f_i R^2-smooth (e.g. logistic regression with features bounded by R) and F mu-strongly convex, and proves exponential convergence with O(d) iteration cost. The proof is a two-step Lyapunov argument (distance to optimum plus stored-gradient errors), and the chapter ends with a table of rates and experiments comparing GD, SGD and SAGA with their theoretical step sizes on l2-regularized logistic regression. The book is the project's starting point.
main_result: Proposition 5.9 (Convergence of SAGA; verified in the PDF): if z_i^(0) = f_i'(theta_0) for all i and gamma = 1/(4R^2), then E||theta_t - eta*||^2 <= (1 - min{1/(3n), 3 mu/(16 R^2)})^t (1 + n/4) ||theta_0 - eta*||^2 (eq. 5.30). Proof structure (verified): Step 1 expands ||theta_t - eta*||^2, uses unbiasedness, ||a + b||^2 <= 2||a||^2 + 2||b||^2, cocoercivity of each f_i (Prop. 5.4) giving E||f_i'(theta_{t-1}) - f_i'(eta*)||^2 <= R^2 (theta_{t-1} - eta*)^T F'(theta_{t-1}) (eq. 5.31, using F'(eta*) = 0), and variance <= second moment, yielding E||theta_t - eta*||^2 <= ||theta_{t-1} - eta*||^2 - 2 gamma (1 - gamma R^2)(theta_{t-1} - eta*)^T F'(theta_{t-1}) + (2 gamma^2/n) sum_i ||f_i'(eta*) - z_i^(t-1)||^2; Step 2 shows E sum_i ||f_i'(eta*) - z_i^(t)||^2 <= (1 - 1/n) sum_i ||f_i'(eta*) - z_i^(t-1)||^2 + R^2 (theta_{t-1} - eta*)^T F'(theta_{t-1}); combining with Delta = 3 gamma^2 and strong convexity (theta - eta*)^T F'(theta) >= mu ||theta - eta*||^2 gives the contraction of V_t = ||theta_t - eta*||^2 + 3 gamma^2 sum_i ||z_i^(t) - f_i'(eta*)||^2 by 1 - min{1/(3n), 3 mu/(16 R^2)}; initialization plus Lipschitz continuity gives the factor 1 + 3n/16 <= 1 + n/4. Consequences stated (verified): after an effective pass (n iterations) the contraction is exp(-min{1/3, 3 mu n/(16 R^2)}); t >= max{3n, 16 R^2/(3 mu)} log(2n/eps), so t = 3n + (16 R^2/(3 mu)) log(2n/eps) iterations suffice, running time d(3n + 16 R^2/(3 mu)) log(2n/eps) versus d n (R^2/mu) log(1/eps) for GD with step 1/R^2: 'We replace the product of n and condition number kappa = R^2/mu by a sum', with kappa = R^2/mu explicitly noted as 'larger than L/mu, where L is the smoothness constant of F' (an L_max-type constant). Experiments (Fig. 5.4, verified): l2-regularized logistic regression, d = 40 Gaussian inputs, lambda = R^2/n, n = 1,000 (top) and n = 10,000 (bottom), GD/SGD/SAGA all with theoretical step sizes; 'SAGA gets to machine precision after 50 effective passes over the data in these two cases'.
relevance: The object of study for every hypothesis: A1-A4 build on its n + kappa complexity (a sum replacing n kappa) and its Lyapunov style; B1 modifies its update theta_t = theta_{t-1} - gamma P^{-1} g_t; B2 replaces the strong-convexity step (theta - eta*)^T F'(theta) >= mu||theta - eta*||^2 by mu_eff(t); B3 instruments exactly the inequalities listed in the proof (square norm, cocoercivity eq. 5.31, variance <= second moment, strong convexity, min of two rates, Lipschitz at init). Pipeline: the book's own experiment (d = 40, lambda = R^2/n, n = 1,000 and 10,000) is the natural first test case. | Baseline for the whole project (A1-B3): the exact statement, step size and Lyapunov proof whose inequalities are instrumented in B3 and whose rate (n + kappa) log(1/eps) is compared with the lower bound Omega((n + sqrt(n kappa)) log(1/eps)) of A1 and the accelerated rate of A3; the notation (theta, eta*, R^2, mu, z_i) is the one the project's lower-bound section should adopt when translating the Lan-Zhou / Han et al. conventions. | Pipeline/B3 (the reference proof): defines exactly the chain of inequalities to be instrumented (square-norm, cocoercivity, variance <= second moment, strong convexity, min of two rates, Lipschitz at initialization) and the Lyapunov structure whose tightness is tested; A4/B2: the book's own experiments use theoretical step sizes on logistic regression, the baseline against which the theory-practice gap is measured; B1: the proof is written in the Euclidean norm, so each step's dependence on P is visible. | Baseline for everything. (A1)/(A4): lambda = R^2/n makes kappa = n, exactly the boundary where n + sqrt(n kappa) = 2n, so acceleration cannot help; the kappa >> n regime of (A4) requires lambda << R^2/n. (B2)/(B3): the proof's constants R^2 (max norm, factor-4 slack vs ||x_i||^2/4) and mu = lambda are the global quantities to compare with trajectory-dependent mu_eff(t) and local Hessians. Pipeline: the book's own synthetic generator (Gaussian x, noisy linear labels, d = 40) is the natural starting point.

title: A Proximal Stochastic Gradient Method with Progressive Variance Reduction
authors: Lin Xiao, Tong Zhang
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization 24(4):2057-2075
summary: Prox-SVRG extends SVRG to composite objectives P = (1/n) sum_i f_i + R with a proximal step and, importantly, to non-uniform sampling with probabilities q_i. The rate depends on the weighted constant L_Q = max_i L_i/(q_i n), which equals L_max for uniform sampling and the average Lbar = (1/n) sum_i L_i when q_i is proportional to L_i - the first rigorous proof that importance sampling replaces L_max by the mean. Experiments on l1-regularized logistic regression study the sensitivity to the step size and to the epoch length.
main_result: Theorem 1 (verified verbatim; each f_i convex and L_i-smooth, P mu-strongly convex, x~_s = average of the inner iterates): let L_Q = max_i L_i/(q_i n), 0 < eta < 1/(4 L_Q) and m large enough that rho = 1/(mu eta (1 - 4 L_Q eta) m) + 4 L_Q eta (m + 1)/((1 - 4 L_Q eta) m) < 1 (eq. 14); then E P(x~_s) - P* <= rho^s [P(x~_0) - P*]. Remarks (verified): with eta = theta/L_Q, rho <= (L_Q/mu)/((1 - 4 theta) theta m) + 4 theta/(1 - 4 theta) for m >> 1; theta = 0.1 and m = 100 L_Q/mu give rho ~ 5/6, hence overall complexity O((n + L_Q/mu) log(1/eps)); q_i = L_i/sum_j L_j minimizes L_Q to Lbar = (1/n) sum_i L_i. Corollary 2 (verified): non-strongly convex case by adding (eps/2)||x||^2. Proof: variance bound E||v_k - grad F(x_{k-1})||^2 <= 4 L_Q [P(x_{k-1}) - P* + P(x~) - P*] (Corollary 3, verified) plus non-expansiveness of the prox; no Lyapunov function, telescoping over an epoch as in SVRG. Practice (verified): 'we can also set x~_s to be the last iterate x_m ... we did not observe much difference in the convergence speed'; on rcv1 with m = 2n, 'The best choice of eta = 0.1/L matches our theoretical analysis'; convergence slows if the step is too large or too small (Figs. 2-3).
relevance: B3: provides the L_max vs Lbar comparison in its clearest form (L_Q) and an experiment where the theoretical step 0.1/L is also the empirically best one, a counter-example to the usual gap worth reproducing on the anisotropic instances. A1: sampling-dependent constant in the n + kappa term. A2: the prox-SVRG estimator is what the naive acceleration plugs into Nesterov's scheme.

title: Optimal Mini-Batch and Step Sizes for SAGA
authors: Nidham Gazagnadou, Robert M. Gower, Joseph Salmon
venue: Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2019), PMLR 97:2142-2150
summary: Uses the JacSketch analysis of b-nice minibatch SAGA, whose step size depends on the expected smoothness constant L(b), and derives computable bounds on L(b) (a simple combinatorial bound, a Bernstein matrix-concentration bound, and a 'practical' estimate), turning the theory into an explicit rule for the step size and the minibatch size. The resulting step sizes are much larger than earlier ones for b > 1, the total complexity decreases linearly in b up to an optimal b*, and the rule performs comparably to grid search on real data.
main_result: Theorem 1 (verified; b-nice sampling, f_i L_i-smooth plus lambda-regularization, f L-smooth and mu-strongly convex; combining Thm 3.6 and eq. (103) of Gower et al.): with step gamma = (1/4) / max{L(b) + lambda, (1/b)((n - b)/(n - 1))(L_max + lambda) + mu n/(4b)} (eq. 14), E||w^k - w*||^2 <= eps C after K_iter(b) = max{4(L(b) + lambda)/mu, n/b + ((n - b)/(n - 1)) 4(L_max + lambda)/(b mu)} log(1/eps) iterations (eq. 15), with C = ||w^0 - w*||^2 + (a multiple of 1/(2 L_max)) sum_i ||J_{:i}^0 - grad f_i(w*)||^2; for b = 1 this is gamma = 1/(4 L_max + n mu) and K = (n + 4 L_max/mu) log(1/eps) (up to lambda). Proposition 1 (verified): L(b) = max_i (1/C(n-1,b-1)) sum_{B ni i, |B| = b} L_B. Theorem 2 (verified, simple bound): L(b) <= L_simple(b) = (n(b - 1))/(b(n - 1)) Lbar + ((n - b)/(b(n - 1))) L_max; a Bernstein bound and the estimate L_practical(b) = (n(b - 1))/(b(n - 1)) L + ((n - b)/(b(n - 1))) L_max (verified: 'L_practical(1) = L_max and L_practical(n) = L ... it is not an upper bound of L', justified by a mid-step of the Bernstein proof) are also given; the total complexity K_total(b) = b K_iter(b) is minimized at an explicit b* and the step size grows with b. Constants: expected smoothness L(b), between L (smoothness of f) and L_max.
relevance: B3: provides the formula connecting the step size to data geometry (L_max, Lbar, L of the full Hessian), which is exactly what changes with feature-covariance anisotropy; the project can compute L(b), L_simple and L_practical on its instances and check which bound is tight. A1/pipeline: minibatch SAGA baselines and theory-driven step sizes instead of grid search. | B3 (central for the experimental design): the constant that governs SAGA on logistic regression is L(F) (feature-covariance dependent) for b > 1 and L_max for b = 1, which is exactly where anisotropy enters; gives the practical reference step sizes for the A4 baseline runs.

title: Towards closing the gap between the theory and practice of SVRG
authors: Othmane Sebbouh, Nidham Gazagnadou, Samy Jelassi, Francis Bach, Robert M. Gower
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (NeurIPS 2019)
summary: Addresses the mismatch between SVRG theory (inner loop m of order kappa, reset to an averaged iterate, small step) and practice (m = n, larger steps, continuing from the last iterate). It analyzes two practical variants under arbitrary sampling: Free-SVRG (inner loop of any length m, last iterate carried over, reference point a weighted average of iterates) and L-SVRG-D (loopless with decreasing step sizes), with new Lyapunov functions based on expected smoothness and a new expected residual constant. The theory then gives optimal loop length, minibatch size and step size, confirmed experimentally.
main_result: Constants: expected smoothness L (Lemma 4.1, from Theorem 3.6 of JacSketch) and expected residual rho (Lemma 4.2: E_D||grad f_v(x) - grad f_v(x*) - grad f(x)||^2 <= 2 rho (f(x) - f(x*))), with closed forms L(b), rho(b) for b-nice sampling and L(1) = L_max. Theorem 4.1 (verified, Free-SVRG): with Lyapunov phi_s = ||x_m^s - x*||^2 + psi_s, psi_s = 8 gamma^2 S_m (f(w_s) - f(x*)) (w_s the weighted-average reference point, S_m a sum of the weights), and step gamma <= 1/(2(L + 2 rho)), E phi_s <= beta^s phi_0 with beta = max{(1 - gamma mu)^m, 1/2}. Corollary 4.1 (verified): total complexity C_m(b) = 2(n/m + 2b) max{(L(b) + 2 rho(b))/mu, m} log(1/eps). Corollary 4.3 (verified, b = 1): gamma = 1/(2(L(1) + 2 rho(1))) = 1/(6 L_max) and C_m(1) = 18 (n + L_max/mu) log(1/eps) for every m in [min(n, L_max/mu), max(n, L_max/mu)]; Corollary 4.2 (b = n, m = 1): 6 n (L/mu) log(1/eps), recovering GD up to a factor 6. Proposition 6.1 (verified): optimal loop m*(b) = (L(b) + 2 rho(b))/mu, with m*(1) = 3 L_max/mu, and 'm = n is a perfectly safe choice'. Theorem 5.1 (verified; L-SVRG-D, reset probability p): with phi_k = ||x^k - x*||^2 + 8 gamma_k^2 L (f(w^k) - f(x*))/(p(3 - 2p)) and step gamma <= 1/(2 zeta_p L), zeta_p = (7 - 4p)(1 - (1 - p)^{3/2})/(p(2 - p)(3 - 2p)) (Remark 5.1: zeta_p increasing with 7/4 <= zeta_p <= 3, so gamma ~ 2/(7L) for small p), E phi_k <= beta^k phi_0 with beta = max{1 - (2/3) gamma mu, 1 - p/2}. Proposition 6.2 / Table 1: optimal minibatch b* for m = n and m = n/b in closed form, different from 1 in a range of regimes, explaining why minibatching helps in practice. Documented gap addressed (verified): 'the classical SVRG analysis given in [13] requires m >= 20 L_max/mu' and a reset to the average of inner iterates, while practice uses m = n and the last iterate.
relevance: B3: the paper's whole purpose is a theory-vs-practice gap for a VR method, and it shows the gap can be closed by changing the Lyapunov function rather than the algorithm - the model for the project's diagnosis; its constants (1/(6 L_max), factor 18) can be compared with Bach's (1/(4R^2), 1 + n/4). A2/A3: Free-SVRG and L-SVRG-D are the non-accelerated counterparts of the loopless accelerated method, in the same expected-smoothness language. | A2/A3: loopless/Free variants are the base of L-Katyusha and the SVRG estimator used in naive acceleration; A4/B3: parameter choices for the SVRG baseline and identification of inner-loop/averaging conventions as part of the theory-practice gap.

title: Stop Wasting My Gradients: Practical SVRG
authors: Reza Babanezhad Harikandeh, Mohamed Osama Ahmed, Alim Virani, Mark Schmidt, Jakub Konecny, Scott Sallinen
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28 (NIPS 2015), pp. 2251-2259
summary: A collection of practical improvements to SVRG with analysis: the full gradient at the snapshot may be computed inexactly (growing batches) without losing the linear rate as long as the error decays, a mixed SG/SVRG iteration, exploiting support vectors to skip gradient evaluations, a justification of the commonly used regularized SVRG update, mini-batch selection strategies, and a look at generalization error. It also records the standard practical settings of SVRG that differ from the theory.
main_result: Setting: f mu-strongly convex, f_i convex with L-Lipschitz gradients (L = L_max); rho(a, b) = (1/(1 - 2 a eta)) (1/(m mu eta) + 2 b eta), so that the Johnson-Zhang rate is rho = rho(L, L). Proposition 1 (verified; inexact snapshot gradient mu_s = grad f(x^s) + e_s, x^{s+1} chosen randomly among the inner iterates, iterates within distance Z of x*): E[f(x^{s+1}) - f*] <= rho E[f(x^s) - f*] + Z E||e_s|| + E||e_s||^2/(1 - 2 L eta); hence the exact linear rate is retained if max{E||e_s||, E||e_s||^2} <= rho~^s for some rho~ < rho, which growing-batch SVRG (batch |B_s| increasing to n, Algorithm 1) achieves, and any linearly decaying error keeps a linear rate. Proposition 2 (verified; mixed SG/SVRG method, alpha = |B_s|/n, E||f_i'(x)||^2 <= sigma^2): E[f(x^{s+1}) - f*] <= rho(L, alpha L) E[f(x^s) - f*] + Z E||e_s|| + [E||e_s||^2 + alpha(1 - alpha)-weighted sigma^2 term]/(1 - 2 L eta), so the variance term vanishes as alpha -> 1. Documented practice (verified verbatim): 'While this result relies on constants we may not know in general, practical choices with good empirical performance include setting m = n, eta = 1/L, and using x^{s+1} = x_m rather than a random iterate.' Section 6 shows the regularized SVRG update is justified and converges faster; Section 5 gives the support-vector skipping heuristic.
relevance: B3: an explicit record of the practical SVRG configuration (m = n, eta = 1/L, last iterate) that theory did not cover in 2015 - the quantitative gap the project's tightness ratios should attribute to specific inequalities. Pipeline: growing-batch and support-vector tricks for cheaper instrumentation runs on logistic regression.

title: Breaking the Span Assumption Yields Fast Finite-Sum Minimization
authors: Robert Hannah, Yanli Liu, Daniel O'Connor, Wotao Yin
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 31 (NeurIPS 2018)
summary: Shows that methods whose iterates stay in the span of sampled component gradients (SAGA, SAG, SDCA without duality, Finito/MISO) need Omega(n ln(1/eps)) iterations when kappa = O(n), whereas SVRG and SARAH - 'hybrid' methods mixing full and component gradients - can be re-parameterized (epoch length m = n + 121 Q and a specific step) to need only O(n ln(1/eps)/(1 + (ln(n/Q))_+) + n + Q) iterations, a speedup of up to 1 + (ln(n/kappa))_+ proved optimal by matching lower bounds. It also explains why the empirically best SVRG step sizes (0.1/L, 0.5/L) are far below 1/L.
main_result: Theorem 1 (verified; Prox-SVRG of Xiao-Zhang with sampling q_i, L_Q = max_i L_i/(n q_i), Q = L_Q/mu): E[F(x^k) - F*] <= rho^k [F(x^0) - F*] with rho the Xiao-Zhang constant (eq. 2.2, printed as rho = (1 + mu eta (1 + 4 m L_Q eta))/(mu eta m (1 - 4 L_Q eta))). Corollary 2 (verified): with m = n + 121 Q and an explicit step eta of order 1/(2 L_Q), rho <= 100/(121 + n/Q), hence K(eps) = O( n ln(1/eps)/(1 + (ln(n/Q))_+) + n + Q ) iterations (eq. 2.3); Corollary 1 (verified): to reach eps = 1/n^alpha with kappa = n^beta, alpha, beta in (0,1), modified SVRG needs O(n) iterations whereas span-assumption algorithms need O(n ln n) (Lan and Zhou, 2017) for sufficiently large d. Corollary 3 (restated from Lan and Zhou 2017): any randomized algorithm satisfying the span assumption needs Omega((n + sqrt(n kappa)) ln(1/eps))-type iterations, so the speedup is optimal; Theorem 2 gives a matching lower bound for SVRG/SARAH; the same modification works for SARAH. Remark 1 (verified): the optimal probabilities are q_i proportional to L_i (L_Q = Lbar). On step sizes (verified verbatim): the paper recalls that Johnson-Zhang suggest eta = 0.1/L ('linear convergence rate 1/4 <= rho <= 1/2 for m >= 50 kappa'), Xiao-Zhang eta = 0.1/L with m = 100 kappa (rho ~ 5/6, and eta = 0.01/L 'works nearly as well'), Nguyen et al. eta = 0.5/L with m = 4.5 kappa (rho ~ 7/9), and states 'This result helps explain why the optimal step size observed in prior work appears to be much smaller than the "standard" gradient descent step of 1/L.'
relevance: A1: the precise source for the second half of hypothesis A1 - under the span assumption with i.i.d. uniform sampling the n log(1/eps) term is unavoidable, while breaking the assumption (full-gradient epochs) gains the factor log(n/kappa) when kappa << n; it also restates the Lan-Zhou lower bound in the needed form. A4: defines the regime kappa vs n in which the empirical exponents should be measured and warns that SVRG-type methods can beat SAGA by a log factor there. B3: explains small theoretical step sizes as an artifact of long epochs, a hypothesis testable with the tightness ratios. | A1: this is the source of the project's second sentence; the exact statements are Theorem 2 / Theorem 4 / eq. 1.3 above, and the project should rephrase 'arbitrary index sequence' as 'algorithms not restricted to i.i.d. component-gradient spans (e.g. full-gradient steps as in SVRG/L-Katyusha), analysed in the oblivious p-CLI class', with the (1 + (ln(n/kappa))_+) factor appearing only when kappa = O(n). A2/A3: L-Katyusha and loopless SVRG use full gradients (reference point), so they live outside the span class; their n-dependence can legitimately be better than SAGA's n ln(1/eps) when kappa << n. A4: predicts that on the block instance SAGA shows n ln(1/eps) while SVRG-type methods show n ln(1/eps)/ln(n/kappa) in the regime kappa << n; the experiments should separate the regimes kappa >> n and kappa << n. B3: the (1 - 2/n)^k block-progress argument is itself an 'inequality to instrument' (fraction of untouched blocks). | A1 (directly the project's claim): proves that for an arbitrary/non-span index usage the sqrt(n kappa) term survives while the n log(1/eps) term weakens by a factor 1 + ln(n/kappa) when kappa << n; A4: VRADA's experiments cite it to explain why SVRG matches accelerated methods at small kappa.

title: Lectures on Convex Optimization
authors: Yurii Nesterov
venue: Springer Optimization and Its Applications, vol. 137, Springer International Publishing (2nd edition of 'Introductory Lectures on Convex Optimization: A Basic Course', Kluwer 2004); ISBN 978-3-319-91577-7
summary: The standard reference for the smooth convex analysis used in every variance-reduction proof: function classes F^{1,1}_L (convex, L-Lipschitz gradient) and S^{1,1}_{mu,L} (strongly convex), the basic inequalities (descent lemma, cocoercivity, strong-convexity inequalities), the gradient method with its rates, Nesterov's lower bounds for first-order methods and the accelerated (fast) gradient method. Bach's Chapter 5 and the SAG/SVRG/SAGA papers all draw their one-line inequalities from this book.
main_result: Chapter 2 (smooth convex optimization). Theorem 2.1.5 (the standard citation for cocoercivity, confirmed from several citing papers; the book itself could not be opened): for convex f with L-Lipschitz gradient, f(y) >= f(x) + <grad f(x), y - x> + (1/(2L))||grad f(x) - grad f(y)||^2 and <grad f(x) - grad f(y), x - y> >= (1/L)||grad f(x) - grad f(y)||^2 - the inequality Bach's Prop. 5.4 and eq. (5.31) of Prop. 5.9 rely on, in the form E||f_i'(theta) - f_i'(eta*)||^2 <= R^2 (theta - eta*)^T F'(theta). Section 2.1.3 (strongly convex functions): <grad f(x) - grad f(y), x - y> >= mu ||x - y||^2 and, for f in S^{1,1}_{mu,L}, <grad f(x) - grad f(y), x - y> >= (mu L/(mu + L))||x - y||^2 + (1/(mu + L))||grad f(x) - grad f(y)||^2; the gradient method with step 2/(mu + L) satisfies ||x_k - x*|| <= ((Q - 1)/(Q + 1))^k ||x_0 - x*|| with Q = L/mu. Section 2.1.4 (lower bounds): for any first-order (span-based) method on S^{1,1}_{mu,L} in high dimension, ||x_k - x*|| >= ((sqrt Q - 1)/(sqrt Q + 1))^k ||x_0 - x*||, i.e. Omega(sqrt(Q) log(1/eps)) iterations; Section 2.2: the accelerated gradient method attains O(sqrt(Q) log(1/eps)). (Theorem numbering as in the 2004 edition, which the 2018 edition retains for Chapter 2 according to citing papers; not re-verified in the book itself.)
relevance: B3: the cocoercivity and strong-convexity inequalities instrumented in the project are exactly Nesterov's Theorem 2.1.5 and Section 2.1.3; their tightness is attained only for quadratics, which frames the geometry-dependent bottleneck analysis. A1/A2: the span-based lower bound and the accelerated method on a single function are the templates that Lan-Zhou/Woodworth-Srebro and Katyusha extend to finite sums. B2: mu_eff(t) is the trajectory-dependent version of the strong-convexity inequality.

title: Optimization Methods for Large-Scale Machine Learning
authors: Leon Bottou, Frank E. Curtis, Jorge Nocedal
venue: SIAM Review 60(2):223-311
summary: Comprehensive survey of stochastic optimization for machine learning: a unified analysis of the stochastic gradient (SG) method under a general noise model (Section 4), then a taxonomy of methods beyond SG organized along two axes, noise reduction (dynamic sampling, gradient aggregation: SVRG, SAGA, SAG, iterate averaging) and second-order information (Section 5-6). It is the standard reference placing variance reduction within the landscape of large-scale optimization, and it explicitly discusses the regimes in which gradient aggregation methods are or are not preferable to SG.
main_result: Section 4 (verified): Theorem 4.6 (strongly convex objective, fixed stepsize alpha_k = alphabar with 0 < alphabar <= mu/(L M_G) under Assumptions 4.1, 4.3, 4.5): E[F(w_k) - F*] <= alphabar L M/(2 c mu) + (1 - alphabar c mu)^{k-1} (F(w_1) - F* - alphabar L M/(2 c mu)), i.e. linear convergence to a noise ball proportional to the step; Theorem 4.7 (diminishing stepsizes alpha_k = beta/(gamma + k)): E[F(w_k) - F*] <= nu/(gamma + k). Section 5.3 'Gradient Aggregation' (verified): SVRG (Algorithm 5.1, estimator g~_j = grad f_{i_j}(w~_j) - (grad f_{i_j}(w_k) - grad R_n(w_k))), for which, with strongly convex R_n (constant c) and (alpha, m) such that rho := (1/(1 - 2 alpha L))(1/(m c alpha) + 2 alpha L) < 1, E[R_n(w_{k+1}) - R_n*] <= rho E[R_n(w_k) - R_n*], each outer iteration costing 2m + n component gradients; SAGA (Algorithm 5.2, estimator (5.14)) with the same per-iteration cost as SG and a linear rate; Section 5.3.3 commentary (verified): the computing time of SVRG, SAGA and SAG is T(n, eps) ~ (n + kappa) log(1/eps), which grows with n, versus ~ kappa^2/eps (often kappa/eps in practice) for SG, so gradient aggregation methods 'cannot beat SG' for very large n and small eps requirements but 'there exists a regime with kappa >= n in which gradient aggregation methods may be superior, and perhaps even easier to tune'. Section 5.1-5.2: noise reduction by dynamic sampling (Theorem 5.1: geometric growth of the sample size keeps the linear rate) and the classical results of Robbins-Monro, Polyak-Juditsky averaging.
relevance: Pipeline/introduction: the canonical survey to position variance reduction against SG and to state the (n + kappa) log(1/eps) vs kappa/eps trade-off that motivates A1/A4 (which regime of n vs kappa the experiments should explore). B3: its SG analysis with a general noise model (Theorems 4.6-4.7) is the baseline against which the 'absorbed variance' of VR methods is measured.

title: A Convergent Incremental Gradient Method with a Constant Step Size
authors: Doron Blatt, Alfred O. Hero, Hillel Gauchman
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization 18(1):29-51
summary: Introduces the incremental aggregated gradient (IAG) method: at each iteration only one component gradient is recomputed and the iterate moves along the sum of the stored (possibly stale) component gradients, with a constant step size. This is the deterministic ancestor of SAG (Le Roux et al. describe SAG as a randomized IAG) and the first finite-sum method with a memory of past gradients. Convergence is proved for a cyclic order with constant step; a global linear rate is shown only for quadratics.
main_result: From the abstract (verified via Crossref): the method 'requires a single gradient evaluation per iteration and uses a constant step size'; when the gradient is bounded and Lipschitz continuous, the method visits infinitely often regions in which the gradient is small; under certain unimodality assumptions global convergence is established; 'In the quadratic case, a global linear rate of convergence is shown'; applications to distributed optimization in wireless sensor networks and numerical comparisons with other incremental gradient methods. No explicit rate in terms of n and kappa for general smooth strongly convex sums (this was supplied by Gurbuzbalaban-Ozdaglar-Parrilo 2017 and, for the randomized version, by Le Roux-Schmidt-Bach 2012).
relevance: A1: the deterministic-order baseline for the 'arbitrary index sequence' part of the hypothesis - the same memory structure as SAG/SAGA but with a cyclic order, which is what the lower bound for arbitrary sequences must cover. Foundations: establishes that gradient memory alone (without randomness) already yields constant-step convergence, separating the role of the memory from the role of i.i.d. sampling in Bach's Prop. 5.9 (where the 1/n refresh rate comes from uniform sampling).

title: On the Convergence Rate of Incremental Aggregated Gradient Algorithms
authors: Mert Gurbuzbalaban, Asuman Ozdaglar, Pablo A. Parrilo
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization 27(2):1035-1048
summary: First explicit linear rate for the deterministic IAG method of Blatt et al. (components processed in a deterministic, e.g. cyclic, order with a memory of past gradients) for a finite sum of smooth functions whose sum is strongly convex, via a Lyapunov argument on the distance to the optimum perturbed by bounded gradient delays; an aggregated method with momentum is also shown to converge linearly. The rate is quadratic in both the delay (n for cyclic order) and the condition number, in contrast with the n + kappa rate of randomized SAG/SAGA.
main_result: Setting (verified): f = sum_{i=1}^m f_i with convex, continuously differentiable components and L-Lipschitz gradients, f mu-strongly convex, Q = L/mu; gradient delays bounded by K (K = m - 1 for the original cyclic IAG, verified). Theorem 3.3 (verified): for a constant step 0 < alpha < alphabar := a mu/(K L (mu + L)) with a = 8/25, the IAG iterates are globally linearly convergent; with alpha = alphabar/2, ||x_k - x*|| <= (1 - c_K/(Q + 1)^2)^k ||x_0 - x*|| and f(x_k) - f* <= (L/2)(1 - c_K/(Q + 1)^2)^{2k} ||x_0 - x*||^2, where c_K = (2/25)(K(2K + 1))^{-1} (eqs. 21-22).
