Hence the iteration complexity is O(K^2 Q^2 log(1/eps)) = O(m^2 kappa^2 log(1/eps)) for the cyclic order, versus O((m + kappa) log(1/eps)) for randomized SAG/SAGA; the abstract (verified) stresses that 'no theoretical analysis with explicit rate results was previously given in the literature ... most of the recent efforts concentrated on the randomized versions'. Proof: a Lyapunov/perturbation argument bounding the gradient error E_k by the delayed distances.
relevance: A1: quantifies the price of a deterministic (arbitrary) index sequence for span-based memory methods - the rate degrades from n + kappa to n^2 kappa^2 in the worst-case analysis - which is the backdrop of the 'arbitrary index sequence' part of the hypothesis and of Finito/SDCA's unproven permutation sampling. B3: the proof isolates the delayed-gradient error term, i.e. the deterministic analogue of the stored-gradient error sum in Bach's Lyapunov V_t, so its looseness can be compared with the randomized 1/n refresh step.

title: A Lower Bound for the Optimization of Finite Sums
authors: Alekh Agarwal, Leon Bottou
venue: ICML 2015, PMLR 37:78-86 (arXiv:1410.0723; v4 of 4 Oct 2015 adds an erratum)
summary: First lower bound specific to finite sums F = (1/n) sum_i f_i with each f_i smooth and F mu-strongly convex, in the Incremental First-order Oracle (IFO) model where a query (x, i) returns (g_i(x), g_i'(x)). Using a Nemirovsky-Yudin-style resisting oracle in l2 and an interleaved-coordinate decomposition into n Nesterov chain functions, they prove that no IFO algorithm can reach relative accuracy eps in fewer than Omega(n + sqrt(n(kappa-1)) log(1/eps)) IFO calls. The arXiv v4 erratum states that the result (both Theorems 1 and 2) holds for DETERMINISTIC algorithms only, because the resisting-oracle construction cannot handle randomized algorithms; the authors say they believe a comparable bound holds for randomized methods (later established by Lan-Zhou for fixed sampling distributions and by Woodworth-Srebro for arbitrary randomized algorithms). VERIFIED: arXiv API (title, authors, v4 dated 2015-10-04, comment 'Added an erratum'), PMLR v37 page (pp. 78-86), and the PMLR and arXiv PDFs (theorem numbering checked).
main_result: Oracle model (Definitions 1-3): IFO query (x, i) -> (g_i(x), g_i'(x)); an IFO algorithm depends on f only through IFO calls; K calls at x_0..x_{K-1}, output x_K. Setting: each g_i convex and (L-mu)-smooth, f = (mu/2)||x||^2 + (1/n) sum_i g_i, so f is mu-strongly convex and L-smooth, kappa = L/mu, domain l2 (infinite-dimensional, to exclude finite-termination methods). Theorem 1 (main theorem; NOT 'Theorem 4', which is ar5iv's sequential renumbering): for any IFO algorithm making K calls there is f in the class with ||x*_f|| = gamma and ||x*_f - x_K|| >= gamma q^{2t}, q = (sqrt(1+(kappa-1)/n) - 1)/(sqrt(1+(kappa-1)/n) + 1), t = 0 if K < n and t = K/n otherwise. Corollary 1 (not 'Corollary 5'): reaching ||x_K - x*|| <= eps ||x*|| (eps < 1) needs K = Omega(n + sqrt(n(kappa-1)) log(1/eps)); the n term is because every g_i must be queried at least once (Proposition 2: if K < n some block is never queried and its minimizer can be placed at distance gamma), the log term comes from the per-block Nesterov chain. Erratum (v4): holds for deterministic algorithms only (deterministic index selection and query points); does not cover SAG/SVRG/SAGA-type randomized index choice. Hard instance (Definition 4): orthonormal interleaved coordinate families Q_i = [e_i, e_{n+i}, e_{2n+i}, ...], i = 1..n; f(x) = (mu/2)||x||^2 + (1/n) sum_i h_i(Q_i^T x), each h_i a Nesterov chain function N_{mu,L} (Definition 9, tridiagonal Hessian) with minimizer (rho q^i)_i scaled so that ||y*|| = gamma/sqrt(n). Appendix A: Theorem 2 ('Nemirovsky-Yudin'; not 'Theorem 11') is the single-function bound ||x_f - x_K|| >= gamma q^{2K} with q = (sqrt(kappa)-1)/(sqrt(kappa)+1); Lemma 3 (not 'Lemma 20') shows that one may assume without loss of generality that the FINAL output x_K lies in Span{x_0..x_{K-1}, f'(x_0)..f'(x_{K-1})} (the only span-type assumption, imposed on the last point only, unlike Nesterov's assumption on all iterates); Definition 11 (not 'Definition 26') is the resisting oracle built by Gram-Schmidt on the queries, Proposition 7 (not 'Proposition 28') keeps the minimizer at distance >= q^{2K}||y*|| from the span of the first K queries; Jensen over the n blocks gives ||x_K - x*||^2 >= gamma^2 q^{4K/n}.
relevance: A1: the original statement of the Omega(n + sqrt(n kappa) log(1/eps)) bound and the clearest statement that a span-type assumption on the output + DETERMINISTIC (arbitrary) index sequence suffice for the sqrt(n kappa) term; must be cited with the erratum (deterministic only). A4: q = (sqrt(1+(kappa-1)/n)-1)/(sqrt(1+(kappa-1)/n)+1) gives the exact predicted per-block contraction, i.e. a kappa^(1/2) exponent in the regime kappa >> n. Pipeline: the resisting-oracle instance is algorithm-dependent (adaptive), so for numerical experiments the project should prefer the fixed block instances of Lan-Zhou / Zhang-Shu-He or the Hessian-partitioned instance of Han-Xie-Zhang.

title: An optimal randomized incremental gradient method
authors: Guanghui Lan, Yi Zhou
venue: Mathematical Programming 171(1-2):167-215, 2018 (published online 28 June 2017; arXiv:1507.02000, v3 Oct 2015)
summary: Introduces the randomized primal-dual gradient (RPDG) method, which computes one randomly selected component gradient per iteration and achieves O((m + sqrt(m L/mu)) log(1/eps)) gradient evaluations, and proves a matching lower complexity bound for the class of randomized incremental gradient methods that sample i_t independently from a fixed (arbitrary) distribution and keep iterates in the linear span of past component gradients. The paper explicitly notes (Sections 1 and 3) that Agarwal-Bottou's bound is 'deterministic by construction' (as the authors acknowledged at ISMP 2015) and therefore not applicable to randomized incremental gradient methods; this is the first valid lower bound for the randomized class. The hard instance is a block-separable sum of scaled Nesterov chain quadratics, one chain per component. VERIFIED: arXiv API, Crossref DOI (Math. Prog. 171(1-2):167-215), and arXiv v3 PDF (theorem statements and equation numbers checked).
main_result: Algorithm class (eqs. 3.40-3.41 of arXiv v3): indices i_t independent with Prob{i_t = i} = p_i, p_i >= 0, sum p_i = 1 (arbitrary FIXED, non-adaptive distribution, uniform as a special case); span assumption x^k in x^0 + Lin{grad f_{i_1}(x^0), ..., grad f_{i_k}(x^{k-1})}. Problem convention: Psi(x) = sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x) + mu w(x) (a SUM, not an average), L = sum_i L_i, C = L/mu. Hard instance (3.37)-(3.39): x = (x_1, ..., x_m), x_i in R^{n~} (n~ = n/m), Psi(x) = sum_i [ f_i(x_i) + (mu/2)||x_i||^2 ], f_i(x_i) = (mu(Q-1)/4) [ (1/2) <A x_i, x_i> - <e_1, x_i> ], A symmetric tridiagonal with 2 on the diagonal and -1 on the off-diagonals except the last diagonal entry kappa_A = (sqrt(Q)+3)/(sqrt(Q)+1); then 0 <= A <= 4I, L_i = mu(Q-1), each block has condition number Q, and the unique minimizer is x*_{i,j} = q^j (Lemma 8, eq. 5.38) with q = (sqrt(Q)-1)/(sqrt(Q)+1) (eq. 3.42). Lower bound: Theorem 3 of arXiv v3 (the list's 'Theorem 3.2' is not the arXiv numbering; the journal numbering was not checked): for any randomized incremental gradient method of the class, E||x^k - x*||^2 / ||x^0 - x*||^2 >= (1/2) exp( -4k sqrt(Q) / ( m (sqrt(Q)+1)^2 - 4 sqrt(Q) ) ) (eq. 3.43) provided the dimension n >= n(m,k) = m log[ (1 - (1-q^2)/m)^k / 2 ] / (2 log q) (eq. 3.44; dimension must grow with k). Corollary 3: the number of gradient evaluations to reach E||x_bar - x*||^2 <= eps is at least Omega( (sqrt(mC) + m) log(||x^0 - x*||^2/eps) ) for n sufficiently large; intermediate form (3.45): k >= [ (m/2)(sqrt(Q)/2 + 1) - 1 ] log(||x^0-x*||^2/(2 eps)); the proof counts the realized number k_i of evaluations of grad f_i (multinomial), each adding at most one nonzero coordinate to block i, and uses convexity of q^{2 k_i}. Translation to Bach's average convention F = (1/m) sum_i g_i with g_i := m [ f_i(x_i) + (mu/2)||x_i||^2 ]: each g_i is m mu Q-smooth, kappa = mQ, i.e. per-block condition number Q = kappa/m, and the bound reads Omega( (m + sqrt(m kappa)) log(1/eps) ), including the m log(1/eps) term (a coupon-collector effect of i.i.d. sampling). Corollary 4: same instance gives Omega(m sqrt(Q_Psi) log(1/eps)) for randomized block coordinate descent.
relevance: A1: THE reference for i.i.d. (arbitrary fixed distribution) sampling + span assumption => Omega((n + sqrt(n kappa)) log(1/eps)); shows the n log(1/eps) term is a consequence of i.i.d. sampling on a block-separable instance (which Hannah et al. later exploit). A4: the block instance with per-block condition number Q = kappa/n is exactly the instance to implement for measuring kappa^1 (SAGA) vs kappa^(1/2) (L-Katyusha) exponents; q^{2 k_i} gives an exact per-block progress law. Pipeline: explicit matrices (tridiagonal A with modified last entry) and explicit optimum x*_{i,j} = q^j make the optimality gap computable in closed form. B1: separable instance shows what a preconditioner P could exploit (block structure) and why the span assumption must be formulated per block. | A1 and A3: the lower bound is the one L-Katyusha's rate is compared against (Kovalev et al. cite it as the optimality reference; ANITA matches it); the construction with an arbitrary index distribution is directly relevant to the project's 'arbitrary index sequence' variant of A1 (Hannah et al. 2018 reword its Corollary 3 as the span-assumption bound). RPDG itself is a direct accelerated method without an explicit negative-momentum term (acceleration via a dual/game formulation) - a useful counterpoint when arguing what is essential in A3. | (A1): the span-based lower bound with i.i.d. sampling. (A4)/pipeline: the explicit hard instance (block-separable chain quadratics with per-block smoothness mu(Q-1), known x*, known kappa) is the natural synthetic benchmark for measuring the kappa^1 vs kappa^{1/2} exponents; the dimension requirement n_(m,k) tells how large d must be for the lower-bound behaviour to be observable over k iterations.

title: Tight Complexity Bounds for Optimizing Composite Objectives
authors: Blake E. Woodworth, Nathan Srebro
venue: NIPS 2016, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (arXiv:1605.08003; v3 of April 2019 corrects Appendix C)
summary: Gives tight upper and lower bounds for minimizing (1/m) sum_i f_i with gradient and prox oracles of the components, for deterministic and randomized algorithms, in smooth/nonsmooth and convex/strongly convex settings. The lower bounds for randomized algorithms do not use a span assumption: the algorithm may choose the component index and the query point adaptively and randomly, and the argument draws random orthonormal directions in a sufficiently large dimension so that each query reveals at most one new direction with high probability (Yao's principle). Shows a real gap between deterministic (AGD optimal, Omega(m sqrt(kappa) log)) and randomized (accelerated SVRG optimal, Omega(m + sqrt(m kappa) log)) methods, and that a gradient oracle suffices for the optimal rate. VERIFIED: arXiv API (v3 updated 2019-04-04), NeurIPS 2016 proceedings index (authors listed as 'Blake E Woodworth, Nati Srebro'), and arXiv v3 PDF (Theorems 4, 7, 8, constants 73 and 161m, and the Appendix C acknowledgement of Carmon-Duchi-Hinder-Sidford checked).
main_result: Oracle: query (x, i, beta) returns f_i(x), grad f_i(x) (or subgradient) and prox_{f_i}^beta(x); the algorithm picks i adaptively; deterministic algorithms produce identical queries for identical answers, randomized ones may flip coins. Deterministic, gamma-smooth lambda-strongly convex (Theorem 4, gamma/lambda > 73): Omega( m sqrt(gamma/lambda) log( lambda eps_0 / (gamma eps) ) ) queries, in dimension d = O(m sqrt(gamma/lambda) log(lambda eps_0/(gamma eps))) (adversarially chosen orthonormal vectors v_r; one 'round' = block of queries revealing about m/2 distinct components). Randomized (in expectation, no span assumption): Theorem 7 (gamma-smooth convex, ||x*|| <= B): Omega( m + sqrt(m gamma B^2 / eps) ) in dimension d = O((gamma^2 B^4/eps^2) log(m gamma B^2/eps)); Theorem 8 (gamma-smooth, lambda-strongly convex, gamma/lambda > 161 m): Omega( m + sqrt(m gamma/lambda) log( (eps_0/eps) sqrt(m lambda/gamma) ) ) in dimension d = O( (gamma m/(lambda eps)) log^4( eps_0^2 lambda m/(gamma eps^2) ) log( gamma m^2/(lambda eps) ) ); note there is no 'm log(1/eps)' term (the m term is additive); Theorems 5-6 (Lipschitz): Omega(m + sqrt(m) L B/eps) and Omega(m + sqrt(m) L/sqrt(lambda eps)). The paper states that the large dimension is the price of omitting the span assumption (with the span assumption the dimension needed is only of the order of the number of queries). Randomized hard instance (Appendix C): for each pair of components, random orthonormal chain directions v_{i,r}, chain links split between the two components of the pair (even/odd links), with a 'flat' link function phi_c (zero on [-c, c]) so that a query reveals a new direction only if the iterate already has non-negligible inner product with it; lemmas show that with d large every oracle answer lies in span({x} U already-revealed vectors) with probability >= 3/4, giving about m k queries. Comments on prior work (Section 1): Agarwal-Bottou's bound holds only for deterministic algorithms (and is loose there); Lan's bound is for a restricted class of randomized algorithms (fixed sampling distribution). v3 corrects the randomized proofs in Appendix C after an issue pointed out by Carmon, Duchi, Hinder and Sidford, 'in a manner resembling' their work.
relevance: A1: the reference for ARBITRARY/ADAPTIVE index sequences and query points without the span assumption: the sqrt(n kappa) log term survives for any randomized algorithm (in large enough dimension), while the n log(1/eps) term is NOT present (only an additive n), which is exactly the regime distinction behind the project's second sentence of A1. A2/A3: identifies accelerated SVRG/Katyusha-type methods as optimal in the randomized class. Pipeline: the dead-zone chain with random directions needs dimension d ~ kappa n / eps (polylog), so for numerics prefer the span-based block instances; the report should note that the price of removing the span assumption is dimension. | A1 and A3: the lower bound that certifies L-Katyusha's rate as optimal (cited by Kovalev et al., Driggs et al., ANITA); together with Lan-Zhou 2018 and Hannah et al. 2018 it delineates exactly which n-term (m versus m log(1/eps)) is tight, which matters for the project's 'arbitrary index sequence' discussion in A1. | (A1): the lower bound without the span assumption and with algorithmic randomness only, complementing Lan-Zhou; the paper is purely theoretical, so its chain instance must be turned into a benchmark by the project (pipeline), with the caveat that the required dimension exceeds the number of queries, which limits how far the Omega(sqrt(m kappa)) behaviour can be reproduced empirically (A4).

title: Dimension-Free Iteration Complexity of Finite Sum Optimization Problems
authors: Yossi Arjevani, Ohad Shamir
venue: NIPS 2016, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (arXiv:1606.09333)
summary: Points out that earlier finite-sum lower bounds (Agarwal-Bottou, Lan) only apply when the number of iterations is below about d/n (dimension-dependent) or to deterministic algorithms, and provides dimension-free lower bounds for 'oblivious' canonical linear iterative (CLI) algorithms, whose update coefficients are scheduled in advance given (L, mu, n) and do not depend on the function (covering SAG, SAGA, SVRG, SDCA, SDCA without duality, accelerated proximal SDCA, GD, AGD, heavy ball and stochastic coordinate descent with fixed step sizes). The bounds are proved by a polynomial/Chebyshev argument on a two-coordinate quadratic family rather than by a resisting oracle, and hold for any number of iterations and under any source of randomness. VERIFIED: arXiv API, NeurIPS 2016 proceedings index, and arXiv PDF (Theorems 2-5 checked).
main_result: Algorithm class (Definitions 1-3): CLI w_i^{(k+1)} in sum_j O_f(w_j^{(k)}; theta_{ij}^{(k)}) where the oracle is the generalized first-order oracle O(w; A, B, C, j) = A grad f_j(w) + B w + C (j = component index) or a steepest coordinate-descent oracle, possibly randomized; oblivious = the parameters theta do not depend on previously acquired oracle answers (step sizes scheduled in advance given side-information L, mu, n); stationary = parameters fixed across iterations. Theorem 2 (finite sums, f_i L-smooth, F mu-strongly convex, kappa = L/mu): any oblivious (possibly stochastic) CLI with first-order and coordinate-descent oracles needs Omega~( n + sqrt(n(kappa-1)) ln(1/eps) ) iterations, independently of the dimension d; the paper states the bound is tight (attained by SAG + an acceleration scheme / accelerated SDCA) and holds for any number of iterations regardless of d and n. Theorem 5 (the n term): for ANY stochastic algorithm that only uses incremental oracles (answers depending on at most one component), with kappa > 3, at least n iterations are needed (Yao's principle). Theorem 3 (smooth convex, n = 1): Omega( (L(delta-2)/eps)^{1/delta} ) for delta in (2,4); Theorem 4 (dual regularized loss minimization with linear predictors): Omega~( n + sqrt(nL/lambda) ln(1/eps) ), attained by accelerated proximal SDCA. Hard instance (finite sums): quadratics f_i(w) = (1/2) w^T Q_{eta_i} w - q^T w where Q_{eta_i} has a 2x2 coupling block with diagonal (L+mu)/2 and off-diagonal eta_i, and mu on the remaining diagonal; since oblivious iterates are polynomials in eta of degree bounded by the iteration count, Chebyshev-type approximation bounds give the rate; the proof is non-constructive (existence of a bad eta) and uses only two coupled coordinates, hence dimension-free. Contrast (Section 1): Agarwal-Bottou's resisting oracle does not apply to stochastic algorithms; Lan's n disjoint Nesterov quadratics give a bound restricted to about d/n iterations and need the span assumption (which excludes SVRG-type full gradient steps and coordinate descent).
relevance: A1: dimension-free version of Omega(n + sqrt(n kappa) ln(1/eps)) valid for SAGA/SVRG/SAG with fixed step sizes (exactly the setting of Bach's Proposition 5.9, gamma = 1/(4R^2) is oblivious); also proves the additive n term for any incremental-oracle algorithm. A2/A3: the lower bound is tight for accelerated methods in the oblivious class, so Katyusha-type negative momentum with step sizes depending only on (L, mu, n) is admissible and optimal. B2: oblivious means the algorithm cannot exploit trajectory-dependent constants such as mu_eff(t); the lower bound is in terms of the worst-case kappa, the right baseline for the theory-practice gap analysis. Pipeline: the 2x2 coupled-quadratic family is cheap to implement as a sanity check that SAGA's rate degrades like kappa (not sqrt(kappa)). | A1: the second, complementary lower bound (oblivious/CLI model with fixed sampling distribution and coefficients) next to Lan-Zhou (span of sampled gradients) and Woodworth-Srebro (oracle model); the 'oblivious' assumption is the counterpart of the span assumption that Hannah et al. break, which is exactly the project's 'arbitrary index sequence' discussion. A3: optimality reference used by the Catalyst and estimate-sequence papers for the accelerated rate.

title: On the Iteration Complexity of Oblivious First-Order Optimization Algorithms
authors: Yossi Arjevani, Ohad Shamir
summary: Studies first-order algorithms that are 'oblivious' (p-CLI: p previous points combined linearly with gradients, coefficients scheduled regardless of the function, except through side-information such as L and mu). With L and mu known, any such algorithm needs Omega~(sqrt(L/mu) ln(1/eps)) iterations on L-smooth mu-strongly convex functions and Omega(sqrt(L/eps)) on smooth convex ones, independently of the dimension (unlike Nemirovsky-Yudin/Nesterov bounds which need k <= d/2). Without knowledge of mu, no oblivious algorithm can beat Omega~((L/mu) ln(1/eps)); time-invariant step sizes cannot beat Omega(L/eps) on smooth convex functions. SAG, SAGA, SDCA without duality and SVRG are named as stationary stochastic p-CLIs subject to the same lower bounds. VERIFIED: arXiv API, PMLR v48 page (pp. 908-916), and arXiv PDF (Definitions 2-3, Theorems 1-2, Corollary 1 checked).
main_result: Class (Definition 2, first-order p-CLI): x_i^{(k+1)} = sum_{j=1}^p ( A_{ij}^{(k)} grad f + B_{ij}^{(k)} )(x_j^{(k)}), with linear coefficient operators, the equality holding for expected iterates in the stochastic case; stationary: coefficients constant in k; oblivious: coefficients may vary with k but depend only on side-information (L, mu, ...), not on f. Iteration complexity (Definition 3): minimal K such that the sub-optimality of E x^{(k)} < eps for all k >= K. Theorem 1 (L and mu given): any oblivious, possibly stochastic, p-CLI needs Omega~( sqrt(kappa) ln(1/eps) ) iterations for mu > 0 and Omega( sqrt(L/eps) ) for mu = 0, for any p and any dimension d (dimension-free). Theorem 2 (only L given, mu unknown): if the iteration complexity is O~( kappa^alpha ln(1/eps) ) then alpha >= 1, i.e. Omega~( kappa ln(1/eps) ), attained by GD with step 1/L. Corollary 1: stationary p-CLIs over L-smooth convex functions need Omega(L/eps) iterations (so acceleration necessarily uses time-varying schedules). Hard instance: quadratics f(x) = (1/2) x^T Q x + q^T x with Q = eta I, eta in [mu, L]; oblivious coefficients do not depend on eta, so the k-th iterate is a polynomial in eta of degree <= k and Chebyshev polynomials give the ((sqrt(kappa)-1)/(sqrt(kappa)+1))^k rate; the smooth-only case uses a separate approximation lemma. Finite sums: SAG, SAGA, SDCA without duality and SVRG are stationary stochastic p-CLIs subject to the same bounds on their expected iterates; the paper does not state an Omega(n + sqrt(n kappa)) bound (that is in the NIPS 2016 companion paper).
relevance: A2/A3: formalizes why plugging a fixed-step SVRG estimator into a stationary scheme cannot be accelerated and why acceleration requires time-varying/mu-dependent coefficients (Katyusha's parameters depend on mu). A1: dimension-free Omega(sqrt(kappa) ln(1/eps)) baseline that holds for any number of iterations, complementing Nesterov's k <= d/2 restriction. B2: the Chebyshev argument quantifies that worst-case over eta in [mu, L] is what forces kappa dependence; a trajectory-dependent mu_eff(t) > mu is precisely an escape from this worst case, which the project can test.

title: Lower Complexity Bounds of Finite-Sum Optimization Problems: The Results and Construction
authors: Yuze Han, Guangzeng Xie, Zhihua Zhang
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 25(2):1-86, 2024 (paper 21-0264; arXiv:2103.08280, v5 Jan 2023)
summary: Unified lower bounds for finite-sum minimization and minimax problems under Proximal Incremental First-order Oracles (PIFO: component value, gradient and prox), including loopless methods that may call the full gradient with probability q <= c_0/n per step. The hard instances partition the ROWS of the bidiagonal factor B of Nesterov's tridiagonal matrix into n groups (l == i-1 mod n), so that from the k-th chain subspace only the single component i == k+1 (mod n) can extend the support (zero-chain property), giving geometric waiting times and lower bounds with a much smaller dimension than Woodworth-Srebro or Lan-Zhou. For strongly convex smooth minimization they recover Omega((n + sqrt(kappa n)) log(1/eps)) for kappa = Omega(n) and the Hannah et al. form Omega(n + (n/(1+(log(n/kappa))_+)) log(1/eps)) for kappa = O(n); they conclude that proximal oracles are not much more powerful than gradient oracles for smooth components. VERIFIED: arXiv API (v5, 'We fix some typos'), JMLR page (vol. 25, paper 2, pp. 1-86, 2024), and arXiv PDF (Definition 3.1, Corollary 4.4, Lemma 4.5, Theorems E.6/E.7/E.9, Definition E.12 checked).
main_result: Oracle/algorithm (Definition 3.1): PIFO returns (f_i(x), grad f_i(x), prox_{f_i}^gamma(x)) (IFO = without prox); at each step i_t is sampled from a FIXED distribution D over [n] (uniform, p_i proportional to L_i or L_i^2), independent of a Bernoulli(q) coin, q <= c_0/n, that triggers a full-gradient call (loopless SVRG/Katyusha have q = Theta(1/n)); linear-span protocol: x_{t+1} in the span of previous iterates, component gradients, prox outputs and full gradients; complexity = number of PIFO calls (a full-gradient call costs n). Theorem E.6 (each f_i L-smooth, f = (1/n) sum f_i mu-strongly convex, n >= 2, kappa = L/mu >= 2, eps <= L R^2/4): the PIFO complexity is Omega( (n + sqrt(kappa n)) log(1/eps) ) for kappa = Omega(n), and Omega( n + ( n/(1 + (log(n/kappa))_+) ) log(1/eps) ) for kappa = O(n); the construction only needs dimension O(1 + sqrt(kappa/n) log(1/eps)) (versus O~(kappa n/eps) in Woodworth-Srebro). Theorem E.7 (convex): Omega(n + R sqrt(nL/eps)), dimension O(1 + R sqrt(L/(n eps))). Theorem E.9 (f_i L-average smooth, f mu-strongly convex, n >= 4): Omega( (n + n^{3/4} sqrt(kappa)) log(1/eps) ) for kappa = Omega(sqrt(n)) and Omega( n + ( n/(1 + (log(sqrt(n)/kappa))_+) ) log(1/eps) ) for kappa = O(sqrt(n)). Theorems E.8/E.11 (nonconvex, mu-weakly convex): Omega( n + (Delta/eps^2) min{L, sqrt(n|mu|L)} ) (smooth) and Omega( n + (Delta/eps^2) min{sqrt(n) L, n^{3/4} sqrt(|mu| L)} ) (average smooth). Hard instance for minimization (Section 6.1 and Appendix E.4): B(m, omega, zeta) in R^{(m+1) x m} with rows b_l (omega in the top-left entry, +1/-1 bidiagonal pattern, zeta in the bottom-right), A = B^T B tridiagonal with diagonal (omega^2+1, 2, ..., 2, zeta^2+1) and -1 off-diagonal (Nesterov's matrix); row index sets L_i = { l : 0 <= l <= m, l == i-1 (mod n) }; component functions (eq. 15) r_i(x) = (n/2) sum_{l in L_i} (b_l^T x)^2 + (c_1/2)||x||^2 + c_2 sum_j Gamma(x_j) - c_3 n <e_1, x> [linear term only for i = 1], r = (1/n) sum_i r_i, Gamma the Carmon et al. nonconvex bump (c_2 = 0 in the convex cases); strongly convex instantiation (Definition E.12): alpha = sqrt( 2(kappa-1)/n + 1 ), f_{SC,i}(x) = lambda r_i( x/beta; m, omega = 0, zeta = sqrt(2/(alpha+1)), c^{SC} ) with c^{SC} = ( 2n/(kappa-1), 0, 1 ), lambda = 2 mu R^2 alpha n/(kappa-1), beta = 2 R sqrt(alpha) n/(kappa-1) (Proposition E.13: f_{SC,i} is L-smooth and mu-strongly convex); zero-chain (Lemma 6.1): if x lies in F_k = span{e_1..e_k}, then grad r_i(x) and prox_{r_i}^gamma(x) lie in F_{k+1} if i == k+1 (mod n) and in F_k otherwise, so T_k - T_{k-1} (first time the support reaches k) is geometric (Corollary 4.4 / E.3), and Lemma 4.5 / E.4 converts a lower bound on the gap over F_M into a number of PIFO calls. Comparison (Section 6): Lan-Zhou and Zhou-Gu partition the VARIABLE into blocks and need higher dimension; this construction partitions the Hessian; Hannah et al. cover oblivious p-CLI algorithms (where preconditioning can violate the linear span) but not proximal oracles; in the smooth strongly convex and convex cases upper and lower bounds match up to logs (Point-SAGA, Katyusha, Li 2021), while a sqrt(n) gap remains for nonconvex smooth components (closed by Peng-Tang-Jia 2026).
relevance: A1: the most complete and recent refereed statement of the project's lower bound, including the Hannah-type regime split and the loopless (full-gradient-with-probability-q) protocol used by L-Katyusha; also the clearest 'implementable' instance with a closed-form parametrization (alpha, lambda, beta, c^{SC}). A3: the oracle protocol explicitly covers loopless Katyusha-type algorithms, so the optimal rate of A3 is matched against this bound. A4/pipeline: implement r_i with B(m, 0, zeta) rows partitioned mod n; the chain support T_k gives a direct observable ('how many coordinates are activated') to plot against gradient count for SAGA vs L-Katyusha. B1: proximal (and hence quadratic/preconditioned, P = Hessian-like) oracles on smooth components do not change the worst-case rate, a negative result for B1's hope that a preconditioner P changes the n + sqrt(n kappa) scaling.

title: Lectures on Convex Optimization (2nd edition)
authors: Yurii Nesterov
venue: Springer Optimization and Its Applications vol. 137, Springer, Cham, 2018 (2nd edition of 'Introductory Lectures on Convex Optimization: A Basic Course', Kluwer, Applied Optimization vol. 87, Boston, 2004, DOI 10.1007/978-1-4419-8853-9)
summary: Textbook source of the classical black-box lower bounds for smooth convex (Theorem 2.1.7) and smooth strongly convex (Theorem 2.1.13) minimization under the linear-span assumption (Assumption 2.1.4), proved by exhibiting the 'worst function in the world', a chain-structured quadratic with tridiagonal Hessian. These two theorems and this quadratic are the building blocks of every finite-sum lower bound in this theme (Agarwal-Bottou, Lan-Zhou, Hannah et al., Zhou-Gu, Xie et al., Han et al.). Chapter 2 of the 2018 edition keeps the Section 2.1 structure and theorem numbering of the 2004 edition. VERIFIED: existence of both editions via Crossref (2018: Springer International, ISBN 9783319915777/9783319915784; 2004: Springer US/Kluwer, Applied Optimization); the theorem numbering 2.1.7 / 2.1.13 was confirmed from the open-access JOTA 2021 paper of Madden, Becker and Dall'Anese (DOI 10.1007/s10957-021-01836-9), which writes 'Nesterov presents the lower bounds in Theorems 2.1.7 and 2.1.13 respectively of [32]' with [32] = the 2018 Springer 2nd edition; the book pages themselves could not be opened (publisher pages require login; downloading a hosted copy was declined by the permission system), so the statements below are as reproduced by the search agent from Nesterov's 1998 lecture-note draft (where they are numbered 2.1.6 and 2.1.12).
main_result: Assumption 2.1.4 (linear-span / black-box first-order method): x_k in x_0 + Lin{ f'(x_0), ..., f'(x_{k-1}) }, k >= 1. Theorem 2.1.7 (smooth convex, class F_L^{infty,1}(R^n)): for any k with 1 <= k <= (n-1)/2 and any x_0 there exists f such that any method satisfying Assumption 2.1.4 has f(x_k) - f* >= 3 L ||x_0 - x*||^2 / (32 (k+1)^2) and ||x_k - x*||^2 >= (1/32) ||x_0 - x*||^2; hard function f_k(x) = (L/4) { (1/2) [ (x^{(1)})^2 + sum_{i=1}^{k-1} (x^{(i)} - x^{(i+1)})^2 + (x^{(k)})^2 ] - x^{(1)} }, Hessian (L/4) A_k with A_k the tridiagonal (2, -1) matrix padded by zeros, 0 <= A_k <= 4 I; minimizer x_k^{(i)} = 1 - i/(k+1) for i <= k; the span of gradients stays in {x : x^{(i)} = 0 for i > k} after k steps because A is tridiagonal. Theorem 2.1.13 (smooth strongly convex, class S_{mu,L}^{infty,1} on l2, infinite-dimensional to avoid finite termination): for any x_0, any mu > 0 and Q_f > 1 there exists f in S_{mu, mu Q_f}^{infty,1}(l2) such that any method satisfying Assumption 2.1.4 has ||x_k - x*||^2 >= ( (sqrt(Q_f)-1)/(sqrt(Q_f)+1) )^{2k} ||x_0 - x*||^2 and f(x_k) - f* >= (mu/2) ( (sqrt(Q_f)-1)/(sqrt(Q_f)+1) )^{2k} ||x_0 - x*||^2; hard function f_{mu,Q_f}(x) = ( mu (Q_f - 1)/4 ) { (1/2) [ (x^{(1)})^2 + sum_{i>=1} (x^{(i)} - x^{(i+1)})^2 ] - x^{(1)} } + (mu/2) ||x||^2, Hessian (mu(Q_f-1)/4) A + mu I with A the infinite tridiagonal (2, -1) operator, so mu I <= f'' <= mu Q_f I; optimality condition 2((Q_f+1)/(Q_f-1)) x^{(1)} - x^{(2)} = 1 and x^{(k+1)} - 2((Q_f+1)/(Q_f-1)) x^{(k)} + x^{(k-1)} = 0, solved by (x*)^{(k)} = q^k with q = (sqrt(Q_f)-1)/(sqrt(Q_f)+1); since f'' is tridiagonal and f'(0) is proportional to e_1, x_k has only its first k coordinates nonzero, hence ||x_k - x*||^2 >= sum_{i > k} q^{2i} = q^{2k} ||x_0 - x*||^2. Consequence: Omega( sqrt(Q_f) log(1/eps) ) iterations, matching accelerated gradient. The bounds are 'uniform in the dimension' only for k <= (n-1)/2 in dimension n (hence l2 in the strongly convex case).
relevance: A1: the one-component (n = 1) base case and the exact chain function that all finite-sum hard instances replicate n times (Lan-Zhou, Hannah, Zhang-Shu-He: one chain per variable block; Han-Xie-Zhang: chain links distributed over components); the project's lower-bound section should start from Assumption 2.1.4 and Theorem 2.1.13 and explain how 'one new coordinate per gradient' becomes 'one new coordinate per sampled block'. A4: q = (sqrt(Q)-1)/(sqrt(Q)+1) with Q = 1 + (kappa-1)/n is the exact per-block decay the experiments should see. Pipeline: closed-form minimizer q^k and tridiagonal Hessian make the optimality gap computable exactly; the finite-dimensional truncation with modified last entry (Lan-Zhou, Han et al.) keeps x* geometric. Cite this edition (the one the project quotes as 'Thm 2.1.13'); the 2004 edition has the same numbering and may be cited instead.

title: Problem Complexity and Method Efficiency in Optimization
authors: Arkadii S. Nemirovsky, David B. Yudin (translated by E. R. Dawson)
venue: Wiley-Interscience Series in Discrete Mathematics, John Wiley & Sons, New York, 1983 (xv + 388 pp., ISBN 0-471-10345-4; translation of the 1979 Russian original)
summary: The founding monograph of information-based complexity for convex optimization: it formalizes the black-box (oracle) model in which a method only learns a function through local oracle answers, introduces the 'resisting oracle' technique, and proves the first lower bounds for first-order methods, including the Omega(1/k^2)-type bound for smooth convex minimization and the sqrt(kappa) dependence for smooth strongly convex problems in the regime where the number of iterations is below the dimension, as well as Omega(1/eps^2) for nonsmooth Lipschitz convex problems and dimension-dependent bounds for cutting-plane methods. Agarwal-Bottou (Appendix A, Theorem 2 'Nemirovsky-Yudin') and Nesterov's chain-function presentation both descend from it. VERIFIED: UPenn library record (Wiley-Interscience series, 1983, 'translated by E.R. Dawson', ISBN 0471103454) and Crossref-indexed book reviews (SIAM Review 27(2):264-265, 1985, DOI 10.1137/1027074; J. Oper. Res. Soc. 35:455, 1984; Math. Comput. Simul. 26:75, 1984). Theorem numbers inside the book were not checked (book not available online).
main_result: Oracle model: a method for a problem class P is a sequence of rules producing query points x_k from the oracle answers (f(x_j), f'(x_j)) at previous points; complexity = minimal number of oracle calls guaranteeing accuracy eps over the whole class; lower bounds are obtained by a resisting oracle that answers consistently with a function whose minimizer is far from everything revealed so far. Classical results (as cited by Nesterov 2004/2018 and Agarwal-Bottou 2015): for L-smooth convex functions and black-box first-order methods, after k <= about n/2 iterations the worst-case error is Omega( L ||x_0 - x*||^2 / k^2 ); for L-smooth mu-strongly convex functions the worst-case contraction per iteration is at least (sqrt(kappa)-1)/(sqrt(kappa)+1) in distance (Omega(sqrt(kappa) log(1/eps)) iterations) as long as the iteration count is below the dimension; for Lipschitz convex functions Omega(1/eps^2) oracle calls in high dimension and Omega(n log(1/eps)) in dimension n. These bounds are 'uniform in dimension' only up to k ~ dimension, which is why finite-sum constructions either use l2 (Agarwal-Bottou, Nesterov), let the dimension grow with k (Lan-Zhou, Woodworth-Srebro, Han et al.) or abandon the oracle model for a structural/oblivious one (Arjevani-Shamir).
relevance: A1: historical root of the oracle model and of the resisting-oracle proof used by Agarwal-Bottou (and the reason their bound is deterministic-only); the project's statement 'any span-based method needs ...' should be phrased in this black-box language. Pipeline: explains why the hard instances need dimension at least proportional to the number of iterations (or infinite dimension) and why experiments must choose d large enough relative to the number of epochs.

title: Limitations on Variance-Reduction and Acceleration Schemes for Finite Sum Optimization
authors: Yossi Arjevani
venue: NIPS 2017, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (proceedings title: 'Limitations on Variance-Reduction and Acceleration Schemes for Finite Sums Optimization'); arXiv:1706.01686 (v2 Dec 2017)
summary: Three negative results delimiting when variance reduction and acceleration are possible on finite sums. (1) The finite-sum structure alone is not enough for an (n + kappa) ln(1/eps) rate: if the oracle returns a component without revealing its index, n^2/2 calls are needed to reach accuracy (kappa+1)/(40 n^2), so knowing WHICH f_i is being queried is essential to variance reduction. (2) For oblivious CLI finite-sum algorithms (SAG, SAGA, SDCA, SVRG, ...) whose side-information does not include mu, the complexity is Omega~(n + kappa ln(1/eps)): acceleration to (n + sqrt(n kappa)) ln(1/eps) requires the strong convexity parameter explicitly. (3) For smooth convex finite sums, stationary algorithms need Omega(n + L/eps) and oblivious ones Omega(n + sqrt(nL/eps)), both tight (SDCA, accelerated SDCA). VERIFIED: arXiv API, NeurIPS 2017 proceedings index (single author, title with 'Finite Sums'), and arXiv PDF (Theorems 1-4, Corollary 1, Lemma 1 checked).
main_result: Theorem 1 (index-hiding stochastic oracle, i.i.d. draws of a component without its identity): for L-smooth mu-strongly convex components with condition number kappa, any algorithm needs at least n^2/2 oracle calls to reach accuracy (kappa+1)/(40 n^2) (parts 2-3: analogous bounds for smooth convex and for Lipschitz strongly convex components); Corollary 1: linear convergence with linear dependence on n requires knowing the component index. Construction: two problems built from f^{+/-}(w) = (1/2)(w +/- q)^T A (w +/- q) with the sign hidden; information-theoretic (bias-estimation) argument. Theorem 2 (oblivious finite-sum algorithms with first-order and coordinate-descent oracles, side-information without mu): iteration complexity Omega~( n + kappa ln(1/eps) ), hence no O~((n + sqrt(n kappa)) ln(1/eps)) unless mu is given (the n part holds for any finite-sum algorithm by Arjevani-Shamir 2016 Theorem 5; tight up to logs, attained by SAG); instance: identical components built from the 2x2 coupled quadratic Q_mu, transferred via a restarting scheme. Theorem 3 (stationary algorithms, smooth convex finite sums): Omega(n + L/eps), attained by SDCA; Theorem 4 (oblivious): Omega(n + sqrt(nL/eps)), attained by accelerated SDCA.
relevance: A2/A3: explains why naive acceleration (A2) with an SVRG estimator and mu-free parameters cannot reach sqrt(n kappa) and why Katyusha/L-Katyusha parameters (step, momentum, negative momentum weight) must depend explicitly on mu (or on an estimate; the project's mu_eff(t) in B2 is exactly such an estimate, so B2 is also a question about adaptivity to unknown mu). A1: the n^2 index-hiding result shows that the Omega(n) term in A1 is about identities of components, not just about counting data points; the identical-component instance is a two-coordinate quadratic easy to add to the experimental suite. B1: preconditioning by P does not supply mu; Theorem 2 still applies to oblivious preconditioned schemes.

title: Lower Bound for Randomized First Order Convex Optimization
authors: Blake Woodworth, Nathan Srebro
venue: arXiv:1709.03594 (v2, 3 Nov 2017), 8-page technical note (unpublished)
summary: A self-contained, explicit-construction proof of the Omega(L^2 B^2/eps^2) first-order lower bound for convex Lipschitz minimization that holds for RANDOMIZED algorithms without any span assumption, provided the dimension is large (polynomial in 1/eps). The technique (random orthonormal 'chain' directions, a resisting subgradient oracle returning the smallest maximizing index, Yao's principle, and a lemma showing that queries stay nearly orthogonal to unrevealed directions with high probability) is the one used in the finite-sum randomized bounds of Woodworth-Srebro 2016; the note isolates it in the simplest setting and acknowledges a correction of Lemma 3 pointed out by Carmon, Duchi, Hinder and Sidford. VERIFIED: arXiv API (v2 2017-11-03, '8 pages') and arXiv PDF (Theorem 1 with the d >= 2 L^8 B^8/eps^8 log(...) condition checked). No published venue was found (DBLP/Crossref returned nothing), so it should be cited as an arXiv note.
main_result: Theorem 1: for L, B > 0 and eps in (0, LB/2), if d >= 2 L^8 B^8/eps^8 * log(L^4 B^4/eps^4), then for any randomized algorithm there is a convex L-Lipschitz f with ||x*|| <= B and a first-order oracle such that Omega(L^2 B^2/eps^2) oracle calls are needed in expectation to find an eps-suboptimal point. Hard family: f(x) = max_{1 <= j <= k} ( <x, v_j> - j c ), k = 1/(4 eps^2), c = eps/k, (v_j) a uniformly random orthonormal set; the oracle returns the subgradient v_l for the smallest maximizing index l; any x with <x, v_j> > -c/2 for some j is not eps-suboptimal; Lemmas 3-4 (rotation invariance of unqueried directions; high-probability event for d large) show each query reveals at most one new v_j, so about 15k/16 queries are needed. The authors note the polynomial dimension requirement is likely improvable and remark that for finite-sum objectives randomization provably helps (contrast with this note's single-function setting). The note has no finite-sum theorem; it refers to the 2016 paper for the randomized finite-sum bounds.
relevance: A1: documents precisely how one removes the span assumption and allows arbitrary/adaptive index and query choices (the 'arbitrary index sequence' part of A1) and what it costs (dimension polynomial in 1/eps); useful to justify in the report why the project's numerical hard instance keeps the span-based block construction. Pipeline: not to be implemented directly (dimension too large).

title: Lower Bounds for Smooth Nonconvex Finite-Sum Optimization
authors: Dongruo Zhou, Quanquan Gu
summary: IFO lower bounds for finite sums under the weaker 'average smoothness' assumption E_i ||grad f_i(x) - grad f_i(y)||^2 <= L^2 ||x - y||^2 (and under individual smoothness), covering strongly convex, convex and nonconvex objectives, for linear-span randomized algorithms with ANY randomized index sequence (Yao's minimax principle). Under average smoothness the strongly convex bound becomes Omega(n + n^{3/4} sqrt(kappa) log(1/eps)) (matching KatyushaX), showing that the n^{1/2} vs n^{3/4} difference between individual and average smoothness is real. The construction places a scaled Nesterov/Carmon chain in each of n orthogonal T-dimensional blocks (variable partition), as in Lan-Zhou. VERIFIED: arXiv API, PMLR v97 page (pp. 7574-7583), and arXiv PDF (Definitions 3.1-3.3, Propositions 3.5/3.11, Theorems 4.1/4.2/4.5/4.7, Remarks 4.3/4.8, Yao's minimax theorem for 'any randomized index sequence' checked).
main_result: Model: IFO returns (f_i(x), grad f_i(x)); linear-span randomized first-order algorithm (Definition 3.3): x^{t+1} in span{x^0, ..., x^t, grad f_{i_0}(x^0), ..., grad f_{i_t}(x^t)} with i_t random indices of arbitrary (possibly adaptive) law; lower bounds are stated for any randomized index sequence via Yao's minimax theorem; (l, L)-smoothness = l I <= Hessian <= L I; L-average smoothness as above (implied by individual smoothness). Delta = F(x^0) - inf F, B = dist(x^0, argmin F). Theorem 4.1 (F sigma-strongly convex, {f_i} L-average smooth, eps <= 8 Delta n^{7/4} sigma^{3/2} L^{-3/2}): Omega( n + n^{3/4} sqrt(L/sigma) log( n sigma Delta/(L eps) ) ) IFO calls, in dimension d = O(n + n^{3/4} sqrt(L/sigma) log(1/eps)). Theorem 4.2 (convex, average smooth, eps <= L B^2/4): Omega( n + n^{3/4} B sqrt(L/eps) ), d = O(n + n^{3/4} B sqrt(L/eps)). Theorem 4.5 (nonconvex sigma-almost convex, average smooth): Omega( (Delta/eps^2) [ n^{3/4} sqrt(sigma L) ^ sqrt(n) L ] ). Theorem 4.7 (each f_i in S^{(-sigma, L)}): Omega( (Delta/eps^2) [ sqrt(n sigma L) ^ L ] ). Hard instance: orthonormal row blocks U^{(i)} in R^{T x Tn} with U^{(i)} U^{(i)T} = I and U^{(i)} U^{(j)T} = 0; f_bar_i(x) = sqrt(n) f(U^{(i)} x), f_i(x) = lambda f_bar_i(x/beta), where f is the Nesterov chain quadratic (strongly convex f_N^sc / convex f_N^c, Definitions 3.6/3.8 with Propositions 3.7/3.9 quoting Nesterov's Chapter 2.1) or Carmon et al.'s nonconvex chain with the Gamma bump (Proposition 3.11 quoting Carmon et al. Lemmas 2-4); zero-chain property (Propositions 3.5, 3.11): an IFO call at a point in the span of the first t directions extends the span by at most one direction, and fewer than nT/2 calls can touch at most n/2 components; the sqrt(n) scaling of each block is what turns individual smoothness into average smoothness and produces the n^{3/4}. Matching upper bounds (Remarks 4.3-4.8): KatyushaX (strongly convex / convex, average smooth), SDCA without duality (l = sigma), Natasha / RapGrad / StagewiseKatyusha (individual smoothness, sigma = O(L/n)); the sqrt(n) gap for nonconvex individual smoothness is left open (closed by Peng-Tang-Jia 2026).
relevance: A1: refinement showing that the Omega(n + sqrt(n kappa) log(1/eps)) bound presumes INDIVIDUAL smoothness (each f_i R^2-smooth as in Bach's Prop. 5.9); if only average smoothness holds the bound is n^{3/4} sqrt(kappa), relevant when the project varies feature-covariance anisotropy (B3), which changes the spread of individual L_i. B1: a preconditioner P changes individual vs average smoothness constants differently; the project can test whether the P^{-1}-SAGA rate tracks max_i L_i(P) or the average. Pipeline: variable-partition construction with explicit U^{(i)} blocks (coordinate selectors) is the same template as Lan-Zhou.

title: A General Analysis Framework of Lower Complexity Bounds for Finite-Sum Optimization
authors: Guangzeng Xie, Luo Luo, Zhihua Zhang
venue: arXiv:1908.08394 (v1, 22 Aug 2019), unpublished preprint, superseded by Han-Xie-Zhang (JMLR 2024)
summary: Introduces the 'partition the tridiagonal matrix into n groups' technique for PIFO (gradient + proximal) lower bounds: the rows of the bidiagonal factor B of Nesterov's matrix are assigned to components by l == i-1 (mod n), so only one specific component can extend the current chain subspace. For f_i L-smooth and mu-strongly convex with i.i.d. sampling from a fixed distribution (p_j), it proves Omega((n + sqrt(kappa n)) log(Delta/eps)) PIFO calls with dimension only O(sqrt(kappa/n) log(Delta/eps)), matching Point-SAGA and Katyusha and tightening the n-dependence relative to Woodworth-Srebro; also n^{3/4} bounds under average smoothness extending Zhou-Gu to proximal oracles. VERIFIED: arXiv API (authors Xie, Luo, Zhang; v1 only) and arXiv PDF (Proposition 2.5, Lemma 2.6, Corollary 2.7, Lemma 2.8, Theorems 3.1/3.3/3.5/3.7, constants n/2 + 1 and 0.00327 checked). No published version found (DBLP/Crossref returned nothing).
main_result: Model: f = (1/n) sum f_i, each f_i L-smooth and mu-strongly convex, kappa = L/mu; PIFO returns [f_i(x), grad f_i(x), prox_{f_i}^gamma(x)] (IFO without prox); PIFO algorithm: iterates in the span of past iterates, component gradients and prox outputs; index i_t random with P(i_t = j) = p_j fixed (WLOG x_0 = 0 and p_1 <= ... <= p_n by reindexing). Theorem 3.1 (kappa >= n/2 + 1, eps/Delta <= 0.00327): Omega( (n + sqrt(kappa n)) log(Delta/eps) ) PIFO calls, in dimension d = O( sqrt(kappa/n) log(Delta/eps) ); tight against Point-SAGA. Theorem 3.3 (convex, eps <= L B^2/4): Omega( n + B sqrt(nL/eps) ), d = O(1 + B sqrt(L/(n eps))) (same bound as Woodworth-Srebro with much smaller dimension, Remark 3.4). Theorem 3.5 (average smooth, strongly convex, eps/Delta <= 0.00327): Omega( (n + n^{3/4} sqrt(kappa)) log(Delta/eps) ), d = O(n^{-1/4} sqrt(kappa) log(Delta/eps)). Theorem 3.7 (average smooth convex): Omega( n + B n^{3/4} sqrt(L/eps) ). Construction: B(m, omega) with bidiagonal rows, A = B^T B tridiagonal; row l goes to group L_i = { l : l == i-1 (mod n) }; r_i uses only its rows, the linear term only in f_1; r = (1/n) sum r_i; Proposition 2.5: each r_i is (4 lambda_1 + 2 lambda_2)-smooth and lambda_2-strongly convex, with an explicit average smoothness constant; Lemma 2.6: at x in F_k the gradient/prox of r_i leaves F_k only if k == i-1 (mod n) ('there exists only one' informative component); Corollary 2.7: T_k = sum of k independent geometric variables with success probabilities p_j; Lemma 2.8: high-probability lower bound on the sum gives the query bound. Any PIFO lower bound is also an IFO lower bound (Table 1).
relevance: A1: the first version of the Hessian-partition instance with the sharpest dimension requirement; the regime condition kappa >= n/2 + 1 makes explicit that the sqrt(kappa n) log(1/eps) form is a large-kappa statement. A3: Point-SAGA/Katyusha optimality against PIFO shows proximal steps cannot improve the rate, relevant when the project compares L-Katyusha with proximal variants. Pipeline: Lemma 2.6 gives a per-step observable (which component is 'informative') that can be logged in experiments. Prefer citing the refereed successor han2024lower for the final statements.

title: Tight Lower Complexity Bounds for Strongly Convex Finite-Sum Optimization
authors: Min Zhang, Yao Shu, Kun He
venue: arXiv:2010.08766 (v1 Oct 2020, v2 19 June 2022), unpublished preprint
summary: Lower bounds for randomized incremental gradient methods (SAG, SAGA, SVRG, SARAH, Katyusha, KatyushaX, SDCA without duality) that, according to the authors, remove the assumptions of a deterministic algorithm (Agarwal-Bottou) or of a predefined component-selection distribution (Lan-Zhou): the proof counts the realized number of queries K_i to each component along the run, so arbitrary (history-dependent) index sequences are covered as long as 'every query to the gradient of f_i can only discover a new coordinate' (zero-chain / span-type property, stated explicitly in the proof of Theorem 3.1). For individually (mu, L)-smooth components they obtain Omega((n + sqrt(n L/mu)) log(B^2 mu/(4 eps))) when L/mu > (7/2) n and Omega(n + (n/log(n mu/L)) log(1/(n eps))) when n >> L/mu (matching Hannah et al.'s modified SVRG), with accuracy thresholds independent of n and kappa; under average smoothness, Omega((n + n^{3/4} sqrt(L/mu)) log(B^2 mu/(4 eps))) for L/mu >= (9/4) sqrt(n). Hard instance: Lan-Zhou-type block chains with per-block condition number (kappa-1)/n + 1. VERIFIED: arXiv API (v2 2022-06-19) and arXiv PDF (Theorems 3.1-3.2 with the conditions L/mu > 7n/2 and L/mu >= (9/4) sqrt(n), the K_i counting argument and the zero-chain wording checked). No published version found.
main_result: Oracle: IFO (x, i) -> (f_i(x), grad f_i(x)); class: randomized incremental gradient methods; no fixed sampling distribution is assumed (the argument uses the realized counts K_i of queries to grad f_i with K = sum_i K_i, so deterministic/adaptive selection is not excluded by the proof as written), with the explicit zero-chain property that each query of grad f_i can reveal at most one new coordinate of block i (so x^K has at most min(K_i, p) nonzero coordinates in block i). Theorem 3.1 (each f_i mu-strongly convex and L-smooth, n >= 2, 0 < eps < B^2 mu/4, B = ||x^0 - x*||): if L/mu > (7/2) n, at least Omega( (n + sqrt(nL/mu)) log( B^2 mu/(4 eps) ) ) IFO queries are needed, in dimension d = O((n + sqrt(nL/mu)) log(1/eps)); if n >> L/mu, at least Omega( n + ( n/log(n mu/L) ) log( 1/(n eps) ) ) queries, in dimension d = O(n + (n/log(n mu/L)) log(1/(n eps))). Theorem 3.2 (F mu-strongly convex, f_i L-average smooth, L/mu >= (9/4) sqrt(n)): Omega( (n + n^{3/4} sqrt(L/mu)) log( B^2 mu/(4 eps) ) ), d = O((n + n^{3/4} sqrt(L/mu)) log(1/eps)). Hard instance (Theorem 3.1): p = d/n coordinates per block; f_i(x) = ((L-mu)/4) ( (1/2) <x, A_i x> - <e_{(i-1)p+1}, x> ) + (mu/2)||x||^2 with A_i the block-tridiagonal matrix supported on block i (2 on the diagonal, -1 off-diagonal, last diagonal entry xi = [ sqrt((kappa-1)/n + 1) + 3 ] / [ sqrt((kappa-1)/n + 1) + 1 ], kappa = L/mu), block minimizer geometric with ratio q = ( sqrt((kappa-1)/n + 1) - 1 ) / ( sqrt((kappa-1)/n + 1) + 1 ); average-smooth version: scale (sqrt(n) L - n mu)/4, extra term (n mu/2) <x, B_i x>, xi = (sqrt(kappa) + 3 n^{1/4})/(sqrt(kappa) + n^{1/4}), q = (sqrt(kappa) - n^{1/4})/(sqrt(kappa) + n^{1/4}); convexity of x -> q^x over the realized counts gives the bound. The paper claims tightness against Katyusha / VRADA and SDCA without duality / KatyushaX; it notes that L/mu = O(sqrt(n)) under average smoothness remains open. Caveat: unrefereed preprint; the 'arbitrary index sequence' claim holds only under the explicit zero-chain/span-type property.
relevance: A1: the closest formal statement to the project's sentence 'for an arbitrary index sequence the sqrt(n kappa) term survives but the n log(1/eps) term weakens by a factor log(n/kappa) when kappa << n': Theorem 3.1 gives exactly Omega(n + sqrt(n kappa) log(1/eps)) for kappa >~ n and Omega(n + (n/log(n/kappa)) log(1/(n eps))) for n >> kappa without a predefined sampling distribution (but still under the span/zero-chain property); cite together with Hannah et al. and Han et al. Theorem E.6, and flag that it is unpublished. A4/pipeline: the instance with per-block condition number (kappa-1)/n + 1 and the explicit xi, q is directly implementable and identical in spirit to Lan-Zhou.

title: Dense Weak Hiding: Closing Complexity Gaps in Nonconvex and PL Finite-Sum Optimization under Individual Smoothness
authors: Yuxing Peng, Zhiqing Tang, Weijia Jia
venue: arXiv:2609.00045 (v1 30 Aug 2026, v3 10 Oct 2026), 56 pages, 7 figures, preprint
summary: Most recent refinement (2026): lower bounds for RANDOMIZED IFO algorithms in which both the component index and the query point may depend on the entire history (no span assumption, large dimension), under individual smoothness. It closes the sqrt(n) gap left open by Zhou-Gu for nonconvex finite sums (Omega(n + sqrt(n) Delta L_max/eps^2), so PAGE and SPIDER are minimax optimal up to constants) and gives new bounds under the global Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition in both the large- and small-condition-number regimes, the latter exhibiting the same n log(1/eps)/(1 + log(sqrt(n)/kappa)) structure as Hannah et al. / Han et al. The technique, 'dense weak hiding', spreads each hidden chain direction over all components so that single queries are weakly informative while the average still reveals it, and uses high dimension to prevent premature activation. VERIFIED: arXiv API (title, authors, dates, '56 pages, 7 figures') and arXiv PDF headings (Theorem 3.1 nonconvex lower bound, Corollary 3.2 tight IFO complexity, Theorem 3.3 tight PL complexity); theorem-level constants not checked.
main_result: Model: randomized IFO algorithms; the choice of component i_t and of the query point may depend on the full history (fully adaptive, no linear-span restriction); individual smoothness L_max (and mean-squared smoothness L_ms). Theorem 3.1 / Corollary 3.2 (nonconvex): Omega( n + sqrt(n) Delta L_max / eps^2 ) IFO calls to find an eps-stationary point, matching the O(n + sqrt(n) Delta L_max/eps^2) of PAGE/SPIDER under individual and mean-squared smoothness. Theorem 3.3 (global PL condition with kappa_max = L_max/mu): for kappa_max >= sqrt(n), Omega( n + kappa_max sqrt(n) log(Delta/eps) ); for 3 <= kappa_max <= sqrt(n), Omega( n + n log(Delta/eps) / (1 + log( sqrt(n)/kappa_max )) ); restarted PAGE attains matching upper bounds in terms of kappa_ms = L_ms/mu. Technique: each hidden direction is distributed densely across all n components with small weight ('weak hiding'), so any single component query reveals little, while the direction is preserved in the average; a large dimension makes early activation of later chain stages unlikely within the query budget; balancing the cost of revealing a stage against the number of stages allowed by individual smoothness yields the missing sqrt(n) factor.
relevance: A1: shows the 2026 state of the art for fully adaptive index/query choice: the 'n log(1/eps) weakened by a log-type factor in the small-kappa regime' structure of A1 persists for arbitrary (history-dependent) index sequences, at least under PL (note the thresholds are at kappa ~ sqrt(n) and the large-kappa term is kappa sqrt(n), not sqrt(n kappa), because PL is weaker than strong convexity). B2: PL/mu_eff-type conditions are exactly what the project's trajectory-dependent curvature mu_eff(t) measures; this paper gives the matching lower-bound landscape for PL. Pipeline: not to be implemented (high-dimensional dense instance), but to be cited as the newest refinement; flag as an unrefereed preprint.

title: An Optimal Algorithm for Decentralized Finite-Sum Optimization
authors: Hadrien Hendrikx, Francis Bach, Laurent Massoulie
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization 31(4):2753-2783, 2021 (arXiv:2005.10675, May 2020, arXiv title 'An Optimal Algorithm for Decentralized Finite Sum Optimization')
summary: From Bach's group (the project builds on Bach's lecture notes): proposes ADFS, an accelerated decentralized stochastic proximal algorithm for sums of n x m smooth strongly convex functions spread over n nodes, and proves a black-box lower bound showing it is optimal among decentralized algorithms. The lower bound's computation term, (m + sqrt(m kappa_s)) log(1/eps) per node, is the single-machine finite-sum lower bound of this theme, recovered inside a decentralized model where the node chooses one sample index per local step (possibly randomly) and local memories satisfy a span assumption; the communication term is tau sqrt(kappa_l/gamma) log(1/eps). The hard instance splits a Nesterov chain both across nodes (Scaman et al.-style) and across samples (f_{i,j}(x) = f_i(e_j^T x)). VERIFIED: arXiv API, Crossref DOI (SIAM J. Optim. 31(4):2753-2783), and arXiv PDF (Section 4.1 black-box model, Theorem 4.1, Corollaries 4.2-4.3 checked; the paper uses section-based numbering, not 'Theorem 1 / Corollary 2 / Corollary 3').
main_result: Model (Section 4.1, following Scaman et al.): n nodes, local objectives f_i = sum_{j=1}^m f_{i,j}, f_{i,j} convex and L_{i,j}-smooth, f_i sigma_i-strongly convex, kappa_l >= L_i/sigma_i (local), kappa_s >= L_{i,j}/sigma_i (stochastic/sample condition number); black-box procedure: node i keeps a memory M_{i,t}; at each local step it picks ONE sample index (chosen by the algorithm, possibly at random) and may compute the gradient, conjugate gradient or proximal operator of that f_{i,j} only; computation memory = span of past iterates and oracle outputs (span assumption); communication memory = span of neighbours' memories at time t - tau (delay tau); output from own memory. Theorem 4.1 (in l2): for a graph of size n and diameter Delta there exist such local functions with 2 (1 - q^2)/(1 - q) * E[ ||theta^t - theta*||^2 / ||theta^0 - theta*||^2 ] >= ( 1 - 2m/(m + sqrt(m kappa_s/3)) )^{4 ceil(t)/m} + ( 1 - 2/(1 + sqrt(kappa_l/3)) )^{2 + 2 ceil(t)/(Delta tau)}, q = (sqrt(kappa_l/3) - 1)/(sqrt(kappa_l/3) + 1) (first term: computation, second: communication). Corollary 4.2 (centralized lower bound): time to reach precision eps is Omega( (m + sqrt(m kappa_s) + tau Delta sqrt(kappa_l)) log(1/eps) ). Corollary 4.3 (decentralized, gossip matrix with spectral gap gamma): Omega( (m + sqrt(m kappa_s) + tau sqrt(kappa_l/gamma)) log(1/eps) ). Construction: node-level chain as in Scaman et al. (2017) so that only a few nodes can make progress at a time, and sample-level splitting f_{i,j}(x) = f_i(e_j^T x) following the single-machine finite-sum construction, i.e. a Nesterov chain distributed over nodes and samples.
relevance: A1: an independent (Bach-group) restatement of the Omega((m + sqrt(m kappa_s)) log(1/eps)) finite-sum lower bound with the span assumption and algorithm-chosen (possibly random) sample indices, in the same notation style as the course; A3: ADFS is an accelerated proximal method whose optimality is certified against this bound, so the project can cite it as evidence that acceleration in the Lyapunov style of Bach's notes reaches the lower bound. Pipeline: the single-node case (n = 1, tau irrelevant) of Theorem 4.1 gives a ready-made inequality E||theta^t - theta*||^2 >= c (1 - 2m/(m + sqrt(m kappa_s/3)))^{4t/m} to plot against SAGA/L-Katyusha trajectories.

title: Oracle Complexity of Second-Order Methods for Finite-Sum Problems
authors: Yossi Arjevani, Ohad Shamir
summary: Asks whether component Hessians help finite-sum optimization and answers negatively in the worst case: for algorithms that combine past points, gradients and (block-structured combinations of at most n/2 recent) component Hessians through linear-algebraic operations, with oblivious index choice, Omega(n + sqrt(n mu/lambda) log(...)) second-order oracle calls are needed even when all components are quadratics; with adaptive index choice the same holds with probability one at the cost of exponentially larger dimension. The hard instance randomly assigns each chain coupling (w_l - w_{l+1})^2 to one component, which is a template for hard instances against adaptive index selection. VERIFIED: arXiv API, PMLR v70 page (pp. 205-213), and arXiv PDF (Theorems 1-3, Assumptions 1-2 checked).
main_result: Theorem 2 (finite sums, quadratic components; notation: mu = smoothness, lambda = strong convexity, so mu/lambda = kappa): oracle returns (f_i(w), grad f_i(w), Hessian f_i(w)) for a chosen i; Assumption 1 (linear-algebraic computations): iterates are generated from previous points and gradients by linear combinations and by multiplication with matrices sharing the block-diagonal structure of a combination of at most n/2 of the most recent component Hessians (covers Newton-type steps on those Hessians, truncated SVD, prox of quadratics; excludes forming the full averaged Hessian); Assumption 2 (index obliviousness): indices chosen independently of f_1..f_n (covers uniform sampling and deterministic passes). For n > 1, mu > lambda > 0, eps in (0, c) and dimension d = O~(1 + sqrt(mu/(lambda n))), any such (possibly randomized) algorithm needs Omega( n + sqrt(n mu/lambda) log( (lambda/mu)^{3/2} sqrt(n)/eps ) ) oracle calls in expectation. Theorem 3: without Assumption 2 (adaptive indices) the same bound holds with probability 1 but with d = n^{O~(1 + sqrt(mu/(lambda n)))}. Theorem 1 (single function, second-order oracle, deterministic algorithms, mu > 8 lambda, d = O~(sqrt(mu/lambda))): at least c (sqrt(mu/(8 lambda)) - 1) log( (lambda/mu)^{3/2}/(c' eps) ) calls, i.e. Omega(sqrt(kappa) log(1/eps)): second-order information does not help without Hessian Lipschitzness. Hard instance (Theorem 2): quadratics; indices j_1, ..., j_{d-1} drawn uniformly at random; component f_i contains the coupling term (w_l - w_{l+1})^2 iff j_l = i, plus shared terms and a regularizer; iterates stay in a chain subspace until the algorithm queries f_{j_l}, which advances the support by O(1) coordinates; about n calls per advance; a separate Omega(n) argument since each call reveals information about one component only.
relevance: B1: directly relevant to the quadratic/preconditioned SAGA modification: preconditioning by P built from component Hessians (or any block-structured combination of up to n/2 of them) cannot beat Omega(n + sqrt(n kappa) log(1/eps)) in the worst case, so B1 should look for gains in constants or in favorable geometries (B3), not in the rate. A1: the random assignment of chain couplings to components is the simplest template for a hard instance that resists adaptive index selection (complements Woodworth-Srebro's dimension-based approach).

title: On Lower and Upper Bounds in Smooth and Strongly Convex Optimization
authors: Yossi Arjevani, Shai Shalev-Shwartz, Ohad Shamir
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 17(126):1-51, 2016 (arXiv:1503.06833, March 2015, arXiv title 'On Lower and Upper Bounds for Smooth and Strongly Convex Optimization Problems')
summary: ADDED (missing framework reference): the paper that introduces the structure-based, dimension-free approach on which both Arjevani-Shamir 2016 papers, Arjevani 2017 and Hannah et al.'s Theorem 4 build (they all cite 'the framework of Arjevani et al. (2015)'). It models optimization algorithms on quadratics as p-SCLI (stationary canonical linear iterative) methods, i.e. recursive applications of linear operators depending on the last p points, connects their convergence rate to the maximal root modulus of characteristic polynomials, and derives lower bounds that hold in the regime where the dimension is fixed (unlike Nemirovsky-Yudin/Nesterov bounds, valid only when the dimension scales with the number of iterations). SDCA is the motivating case study and SAG/SVRG-type methods are shown to fit the framework. VERIFIED: JMLR page (vol. 17, paper 126, pp. 1-51, 2016) and arXiv API; theorem headings read from the arXiv PDF (Definitions 2-3, Theorems 4, 5, 8, Corollary 7); the exact constants were not checked.
main_result: Framework (Section 2-3): a p-SCLI algorithm on quadratics f_{A,b}(x) = (1/2) x^T A x + b^T x generates x^{(k+1)} = sum_{j=0}^{p-1} C_j(A) x^{(k-j)} + N(A) b with coefficient matrices that are polynomial (or more general) functions of A; Definition 2: characteristic polynomial of the algorithm; Definition 3 (consistency): the fixed point must be the minimizer for all A in the class; Theorem 4: the convergence rate is governed by the maximal modulus of the roots of the characteristic polynomial; Theorem 5 / Corollary 7: consistency forces constraints on the coefficient polynomials, giving a 'plug-and-play' scheme for lower bounds via polynomial root bounds. Theorem 8 (main lower bound, as stated in the arXiv version): for consistent p-SCLI algorithms with scalar or diagonal inversion matrices over L-smooth mu-strongly convex quadratics, the iteration complexity is bounded below by Omega(kappa^{1/p} ln(1/eps)) (p-th root of the condition number), independently of the dimension; tight for p = 1 (gradient descent) and p = 2 (accelerated gradient descent / heavy ball); the authors note Theorem 8 is not tight for general p and conjecture that Omega(sqrt(kappa) ln(1/eps)) holds for any p. Upper bounds: a systematic derivation of Nesterov's accelerated gradient method as the optimal 2-SCLI. Stochastic finite-sum methods (SDCA, SAG, SVRG) are stochastic p-SCLIs whose expected iterates follow the same recursions, so the bounds apply to their bias.
relevance: A1/A2: the origin of the 'oblivious / CLI' algorithm class used by arjevani2016dimension, arjevani2016iteration, arjevani2017limitations and by Hannah et al.'s Theorem 4; needed to state precisely which algorithm class the dimension-free finite-sum lower bounds cover (fixed-step SAGA with gamma = 1/(4R^2) as in Bach's Prop. 5.9 is a stationary 1-SCLI in expectation). A3: explains why acceleration needs p >= 2 memory (momentum) and mu-dependent coefficients. B2: the polynomial/root-modulus view makes precise what a trajectory-dependent effective curvature could gain over the worst-case root bound.

title: Katyusha: The First Direct Acceleration of Stochastic Gradient Methods
authors: Zeyuan Allen-Zhu
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 18(221):1-51, 2018 (conference version STOC 2017; arXiv:1603.05953, v6 Sept 2018)
summary: ADDED (matching upper bound): the algorithm whose rate O((n + sqrt(n kappa)) log(1/eps)) certifies that the lower bounds of this theme are tight (every lower-bound paper in the list states 'matching Katyusha'). Katyusha adds a 'negative momentum' (Katyusha momentum) toward a reference snapshot point on top of Nesterov momentum inside an SVRG-type variance-reduced method, which makes the variance of the stochastic gradient absorbable and yields the optimal accelerated rate for convex finite sums, with optimal parallel linear speed-up in the mini-batch setting. VERIFIED: JMLR page (vol. 18, paper 221, pp. 1-51, 2018), arXiv API (v6, 'Appeared in STOC 2017 and JMLR 2018'), and a local copy of the arXiv PDF (Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 3.2 checked).
main_result: Theorem 2.1 (each f_i convex and L-smooth, psi sigma-strongly convex, epoch length m, step parameters depending on (L, sigma, m)): Katyusha(x_0, S, sigma, L) satisfies E[F(x^S) - F(x*)] <= O( (1 + sqrt(sigma/(3Lm)))^{-Sm} ) (F(x_0) - F(x*)) if m sigma/L <= 3/4, and O(1.5^{-S}) (F(x_0) - F(x*)) otherwise; Corollary 3.2 (HOOD property): the total stochastic gradient complexity to halve the objective gap is T(L, sigma) = O( n + sqrt(nL/sigma) ), i.e. O( (n + sqrt(n kappa)) log(1/eps) ) gradient evaluations for eps accuracy, matching the Omega((n + sqrt(n kappa)) log(1/eps)) lower bounds of Lan-Zhou / Woodworth-Srebro / Arjevani-Shamir (individual smoothness). Section 3-4: reductions to non-strongly convex and non-smooth settings (Corollaries 3.5-3.7) and Katyusha^ns with O(n log(1/eps) + sqrt(nL/eps)) for convex objectives; mini-batch parallel speed-up. The loopless variant with the same rate is L-Katyusha (Kovalev, Horvath, Richtarik 2020), which is the algorithm of the project's A3.
relevance: A3: the reference statement and proof template of the corrected acceleration (negative momentum toward a reference point) that the project reproduces in Lyapunov style; its rate is exactly what the lower bounds of this theme show to be optimal, which is the point of the project's title. A2: Section 1 of the paper explains why naive Nesterov momentum on top of a stochastic estimator fails (counterexamples), motivating A2 vs A3. A4: predicts the kappa^(1/2) exponent for L-Katyusha on the hard instances. | A2: Sec. 1 ('counterexamples exist and prevent Nesterov's momentum from providing similar acceleration, even if the problem is convex and finite-sum'; 'momentum is dangerous if stochastic gradients are present ... when naively equipped with momentum, stochastic gradient methods are very prone [sic: prune] to error accumulation') and Remark 5.7 answer key question (i): the proof term that cannot be absorbed is the inner product <grad f(x_{k+1}), xtilde - x_{k+1}> in the tight variance bound (the loose classical bound 4L(f(xtilde) - f(x*)) is insufficient for acceleration). A3: the 'magnet' interpretation (Section 1.1: weight tau_2 = 0.5 keeps x_{k+1} close to xtilde so the estimator stays accurate; 'counteracting a fraction of the positive momentum') answers (ii); parameters tau_1, tau_2, alpha, m give the loopy analogue of L-Katyusha's theta_1, theta_2, eta, p (iii). A4/pipeline: experiments on ridge/Lasso/logistic with lambda in {1e-4, 1e-6, 1e-7} versus SVRG, SAGA, Catalyst-SVRG, APCG; Figure 1 shows that with tau_2 = 0 (naive Nesterov + SVRG) the method is no longer accelerated - a ready-made design for the A2 vs A3 experiment (iv). | (A3)/(A4): the canonical way to control kappa in VR experiments is to sweep lambda over decades at fixed data; with average-norm scaling, L ~ 1/4 + lambda for logistic, so lambda = 1e-6 gives kappa ~ 2.5e5 >> n for a9a, exactly the regime where the sqrt(n kappa) vs kappa separation is visible; also the empirical warning that naive/Catalyst-style acceleration can be slower (A2).

title: Lower Bounds for Finding Stationary Points I
authors: Yair Carmon, John C. Duchi, Oliver Hinder, Aaron Sidford
venue: Mathematical Programming 184(1-2):71-120, 2020 (published online 7 June 2019; arXiv:1710.11606, v3 Aug 2019)
summary: ADDED (technique reference): the paper that formalizes the 'zero-chain' and 'robust zero-chain' notions (Definitions 3 and 4) and the random-rotation argument for randomized algorithms that the finite-sum lower bounds of Zhou-Gu (Propositions 3.5/3.11), Xie-Luo-Zhang, Han-Xie-Zhang (the Gamma bump, Lemma 6.1) and Zhang-Shu-He ('f is a first-order zero-chain (Carmon et al.)') build on; it also pointed out the issue in the randomized proofs of Woodworth-Srebro 2016 (Appendix C) and 2017, which were then corrected 'in a manner resembling' this paper. Its own subject is nonconvex: for any (randomized) algorithm there is a function with Lipschitz p-th derivatives requiring eps^{-(p+1)/p} queries to find an eps-stationary point, so gradient descent (p = 1) and cubic regularization (p = 2) are worst-case optimal. VERIFIED: arXiv API, Crossref DOI (Math. Prog. 184(1-2):71-120), and arXiv PDF (Definitions 3-4 'p-th order zero-chain' / 'robust zero-chain', Section 4-5 structure checked).
main_result: Definition 3 (p-th order zero-chain): f is a p-th order zero-chain if supp{x} subset {1, ..., i-1} implies supp{grad^{(q)} f(x)} subset {1, ..., i} for q <= p (Nesterov's chain quadratic is a first-order zero-chain); Observation/Proposition: for zero-respecting (and hence, via a resisting-rotation argument, all deterministic) algorithms, each oracle query extends the support by at most one coordinate, so T coordinates need T queries. Definition 4 (robust zero-chain): |x_j| < 1/2 for all j >= i implies f(y) = f(y_1, ..., y_i, 0, ..., 0) in a neighborhood; with a uniformly random orthogonal rotation U and f_U(x) = f(Ux), an adapted Woodworth-Srebro lemma shows that randomized algorithms also reveal at most one new direction per query with high probability, in dimension polynomial in the query budget. Main theorems: for functions with Lipschitz p-th derivatives, any randomized algorithm needs Omega(eps^{-(p+1)/p}) queries to find an eps-stationary point (Omega(eps^{-2}) for first-order methods on smooth functions), sharp to within constants. The chain construction uses the bump function Gamma and the 'Psi/Phi' nonconvex chain later reused as the Gamma term in Zhou-Gu and Han-Xie-Zhang.
relevance: A1/pipeline: supplies the clean 'zero-chain' vocabulary and lemma the project should use to explain why, on the block instances, one component gradient activates at most one new coordinate (the observable to log in the experiments), and the random-rotation device that extends span-based bounds to arbitrary randomized algorithms; cite when discussing the dimension requirements of the no-span-assumption bounds (Woodworth-Srebro, Peng-Tang-Jia). Not to be implemented (nonconvex setting).

title: A Universal Catalyst for First-Order Optimization
authors: Hongzhou Lin, Julien Mairal, Zaid Harchaoui
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28 (NeurIPS 2015), pp. 3384-3392 (pages per OpenAlex); arXiv:1506.02186
summary: Generic acceleration scheme: an inexact accelerated proximal-point outer loop whose subproblems F + (kappa/2)||x - y_k||^2 are solved approximately by any linearly convergent method M (GD, block coordinate descent, SAG, SAGA, SDCA, SVRG, MISO/Finito). Yields Nesterov-type acceleration and support for non-strongly convex objectives at the price of logarithmic factors, with practical gains mainly on ill-conditioned problems.
main_result: With kappa chosen so that the condition number (L + kappa)/(mu + kappa) of the subproblems is of order n, incremental methods SAG/SAGA/SVRG/MISO/SDCA (complexity O((n + L/mu) log(1/eps)) alone) become O~((n + sqrt(n L/mu)) log(1/eps)) for mu > 0 and O~(sqrt(n L/eps)) for mu = 0; O~ hides logarithmic factors in the condition number. Table 1 (NeurIPS version) only presents the case n <= L/mu when mu > 0 and states that 'for all incremental algorithms, there is indeed no acceleration otherwise'. Full gradient descent becomes O~(n sqrt(L/mu) log(1/eps)); accelerated methods are not further accelerated. Experiments (Sec. 5) on logistic regression: huge speed-up for MISO in the 'small mu' regime, SAGA without acceleration best on ocr, attributed to adaptivity to the unknown local strong convexity mu' >= mu near the solution ('when mu'/L >= 1/n ... acceleration does not occur').
relevance: A3 (indirect acceleration): the 'black-box' alternative to negative momentum - the extra log factor versus Katyusha is the price of not having a direct Lyapunov argument (SSNM intro: 'APPA and Catalyst ... result in additional log factors'). A4/B2: the authors state gains appear 'particularly on ill-conditioned problems', and the ocr experiment is an early published instance of the local-strong-convexity effect of B2. Pipeline: candidate baseline (Catalyst-SAGA) for the kappa-sweep.

title: Catalyst Acceleration for First-order Convex Optimization: from Theory to Practice
authors: Hongzhou Lin, Julien Mairal, Zaid Harchaoui
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 18(212):1-54; arXiv:1712.05654
summary: Long version of Catalyst: full global complexity analysis of the inexact accelerated proximal point scheme, warm-start strategies and stopping criteria that make the acceleration effective in practice, and extensive experiments. The authors insist that acceleration depends on solving the subproblems to the right accuracy with the right warm start.
main_result: Table 1: without Catalyst SAG/SAGA/MISO/SDCA/SVRG need O((n + Lbar/mu) log(1/eps)) (mu > 0); with Catalyst O~((n + sqrt(n Lbar/mu)) log(1/eps)) (mu > 0) and O~(sqrt(n Lbar/eps)) (mu = 0), where O~ hides logarithmic factors; full gradient O(n L/mu log(1/eps)) becomes O~(n sqrt(L/mu) log(1/eps)); accelerated methods (Acc-FG, Acc-SDCA): 'no acceleration'. Rule: choose kappa so that (Lbar + kappa)/(mu + kappa) is of order n, then the inner complexity is O(n log(1/eps)). Results are optimal up to logarithmic factors (citing Woodworth-Srebro and Arjevani-Shamir lower bounds). Experiments (logistic, Elastic-net, Lasso on covtype, real-sim, rcv1, alpha): 'significant improvements are achieved as expected by the theory for the ill-conditioned problems'.
relevance: A3: explains why reduction-based acceleration loses a log(kappa) factor compared with direct methods (L-Katyusha), useful for the discussion of optimality in the project's rate statement. A4/B3: experimental evidence that acceleration helps only in the ill-conditioned regime (kappa >> n) - consistent with the project's expected kappa^{1/2} versus kappa^1 exponents (iv).

title: Un-regularizing: approximate proximal point and faster stochastic algorithms for empirical risk minimization
authors: Roy Frostig, Rong Ge, Sham M. Kakade, Aaron Sidford
venue: ICML 2015, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 37:2540-2548; arXiv:1506.07512
summary: Introduces the Approximate Proximal Point Algorithm (APPA): minimizing a mu-strongly convex F is reduced to approximately minimizing a sequence of heavily regularized problems F(x) + (lambda/2)||x - x_k||^2, each solved by a fast linearly convergent stochastic method (SVRG/SDCA/APCG). This 'reaps the computational benefits of adding a large strongly convex regularization term without incurring a corresponding bias', giving accelerated running times for ERM (notably least squares) in a black-box way, contemporaneous with Catalyst.
main_result: Theorem 1.1 (Accelerated Approximate Proximal Point Algorithm): given an oracle returning, for any centre x_0 and c > 0, a point with E f_lambda(x_c) - min f_lambda <= (1/c)(f_lambda(x_0) - min f_lambda) for the regularized objective f_lambda = f + (lambda/2)||x - x_0||^2, a mu-strongly convex f is minimized to accuracy eps with O(sqrt(lambda/mu) log(1/eps)) oracle calls, each requiring only constant relative accuracy (c polynomial in lambda/mu). Theorems 2.2-2.3: SVRG and APCG are such primal oracles with runtime O(nd min{kappa_lambda, ...} log c) / O(nd sqrt(kappa_lambda) log c). Combined (Secs. 3-4), ERM is solved in O~(d(n + sqrt(n kappa)) log(1/eps)) time with O~ hiding polylogarithmic factors in n, L, mu, lambda (summarized by later papers, e.g. Zhou et al. 2019 Table 1 and Lan et al. 2019, as optimal up to log factors).
relevance: A3: the second 'indirect' acceleration route; same role as Catalyst in the discussion of why direct negative-momentum methods avoid the extra log(kappa). B1: the regularized subproblem F + (lambda/2)||x - x_k||^2 is a proximal (identity-preconditioned) modification of the finite sum - a conceptual relative of the project's P-preconditioned SAGA step.
