title: Accelerated Proximal Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent for Regularized Loss Minimization
authors: Shai Shalev-Shwartz, Tong Zhang
venue: ICML 2014, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 32(1):64-72; journal version Mathematical Programming 155(1-2):105-145, 2016 (DOI 10.1007/s10107-014-0839-0); arXiv:1309.2375
summary: Proximal SDCA accelerated by an inner-outer (proximal-point / Nesterov) iteration: the inner loop runs Prox-SDCA on a problem with an added quadratic term. First method with the O(n + sqrt(n kappa)) dependence for regularized ERM (the Gower et al. survey credits it as first achieving the optimal complexity). Experiments confirm the gains for small lambda.
main_result: For min (1/n) sum phi_i(X_i^T w) + lambda g(w) with (1/gamma)-smooth losses and 1-strongly convex g, an eps-accurate solution is found with probability >= 1 - delta in time O(d (n + min{1/(lambda gamma), sqrt(n/(lambda gamma))}) log(1/delta) log(1/eps) max{1, log^2(1/(lambda gamma n))}) = O~(d (n + min{1/(lambda gamma), sqrt(n/(lambda gamma))})), with 1/(lambda gamma) playing the role of the condition number: O~(dn) when kappa = O(n), O~(d sqrt(n/(lambda gamma))) when kappa >> n, improving on accelerated gradient descent O~(d n sqrt(1/(lambda gamma))). Theorem 1 gives the inner Prox-SDCA rate T >= (n + R^2/(lambda gamma)) log(...). Smoothed version for Lipschitz losses: O~(d (n + min{1/(lambda eps), sqrt(n/(lambda eps))})).
relevance: A3 context: historically the first accelerated finite-sum rate; the inner-outer structure (acceleration on a regularized surrogate) is the dual precursor of Catalyst/APPA and shows the extra log factors of indirect acceleration. A1/A4: makes explicit the two regimes kappa = O(n) (linear in n, no benefit from acceleration) versus kappa >> n (sqrt(n kappa)) that the project's kappa-sweep must separate.

title: An Accelerated Randomized Proximal Coordinate Gradient Method and its Application to Regularized Empirical Risk Minimization
authors: Qihang Lin, Zhaosong Lu, Lin Xiao
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization 25(4):2244-2273 (DOI 10.1137/141000270); arXiv:1407.1296 (July 2014, arXiv title without 'Randomized'); a short version appeared at NeurIPS 2014 (not verified here)
summary: APCG: an accelerated randomized proximal coordinate gradient method for composite problems with block-separable regularizer; applied to the dual of regularized ERM it accelerates SDCA with an implementation that avoids full-dimensional vector operations. For ill-conditioned ERM it improves over SDCA/SAG/SVRG by replacing kappa with sqrt(n kappa).
main_result: For regularized ERM with lambda-strongly convex regularizer, (1/gamma)-smooth losses and ||a_i|| <= R, APCG reaches E[D* - D(x^{(k)})] <= eps after k >= (n + sqrt(n R^2/(lambda gamma))) log(C/eps) iterations (each costing O(d)), i.e. O((n + sqrt(n kappa)) log(1/eps)) with kappa = R^2/(lambda gamma), versus O((n + R^2/(lambda gamma)) log(1/eps)) for SDCA/SAG/SVRG; the result 'can be much better for ill-conditioned problems, i.e., when the condition number R^2/(lambda gamma) is much larger than n'; the accelerated full-gradient method needs O(sqrt(n ||A||_2^2/(lambda gamma)) log(1/eps)) <= O(sqrt(n^2 R^2/(lambda gamma)) log(1/eps)), a factor up to sqrt(n) worse. The paper notes that accelerated SDCA (Shalev-Shwartz and Zhang) 'achieves the same complexity O((n + sqrt(n kappa)) log(1/eps))' via an inner-outer scheme. Experiments: ill-conditioned setting with lambda from 1e-5 to 1e-8.
relevance: A3 context (dual/coordinate route to the optimal rate without negative momentum: acceleration happens in a coordinate-descent sense on the dual, where the stochastic estimator is exact per coordinate, which is why no variance-absorption issue arises - a useful contrast for explaining what is special about primal SVRG-type estimators). A1: the regime statement 'much better for ill-conditioned problems, i.e. when kappa >> n'.

title: Stochastic Primal-Dual Coordinate Method for Regularized Empirical Risk Minimization
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Lin Xiao
venue: ICML 2015, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 37:353-361 (proceedings.mlr.press/v37/zhanga15.html); journal version Journal of Machine Learning Research 18(84):1-42, 2017; arXiv:1409.3257
summary: SPDC rewrites regularized ERM as a convex-concave saddle point problem and alternates a maximization over a randomly chosen dual coordinate with a primal minimization plus an extrapolation (momentum) step on the primal variable. Mini-batch and weighted-sampling variants are given; experiments show performance comparable to or better than SDCA/SAG/SVRG-type methods, especially for ill-conditioned problems.
main_result: Iteration complexity O((n + sqrt(kappa n)) log(1/eps)) with kappa = R^2/(lambda gamma) (R = max ||a_i||, losses (1/gamma)-smooth, regularizer lambda-strongly convex), i.e. batch complexity O((1 + sqrt(kappa/n)) log(1/eps)), compared with O((n + kappa) log(1/eps)) (batch O((1 + kappa/n) log(1/eps))) for SDCA/SAG/SVRG and O((1 + sqrt(kappa)) log(1/eps)) full passes for accelerated full gradient. Section 1.1: in statistical learning lambda is usually of order 1/sqrt(n) or 1/n, so kappa is of order sqrt(n) or n (or larger when strong convexity is added only for numerical regularization), and the actual conditioning may be better than kappa if the empirical loss is itself strongly convex.
relevance: A3 context: primal-dual extrapolation is another way to obtain the optimal rate; the extrapolation step is a momentum on the primal variable that is safe because the dual coordinate update is exact. A1/A4: gives the typical statistical scaling kappa ~ sqrt(n) to n, useful to argue which regime of the project's (n, kappa) grid is practically relevant; B2: the remark on hidden strong convexity of the empirical loss anticipates mu_eff > mu.

title: Random Gradient Extrapolation for Distributed and Stochastic Optimization
authors: Guanghui Lan, Yi Zhou
summary: RGEM is a randomized incremental gradient method derived from a dual (game) view of Nesterov's acceleration: at each iteration one component is selected, its gradient is extrapolated, and no exact full gradient is ever computed, not even at the initial point. It attains the optimal accelerated complexity for finite sums and extends to stochastic finite sums and distributed settings with O(log(1/eps)) communication rounds.
main_result: For (1/m) sum_i f_i(x) + mu w(x) with f_i smooth and w strongly convex, RGEM 'does not require any exact gradient evaluation even for the initial point' but achieves the optimal O(log(1/eps)) complexity in the number of component-gradient evaluations, i.e. O((m + sqrt(mL/mu)) log(1/eps)) (as tabulated in Lan-Li-Zhou 2019); for stochastic finite-sum problems it keeps the optimal O(1/eps) stochastic-gradient complexity (up to a log factor), independent of m, with O(log(1/eps)) communication rounds each involving a single agent.
relevance: A3 context: shows that the optimal rate can also be obtained with a gradient-extrapolation (rather than snapshot) mechanism; relevant to the discussion of what replaces the 'reference point' in SAGA-like memory-based accelerated schemes (compare SSNM). Pipeline: alternative accelerated baseline that, like SAGA, never computes full gradients.

title: A unified variance-reduced accelerated gradient method for convex optimization
authors: Guanghui Lan, Zhize Li, Yi Zhou
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (NeurIPS 2019), pp. 10462-10472 (pages per OpenAlex); arXiv:1905.12412
summary: Varag is an accelerated SVRG-type randomized incremental gradient method whose single step-size policy adapts to the condition number, giving optimal rates for smooth convex finite sums with or without strong convexity, without restarts or perturbation. It is the first accelerated RIG method with optimal linear convergence when strong convexity sits in the data-fidelity term, extends to error-bound conditions and to stochastic finite sums. Its inner update also mixes the snapshot into the convex combination (negative-momentum-like).
main_result: Table 2 (unified results, m components, D_0 = 2[psi(x^0) - psi*] + 3L V(x^0, x*)): O(m log(1/eps)) gradient evaluations if m >= D_0/eps or m >= 3L/(4mu); O(m log m + sqrt(mL/eps)) if m < D_0/eps <= 3L/(4mu); O(m log m + sqrt(mL/mu) log((D_0/eps)/(3L/(4mu)))) if m < 3L/(4mu) <= D_0/eps (this last term is below O(sqrt(mL/mu) log(1/eps))). Comparison table: RPDG, Catalyst, Katyusha, RGEM all O((m + sqrt(mL/mu)) log(1/eps)) for strongly convex problems (Catalyst/RPDG/Katyusha via perturbation in the non-strongly convex case, Catalyst with an extra log); Theorem 3 extends the results to the error-bound condition.
relevance: A3: an alternative direct accelerated method with an explicit regime split (m vs 3L/(4mu)) that mirrors the two regimes of the project (n >= kappa: O(n log 1/eps), n << kappa: sqrt(n kappa)); the 3/4 threshold also appears in MiG/SSNM. A1/A4: the m >= 3L/(4mu) => O(m log(1/eps)) statement is the theoretical basis for the project's expectation that acceleration gives nothing when kappa << n.

title: A Simple Stochastic Variance Reduced Algorithm with Fast Convergence Rates
authors: Kaiwen Zhou, Fanhua Shang, James Cheng
venue: ICML 2018, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 80:5980-5989; arXiv:1806.11027
summary: MiG keeps only the Katyusha (negative) momentum and drops Nesterov's momentum: the inner iterate is a two-point convex combination y = theta x + (1 - theta) xtilde of the current variable and the SVRG snapshot, which still achieves the best-known rates for strongly and non-strongly convex problems. The lighter structure enables sparse and asynchronous variants; experiments on l2-logistic regression and ridge regression with lambda from 1e-4 down to 1e-8 show practical gains.
main_result: Theorem 1 (strongly convex, m = Theta(n); Table 2: theta = sqrt(m/(3 kappa)) and eta = 1/(3 theta L) when m/kappa <= 3/4, theta = 1/2 and eta = 2/(3L) otherwise): oracle complexity O(sqrt(kappa n) log((F(x_0) - F*)/eps)) if m/kappa <= 3/4 and O(n log((F(x_0) - F*)/eps)) otherwise, i.e. O((n + sqrt(kappa n)) log((F(x_0) - F*)/eps)), 'the best-known oracle complexity for stochastic first-order algorithms, e.g., APCG, SPDC, and Katyusha'. Section 3.1 ('Choice of x_0^{s+1}'): if each epoch is restarted from the snapshot xtilde^s instead of the last iterate, 'the overall oracle complexity will degenerate to a non-accelerated one for some ill-conditioned problems, which is O((n + kappa) log(1/eps))'. Appendix: 'MiG uses only Katyusha Momentum (negative momentum) to achieve acceleration ... To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to yield an acceleration without using Nesterov's Momentum'.
relevance: A2/A3 (key for question ii): isolates the negative-momentum term as the ingredient responsible for acceleration - the opposite ablation of Katyusha's tau_2 = 0 experiment; together they show Nesterov momentum alone fails while negative momentum alone suffices. Pipeline: the simplest accelerated SVRG-type baseline to implement next to L-Katyusha; experiments sweep lambda (1e-4 ... 1e-8), relevant to A4.

title: Direct Acceleration of SAGA using Sampled Negative Momentum
authors: Kaiwen Zhou, Qinghua Ding, Fanhua Shang, James Cheng, Danli Li, Zhi-Quan Luo
venue: AISTATS 2019, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 89:1602-1610; arXiv:1806.11048 (arXiv version single-authored by Kaiwen Zhou)
summary: SSNM is the first direct acceleration of SAGA: since SAGA has no snapshot point where a full gradient is known, the negative momentum is taken toward a randomly sampled entry of SAGA's table of past points (a 'coupled table'), using a double sampling (i_k for the gradient, an independent I_k for the momentum). The proof uses the SAGA Lyapunov function and reaches the optimal strongly convex complexity; experiments on ill-conditioned logistic regression compare SAGA, SSNM, Katyusha and MiG.
main_result: Theorem 1 (strongly convex): with Lyapunov T^k = (1/(n eta mu)) [(1/n) sum_i F_i(phi_i^k) - F(x*) - (1/n) sum_i <grad F_i(x*), phi_i^k - x*>] + (1/(2 eta n)) ||x_k - x*||^2 ('the same as the one in SAGA') and tau = n eta mu/(1 + eta mu), E[T^{k+1}] <= (1 + eta mu)^{-1} T^k. (I) ill-conditioned, n/kappa <= 3/4, eta = sqrt(1/(3 mu n L)): E||x_{K+1} - x*||^2 <= (1 + sqrt(1/(3 n kappa)))^{-K} ((2/mu)(F(x_1) - F*) + ||x_1 - x*||^2), i.e. O(sqrt(kappa n) log(1/eps)); (II) n/kappa > 3/4, eta = 1/(2 mu n): contraction (1 + 1/(2n))^{-K}, i.e. O(n log(1/eps)); overall O((n + sqrt(kappa n)) log(1/eps)). Proof insight (Sec. 3-4): 'the major task of the negative momentum is to cancel the additional inner product term shown in the variance bound'. Experiments (a9a with lambda = 1e-6, 1e-7; covtype with lambda = 1e-8, 1e-9): 'Around 3 times slow-down when kappa is 10 times larger ... approximately sqrt(10) times slow-down ... is recorded for all the accelerated methods. In comparison, SAGA shows significant slow-down when kappa is increased ... This observation justifies the sqrt(kappa) dependency for accelerated methods'; accelerated methods look worse during the first passes on a9a, conjectured because 'the objective is locally well-conditioned'.
relevance: A3: the accelerated method closest to Bach's SAGA setting - same Lyapunov structure as Bach's Prop. 5.9 (table term + distance term) and an explicit statement of which proof term (the inner product in the variance bound) the negative momentum cancels (ii). A4 (key for question iv): the only paper found that explicitly reports the empirical kappa-scaling (sqrt(10) per decade of kappa for Katyusha/MiG/SSNM versus a much larger slowdown for SAGA), i.e. the kappa^{1/2} vs kappa^1 exponents the project wants to measure, though only over two lambda values per dataset. B2: the 'locally well-conditioned around the initial point' remark is exactly the trajectory-dependent effective-curvature effect of B2.

title: Stochastic Proximal Gradient Descent with Acceleration Techniques
authors: Atsushi Nitanda
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 27 (NeurIPS 2014), pp. 1574-1582 (pages per OpenAlex)
summary: Acc-Prox-SVRG: the first attempt to combine Nesterov's acceleration with the SVRG variance-reduced estimator, in a mini-batch setting. The abstract states that the advantage over both accelerated proximal gradient (APG) and Prox-SVRG is obtained only 'with the appropriate mini-batch size', and the analysis makes the acceleration depend on the mini-batch size b (content confirmed from the NeurIPS PDF).
main_result: Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 (p. 6): for small momentum parameter p, with eta = min{(pb)^2 (n-1)^2 mu/(64 (n-b)^2 L^2), 1/(2L)}: if the mini-batch size b is below a threshold b_0 the learning rate is the first term and the overall complexity (component gradient evaluations) is O((n + ((n-b)/(n-1)) kappa) log(1/eps)) (eq. 26); otherwise eta = 1/(2L) and the complexity becomes O((n + b sqrt(kappa)) log(1/eps)) (eq. 27). Table 1 compares with Prox-SVRG O((n + kappa) log(1/eps)) and APG O(n sqrt(kappa) log(1/eps)). Allen-Zhu (Remark 5.7) restates this as total work O(n + ((n-b)/(n-1)) L/sigma + b sqrt(L/sigma)); Nitanda (2016) restates it as O((n + n kappa/(n + sqrt(kappa))) log(1/eps)) = O~((n + min{kappa, n sqrt(kappa)}) log(1/eps)), half the harmonic mean of the SVRG term kappa and the accelerated-full-gradient term n sqrt(kappa): acceleration over SVRG appears only when sqrt(kappa) > n.
relevance: A2 (central for key question i): the concrete instance of 'plugging the SVRG estimator into Nesterov's algorithm'; with b = 1 the variance term cannot be absorbed and the bound is the non-accelerated O((n + kappa) log(1/eps)); only a large mini-batch shrinks the variance enough, which is why Allen-Zhu writes it 'requires mini-batch size to be very large in order to be accelerated' and treats tau_2 = 0 in Katyusha as this method. Pipeline: the natural 'naive acceleration' baseline for the A2 experiment.

title: Estimate Sequences for Variance-Reduced Stochastic Composite Optimization
authors: Andrei Kulunchakov, Julien Mairal
venue: ICML 2019, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 97:3541-3550; arXiv:1905.02374
summary: Extends Nesterov's estimate sequences to stochastic composite optimization so that SGD, SAGA-, SVRG- and MISO-type methods are all viewed as iteratively minimizing a surrogate; this gives a generic convergence proof, SVRG variants that adapt to strong convexity, robustness to stochastic (perturbation) noise, and a new accelerated SVRG whose variance is controlled 'in a similar manner to Katyusha' with an anchor point updated with probability 1/n. Experiments on l2-logistic regression with lambda = 1/(10n) and 1/(100n), with and without DropOut noise.
main_result: Accelerated random-SVRG (Algorithm 2; Proposition 4 variance bound sigma_k^2 <= 2 L_Q (f(xtilde_{k-1}) - f(y_{k-1}) - <grad f(y_{k-1}), xtilde_{k-1} - y_{k-1}>) + 3 rho_Q sigmatilde^2; Theorem 4 with step sizes eta_k <= min{1/(3 L_Q), 1/(15 mu_k n)}; Corollary 8): complexity O((n + sqrt(n L_Q/mu)) log((F(x_0) - F*)/eps)) + O(rho_Q sigmatilde^2/(mu eps)) stochastic gradient evaluations, where sigmatilde^2 is the variance of the gradient perturbations (zero for exact finite sums, 'the optimal complexity for finite sums (Arjevani & Shamir, 2016)'), L_Q the smoothness constant under sampling distribution Q, rho_Q = 1 for uniform sampling; with constant step size the iterates converge linearly to a ball of radius O(rho_Q sigmatilde^2 min{1/sqrt(n mu L_Q), 1/(mu n)}). Experimental observations: 'Acceleration is more effective when the problem is badly conditioned - that is, when lambda = 1/(100n)'; with lambda = 1/(10n) non-accelerated methods 'already perform well ... This may be due to hidden strong convexity' giving a regime where the complexity is O(n log(1/eps)).
relevance: A3: a third proof technique (estimate sequences, i.e. Nesterov's own Lyapunov-like potential) for the accelerated rate, with a loopless anchor updated w.p. 1/n exactly as in L-Katyusha - useful to cross-check the Lyapunov constants. A4/B2: the 'hidden strong convexity' remark is a published instance of the project's mu_eff(t) >= mu explanation for the theory-practice gap, and the lambda = 1/(10n) vs 1/(100n) comparison is a two-point kappa sweep (iv).

title: Estimate Sequences for Stochastic Composite Optimization: Variance Reduction, Acceleration, and Robustness to Noise
authors: Andrei Kulunchakov, Julien Mairal
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 21(155):1-52; arXiv:1901.08788
summary: Journal (long) version of the estimate-sequence framework: unified analysis of SGD, SAGA, SVRG, MISO/Finito/SDCA as surrogate minimization ('procedures that iteratively minimize a surrogate of the objective'), with generic strategies to make them robust to stochastic noise and a new accelerated SGD and a new accelerated SVRG algorithm 'that is robust to stochastic noise'.
main_result: Same accelerated-SVRG guarantee as the ICML version: O((n + sqrt(n L/mu)) log(1/eps)) for exact finite sums plus an O(sigmatilde^2/(mu eps)) term under additive gradient noise; non-accelerated variants obtain O((n + L/mu) log(1/eps)) + noise term; all proofs go through a single estimate-sequence (potential) inequality per iteration.
relevance: A3: provides a complete, self-contained Lyapunov/estimate-sequence derivation of the accelerated rate that can be compared line by line with the project's reproduction of the L-Katyusha proof; B3: the per-iteration surrogate inequality lists exactly the inequalities one would instrument for a tightness-ratio diagnosis.

title: Accelerating variance-reduced stochastic gradient methods
authors: Derek Driggs, Matthias J. Ehrhardt, Carola-Bibiane Schonlieb
venue: Mathematical Programming 191(2):671-715 (published online 2020; DOI 10.1007/s10107-020-01566-2); arXiv:1910.09494
summary: Proposes a universal momentum framework (linear-coupling style, no anchor point) that accelerates any gradient estimator satisfying an 'MSEB' property (bounds on the mean-squared error and bias of the estimator): SAGA, SVRG, SARAH and SARGE. The introduction gives the clearest published discussion of what the Katyusha anchor term does and why negative momentum is estimator-specific (it needs a point where the full gradient is known, so it cannot be applied to SAGA). The price of dropping it is an n^{2/3} instead of sqrt(n) factor in the strongly convex rate.
main_result: Theorem 13 (SAGA estimator, mini-batch b <= 4 sqrt(2) n^{2/3}): non-strongly convex: with gamma_k = b^3 (k + 4n/b + 4)/(192 n^2 L), tau_k = b^3/(96 n^2 L gamma_k), E F(y_T) - F* <= (4n/b + 2)(4n/b + 4) K_1/(T + 4n/b + 3)^2 (O(n^2/T^2), matching Katyusha); mu-strongly convex: with gamma = min{b^{3/2}/(4n sqrt(6 mu L)), b/(4 n mu)} and the momentum parameter tied to mu as in Theorem 6, E||z_T - x*||^2 <= (1 + min{b^{3/2} sqrt(mu)/(4n sqrt(6L)), b/(4n)})^{-T} K_2; with b = n^{2/3} this gives O(n^{2/3} sqrt(kappa) log(1/eps)) stochastic gradients, 'slightly worse than the results proven for Katyusha, which requires O(sqrt(n)) stochastic gradient evaluations per iteration to match the convergence rate of full-gradient methods'; Theorem 14 gives the SVRG analogue with b <= 32 p^2, p = n^{1/3}. Introduction: the anchor updates x_{k+1} = tau_1 z_k + tau_2 xtilde + (1 - tau_1 - tau_2) y_k 'attract the current iterate toward a safe point xtilde where we know the full gradient'; 'negative momentum is effectively a variance-reduction technique'; Catalyst's rates are a logarithmic factor worse than Katyusha's, RPDG matches Katyusha in the strongly convex case.
relevance: A2/A3 (key questions i-ii): quantifies what is lost without the reference-point term - acceleration in kappa is still possible (sqrt(kappa)), but the n-dependence degrades from sqrt(n) to n^{2/3} because the estimator's MSE must then be controlled by the step-size/mini-batch alone; explains why SAGA (no snapshot) is harder to accelerate directly (B1-type structural remark). A4: experiments (ridge lambda = 1/n, Lasso lambda = 1/sqrt(n)) compare accelerated SAGA/SVRG/SARAH/SARGE with Katyusha-type methods.

title: Variance Reduction via Accelerated Dual Averaging for Finite-Sum Optimization
authors: Chaobing Song, Yong Jiang, Yi Ma
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020), pp. 833-844 (pages per OpenAlex); arXiv:2006.10281
summary: VRADA combines the MiG-style two-point coupling with the snapshot (negative momentum) and accelerated dual averaging, with a single parameter setting and a unified 'generalized estimate sequence' analysis for general convex (sigma = 0) and strongly convex (sigma > 0) problems. It improves the n log n term to n log log n and matches lower bounds in both strongly convex regimes; experiments on a9a/covtype logistic regression with lambda in {0, 1e-8, 1e-4} compare SVRG, Katyusha, MiG and VRADA.
main_result: An O(1/n)-accurate solution in O(n log log n) stochastic gradient evaluations in both settings (improving O(n log n)); matches the general convex lower bound up to a log log n factor and the strongly convex lower bounds 'in both regimes n <= Theta(kappa) and n >> kappa'; strongly convex complexity O((n + sqrt(n kappa)) log(1/eps)) or O(n log log n + sqrt(n kappa) log(1/eps)); table lists Katyusha^sc as O(sqrt(n kappa) log(1/eps)) for n <= kappa and O(n log(1/eps)) for n >> kappa. Experiments: for lambda = 1e-8 (large kappa) VRADA beats Katyusha^sc and MiG^sc; for lambda = 1e-4 (small kappa) SVRG is 'competitive with VRADA, which partly verifies the theoretical results for SVRG [Hannah et al. 2018]'.
relevance: A3: shows the negative-momentum coupling is compatible with dual averaging and gives a fully unified Lyapunov analysis; A1/A4: the explicit two-regime discussion (n <= kappa vs n >> kappa) and the experimental observation that non-accelerated SVRG matches accelerated methods when kappa << n support the project's prediction that the kappa^{1/2} exponent is only visible for kappa >> n (iv).

title: ANITA: An Optimal Loopless Accelerated Variance-Reduced Gradient Method
authors: Zhize Li
venue: arXiv:2103.11333 (v1 March 2021, v3 September 2022); no journal/conference reference listed on arXiv
summary: A loopless accelerated SVRG-type method (coin-flip reference point like L-SVRG/L-Katyusha, but handling both mu = 0 and mu > 0) with a 'dynamic multi-stage' analysis. It is optimal in the strongly convex case (matching the Lan-Zhou lower bound) and is the first to reach O(n) complexity in the general convex large-scale regime n >= 1/eps^2 (matching the Omega(n) lower bound of Woodworth-Srebro), improving Varag's O(n log(1/eps)) and Katyusha's O(n/sqrt(eps)); experiments show faster convergence than Varag.
main_result: Theorem 2 (strongly convex): with p_t = p, theta_t = (1/2) min{1, sqrt(mu/(pL))}, eta_t <= 1/(L theta_t (1 + 1/(1 - theta_t))), alpha_t = 1 + mu eta_t, the potential Phi_t = f(w_t) - f* + ((1 + mu eta) p theta/(2 eta)) ||x_t - x*||^2 satisfies E[Phi_t] <= (1 - 4 p theta/5)^t Phi_0; with p = 1/n this gives O((n + sqrt(nL/mu)) log(1/eps)), matching the Lan-Zhou lower bound. Theorem 1 (general convex): two-phase parameters (p_t = 1/(n+1), theta_t = 1 - 1/(2 sqrt n) for t <= t_1, then p_t = max{4/(t - t_1 + 3 sqrt n), 4/(n+3)}, theta_t = 2/(p_t (t - t_1 + 3 sqrt n))) give E[f(w_t) - f*] <= 32||x_0 - x*||^2/(eta_{t-1} p_{t-1} (t - t_1 + 3 sqrt n)^2), yielding O(n) stochastic gradients when n >= 1/eps^2.
relevance: A3: a second loopless accelerated method with an explicit two-term potential (function value at the reference point + distance), whose contraction factor 1 - 4p theta/5 can be compared with L-Katyusha's min{sigma/(6 theta_1), theta_1/(2n)}; useful for the project's 'Lyapunov-style' reproduction and for choosing theta/p in experiments.

title: Dissipativity Theory for Accelerating Stochastic Variance Reduction: A Unified Analysis of SVRG and Katyusha Using Semidefinite Programs
authors: Bin Hu, Stephen Wright, Laurent Lessard
venue: ICML 2018, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 80:2038-2047; arXiv:1806.03677
summary: Casts SVRG and Katyusha as jump/stochastic linear systems and uses dissipativity theory from control (energy-conservation 'supply rates') so that convergence certificates - i.e. quadratic Lyapunov functions - are found by solving small semidefinite programs. The approach 'recovers existing convergence results for SVRG and Katyusha and generalizes the theory to alternative parameter choices', and is presented as complementary to Allen-Zhu's linear-coupling technique.
main_result: Existence of a feasible solution of a small LMI/SDP (built from supply-rate constraints encoding L-smoothness, mu-strong convexity and the SVRG variance bound) certifies linear convergence of the inner loop of SVRG / Katyusha with a given rate; solving the SDP numerically reproduces the published rates and gives rates for alternative (tau_1, tau_2, alpha) choices; new stochastic supply-rate conditions are introduced for the variance-reduced estimator.
relevance: B3/A3: provides a systematic way to see which inequalities (supply rates) are active in the certificate for SVRG versus Katyusha, i.e. exactly the per-inequality bottleneck analysis the project wants to do empirically ('tightness ratio' per inequality); also shows how the negative-momentum weight enters the feasibility of the Lyapunov SDP. B1: the LMI framework extends naturally to preconditioned updates. | A3 (central): the SDP-certified version of the Katyusha/negative-momentum Lyapunov proof; the project's reproduction of the loopless Katyusha proof can be checked line by line against the LMI (each supply rate = one inequality of the chain, each multiplier = its weight). A2: shows the variance of the SVRG estimator is absorbed only when the storage function couples z_k with the reference point. B3: the LMI exposes which inequality limits the rate.

title: First-order and Stochastic Optimization Methods for Machine Learning
authors: Guanghui Lan
venue: Springer Series in the Data Sciences, Springer (DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-39568-1); Chapter 5 'Convex Finite-Sum and Distributed Optimization', pp. 221-303 (DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-39568-1_5)
summary: Graduate textbook. Chapter 5 is devoted to convex finite-sum and distributed optimization and (per its title and the author's underlying papers) presents the randomized primal-dual gradient method RPDG with its game-theoretic derivation, the lower complexity bound Omega((m + sqrt(mL/mu)) log(1/eps)) for randomized incremental gradient methods, random gradient extrapolation (RGEM) and variance-reduced accelerated methods, with complete proofs. (Only bibliographic data verified via Crossref: book, chapter title and page range; chapter content not opened.)
main_result: Textbook statements of: optimal deterministic/randomized first-order complexity for finite sums; RPDG upper bound O((m + sqrt(mL/mu)) log(1/eps)); the matching lower bound for randomized incremental gradient methods; RGEM without full gradients. Other chapters cover Nesterov's accelerated method via the game interpretation (Ch. 3) and stochastic convex optimization (Ch. 4).
relevance: A1/A3: a single self-contained source with the lower bound and a direct accelerated method proved in the same notation, useful to write the project's optimality statement; complements Bach's notes (which stop at SAGA's non-accelerated rate) at textbook level.

title: On the Ineffectiveness of Variance Reduced Optimization for Deep Learning
authors: Aaron Defazio, Leon Bottou
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (NeurIPS 2019); arXiv:1812.04529 (page range not confirmed: OpenAlex lists 1753-1763)
summary: Empirical study asking whether SVRG-type variance reduction helps train modern deep networks: it does not ('naive application of the SVRG technique and related approaches fail, and explore why'). Data augmentation, batch normalization and dropout break the finite-sum structure; measurements on CNNs show the variance reduction actually obtained is small for deep architectures; streaming SVRG variants do not improve on plain SVRG despite handling augmentation in theory.
main_result: Naive application of SVRG and related approaches fails for deep learning; quantified properties of the network (depth/architecture) determine the achievable variance reduction ratio, which becomes negligible for modern CNNs; streaming SVRG offers no gain; code released.
relevance: Scope/limits for the whole project (A4, B2, B3): explains why the project's instrumented study of the proof is done on convex l2-logistic regression, where the finite-sum assumptions of Bach's Prop. 5.9 hold; also a cautionary example that 'variance reduction in theory' does not translate automatically into practice - the same theory-practice gap the B2/B3 diagnostics target, here in the non-convex case.

title: On the insufficiency of existing momentum schemes for Stochastic Optimization
authors: Rahul Kidambi, Praneeth Netrapalli, Prateek Jain, Sham M. Kakade
venue: ICLR 2018 (oral; per the arXiv author comment); a workshop version appeared at the Information Theory and Applications Workshop (ITA) 2018, DOI 10.1109/ITA.2018.8503173; arXiv:1803.05591
summary: Shows that heavy-ball and Nesterov momentum applied to plain stochastic gradients need not accelerate: in the stochastic first-order oracle model there are 'simple problem instances' (linear regression) 'where these methods cannot outperform SGD despite the best setting of its parameters', and these instances are generic rather than pathological; empirically the same holds for NAG; 'HB or NAG's practical performance gains are a by-product of mini-batching'. Proposes ASGD, a different accelerated stochastic scheme that provably improves on HB, NAG and SGD on these instances.
main_result: Theorem (Sec. 3): heavy ball is not optimal in the stochastic first-order oracle model - there exist linear regression instances where its performance (any step size, any momentum) equals or is worse than SGD, while ASGD improves on both; experiments show the suboptimality of HB and NAG is widespread; stated take-home message: 'the only reason for the superiority of momentum methods in practice is mini-batching, which reduces the variance in stochastic gradients'.
relevance: A2 (key question i): the 'counterexamples' Allen-Zhu alludes to for momentum with stochastic gradients; supports the project's hypothesis that momentum amplifies estimator noise unless the noise is controlled (variance reduction + negative momentum) or averaged (mini-batch, as in Nitanda's Acc-Prox-SVRG).

title: First-order methods of smooth convex optimization with inexact oracle
authors: Olivier Devolder, Francois Glineur, Yurii Nesterov
venue: Mathematical Programming 146(1-2):37-75 (DOI 10.1007/s10107-013-0677-5); preprint CORE Discussion Paper 2011/02 / Optimization Online 2010
summary: Introduces the (delta, L)-inexact first-order oracle (covering smoothing, Moreau-Yosida regularization, augmented Lagrangians, inexact subproblem solutions) and analyses the primal, dual and fast gradient methods under it. Central finding (abstract): 'the superiority of fast gradient methods over the classical ones is no longer absolute when an inexact oracle is used. We prove that, contrary to simple gradient schemes, fast gradient methods must necessarily suffer from error accumulation'; the right method depends on the target accuracy and the oracle accuracy; intermediate methods trade off speed and error sensitivity.
main_result: For a (delta, L)-oracle, the primal gradient method reaches f(x_k) - f* <= O(L R^2/k) + delta (Theorem 2 / Sec. 4: 'there is no error accumulation'), while the fast gradient method reaches O(L R^2/k^2) + O(k delta) (Sec. 5.2 'Error accumulation': 'while the first term in (42) decreases as O(1/k^2), the second term is increasing in k, and this FGM used with an inexact oracle is asymptotically divergent'); Sec. 8.3 (Theorems 6-7) proves that error accumulation and divergence are unavoidable for all fast first-order methods: a method with rate O(LR^2/k^p) must accumulate the oracle error at a rate growing with p.
relevance: A2 (root cause for key question i): a stochastic variance-reduced gradient is an inexact oracle whose error delta is proportional to the variance; Nesterov momentum accumulates this error linearly in k, which is exactly the term that cannot be absorbed when one plugs the SVRG estimator into Nesterov's algorithm; negative momentum (A3) acts by keeping delta small (iterates close to the reference point where the estimator is accurate).

title: L-SVRG and L-Katyusha with Arbitrary Sampling
authors: Xun Qian, Zheng Qu, Peter Richtarik
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 22(112):1-47; arXiv:1906.01481
summary: Generalizes L-SVRG and L-Katyusha to arbitrary (mini-batch, importance) sampling via an 'expected smoothness' assumption that bounds the variance of the stochastic gradient estimator by a constant times a Bregman-type distance; recovers the uniform-sampling results, gives nonconvex and general convex variants, and designs importance samplings with linear speed-up in the expected mini-batch size over a range; also connects expected smoothness to ESO to exploit sparsity.
main_result: Theorem 3.2 (arXiv v1 numbering; L-Katyusha under expected smoothness constant L_2, f mu-strongly convex, L_f-smooth), Lyapunov Psi^k = Z^k + Y^k + W^k with Z^k = L(1 + eta sigma)/(2 eta)||z^k - x*||^2, Y^k = (1/theta_1)(P(y^k) - P(x*)), W^k = theta_2/(p q theta_1)(P(w^k) - P(x*)), 0 < q < 1: E_k[Z^{k+1} + Y^{k+1} + W^{k+1}] <= Z^k/(1 + eta sigma) + (1 - (theta_1 + theta_2 - theta_2/q)) Y^k + (1 - p(1 - q)) W^k, and for some q in [2/3, 1), E[Psi^k] <= eps Psi^0 after O((1/p + sqrt(L_f/mu) + sqrt(L_2/(mu p))) log(1/eps)) iterations; with p = 1/n and uniform single-element sampling (L_2 ~ L_max) this is O((n + sqrt(n L_max/mu)) log(1/eps)). Remark 1: Katyusha's proof extends to arbitrary sampling by replacing Lbar/b by L_2.
relevance: A3: the same Lyapunov Psi = Z + Y + W as L-Katyusha with the variance bound abstracted into a single 'expected smoothness' inequality - the cleanest statement of which inequality carries the sampling/variance information in the accelerated proof (B3 instrumentation). B1/B3: importance sampling and mini-batching change only L_2, suggesting how anisotropy of the feature covariance enters the constants.

title: Accelerated Stochastic Gradient Descent for Minimizing Finite Sums
authors: Atsushi Nitanda
venue: AISTATS 2016, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 51:195-203; arXiv:1506.03016 (June 2015)
summary: AMSVRG: combines the linear-coupling accelerated gradient method of Allen-Zhu and Orecchia with SVRG in a mini-batch setting 'like Acc-Prox-SVRG', applicable to non-strongly and strongly convex problems. Its introduction and Table 1 restate the complexity of Acc-Prox-SVRG (Nitanda 2014) in closed form and tabulate it against AGD, SAG, SVRG and SAGA.
main_result: Theorem 3 (strongly convex): overall complexity O((n + n kappa/(n + sqrt(kappa))) log(1/eps)), 'the same as that of Acc-Prox-SVRG', where n kappa/(n + sqrt(kappa)) = (1/2) H(kappa, n sqrt(kappa)) is half the harmonic mean of the SVRG term kappa and the accelerated-full-gradient term n sqrt(kappa), 'whose order is the same as min{kappa, n sqrt(kappa)}' (so the method behaves like SVRG unless sqrt(kappa) > n); non-strongly convex (Theorems 1-2): O~(n + min{L/eps, n sqrt(L/eps)}). Each stage uses growing mini-batches b_{k+1} chosen so that the variance term stays below a constant.
relevance: A2: closed-form evidence that naive Nesterov + SVRG with mini-batches yields only n + min{kappa, n sqrt(kappa)} - acceleration appears only when kappa > n^2 - i.e. the variance has to be beaten down by the mini-batch size (b grows with the momentum), not absorbed by the analysis; contrasts with Katyusha's n + sqrt(n kappa) for b = 1 (A3).

title: Linear Coupling: An Ultimate Unification of Gradient and Mirror Descent
authors: Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Lorenzo Orecchia
venue: 8th Innovations in Theoretical Computer Science Conference (ITCS 2017), LIPIcs vol. 67, pp. 3:1-3:22 (DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2017.3); arXiv:1407.1537 (2014)
summary: Reinterprets Nesterov's accelerated gradient method as a linear coupling of a gradient-descent step (primal progress, good when the gradient is large) and a mirror-descent step (dual progress, good when the gradient is small): the next query point is a convex combination x_{k+1} = tau z_k + (1 - tau) y_k of the mirror iterate z and the gradient iterate y. This gives 'a cleaner interpretation than Nesterov's original proofs' and is the analysis framework of Katyusha (y = gradient step, z = mirror step, plus the snapshot term) and of MiG/VRADA.
main_result: Theorem 4.1: if f is L-smooth w.r.t. a norm and w is 1-strongly convex w.r.t. the same norm, AGM (x_{k+1} = tau_k z_k + (1 - tau_k) y_k; y_{k+1} = Grad(x_{k+1}) gradient step; z_{k+1} = Mirr_{z_k}(alpha_{k+1} grad f(x_{k+1})) mirror step, with alpha_{k+1} = (k+2)/(2L) and tau_k = 1/(alpha_{k+1} L)) outputs y_T with f(y_T) - f(x*) <= 4 L Theta/T^2, Theta any upper bound on the Bregman distance V_{x_0}(x*); the strongly convex case follows by restarting, giving O(sqrt(L/sigma) log(1/eps)); the one-step 'coupling lemma' bounds alpha <grad f(x_{k+1}), z_k - u> by the mirror-step progress plus alpha^2 L (f(x_{k+1}) - f(y_{k+1})).
relevance: A3: the project's reproduction of the L-Katyusha proof is a linear-coupling argument - the Lyapunov terms Z^k (mirror/distance), Y^k (gradient-step function value) and W^k (snapshot) of Kovalev et al. correspond to the z, y and xtilde sequences of this framework; the coupling lemma is the step in which the variance term -(theta_2/(2L theta_1))||g - grad f||^2 appears. A2: explains why plain Nesterov momentum (tau_2 = 0) is the special case without the magnet.

title: Convergence Rates of Inexact Proximal-Gradient Methods for Convex Optimization
authors: Mark Schmidt, Nicolas Le Roux, Francis Bach
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 24 (NeurIPS 2011), pp. 1458-1466 (pages per OpenAlex); arXiv:1109.2415
summary: Analyses the basic and the accelerated proximal-gradient methods when the gradient of the smooth term is computed with an error e_k and/or the proximity operator is computed inexactly (error eps_k). Both methods keep their error-free rates O(1/k) and O(1/k^2) provided the errors decrease at appropriate rates - but the accelerated method needs the errors to decrease faster, because its bound weights the error at iteration i by i: this is the discrete mechanism by which momentum accumulates gradient errors.
main_result: Proposition 1 (basic method, convex): f(x_k) - f* <= (L/(2k)) (||x_0 - x*|| + 2 A_k + sqrt(2 B_k))^2 with A_k = sum_{i<=k} (||e_i||/L + sqrt(2 eps_i/L)), B_k = sum_{i<=k} eps_i/L, so summable errors (e.g. decreasing as O(1/k^{1+delta})) preserve the O(1/k) rate. Proposition 2 (accelerated method, beta_k = (k-1)/(k+2)): f(x_k) - f* <= (2L/(k+1)^2) (||x_0 - x*|| + 2 Atilde_k + sqrt(2 Btilde_k))^2 with Atilde_k = sum_{i<=k} i (||e_i||/L + sqrt(2 eps_i/L)), Btilde_k = sum_{i<=k} i^2 eps_i/L: the series {k ||e_k||} and {k sqrt(eps_k)} must be summable (errors decreasing as O(1/k^{2+delta})) to keep the O(1/k^2) rate, 'an (unsurprisingly) stronger constraint than in the basic case'. Proposition 3 (strongly convex, basic method): ||x_k - x*|| <= (1 - gamma)^k (||x_0 - x*|| + Abar_k) with Abar_k = sum (1 - gamma)^{-i} (||e_i||/L + sqrt(2 eps_i/L)), gamma = mu/L.
relevance: A2 (key question i, in Bach's own line of work): with a stochastic variance-reduced estimator the gradient error does not vanish fast enough, and Proposition 2 shows that the accelerated method then accumulates it with weight k (while the basic method only needs summability) - the elementary reason why plugging the SVRG estimator into Nesterov's algorithm does not accelerate unless the variance is forced down by mini-batches (Nitanda) or by an anchor that ties the error to the suboptimality (A3). Also the template for the deterministic error-accumulation statement of Devolder-Glineur-Nesterov.

title: Statistically Preconditioned Accelerated Gradient Method for Distributed Optimization
authors: Hadrien Hendrikx, Lin Xiao, Sebastien Bubeck, Francis Bach, Laurent Massoulie
venue: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2020), PMLR 119:4203-4227
summary: Distributed ERM where a server holds n subsampled points and uses the local loss phi(x) = f_1(x) + (mu_tilde/2)||x||^2 as a Bregman reference (statistical preconditioner), as in DANE. SPAG is a Nesterov-type accelerated Bregman method whose rate depends on the square root of the relative condition number kappa_{F/phi} between the global loss F and phi. The paper also derives sharp matrix-concentration bounds on kappa_{F/phi} for linear prediction models (logistic/ridge) via uniform Hessian concentration.
main_result: Definition 1: F is L_{F/phi}-smooth and sigma_{F/phi}-strongly convex relative to phi if sigma_{F/phi} grad^2 phi(x) <= grad^2 F(x) <= L_{F/phi} grad^2 phi(x) for all x; relative condition number kappa_{F/phi} = L_{F/phi}/sigma_{F/phi}, and with phi = f_1 + (mu_tilde/2)||.||^2 one has kappa_{F/phi} = 1 + 2 mu_tilde/sigma_F whenever ||grad^2 F - grad^2 f_1|| <= mu_tilde (Section 4). Theorem 1 (SPAG, Assumption 1: F is L_F-smooth, sigma_F-strongly convex, relatively smooth/strongly convex w.r.t. phi, phi itself L_phi-smooth and sigma_phi-strongly convex): (1/A_t)(Phi(x_t) - Phi(x*)) + sigma_{F/phi} D_phi(x*, v_t) <= (1/A_t) D_phi(x*, v_0) with A_t = (1/(4 kappa_{F/phi})) (prod_{tau<t}(1+alpha_tau) - prod_{tau<t}(1-alpha_tau))^2 and alpha_t = 1/(2 sqrt(kappa_{F/phi} G_t)); the gain G_t <= kappa_phi = L_phi/sigma_phi always (Lemma 1), equals 1 for quadratic phi, and converges to 1 geometrically when grad^2 phi is M-Lipschitz (Lemma 2: G_t = min{kappa_phi, 1 + (M/sigma_phi) d_t} with d_t a sum of iterate distances), giving the accelerated rate (1 - 1/sqrt(kappa_{F/phi}))^t up to constants, i.e. O(sqrt(kappa_{F/phi}) log(1/eps)) communication rounds versus O(kappa_{F/phi} log(1/eps)) for non-accelerated preconditioned gradient (DANE-type) methods. Each iteration solves at the server a local problem of the form min_x eta_t <grad F(y_t), x> + psi(x) + (1-beta_t) D_phi(x, v_t) + beta_t D_phi(x, y_t), a finite sum over the n local samples (no communication); the gain-search at most doubles the number of gradient evaluations. Section 4 (linear models with |l_i''| <= 1, ||a_i|| <= R): Theorem 2 (quadratic losses) improves the Hoeffding-type bound mu_tilde = O(R^2/sqrt(n)) by a factor sqrt(n); Theorem 3 removes the dimension dependence for non-quadratic losses via uniform concentration: with probability 1-delta, mu_tilde = 4 (R^2/sqrt(n)) (B sqrt(2) + sqrt(log(1/delta)/2) + R M D) with D the domain radius, i.e. kappa_{F/phi} = 1 + O((R^2/(sigma_F sqrt(n))) (B + sqrt(log(1/delta)) + R M D)); Theorem 4 gives a refined bound for sub-Gaussian inputs.
relevance: B1 (central): gives the exact meaning of 'condition number in the P-metric' (relative smoothness/strong convexity sigma_{F/phi}, L_{F/phi}) that replaces R^2 and mu in Bach's Prop. 5.9 when theta_t = theta_{t-1} - gamma P^{-1} g_t with P = grad^2 phi; shows which proof steps become loose: the Euclidean cocoercivity and strong-convexity inequalities must be rewritten in the P^{-1}/P norms, and the Lyapunov function V_t must use ||theta_t - eta*||_P^2 (= D_phi for quadratic phi). A1/A3: an accelerated Bregman (Nesterov-Stich) scheme with sqrt(kappa) dependence, written in the same Lyapunov style as the project's L-Katyusha proof. B2: kappa_{F/phi} is a data-dependent 'effective' condition number (1 + O(R^2/(mu sqrt(n)))) that can be computed on the project's logistic-regression instances and compared to the trajectory-dependent mu_eff(t). B3/pipeline: the Hessian-concentration bounds explain how the anisotropy of feature covariance enters the preconditioned rate.

title: Relatively Smooth Convex Optimization by First-Order Methods, and Applications
authors: Haihao Lu, Robert M. Freund, Yurii Nesterov
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization 28(1):333-354 (arXiv 1610.05708, Oct. 2016, under the title 'Relatively-Smooth Convex Optimization by First-Order Methods, and Applications')
summary: Introduces relative smoothness and relative strong convexity of f with respect to a reference function h (no norm involved), and analyses the primal gradient scheme x_{k+1} = argmin <grad f(x_k), x> + L D_h(x, x_k) and a dual averaging scheme. Gives O(L D_h(x*,x_0)/k) sublinear and (1 - mu/L)^k linear rates, plus applications (D-optimal design, Poisson inverse problems) where the usual Lipschitz-gradient assumption fails.
main_result: Definition 1.1: f is L-smooth relative to h on Q if f(y) <= f(x) + <grad f(x), y - x> + L D_h(y, x) for all x, y in int Q; Definition 1.2: f is mu-strongly convex relative to h if f(y) >= f(x) + <grad f(x), y - x> + mu D_h(y, x). Proposition 1.1: equivalent characterisations, in particular (for twice differentiable f, h) mu grad^2 h(x) <= grad^2 f(x) <= L grad^2 h(x); Proposition 1.2: closure under sums and under composition with linear maps. Theorem 3.1 (Primal Gradient Scheme, Algorithm 1): if f is L-smooth and mu-strongly convex relative to h then {f(x_k)} is monotonically decreasing and f(x_k) - f(x) <= mu D_h(x, x_0) / ((1 + mu/(L - mu))^k - 1) <= (L/k) D_h(x, x_0) for all x in Q (eq. (26)); for mu > 0 the first bound gives linear convergence at rate (1 - mu/L)^k (eq. (27)), and for mu = 0 the middle term is understood as the limit mu -> 0+. Theorem 3.2 gives the analogous bound for the Dual Averaging Scheme (Algorithm 2). When h(x) = (1/2) x^T P x the scheme is exactly preconditioned gradient descent x_{k+1} = x_k - (1/L_P) P^{-1} grad f(x_k), the relative constants L_P, mu_P are the extreme eigenvalues of P^{-1/2} grad^2 f P^{-1/2}, and the per-iteration cost is one solve with P (O(d^2) dense, O(d) diagonal, or a Cholesky back-solve).
relevance: B1: provides the definitions (relative L_P, mu_P) that the project needs to restate Bach's assumptions 'each f_i is R^2-smooth' and 'F is mu-strongly convex' in the P-metric, and the identity mu_P grad^2 h <= grad^2 f <= L_P grad^2 h which makes the Euclidean proof of Prop. 5.9 go through verbatim after the change of variables theta -> P^{1/2} theta. Pins down which steps become loose: the constants R^2 and mu are replaced by L_P = lambda_max(P^{-1/2} grad^2 f_i P^{-1/2}) (worst over i) and mu_P, while the dimension-free steps (square-norm inequality, variance <= second moment) are unchanged. B2: the relative constants are natural 'effective curvature' quantities to measure along the trajectory.

title: A Descent Lemma Beyond Lipschitz Gradient Continuity: First-Order Methods Revisited and Applications
authors: Heinz H. Bauschke, Jerome Bolte, Marc Teboulle
venue: Mathematics of Operations Research 42(2):330-348
summary: Replaces the Lipschitz-gradient descent lemma by the 'Lipschitz-like/convexity condition' (LC): L h - g convex on int dom h, relative to a Legendre reference function h, which yields the Bregman descent lemma g(x) <= g(y) + <grad g(y), x - y> + L D_h(x, y). The resulting NoLips (Bregman proximal gradient) method has a global O(1/k) rate without any Lipschitz-gradient assumption; applications include Poisson inverse problems and barrier-type references.
main_result: Lemma 1 (descent lemma without Lipschitz gradient continuity): for a Legendre function h and a convex g differentiable on int dom h, (LC) 'L h - g convex on int dom h' is equivalent to g(x) <= g(y) + <grad g(y), x - y> + L D_h(x, y) for all x, y in int dom h (eq. (6)). NoLips: x_{k+1} = argmin_x { f(x) + <grad g(x_k), x> + (1/lambda_k) D_h(x, x_k) }. Theorem 1: with lambda_k = (1 + alpha)/(2L), where alpha = alpha(h) in [0, 1] is the symmetry coefficient of D_h (eq. (8); alpha = 1 iff h is a nondegenerate convex quadratic), the sequence satisfies (i) monotonicity of Psi(x_k) = f(x_k) + g(x_k), (ii) sum_k D_h(x_k, x_{k-1}) < infinity, (iii) convergence of function values, and (iv) the global estimate Psi(x_k) - Psi(u) <= 2L D_h(u, x_0) / ((1 + alpha) k) for all u in dom h; for a quadratic reference h = (1/2)||.||_P^2 (alpha = 1) this is the classical L_P D_h(u, x_0)/k bound of preconditioned proximal gradient with step 1/L_P, each step costing one solve with P. (Statement checked on the authors' accepted manuscript, cmps-people.ok.ubc.ca/bauschke/Research/103.pdf; venue, authors and year confirmed through Crossref; the paper is not on arXiv.)
relevance: B1: the Bregman descent lemma is exactly the 'smoothness upper bound' used in Bach's chapter (f(theta') <= f(theta) + <f'(theta), theta' - theta> + (R^2/2)||theta' - theta||^2) rewritten in the P-metric, i.e. with the constant L_P = sup ||grad^2 f_i||_{P^{-1}-operator norm}; this is the step of the SAGA proof whose constant changes under preconditioning. Together with Lu-Freund-Nesterov it is the standard citation for 'relative smoothness' used by Dragomir-Even-Hendrikx and Hendrikx et al.; the symmetry coefficient alpha(h) quantifies what is lost when the metric is not quadratic.

title: Fast Stochastic Bregman Gradient Methods: Sharp Analysis and Variance Reduction
authors: Radu-Alexandru Dragomir, Mathieu Even, Hadrien Hendrikx
venue: Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2021), PMLR 139:2815-2825
summary: Analyses Bregman SGD for relatively smooth finite sums and proposes Bregman-SAGA, the first variance-reduced method in the relative-smoothness setting. Bregman SGD converges only to a noise-dependent region (exactly under interpolation), while Bregman-SAGA converges linearly to the minimizer at a rate governed by the relative condition number, provided the reference function has enough regularity (a 'gain function' compensating the lack of translation invariance of Bregman divergences). Applications: Poisson tomographic reconstruction and statistical preconditioning for distributed optimization.
main_result: Definition: f is L_{f/h}-relatively smooth and mu_{f/h}-relatively strongly convex w.r.t. h if mu_{f/h} D_h(x,y) <= D_f(x,y) <= L_{f/h} D_h(x,y). Theorem 1 (Bregman SGD, step eta <= 1/(2 L_{f/h}), Assumptions 1-2): E[D_h(x*, x_t)] <= (1 - eta mu_{f/h})^t D_h(x*, x_0) + a noise term of order eta sigma^2/mu_{f/h}, where sigma^2 is the 'relative noise at the optimum' (Assumption 2), so exact convergence iff sigma^2 = 0 (interpolation); Theorem 2: convex case. Section 4, Algorithm 1 (Bregman-SAGA: memory phi_i, g_t = grad f_i(x_t) - grad f_i(phi_i) + (1/n) sum_j grad f_j(phi_j), mirror step with step eta_t); Assumption 3: each f_i is L_{f/h}-relatively smooth, f is mu_{f/h}-relatively strongly convex, and there is a gain function G with D_h(x + v, x) <= G(x,y,v)^2 D_h(y + v, y). Theorem 4: with eta_t = 1/(8 L_{f/h} G_t) and a suitable decreasing G_t, the potential Psi_t = (1/eta_t) D_h(x*, x_t) + 2 H_t (H_t = (1/n) sum_i D_{f_i}(phi_i^t, x*), eq. (16)) satisfies E[Psi_{t+1}] <= (1 - min{eta_t mu_{f/h}, 1/(2n)}) Psi_t (eq. (18)). Corollary 1 (quadratic h, i.e. fixed P-metric, G = 1): E[Psi_t] <= (1 - min{1/(8 kappa_{f/h}), 1/(2n)})^t Psi_0 with kappa_{f/h} = L_{f/h}/mu_{f/h} the relative condition number (eq. (22)). Corollary 2 (h mu_h-strongly convex (equivalently mu_h^{-1}-smooth conjugate) and f L_f-smooth in a norm, constant step eta = mu_h/(8 L_f)): E[Psi_t] <= (1 - min{mu_h mu_{f/h}/(8 L_f), 1/(2n)})^t Psi_0 (eq. (23)), i.e. the rate degrades by the conditioning of h. Proposition 1 / Corollary 3: if h is L_h-smooth with M-Lipschitz Hessian, G(x,y,v) = 1 + 2 M L_h (||y - x|| + ||v||) gives an explicit computable G_t. Cost per step: one mirror step (grad h)^{-1}(grad h(x_t) - eta g_t), i.e. one solve with P for quadratic h, plus O(d) memory update.
relevance: B1 (the key reference): Corollary 1 is literally 'SAGA with a fixed SPD metric P': step 1/(8 L_P) P^{-1}, rate 1 - min{1/(2n), 1/(8 kappa_P)}, to be compared term by term with Bach's Prop. 5.9 (gamma = 1/(4R^2), rate 1 - min{1/(3n), 3 mu/(16 R^2)}, Lyapunov V_t = ||theta_t - eta*||^2 + 3 gamma^2 sum_i ||z_i - f_i'(eta*)||^2). The project can reproduce this corollary in Bach's style by replacing the Euclidean cocoercivity with the P^{-1}-norm cocoercivity implied by relative smoothness and strong convexity with its relative version; the paper also explains (Assumption 3 and the gain function) exactly which inequality breaks for non-quadratic metrics: the square-norm and 'variance <= second moment' steps rely on translation invariance of ||.||^2, which fails for general D_h. A3: the same Bregman-SAGA analysis is the natural starting point for a preconditioned L-Katyusha. B2/B3: the gain function G_t is a trajectory-dependent quantity analogous to mu_eff(t).

title: Solving Ridge Regression using Sketched Preconditioned SVRG
authors: Alon Gonen, Francesco Orabona, Shai Shalev-Shwartz
venue: Proceedings of the 33rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2016), PMLR 48:1397-1405
summary: Ridge regression L(w) = (1/n) sum_i (1/2)(<x_i, w> - y_i)^2 + (lambda/2)||w||^2 in the large n, large d regime. The preconditioned problem L_tilde(w_tilde) = L(P^{-1/2} w_tilde) is solved by prox-SVRG with non-uniform (smoothness-proportional) sampling, whose cost depends on the average condition number, where P^{-1/2} is a sketched preconditioner built from a rank-k randomized block Lanczos approximation of the covariance C in O(ndk log n) time. The analysis translates per-vector Lanczos guarantees into a bound on the average condition number after preconditioning.
main_result: Average condition number kappa_hat = tr(C + lambda I)/lambda_min(C + lambda I) governs the SVRG variant with non-uniform sampling of Xiao-Zhang (recalled as Theorem 2, ref. [21]): runtime O((kappa_hat + n) d log(1/eps)); with uniform sampling the constant would be the maximal smoothness max_i ||P^{-1/2} x_i||^2 instead of the average (discussion after Theorem 2 and Theorem 4). The optimal preconditioner P = C + lambda I makes the average condition number equal to d (but is as expensive as solving the problem). Theorem 4: the average condition number of L_tilde is bounded by tr(P^{-1/2}(C + lambda I)P^{-1/2}) / lambda_min(P^{-1/2}(C + lambda I)P^{-1/2}), with the O(d) bound attained by the whitening matrix. Theorem 1 (main result, sketched preconditioner, assuming lambda >= lambda_d): preprocessing O(ndk log n) (Theorem 3 = block Lanczos guarantee of ref. [8]); then preconditioned SVRG finds an eps-approximate minimizer with probability >= 9/10 in additional time O((kappa_tilde + n + d) d log(1/eps)) with kappa_tilde = (k lambda_k + sum_{i>k} lambda_i)/lambda (or sqrt(n (k lambda_k + sum_{i>k} lambda_i)/lambda) with accelerated SVRG), where lambda_i are the eigenvalues of C (Lemma 1 for the exact truncated-SVD preconditioner, extended to the sketch in Section 5.3); versus kappa_hat = (sum_i lambda_i + lambda d)/lambda without preconditioning, the speed-up ratio is ~ sum_i lambda_i / (k lambda_k + sum_{i>k} lambda_i), large under fast spectral decay. Per-iteration cost after preprocessing is O(d) (the preconditioner is folded into the data P^{-1/2} x_i). (The paper has Theorems 1-4 and Lemmas 1-4; there is no 'Theorem 5'.)
relevance: B1 (quadratic case): the cleanest statement that preconditioning a VR method is equivalent to running it on P^{-1/2}-transformed data, with the smoothness constants R_i^2 = ||P^{-1/2} x_i||^2 in Bach's Prop. 5.9 replaced by (preconditioned) leverage-type quantities; with P = C + lambda I the average condition number is d and the max-type constant is n * max_i (ridge leverage score), which is the 'leverage scores / coherence as condition number after preconditioning' statement the project asks for. A4/B3: suggests the experiment of comparing SAGA on raw vs. whitened features on the project's anisotropic logistic/ridge instances (the kappa^1 exponent should collapse to the effective dimension). A1: the lower bound's n + sqrt(n kappa) scaling applies to the preconditioned problem with kappa replaced by kappa_tilde.

title: A Linearly-Convergent Stochastic L-BFGS Algorithm
authors: Philipp Moritz, Robert Nishihara, Michael I. Jordan
venue: Proceedings of the 19th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2016), PMLR 51:249-258
summary: SLBFGS combines the SVRG variance-reduced gradient with an L-BFGS inverse-Hessian approximation H_r built from subsampled Hessian-vector products (memory M, Hessian batch b_H, refreshed every L steps), updating x_{t+1} = x_t - eta H_r v_t. It is the first stochastic quasi-Newton method with a proven linear rate for strongly convex finite sums; experiments on ridge regression, SVM and matrix completion.
main_result: Assumptions 1-2: lambda I <= grad^2 f_i (subsampled Hessians) <= Lambda I. Lemma 4: the L-BFGS matrices satisfy gamma I <= H_r <= Gamma I with gamma = 1/((d + M) Lambda) and Gamma = ((d + M) Lambda)^{d+M-1} / lambda^{d+M} (exponential in d + M, i.e. extremely loose). Theorem 7: E[f(w_k) - f(w*)] <= alpha^k E[f(w_0) - f(w*)] with alpha = (1/(2 m eta) + eta Gamma^2 Lambda^2) / (gamma lambda - eta Gamma^2 Lambda^2) < 1, provided eta < gamma lambda/(2 Gamma^2 Lambda^2) and m is large enough (condition (8)). The proof only uses the metric through the bounds gamma, Gamma (the variance bound Lemma 6, E||v_t||^2 <= 4 Lambda (f(x_t) - f* + f(w_k) - f*), is Euclidean); the authors note in the discussion that such proofs bound how far the quasi-Newton metric deviates from the identity and therefore give constants that scale poorly. Cost per iteration: O(d(b + M)) for the two-loop recursion plus O(b_H d) Hessian-vector products every L iterations (experiments: b = 20-100, b_H = 10b-20b, L = 10, M = 10, m = N/b).
relevance: B1: shows what happens to the SAGA/SVRG proof when the metric P^{-1} = H_r is only known through gamma I <= H_r <= Gamma I: the rate degrades to the Euclidean rate times gamma/Gamma-type factors, because the proof keeps the Euclidean smoothness/variance inequalities instead of the P-metric ones (this is precisely the 'loose step' the project should identify: the proof does not exploit that H_r approximates the Hessian). B2/B3: motivates measuring the actual spectrum of P^{1/2} grad^2 F P^{1/2} along the trajectory rather than the worst-case bounds. A4: a natural baseline for the empirical-exponent experiments.

title: Stochastic Block BFGS: Squeezing More Curvature out of Data
authors: Robert M. Gower, Donald Goldfarb, Peter Richtarik
venue: Proceedings of the 33rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2016), PMLR 48:1869-1878
summary: Replaces the rank-two BFGS update by a block update that forces the metric H_t to satisfy a sketched inverse-Hessian equation H_t grad^2 f_T(x_t) D_t = D_t for a d x q sketch D_t (q Hessian-vector products on a subsample T), with limited memory M and a factored form. Combined with the SVRG gradient estimator it gives a linearly convergent stochastic quasi-Newton method; experiments on l2-regularized logistic regression on a9a, w8a, gisette, covtype, HIGGS, SUSY, epsilon, rcv1, url.
main_result: Assumption 1: lambda I <= grad^2 f_T(x) <= Lambda I for all subsets T. Lemma 1: the limited-memory block BFGS matrices satisfy gamma I <= H_t <= Gamma I for explicit constants. Theorem 1 (Algorithm 1 with g_t = grad f_{S_t}(x_t) - grad f_{S_t}(w_k) + grad f(w_k), x_{t+1} = x_t - eta H_t g_t, Option II): E[f(w_k) - f(w*)] <= rho^k E[f(w_0) - f(w*)] with rho = (1/(2 m eta) + 2 eta Gamma^2 Lambda (Lambda - lambda)) / (gamma lambda - 2 eta Gamma^2 Lambda^2) < 1 for eta < gamma lambda/(2 Gamma^2 Lambda^2) and m large enough. Cost: the block update costs M q (4d + 2q) flops (q << d, e.g. q ~ sqrt(d) gives O(d^{3/2})), plus O(q^2 d) for D_t^T Y_t and O(q^3) for its Cholesky factor; the sketch requires q Hessian-vector products per iteration on the Hessian batch.
relevance: B1: same message as Moritz et al. but with a richer metric (block sketch of the Hessian): the proof still only exploits gamma I <= H <= Gamma I, so the theoretical rate is governed by (gamma/Gamma) kappa rather than by the relative condition number; the comparison between the two is exactly what B1's 'which steps become loose' question asks. The 'sketch-and-project' viewpoint (metric satisfying a sketched secant equation) is also the natural way to build a cheap fixed P for the project's experiments. B3: provides a large set of logistic-regression benchmarks on which to instrument the inequalities.

title: SVRG meets AdaGrad: Painless Variance Reduction
authors: Benjamin Dubois-Taine, Sharan Vaswani, Reza Babanezhad, Mark Schmidt, Simon Lacoste-Julien
venue: Machine Learning 111(12):4359-4409 (Springer, Dec. 2022); arXiv 2102.09645 (Feb. 2021)
summary: AdaSVRG runs an SVRG outer loop with an AdaGrad inner loop (scalar, diagonal, or full-matrix adaptive metric), so no knowledge of the smoothness constant is needed. For convex smooth finite sums it matches the O(n + 1/eps) gradient complexity of SVRG/SARAH (multi-stage variant) and also gives adaptive inner-loop termination rules based on a phase-transition analysis of AdaGrad.
main_result: Theorem 1 (fixed inner loop m_k = n, step eta_k in [eta_min, eta_max], convex L-smooth f_i, bounded iterates of diameter D): E[f(w_bar_K) - f*] decays as O(1/K)-type terms depending on D, implying O(n/eps) gradient evaluations to reach eps = Theta(1/n); the bound depends on the diameter D instead of ||w_0 - w*|| (shown unavoidable for adaptive methods). Theorem 2 (multi-stage AdaSVRG, I = log(1/eps) stages, K >= 3 outer loops, m_i = 2^{i+1}): O(n log(1/eps) + 1/eps) gradient evaluations to reach 2(1 + sqrt(5)) eps suboptimality, matching SARAH without knowing L; the full-matrix and diagonal variants reach the same complexity up to an extra sqrt(d) L_max factor in the suboptimality. Theorem 4: AdaGrad's preconditioner norm ||G_t|| stays bounded (constant step phase) until T_0 and then grows as O(sqrt(t)); Theorem 3 uses this for adaptive inner-loop sizes. No strongly convex rate is given (left as future work). Cost: O(d) per step (scalar/diagonal), O(d^2) full-matrix.
relevance: B1/B2: a variance-reduced method whose diagonal metric adapts to the local geometry; useful as the 'adaptive P' contrast to a fixed P and as evidence that the Euclidean R^2 constant in Bach's bound can be replaced by data-adaptive quantities without tuning. B3: the phase-transition analysis (Theorem 4) suggests instrumenting the effective step size as a diagnostic alongside the per-inequality tightness ratios. Pipeline: scalar AdaSVRG is a cheap baseline to add to the SAGA/L-Katyusha runs.

title: Stochastic Variance-Reduced Newton: Accelerating Finite-Sum Minimization with Large Batches
authors: Michal Derezinski
venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2025; arXiv 2206.02702 (v1 June 2022, v2 April 2025); also presented at the NeurIPS 2023 OPT workshop
summary: SVRN applies an SVRG-type variance-reduced gradient with large mini-batches inside a stochastic Newton method with a fixed (per outer stage) Hessian estimate H_tilde: x_{t+1} = x_t - eta H_tilde^{-1}((1/m) sum_{i in batch}(grad psi_i(x_t) - grad psi_i(x_tilde_s)) + grad f(x_tilde_s)). Locally, each pass over the data reduces the error by a factor that improves with n, giving an O(log n) acceleration over Subsampled Newton in sequential time while keeping O(log(1/eps)) parallel batch queries. For least squares, leverage-score sampling removes the condition-number dependence.
main_result: Theorem 3 (strongly convex finite sum with Lipschitz Hessian or self-concordance, Hessian alpha-approximation H_tilde of grad^2 f(x_tilde_s) in the sense (1/sqrt(alpha)) grad^2 f <= H_tilde <= sqrt(alpha) grad^2 f, iterate in a local neighbourhood U_f(1/c)): with mini-batch size m >= c alpha^2 kappa log(t/delta) and step eta = min{sqrt(2/alpha), 1}, after t inner iterations the last iterate satisfies, with probability 1 - delta, (f(x_tilde_{s+1}) - f*) / (f(x_tilde_s) - f*) <= (1 - 1/(2 alpha))^t + c alpha^2 kappa log(t/delta)/m. Theorem 1 (informal), n >> kappa >> alpha: parallel time O(alpha log(1/eps)) batch queries and sequential time O(log(1/eps)/log(n)) data passes, versus O(alpha log(1/eps)) passes for Subsampled Newton (Remark 1: O(alpha log n) acceleration that grows with n). Remark 3: the kappa in the batch size comes from sub-sampled gradient estimation; for least squares, Theorem 2 and Lemma 6 (sampling probabilities proportional to leverage scores a_i^T (A^T A)^{-1} a_i, sketched Hessian, O(nd log n + d^3 log d) preprocessing) eliminate the kappa-dependence: SVRN finds x_tilde with f(x_tilde) <= (1 + eps) f* in O(nd log(1/eps)/log(n/d)) time; alternatively a randomized Hadamard transform uniformizes leverage scores so uniform sampling works. Section 5 shows that high coherence (large leverage scores) degrades both Hessian subsampling and the variance-reduction gain; the error is measured in the norm of the inverse Hessian at the optimum (Lemma 3). Cost: O(d^2) per inner step to apply H_tilde^{-1} after an O(d^3) factorization per stage; gradients in batches of size m (parallelizable).
relevance: B1: variance reduction in the Newton metric with explicit constants; the error is measured in the inverse-Hessian norm (Lemma 3), i.e. exactly the P^{-1}-norm bookkeeping that Bach's proof needs when P ~ grad^2 F, and the result quantifies the role of the batch size (alpha^2 kappa log) in making the metric useful. Leverage scores/coherence: the least-squares results make precise that after Hessian preconditioning the remaining difficulty is the coherence of the data (max leverage score), which is the quantity to plot in the project's anisotropy experiments (B3). A1/A4: SVRN's O(log(1/eps)/log n) passes versus the n + sqrt(n kappa) lower bound illustrates that the lower bound of (A1) is for first-order span-based methods only.

title: IQN: An Incremental Quasi-Newton Method with Local Superlinear Convergence Rate
authors: Aryan Mokhtari, Mark Eisen, Alejandro Ribeiro
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization 28(2):1670-1698 (arXiv 1702.00709, Feb. 2017)
summary: IQN keeps, for each component f_i, a copy z_i of the iterate, its gradient and a BFGS matrix B_i, and updates them cyclically; the new iterate minimizes the sum of the per-component quadratic Taylor models evaluated consistently at z_i. It is the first incremental quasi-Newton method with per-iteration cost independent of n (O(p^2) via Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury) and a proven local superlinear rate.
main_result: Setting: f_i mu-strongly convex with L-Lipschitz gradients and Lipschitz Hessians. Update: x^{t+1} = (sum_i B_i^t)^{-1} (sum_i B_i^t z_i^t - sum_i grad f_i(z_i^t)) with one (cyclically chosen) component refreshed per iteration; the aggregate inverse is maintained with rank-two updates in O(p^2) time (memory O(n p^2) for the B_i, O(np) for z_i and gradients). Lemmas 1-3: residual bounds and local linear convergence of the residuals ||x^t - x*|| (Lemma 3 extends the classical Theorem 3.2 of Broyden-Dennis-More to the incremental setting); Proposition 4: the Dennis-More condition holds for each component, and Lemma 5 gives the generalized version needed for the aggregate; Theorem 6: the ratio ||x^t - x*|| / ((1/n) sum_{j=1}^n ||x^{t-j} - x*||) tends to zero; Theorem 7: a subsequence of the residuals converges Q-superlinearly and there is a sequence zeta_t -> 0 superlinearly with ||x^t - x*|| <= zeta_t for all t (R-superlinear convergence). The rate is independent of n per pass but requires O(np^2) memory.
relevance: B1 (variable-metric limit): shows the opposite extreme of a fixed P: a per-component metric that approaches the true Hessians gives superlinear local convergence, so the linear-rate constants of Bach's Prop. 5.9 (R^2/mu) disappear altogether locally; useful for discussing what a 'perfect' P could achieve and the price (O(np^2) memory, O(p^2) per step). A1: cyclic (not i.i.d.) index selection is essential to IQN's analysis, which connects to the project's discussion of arbitrary index sequences in the lower bound (A1). B2: the trajectory-dependent curvature constants in IQN's proof (errors of the last n iterates) are a model for mu_eff(t)-type analyses.

title: A Superlinearly-Convergent Proximal Newton-type Method for the Optimization of Finite Sums
authors: Anton Rodomanov, Dmitry Kropotov
venue: Proceedings of the 33rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2016), PMLR 48:2597-2605
summary: NIM keeps a second-order model m_i^k(x) = f_i(v_i^k) + <grad f_i(v_i^k), x - v_i^k> + (1/2)(x - v_i^k)^T grad^2 f_i(v_i^k)(x - v_i^k) for each component (centres v_i^k), updates one component per iteration (cyclically) and takes a scaled proximal step on the aggregated model plus the nonsmooth term h. It is an incremental Newton-type method with superlinear local and linear global convergence, effective when n is large and d small.
main_result: Theorem 1 (local rate): if the initial points x_0, ..., x_{n-1} are within R of x* (f_i with Lipschitz gradients and Hessians, F mu_f-strongly convex), NIM with unit step and cyclic order converges to x* R-superlinearly (there is z_k -> 0 with ||x_k - x*|| <= z_k and z_{k+1} <= q_k z_k, q_k -> 0); Q-quadratic convergence w.r.t. epochs is shown for a model example. Theorem 2 (global rate): with Lipschitz-continuous gradients and a small enough constant step, ||x_k - x*||^2 <= const c^k ||x_0 - x*||^2 for some c in (0,1) from any initialization. Memory O(nd + d^2) in general (no per-component Hessians are stored; the aggregate H_k = (1/n) sum_i grad^2 f_i(v_i^k) is updated by computing the selected Hessian at the new and old centres), reduced to O(n + d^2) for linear models (only n scalars); per-iteration cost at best O(d^2) (rank updates of H_k and inner solve by conjugate gradients for h = l2, by a fast gradient method otherwise), with an incremental-compatible inexactness criterion for the inner problem. Experiments: l2- and l1-regularized logistic regression (a9a, covtype, protein, SUSY, mnist8m) with lambda = 1/n.
relevance: B1: the 'exact variable metric' endpoint of the preconditioning spectrum for finite sums, with explicit per-iteration (O(d^2)) and memory costs that the project can quote when discussing the cost of applying P^{-1}. A1: cyclic order again, as in IQN. B2: NIM's model is the natural object for computing the trajectory-dependent effective curvature (aggregated Hessians at past centres), i.e. a concrete instance of the quantities in (B2).

title: Communication-Efficient Distributed Optimization using an Approximate Newton-type Method
authors: Ohad Shamir, Nathan Srebro, Tong Zhang
venue: Proceedings of the 31st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2014), PMLR 32(2):1000-1008; arXiv 1312.7853
summary: DANE: each of m machines holding n i.i.d. samples solves a local problem (its own loss corrected by the global gradient and a proximal term mu/2 ||w - w_t||^2) and the solutions are averaged. Because local Hessians concentrate around the global one, DANE behaves like an approximate Newton method whose communication complexity improves with the local sample size n (for quadratics), which is the origin of 'statistical preconditioning'.
main_result: Update: w_i^{(t)} = argmin_w phi_i(w) - <grad phi_i(w^{(t-1)}) - eta grad phi(w^{(t-1)}), w> + (mu/2)||w - w^{(t-1)}||^2, then average. Theorem 2 (quadratic losses, eta = 1): ||w^{(t)} - w_hat|| <= ||I - H_tilde^{-1} H||_2^t ||w^{(0)} - w_hat|| with H = (1/m) sum_i H_i and H_tilde^{-1} = (1/m) sum_i (H_i + mu I)^{-1}. Lemma 1: if lambda <= H <= L and ||H_i - H|| <= beta for all i, then eta = 1 and mu = max{0, 8 beta^2/lambda - lambda} give ||I - H_tilde^{-1} H|| bounded away from 1. Lemma 2 (concentration): if 0 <= grad^2 f(w; z) <= L then with probability >= 1 - delta, max_i ||H_i - H||_2 <= sqrt(32 L^2 log(dm/delta)/n). Theorem 3: for lambda-strongly convex, L-smooth quadratic instantaneous losses, t = O((L/lambda)^2 (log(dm/delta)/n) log(L ||w_0 - w_hat||^2/eps)) DANE iterations give F_hat(w^{(t)}) <= F_hat(w_hat) + eps with probability >= 1 - delta, i.e. O((kappa^2/n) log(1/eps)) rounds. Theorem 4 (general smooth strongly convex losses): linear rate (1 - rho)^t with rho ~ lambda/L for tuned eta, mu (no better than gradient descent). Theorem 5 (single-machine Bregman variant with h = phi_1): if D_h(w; w') <= D_phi(w; w') <= beta^{-1} D_h(w; w') for some beta > 0, then D_h(w_hat; w^{(t)}) <= (1 - beta)^t D_h(w_hat; w^{(0)}) - the precursor of the relative-condition-number analysis. Cost per round: one local finite-sum solve per machine (any solver) and two communications.
relevance: B1: DANE is the origin of the 'statistical preconditioner' P = local Hessian (+ mu I); Theorem 2 and Lemma 2 show how the preconditioned condition number scales as 1 + O(L sqrt(log(d)/n)/lambda) and Theorem 5 is the Bregman/relative-strong-convexity viewpoint that Hendrikx et al. and Dragomir et al. generalize. A1: the (kappa^2/n) rate is loose (see Yuan-Li 2020 for the sharper kappa/sqrt(n)), an example of a proof step (the averaging step) being the bottleneck, in the spirit of (B3). Pipeline: DANE with SAGA/SVRG as the local solver is the simplest 'preconditioned VR' baseline.

title: DiSCO: Distributed Optimization for Self-Concordant Empirical Loss
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Lin Xiao
venue: Proceedings of the 32nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2015), PMLR 37:362-370; long version arXiv 1501.00263, 'Communication-Efficient Distributed Optimization of Self-Concordant Empirical Loss'
summary: DiSCO is an inexact damped Newton method for self-concordant empirical losses in which each Newton step is computed by a distributed preconditioned conjugate gradient method, the preconditioner being the local Hessian of the first machine plus mu I. For ridge, logistic and smoothed-hinge losses with i.i.d. data and regularization ~ 1/sqrt(n), the number of communication rounds does not grow with the sample size and grows only slowly with the number of machines m.
main_result: Assumption A: lambda I <= grad^2 f <= L I; f standard self-concordant. Theorem 2 (long version numbering): if mu upper-bounds ||grad^2 f_1(w_k) - grad^2 f(w_k)||_2 for all k (Hessian similarity), the total number of communication rounds to reach f(w) - f* < eps is T <= 1 + (ceil((f(w_0) - f*)/((1/2) omega(1/6))) + ceil(log_2(2 omega(1/6)/eps))) (2 + sqrt(1 + 2 mu/lambda) log(2L/lambda)) (eq. (27)), i.e. O((f(w_0) - f* + log(1/eps)) sqrt(1 + 2 mu/lambda)) rounds ignoring logs and constants (compare O(sqrt(L/lambda)) for accelerated gradient); Theorem 3 gives the same with an adaptive mu. Corollary 4 (ridge regression, m machines, n samples each, features bounded by B, regularization lambda): with probability 1 - delta, T = O((1 + B/(lambda^{1/2} n^{1/4})) log(1/eps) log(md/delta)) (eq. (44)), hence T = O(m^{1/4} log(1/eps)) when lambda = Theta(1/sqrt(mn)), versus O(m log(1/eps)) for DANE. Corollary 5 (logistic regression): E[T] = O((log(1/eps) + B^3 D/(lambda n^{1/2})) (1 + B d^{1/4}/(lambda^{1/2} n^{1/4}))) and for lambda = Theta(1/(mn)) E[T] = O(m^{3/4} d^{1/4} + m^{1/4} d^{1/4} log(1/eps)); Corollary 6 treats the smoothed hinge loss. Cost: each PCG iteration is one communication round plus a local solve with P = grad^2 f_1(w_k) + mu I (O(d^3) or inner CG) at the master.
relevance: B1: the preconditioner is a statistically estimated Hessian and the convergence depends on the Hessian-similarity parameter mu through sqrt(1 + 2 mu/lambda): the 'square root of the relative condition number' that the project's accelerated preconditioned analysis should reproduce (A3 + B1). The rescaling tricks for self-concordant losses (logistic) show how the constants of the preconditioned rate depend on the feature radius B and dimension d, which is what the project measures in (B3). Together with DANE and SPAG it gives the three canonical statistical-preconditioning rates (kappa^2/n, kappa/sqrt(n), sqrt(kappa/sqrt(n))).

title: Acceleration of SVRG and Katyusha X by Inexact Preconditioning
authors: Yanli Liu, Fei Feng, Wotao Yin
venue: Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2019), PMLR 97:4003-4012
summary: Applies a fixed SPD preconditioner M to SVRG and to Katyusha X (Nesterov-accelerated SVRG for sums of possibly nonconvex functions with strongly convex sum): w_{t+1} = prox^M_{eta psi}(w_t - eta M^{-1} g_t) where g_t is the SVRG estimator and the M-preconditioned proximal mapping is solved inexactly with a fixed number of FISTA (with restart) iterations. Proves that the inexactness does not break linear convergence and that the gradient complexity improves when M captures the curvature of f; experiments on Lasso and logistic regression show about 8x fewer iterations and 7x less time.
main_result: Definitions 1-3: f is L_f^M-smooth under ||.||_M if f(y) <= f(x) + <grad f(x), y - x> + (L_f^M/2)||y - x||_M^2, mu_f^M-strongly convex under ||.||_M analogously, and kappa_f^M = L_f^M/mu_f^M is the condition number under M (kappa_f^M = O(1) when M approximates the Hessian). Algorithm 1 (iPreSVRG): the subproblem argmin_y psi(y) + (1/(2 eta))||y - (w_t - eta M^{-1} g_t)||_M^2 is solved inexactly by p FISTA-with-restart steps (Procedure 1; each FISTA step costs one multiplication by M, 'often cheaper than d gradient computations'); Lemma 1 bounds the resulting error by c(p) ||w_{t+1} - w_t||_M with c(p) = O(kappa(M) ... (1 - 1/sqrt(kappa(M)))^p)-type, so p = O(sqrt(kappa(M)) log(kappa_f^M kappa(M))) suffices (Lemma 2, eq. (4.5)).
