Theorem 1 (iPreSVRG) and Theorem 2 (iPreKatX): under Assumption 1, if 64 kappa_f^M c(p)^2 <= 1, m >= 4 and the step eta is chosen as in Katyusha X, the epoch outputs converge linearly with exactly the rates of SVRG and Katyusha X for sum-of-nonconvex objectives (Allen-Zhu 2018, Theorems D.1 and 4.3, recovered when M = I, Remark 5) with the Euclidean condition number replaced by kappa_f^M: E[F(x_k) - F*] = O((1 + m mu_f^M eta/4)^{-k}) for iPreSVRG and O((1 + (1/2) sqrt(m mu_f^M eta/2))^{-k})-type for iPreKatX (eqs. (4.3)-(4.4)), giving gradient complexities (4.8)-(4.9). Theorems 3-4 (total cost with the FISTA inner solver, M chosen so that kappa(M) is of the order of kappa_f and kappa_f^M is small): when kappa_f > sqrt(n) and kappa_f < n^2 d^{-2}, the gradient complexity of iPreSVRG is smaller than SVRG's by a factor of order kappa_f/sqrt(n) and iPreKatX improves on Katyusha X by a factor of order sqrt(kappa_f)/n^{1/4}; for kappa_f > n^2 d^{-2} the speed-ups saturate at factors involving n and d because the O(d^2) cost of applying a dense M dominates (eqs. (4.10)-(4.13)). Each summand f_i may be nonconvex; a nonsmooth regularizer psi is allowed.
relevance: B1 (direct): this is 'SVRG with a fixed SPD metric' plus its accelerated (Katyusha X) version, with the condition number under M replacing kappa in both the non-accelerated and accelerated rates; the proof technique (error measured in ||.||_M, inexact prox) is the model for the project's preconditioned SAGA/L-Katyusha Lyapunov argument, and the cost analysis makes explicit the trade-off between the d^2 cost of P^{-1} and the gain in kappa. A3/A4: shows the exponent change kappa^1 -> kappa^{1/2} survives preconditioning (iPreKatX), so the project's empirical-exponent experiment can be repeated with P != I. Experiments on Lasso/logistic regression match the project's B3 setting.

title: PROMISE: Preconditioned Stochastic Optimization Methods by Incorporating Scalable Curvature Estimates
authors: Zachary Frangella, Pratik Rathore, Shipu Zhao, Madeleine Udell
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 25(346):1-57 (arXiv 2309.02014, v3 March 2024)
summary: A suite of sketching-based preconditioned variance-reduced methods, SketchySVRG, SketchySAGA and SketchyKatyusha, in which a lazily updated preconditioner P (subsampled Newton, Nystrom or sketch-and-solve approximation of a subsampled Hessian, rank r ~ 10, Hessian batch ~ sqrt(n)) is applied to the VR gradient. Introduces 'quadratic regularity' to prove global linear convergence at a rate governed by the quadratic regularity ratio (equal to 1 for quadratics) instead of the condition number, and shows with default hyperparameters that the methods beat tuned SVRG/SAGA/L-Katyusha/SLBFGS on 51 ridge and logistic regression problems.
main_result: Definition 11 (quadratic regularity on a set C): gamma_l/2 ||w2 - w1||^2_{grad^2 F(w0)} <= F(w2) - F(w1) - <grad F(w1), w2 - w1> <= gamma_u/2 ||w2 - w1||^2_{grad^2 F(w0)} for all w0, w1, w2 in C; ratio q = gamma_u/gamma_l (q = 1 for quadratics; -> 1 near the optimum with Lipschitz Hessians; Proposition 12: L-smooth mu-strongly convex gives the pessimistic bounds gamma_l >= 1/kappa, gamma_u <= kappa). Preconditioner: a zeta-spectral approximation (1 - zeta) P <= grad^2 F(w_j) <= (1 + zeta) P built at update indices; Lemmas 2-3 and Table 4: construction O(b_H r p + r^2 p) (NySSN) or O(b_H p + r^2 p + r^3) (SASSN), application of P^{-1} to a vector in O(r p); Proposition 8: for GLMs a Hessian batch b_H = O(chi d_eff(grad^2 F) log(.)) suffices (chi = ridge leverage coherence, d_eff = sum of ridge leverage scores). Definition 13 (Hessian dissimilarity tau) and Proposition 15: for GLMs tau <= 1 + chi d_eff(A). Proposition 16 (preconditioned expected smoothness): E||grad F_{b_g}(w) - grad F_{b_g}(w')||^2_{P^{-1}} <= 2 L_P (F(w) - F(w') - <grad F(w'), w - w'>) with L_P = [n(b_g - 1)/(b_g(n-1))] gamma_u + [(n - b_g)/(b_g(n-1))] gamma_u^max tau (1 + zeta), so a gradient batch b_g = O(tau) is needed for L_P = O(1) even with a perfect preconditioner. Theorem 18 (SketchySVRG): with eta = 1/(8 L_P) and m = 19 q_bar/(1 - zeta) inner iterations (q_bar the weighted quadratic regularity ratio, Definition 17), E[F(w_hat^{(s)})] - F* <= eps after s = 10 log(1/eps) outer iterations, i.e. at most 10 (n + 19 b_g q_bar/(1 - zeta)) log(1/eps) stochastic gradient queries, independent of kappa; for quadratics with b_g = tau, q_bar <= 2(1 + zeta). Corollary 19 (ridge regression): with b_g = 1 + chi(A) d_eff(A) and m = 48 (1 + zeta)/(1 - zeta) the complexity is O((n + chi d_eff(A)) log(1/eps)) gradients. Theorem 20: local condition-number-free linear convergence of SketchySVRG for any strongly convex finite sum with M-Lipschitz Hessians (b_g = O(tau)). Analogous linear-convergence theorems for SketchySAGA and SketchyKatyusha are in the arXiv report (stated in the JMLR version, Section 5).
relevance: B1 (direct, including SAGA): preconditioned SAGA/SVRG/loopless-Katyusha with a fixed (lazily updated) P and a full Lyapunov analysis in the P-norm; the quadratic regularity constants gamma_u, gamma_l are precisely the constants that replace R^2 and mu in Bach's Prop. 5.9, and Proposition 16 is the preconditioned version of the 'cocoercivity/variance' step with the explicit dependence on the batch size through the Hessian dissimilarity tau - which identifies the step that becomes loose for small batches (b_g = 1, as in Bach's SAGA). Leverage scores/effective dimension: tau <= 1 + chi d_eff and Corollary 19 give the post-preconditioning condition number in terms of ridge leverage coherence and effective dimension. B2: the quadratic regularity ratio measured along the trajectory is exactly a 'trajectory-dependent constant' of the kind hypothesised in (B2). B3/pipeline: the 51-problem ridge/logistic test bed and default hyperparameters are a template for the project's experiments; A3: SketchyKatyusha is the preconditioned counterpart of the project's L-Katyusha. | B1 (central): the analysis of SAGA/SVRG/Katyusha with P^{-1} steps, showing which steps must be rewritten (cocoercivity and strong convexity are replaced by quadratic regularity in the P-norm; the variance/second-moment step is unchanged); B2 (central): an explicitly measured trajectory-dependent effective condition number on logistic regression; B3: ready-made experimental protocol (LIBSVM logistic datasets, epochs-to-accuracy).

title: SketchySGD: Reliable Stochastic Optimization via Randomized Curvature Estimates
authors: Zachary Frangella, Pratik Rathore, Shipu Zhao, Madeleine Udell
venue: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science 6(4):1173-1204 (2024); arXiv 2211.08597 (v1 Nov. 2022, v5 Feb. 2024)
summary: SketchySGD preconditions minibatch SGD with a randomized Nystrom low-rank approximation (rank r, regularization rho) of a subsampled Hessian, refreshed every u iterations, with an automatic learning rate. It converges linearly to a noise ball whose rate is controlled by a preconditioned smoothness constant and the Hessian dissimilarity rather than the condition number; on ill-conditioned least squares it provably beats SGD, and it solves problems whose data would need 840 GB of RAM.
main_result: Assumptions 4.1-4.2: f L-smooth, f_i L_i-smooth (L_max), f mu-strongly convex. Definition 4.3 (relative quadratic regularity, refining the relative smoothness/convexity of Gower et al. 2019 (RSN)) and Definition 4.5 (nu-dissimilarity tau_nu(H(w)) = max_i ||(H + nu I)^{-1/2}(grad^2 f_i + nu I)(H + nu I)^{-1/2}||); Proposition 4.7: for GLMs with sub-Gaussian data and n >= C d_eff log(.) samples, tau_nu is at most the nu-effective dimension d_eff(H(w)) = tr(H(H + nu I)^{-1}) up to logs. Theorem 4.15 (strongly convex): with gradient batch b_g, learning rate eta = min{1/(4 L_P), eps mu/(8 sigma^2)} (L_P the preconditioned expected smoothness, sigma^2 the gradient variance at the optimum), regularization mu <= rho <= L_max, update frequency u and Hessian batch sizes as in Assumption 4.11, after ms = O(((L_P/((1-zeta) mu)) + sigma^2/(mu^2 eps)) (1 + rho/mu) log(2(f(w_0) - f*)/eps))-type iterations the output satisfies E[f(w_hat) - f*] <= eps; Corollary 4.16: linear convergence to the optimum under interpolation (sigma^2 = 0) with eta = 1/(4 L_P). Corollary 4.17 (quadratic f, u = infinity, b_g = tau(H)): ms = O((tau + sigma^2/(mu eps)) log(1/eps)) iterations (O(tau log(1/eps)) if sigma^2 = 0), versus O((L/mu + sigma^2/(mu eps)) log(1/eps)) for minibatch SGD, i.e. the condition number L/mu is replaced by the Hessian dissimilarity tau (<= d_eff for GLMs). Cost: P^{-1} v in O(r p) per iteration; preconditioner construction O(b_H r p) every u iterations via b_H Hessian-vector products.
relevance: B1: companion of PROMISE for the non-VR case: makes precise that a sketched Hessian preconditioner turns kappa into the Hessian dissimilarity tau (effective dimension for GLMs), which is the quantitative answer to 'what the preconditioned rate depends on'. Leverage scores/effective dimension: Proposition 4.7 ties the post-preconditioning constant to d_eff (ridge leverage scores). B3: the Nystrom preconditioner is cheap enough (O(r p) per step) to use as the fixed P in the project's instrumented SAGA runs; comparison SGD vs SketchySGD shows the noise ball sigma^2 term that variance reduction removes (A2/A3 motivation).

title: Leverage Score Sampling for Faster Accelerated Regression and ERM
authors: Naman Agarwal, Sham Kakade, Rahul Kidambi, Yin Tat Lee, Praneeth Netrapalli, Aaron Sidford
venue: Proceedings of the 31st International Conference on Algorithmic Learning Theory (ALT 2020), PMLR 117:22-47 (arXiv 1711.08426, Nov. 2017)
summary: Improves the best known running time for least-squares regression (and a class of ERM problems) from Otilde((n + sqrt(n kappa_sum)) s log(1/eps)) to Otilde((n + sqrt(d kappa_sum)) s log(1/eps)), where kappa_sum = tr(A^T A)/lambda_min(A^T A) and s is the row sparsity, by combining leverage-score sampling (as a preconditioner / sub-sampled problem), proximal point outer loops and accelerated coordinate descent, with an iterative scheme to estimate leverage scores.
main_result: Definition 8: leverage score tau_i(A) = a_i^T (A^T A)^+ a_i in (0,1], sum_i tau_i = rank(A) <= d. Theorem 4 (previous best, accelerated coordinate descent + proximal point): T(A) = Otilde((n + sum_i ||a_i||/sqrt(lambda_min(A^T A))) s(A)) <= Otilde((n + sqrt(n kappa_sum)) s(A)) per log(1/eps). Theorem 5 (new): T(A) = Otilde((nnz(A) + d + sum_i ||a_i|| sqrt(tau_i(A)/lambda_min(A^T A))) s(A)) log(1/eps) <= Otilde((nnz(A) + sqrt(d kappa_sum) s(A)) log(1/eps)), since sum_i ||a_i|| sqrt(tau_i) <= sqrt(sum_i ||a_i||^2 sum_i tau_i) = sqrt(d tr(A^T A)); the improvement is largest when leverage scores are small (tau_i = O(d/n) for Gaussian data). Theorem 10: sampling rows with probabilities built from overestimates u_i of the leverage scores (tau_i <= u_i <= 4 tau_i + [n kappa(A^T A)]^{-1}) yields a spectral approximation and a preconditioned sub-problem solvable in the above time; Lemma 11/Algorithm 2 estimate leverage scores in nearly linear time plus O(1) regression solves. Theorem 7 (ERM with M-'regular' univariate losses f_i(a_i^T x)): total time Otilde(nnz(A) + d M^5 + sqrt(sum_i ||a_i||^2 tau_i M^3 / lambda_min(A^T A)) s(A)) log(1/eps) (Algorithm 4 samples components by leverage scores and uses a variance-reduced estimator a la SVRG inside an off-the-shelf accelerated coordinate solver, Theorem 17).
relevance: A1/B1: shows that for finite sums the sqrt(n kappa) term of the lower bound (A1) is not tight for ill-conditioned but incoherent data: the n in sqrt(n kappa_sum) can be replaced by d = sum of leverage scores, i.e. after leverage-score reweighting/preconditioning the 'condition number' is governed by the leverage scores (coherence) and the effective dimension; this is the sharpest statement of 'leverage scores as the condition number after preconditioning' that the task asks for. B3: suggests plotting max and sum of leverage scores for the project's anisotropic instances to explain theory-practice gaps. A4: gives a prediction for the empirical exponent on incoherent vs. coherent designs.

title: Stochastic Distributed Optimization under Average Second-order Similarity: Algorithms and Analysis
authors: Dachao Lin, Yuze Han, Haishan Ye, Zhihua Zhang
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023), main conference track; arXiv 2304.07504
summary: Finite-sum distributed optimization (master + n - 1 workers) under delta-average second-order similarity (AveSS: (1/n) sum_i ||grad^2 f_i - grad^2 f||^2 <= delta^2) and mu-strong convexity. SVRS combines gradient sliding (proximal steps on the master's local function f_1, i.e. statistical preconditioning) with loopless variance reduction; AccSVRS adds Katyusha-X acceleration. The bounds are smoothness-free, and a nearly matching lower bound shows AccSVRS is near optimal.
main_result: Assumption 1: f_i satisfy delta-AveSS and f is mu-strongly convex (f_i may be nonconvex). Theorem 3.3 (SVRS, one-epoch loopless scheme with step eta = 1/(4 sqrt(n) delta), full-gradient probability p = 1/n, inexact proximal steps satisfying an error-independent criterion (10)): after Otilde(n + sqrt(n) delta/mu) communications in expectation, E f(w_k) - f* <= eps. Theorem 3.6 (AccSVRS, Katyusha X framework, momentum parameter of order n^{-1/4} sqrt(mu/delta)): Otilde(n + n^{3/4} sqrt(delta/mu)) communications. Theorem 4.4 (lower bound for the class of randomized algorithms of Definition 4.1 with proximal-incremental first-order oracle): Omega-tilde(n + n^{3/4} sqrt(delta/mu)) communications, so AccSVRS is optimal up to logs. Section 3.3 also gives total gradient complexity Otilde(n + n^{3/4} sqrt(delta/mu) + L/delta + sqrt(nL/mu))-type when f_1 is L-smooth (each proximal subproblem on f_1 is strongly convex and is solved by a few local steps). Cost per communication round: one proximal subproblem on the master's local function (solved inexactly) plus O(1) worker gradients in expectation.
relevance: A1/A3/B1: the sharpest known rates for 'variance reduction + statistical preconditioning (prox on a reference function) + acceleration': sqrt(n kappa) becomes n^{3/4} sqrt(delta/mu) where delta/mu is the relative (Hessian-similarity) condition number; the matching lower bound is the preconditioned analogue of the project's (A1) and uses a similar hard-instance construction. Also shows that in the preconditioned setting the natural 'condition number' is delta/mu (average Hessian dissimilarity), which the project can estimate on its instances (B2/B3). The proof is Katyusha-X style and therefore close to the Lyapunov style of (A3).

title: Optimal Complexity and Certification of Bregman First-Order Methods
authors: Radu-Alexandru Dragomir, Adrien B. Taylor, Alexandre d'Aspremont, Jerome Bolte
venue: Mathematical Programming 194(1-2):41-83 (2022); arXiv 1911.08510
summary: Proves that the O(1/k) rate of NoLips / Bregman gradient descent is optimal for the class of relatively smooth (h-smooth) convex functions: no Bregman first-order method using the same mirror map can be accelerated in general. The worst-case functions are constructed with an extension of the performance estimation (PEP) framework to Bregman methods.
main_result: Theorem 1 (NoLips convergence rate): for (f, h) in the class B_L(C) of L-relatively-smooth instances and constant step lambda in (0, 1/L], f(x_k) - f(u) <= D_h(u, x_0)/(lambda k) for every u in dom h. Theorem 2 (lower complexity bound): for any N >= 1 and eps in (0,1), there exist (f, h) in B_L(R^{2N+1}) such that any Bregman gradient method satisfying Definition 4 (accessing f only through gradients and h through its mirror map, iterates in the span of the oracle outputs) returns, after at most N calls to each of the primal and mirror oracles, a point x with f(x) - min f >= L D_h(x*, x_0) (1 - eps)/(2N + 1); hence the O(L D_h(x*, x_0)/k) rate of Bauschke-Bolte-Teboulle / Lu-Freund-Nesterov is optimal and Nesterov-type acceleration (O(1/k^2)) is impossible under relative smoothness alone, in contrast with the Euclidean case (quadratic h), where acceleration holds because relative smoothness w.r.t. (1/2)||.||_P^2 is ordinary smoothness after the change of variables x -> P^{1/2} x. Theorem 4: the worst-case value of NoLips is computable as a semidefinite program (PEP).
relevance: A3/B1: delimits exactly when 'preconditioned acceleration' is possible: for a fixed quadratic metric P the project can accelerate preconditioned SAGA/L-Katyusha as in the Euclidean case (the whole Bach proof transfers by the change of variables), whereas for a non-quadratic Bregman metric (e.g. the DANE/SPAG statistical preconditioner f_1 itself) acceleration needs extra structure (Hessian regularity, as in SPAG's Lemma 2 and Dragomir-Even-Hendrikx's gain function). A1: a lower-bound construction technique (PEP-based) complementary to the span-based arguments of (A1).

title: Fastest Rates for Stochastic Mirror Descent Methods
authors: Filip Hanzely, Peter Richtarik
venue: Computational Optimization and Applications 79(3):717-766 (2021); arXiv 1803.07374 (March 2018)
summary: Studies stochastic methods for relatively smooth problems (relative smoothness and strong convexity w.r.t. a separable reference h): relative randomized coordinate descent (relRCD), the first stochastic mirror descent method with a linear rate, and relative SGD (relSGD) with growing step-size parameters. Explicitly leaves variance reduction for relatively smooth ERM as an open problem (later solved by Dragomir-Even-Hendrikx 2021).
main_result: Theorem 2.5 recalls the deterministic rate of Lu-Freund-Nesterov. Theorem 3.2 (relRCD, Algorithm 2, f L-smooth and mu-strongly convex relative to a separable h, uniform coordinate sampling with tau coordinates): a weighted average of iterates satisfies sum_{t=1}^k c_t (E f(x_t) - f*) <= ((L - tau mu/n) D_h(x*, x_0) + ((n - tau)/n)(f(x_0) - f*)) / ((1 - tau mu/(nL))^{-(k-1)} ... ) with the driving factor (1 - tau mu/(n L))^{k-1}, i.e. linear convergence at rate (1 - mu/(nL)) per single-coordinate step (matching Theorem 2.5 when tau = n); Theorem 3.5 gives the non-averaged version via the Lyapunov quantity L D_h(x*, x_t) + f(x_t) - f*; Theorem 3.3: the convex case. Theorem 5.4 / Corollary 5.5 (relSGD, Algorithm 4: x_{t+1} = argmin <g_t, x> + L_t D_h(x, x_t) with E g_t = grad f(x_t)): with L_t increasing (L_t ~ sqrt(k) for convex f) the rate is O(1/sqrt(k)) in the convex case and a conservative-step analysis for mu > 0; Corollary 5.8 covers minibatches. The authors state (Section 5) that the gradient-estimator variance does not vanish and leave variance reduction for relatively smooth ERM as an open research question. For a quadratic reference h(x) = (1/2) x^T B x all results reduce to preconditioned (B-metric) coordinate descent / SGD with L, mu the extreme eigenvalues of B^{-1/2} grad^2 f B^{-1/2}; mirror steps cost O(d) for separable h.
relevance: B1: the Lyapunov function L D_h(x*, x_t) + f(x_t) - f* is the relative-smoothness analogue of the quantities in Bach's SAGA proof and shows how the step 'strong convexity' becomes mu D_h; the paper's open question (variance reduction for relatively smooth ERM) is exactly the question behind (B1), answered in the quadratic case by Dragomir-Even-Hendrikx Corollary 1 and PROMISE. B2: the (1 - mu/(nL)) coordinate rate with relative constants is useful for comparing coordinate-wise (diagonal) preconditioning with full preconditioning.

title: Stochastic Gradient Methods with Preconditioned Updates
authors: Abdurakhmon Sadiev, Aleksandr Beznosikov, Abdulla Jasem Almansoori, Dmitry Kamzolov, Rachael Tappenden, Martin Takac
venue: Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications 201(2):471-489 (May 2024); arXiv 2206.00285 (v1 June 2022, v2 Jan. 2024)
summary: Adds a diagonal preconditioner, estimated by Hutchinson's diagonal-Hessian estimator with momentum (the OASIS preconditioner of Jahani et al.), to the variance-reduced methods SARAH/PAGE and loopless SVRG, yielding Scaled SARAH and Scaled L-SVRG for (possibly nonconvex) finite sums. Gives complexity bounds under smoothness and linear rates under smoothness plus Polyak-Lojasiewicz; the theory is weaker than for the unscaled methods by the preconditioner's eigenvalue ratio, but experiments show gains on badly scaled problems.
main_result: Preconditioner (4)-(6): D_t = beta D_{t-1} + (1 - beta) diag(z_t o grad^2 P_{J_t}(w_t) z_t) with Rademacher z_t and a minibatch Hessian-vector product, then truncated entrywise so that (Lemma 1, re-proving Remark 4.10 of Jahani et al. 2021) alpha I <= D_hat_t <= Gamma I with Gamma = d L. Updates: w_{t+1} = w_t - eta D_hat_t^{-1} v_t with v_t the SARAH/PAGE or L-SVRG estimator. Theorem 1 (nonconvex, L-smooth, step eta <= alpha-scaled bound (8)): Scaled SARAH reaches E||grad P||^2 <= eps^2 in T = O((Delta_0 L/(alpha eps^2))(1 + sqrt((1-p)/p))) iterations (p the full-gradient probability); Theorem 2 (PL with parameter mu): T = O(max{1/p, (L/(alpha mu))(1 + sqrt((1-p)/p))} log(Delta_0/eps)), linear convergence; Theorems 3-4 (Scaled L-SVRG): T = O(max{1/p, L/(alpha p^{2/3} mu)} log(Delta_0/eps)) under PL with the step eta <= min{p/(6 mu), 1/(4L), ...} scaled by alpha. The authors note (Section 5, Table 3) that all bounds for scaled methods are worse than the unscaled ones by factors involving Gamma/alpha (up to d), and discuss in Appendix F.1 ('the worst case') why this gap seems unavoidable with current proof techniques. Cost: O(d) to apply the diagonal preconditioner plus one minibatch Hessian-vector product per iteration for Hutchinson's estimator.
relevance: B1 (diagonal / feature-scaling case): the only published analysis of a diagonal-preconditioned loopless SVRG/SARAH; it exhibits precisely the phenomenon the project wants to explain - the proof only uses alpha I <= D <= Gamma I, so the theoretical rate is worse than the Euclidean one even though practice improves - identifying the smoothness step (Euclidean L instead of the D-relative smoothness) as the loose inequality. B3: Hutchinson's estimator is a cheap way to build the fixed diagonal P for the project's anisotropic logistic-regression experiments, and the paper's Appendix F.1 discussion of why the bounds cannot be improved is directly relevant to the 'bottleneck step per geometry' question.

title: GIANT: Globally Improved Approximate Newton Method for Distributed Optimization
authors: Shusen Wang, Farbod Roosta-Khorasani (Fred Roosta), Peng Xu, Michael W. Mahoney
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 31 (NeurIPS 2018); arXiv 1709.03528
summary: Each of m workers computes an approximate Newton direction with its local Hessian (s local samples) and the driver averages them (the 'GIANT' direction), trading local computation for communication. The analysis is in terms of the row coherence of the (iteration-dependent) data matrix, i.e. the maximal leverage score, and shows linear-quadratic convergence with a local sample size that scales with coherence times d rather than with the condition number; sketches other than uniform sampling (leverage scores, SRHT, Gaussian) remove the coherence dependence.
main_result: Definition 1: row coherence mu(A) = (n/d) max_j ||u_j||_2^2 in [1, n/d] for the column-orthonormal basis U of A (= n/d times the largest leverage score). Theorem 1 (ridge regression X in R^{n x d}, m partitions): if the local sample size satisfies s >= 3 mu d log(md/delta)/eta^2 for eta, delta in (0,1), then with probability 1 - delta ||Delta_t||_2 <= alpha^t sqrt(kappa) ||Delta_0||_2 with alpha = eta/sqrt(m) + eta^2 and kappa the condition number of grad^2 f = (1/n) X^T X + gamma I (contraction in the Hessian norm without the sqrt(kappa)), so the number of communication rounds is logarithmic in 1/eps and does not depend on kappa given s >> mu d (Remark 2: n >= 3 mu d m log(md/delta) suffices). Theorem 2 / Corollary 3 (general smooth losses with L-Lipschitz Hessian, coherence mu_t of A_t = diag(l_i'')^{1/2} X): if s_t >= 3 mu_t d log(md/delta)/eta^2 then ||Delta_{t+1}||_2 <= max{alpha sqrt(lambda_max(H_t)/lambda_min(H_t)) ||Delta_t||_2, (L/lambda_min(H_t)) ||Delta_t||_2^2}-type, i.e. linear-quadratic convergence. Theorem 4: inexact local solves with relative accuracy keep the results. Appendix: leverage-score sampling, Gaussian projections or subsampled randomized Hadamard transforms satisfy the required sketch condition without the coherence factor mu. Cost per round: each worker solves a d x d system with its local Hessian (O(s d^2) or CG) and sends one d-vector.
relevance: B1 and 'leverage scores / coherence': gives the explicit coherence-dependent sample size (3 mu d log(md/delta)/eta^2) needed for a subsampled-Hessian preconditioner to be spectrally accurate, which is the quantitative version of the project's claim that after preconditioning the condition number is controlled by leverage scores/coherence and the dimension; also shows the role of the iteration-dependent coherence of diag(l_i'')^{1/2} X for logistic regression (B2/B3: a trajectory-dependent quantity).

title: AIDE: Fast and Communication Efficient Distributed Optimization
authors: Sashank J. Reddi, Jakub Konecny, Peter Richtarik, Barnabas Poczos, Alex Smola
venue: arXiv preprint 1608.06879 (Aug. 2016); no journal/conference version found on Crossref
summary: Inexact DANE lets each machine solve its DANE subproblem only approximately with any local solver (e.g. SVRG), and AIDE accelerates it with the Catalyst (proximal-point/Nesterov) outer loop. AIDE matches the communication lower bounds for distributed optimization (Arjevani-Shamir) up to logarithmic factors while using only first-order local oracles.
main_result: Theorem 2 (InexactDANE, Option I): if lambda I <= H <= L I, the local functions F_k are delta-related (||grad^2 F_k - grad^2 F|| <= delta), mu = max{0, 8 delta^2/lambda - lambda}, eta = 1 and each local subproblem is solved to a fixed relative accuracy theta, then ||w_t - w_hat|| <= rho_tilde ||w_{t-1} - w_hat|| with rho_tilde = 2/3 if delta^2 <= lambda^2/... (small delta) and 1 - lambda^2/(24 delta^2) otherwise; solving the local problems more accurately does not improve the rate. Corollary 1: t = Otilde((delta^2/lambda^2) log(L ||w_0 - w_hat||^2/eps)) rounds give f(w_t) <= f(w_hat) + eps, and when each H_k is the average of n i.i.d. quadratic Hessians bounded by L, delta = O(L/sqrt(n)) (Corollary 4), hence t = Otilde(((L/lambda)^2/n) log(1/eps)) as for DANE. Theorem 5 (AIDE = Catalyst applied to InexactDANE, Option I): communication complexity reduced to the square root of InexactDANE's, matching the Arjevani-Shamir lower bound up to log factors for delta-related quadratics; Corollary 3 treats the weakly convex case; local computation uses SVRG (Section 7 and Appendix E compare with DiSCO and CoCoA+). Cost per round: one inexact local solve per machine and two communications.
relevance: A3/B1: the Catalyst route to accelerating a (statistically) preconditioned VR method, i.e. 'naive acceleration' by an outer loop instead of the negative-momentum of L-Katyusha; a natural baseline for (A2)/(A3) in the preconditioned setting and for discussing the extra log factor of Catalyst-type acceleration. Theorem 2 also shows a proof whose constant (delta^2/lambda^2) is loose, later sharpened by Yuan-Li 2020 (B3-type diagnosis).

title: On Convergence of Distributed Approximate Newton Methods: Globalization, Sharper Bounds and Beyond
authors: Xiao-Tong Yuan, Ping Li
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 21(206):1-51 (2020); arXiv 1908.02246
summary: Proposes DANE-LS (DANE with backtracking line search and a single-local-solver architecture) and DANE-HB (heavy-ball accelerated), with global convergence and sharper local rates for strongly convex objectives. Shows that the O(kappa^2/n) DANE bound is loose and that the correct dependence is O(kappa/sqrt(n)) (and O(sqrt(kappa/sqrt(n))) with heavy-ball), the looseness coming from the model-averaging step of the original DANE.
main_result: Theorem 3 (quadratic loss, mu I <= H <= L I, ||H_1 - H|| <= delta, step-size condition): DANE-LS outputs ||w^{(t)} - w*|| <= eps after t >= 2 ((mu + 2 delta)/mu) log(||w^{(0)} - w*||/eps) rounds, i.e. the relative condition number is 1 + 2 delta/mu, versus O((delta/mu)^2 log(1/eps))-type bounds for DANE (Shamir et al. 2014, Lemma 1) and InexactDane (Reddi et al. 2016, Corollary 1). Corollary 4 (uniformly distributed samples, Hessians bounded by L): with probability 1 - delta', delta = L sqrt(32 log(p/delta')/n), hence t >= (1 + 2 (L/mu) sqrt(32 log(p/delta')/n)) log(2||w^{(0)} - w*||/eps) = O((1 + kappa/sqrt(n)) log(1/eps)) rounds. Theorem 8 / Theorem 13: global convergence and non-asymptotic local rates of DANE-LS for general strongly convex functions with Lipschitz Hessians. Theorem 15 / Corollary 16 (DANE-HB, quadratic, beta = (1 - sqrt(mu/(mu + 2 delta)))^2): O(sqrt((mu + 2 delta)/mu) log(1/eps)) = Otilde(n^{-1/4} kappa^{1/2} log^{1/4}(p/delta') log(1/eps)) rounds, nearly tight; Theorems 18-19: local rates of DANE-HB for strongly convex functions and global rates for linear prediction models (DANE-HB-LM); Corollaries 35-36: total IFO complexity when local problems are solved by SVRG (terms of order n^{3/4} and n^{1/4} kappa-type).
relevance: B1/B3: a worked example of 'which proof step is loose': the averaging step of DANE costs a square in the relative condition number, and removing it gives the natural O(1 + 2 delta/mu) rate and its accelerated square root - exactly the kind of tightness analysis the project does for Bach's SAGA proof. The explicit relative condition number 1 + 2 delta/mu with delta = L sqrt(32 log(p/delta')/n) is a ready-to-use formula for the preconditioned constants in (B1).

title: A Variance Reduced Stochastic Newton Method
authors: Aurelien Lucchi, Brian McWilliams, Thomas Hofmann
venue: arXiv preprint 1503.08316 (v4 June 2015); no journal/conference version found on Crossref
summary: VITE combines the SVRG variance-reduced gradient with a stochastic quasi-Newton metric (fixed within an epoch), w <- w - eta J_hat_t^{-1} v_t, and proves a geometric rate with constant step for smooth strongly convex objectives without exploiting the specific form of the approximate Hessian, only eigenvalue bounds on it.
main_result: Assumptions A1-A3: strong convexity mu, Lipschitz gradient L, and eigenvalue bounds gamma I <= J_hat_t^{-1} <= Gamma I on the metric, used to define the rescaled constants mu_hat = mu gamma and L_hat = L Gamma (the strong convexity and smoothness constants in the metric). Theorem 1: for 0 < eta < mu_hat/(2 L_hat^2) and an epoch length m large enough that alpha < 1, where alpha is an explicit function of (mu_hat, L_hat, eta, m) of the Johnson-Zhang form (a term decaying in m divided by mu_hat - 2 L_hat^2 eta, plus 2 L_hat^2 eta/(mu_hat - 2 L_hat^2 eta)), the epoch outputs satisfy E[f(w_tilde_s) - f*] <= alpha^s (f(w_tilde_0) - f*) (local geometric rate with constant learning rate); Remark 1: if J_hat_t approximates the Hessian well, plugging Gamma = 1/mu-type and gamma = 1/L-type values gives the step bound 1/(2 mu L)-type; the number of stages to reach eps is s >= log(eps^{-1}(f(w_tilde_0) - f*))/log(alpha^{-1}), with overall complexity O((n + 2m(|A| + |B|)) log(1/eps)) component gradients. Cost per step: O(d) plus the application of the metric (O(M d) for an L-BFGS two-loop form).
relevance: B1: the earliest 'SVRG with a fixed-per-epoch metric' analysis; its rate has the same form as Bach's/Johnson-Zhang's SVRG rate with (mu, L) replaced by the rescaled (mu_hat, L_hat), i.e. the P-metric constants, and is a template for the project's preconditioned proof. Also an example where the proof ignores the structure of the metric (only eigenvalue bounds), hence loose - relevant to (B3).

title: Optimal Gradient Sliding and its Application to Optimal Distributed Optimization Under Similarity
authors: Dmitry Kovalev, Aleksandr Beznosikov, Ekaterina Borodich, Alexander Gasnikov, Gesualdo Scutari
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022), main conference track; arXiv 2205.15136 (arXiv title: 'Optimal Gradient Sliding and its Application to Distributed Optimization Under Similarity')
summary: An inexact accelerated extragradient 'sliding' method for minimizing p + q + r (p L_p-smooth, q convex L_q-smooth, r mu-strongly convex) that attains the optimal number of gradient calls separately for p and q. Applied to distributed optimization under delta-Hessian similarity (p = f - f_1 with L_p = delta, q = f_1), it achieves simultaneously the optimal communication complexity O(sqrt(delta/mu) log(1/eps)) and the optimal local gradient complexity O(sqrt(L/mu) log(1/eps)), closing a long-standing open problem.
main_result: Assumptions 4-6: f_i convex and L-smooth, r mu-strongly convex, delta-related Hessians ||grad^2 f_i(x) - grad^2 f(x)|| <= delta. Theorem 3 (sliding, mu <= L_p <= L_q): O(sqrt(L_q/mu) log(1/eps)) gradients of q and O(sqrt(L_p/mu) log(1/eps)) gradients of p, with the inner subproblem (min_x <grad p(x_g), x> + q(x) + r(x) + prox term) solved to a stopping criterion by accelerated steps (Theorems 1-2). Theorem 5 (distributed, mu <= delta <= L): O(sqrt(delta/mu) log(1/eps)) communication rounds and O(sqrt(L/mu) log(1/eps)) local gradient computations - optimal by the Arjevani-Shamir communication lower bound and the Nesterov local-computation lower bound. Theorem 6: the convex case with O(sqrt(delta/eps) ||x_0 - x*||) rounds and O(sqrt(L/eps) ||x_0 - x*||) local computations; Theorems 7-12 extend to variational inequalities / saddle-point problems. Cost per round: the master solves inexactly a strongly convex local problem built from f_1 (statistical preconditioner) with first-order steps; workers send one gradient each.
relevance: A1/A3/B1: the deterministic (full-gradient-per-round) optimal rate under statistical preconditioning, sqrt(delta/mu), which is the preconditioned analogue of sqrt(kappa) in Nesterov's rate; comparing it with Lin et al.'s n^{3/4} sqrt(delta/mu) (variance-reduced) and the project's sqrt(n kappa) clarifies how the n-dependence and the metric interact. Identifies the 'reference function' f_1 as a Bregman preconditioner (B1) and the constant delta (Hessian dissimilarity) as the quantity that replaces R^2 (B2).

title: Randomized Nystrom Preconditioning
authors: Zachary Frangella, Joel A. Tropp, Madeleine Udell
venue: SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications 44(2):718-752 (2023); arXiv 2110.02820
summary: Nystrom PCG: a randomized rank-l Nystrom approximation A_hat of a PSD matrix A defines a preconditioner for the regularized system (A + mu I) x = b. The preconditioned condition number is bounded by a constant as soon as the rank is of the order of the effective dimension d_eff(mu) = tr(A (A + mu I)^{-1}), and adaptive variants find this rank automatically; experiments on large kernel ridge and data-analysis systems.
main_result: With a randomized Nystrom approximation A_hat = (A Omega)(Omega^T A Omega)^+ (A Omega)^T of rank l (Algorithm 2.1) and the preconditioner P = (1/(lambda_l(A_hat) + mu)) U (Lambda_hat + mu I) U^T + (I - U U^T) (eq. (5.3)), Theorem 5.1 (= Theorem 1.1): if the sketch size is l = 2 ceil(1.5 d_eff(mu)) + 1 then E[kappa_2(P^{-1/2}(A + mu I)P^{-1/2})] < 28; Corollary 5.2: conditioned on kappa_2 <= 56, Nystrom PCG started at x_0 = 0 has relative error (in the preconditioned-matrix norm) < 2 (0.77)^t, so O(log(1/eps)) iterations suffice; Theorem 4.2 gives the analogous accuracy guarantee for the direct Nystrom sketch-and-solve approximation; Section 5 gives adaptive rank selection without knowledge of d_eff. Cost: building the preconditioner O(l nnz(A) + l^2 n) (sketch size proportional to d_eff), applying it O(n l) per iteration.
relevance: B1 and 'effective dimension as the condition number after preconditioning': the linear-algebra core behind SketchySGD/PROMISE/SAPPHIRE preconditioners - the post-preconditioning condition number is O(1) once the rank matches d_eff(mu) = sum of ridge leverage scores. For the project's ridge/logistic experiments (B3) it gives a concrete recipe for a cheap fixed P with provable kappa_P = O(1) at cost O(r d) per SAGA step.

title: Dual-Free Stochastic Decentralized Optimization with Variance Reduction
authors: Hadrien Hendrikx, Francis Bach, Laurent Massoulie
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020); arXiv 2006.14384
summary: DVR is a decentralized variance-reduced method obtained by running Bregman coordinate descent on a dual formulation with a Bregman divergence built from the local functions (hence 'dual-free': only stochastic gradients of the local f_i are needed). It runs as fast as a centralized VR method on a 1/n fraction of the data, with an accelerated (Catalyst) version.
main_result: The dual problem is attacked by randomized Bregman coordinate descent with the reference function phi built from the conjugates of the local losses; the analysis assumes directional relative smoothness D_f(x + t e_i, x) <= L_rel^i D_phi(x + t e_i, x) (eq. (17)) and relative strong convexity D_f(x, y) >= sigma_rel D_phi(x, y) (eq. (18)); Theorem 3: with step eta_t such that eta_t L_rel^i < p_i for all i, the Lyapunov function L_t = D_phi(x*, x_t) + (eta_t/p_min)(F(x_t) - F(x*)) satisfies E[L_{t+1}] <= (1 - eta_t sigma_rel) L_t (the same with the constant 1/L_rel^max in place of eta_t/p_min); Theorem 1 gives the expected time to reach precision eps for DVR with the communication probability p_comm = (1 + sqrt(...(m + s)...))^{-1}-type choice (eq. (14): T = O(((m + s) + communication term)/ ... log(1/eps))), and Theorem 2 the Catalyst-accelerated complexity. (Exact constants of Theorems 1-2 not transcribed from the extracted text.) Cost per step: one local stochastic gradient (Bregman step) or one communication along an edge.
relevance: B1: a concrete instance, by Bach and coauthors, of a variance-reduced method analysed through relative smoothness/strong convexity with a non-Euclidean (dual) Bregman reference, i.e. the Bregman-SAGA machinery the project needs; the 'directional relative smoothness' constants L_rel^i are the per-component analogues of Bach's R^2 in the P-metric. Pipeline: shows how to write a VR proof in the Lyapunov style of Bach's notes when the metric is not Euclidean.

title: SDNA: Stochastic Dual Newton Ascent for Empirical Risk Minimization
authors: Zheng Qu, Peter Richtarik, Martin Takac, Olivier Fercoq
venue: Proceedings of the 33rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2016), PMLR 48:1823-1832; arXiv 1502.02268
summary: A dual method for l2-regularized ERM that at each iteration updates a random subset of tau dual coordinates by solving a proximal subproblem with the corresponding principal submatrix of the Hessian of the (quadratic) dual, thereby using all curvature information of the sampled examples; it provably dominates minibatch SDCA and, for quadratic losses, is a variant of the Iterative Hessian Sketch.
main_result: Assumptions: f has a block-smoothness matrix M (f(x + h) <= f(x) + <grad f(x), h> + (1/2) h^T M h) and a strong-convexity matrix G. Theorem 1: E[f(x_{k+1}) - f*] <= (1 - sigma_m) E[f(x_k) - f*] for the three methods (m = 1, 2, 3), with sigma_1 = lambda_min(G^{1/2} E[(M_S)^+] G^{1/2}) for SDNA (M_S the principal submatrix on the random block S), and Theorem 2: 0 < sigma_3 <= sigma_2 <= sigma_1 <= 1 (SDNA's rate dominates minibatch SDCA-type rates). Theorem 4 (Complexity of SDNA, uniform sampling with tau = E|S|): E[P(w_k) - D(alpha_k)] <= (1 - sigma(S_hat))^k ... with sigma(S_hat) explicit in the data Gram matrix, regularization and tau; Theorem 5: quadratic losses; Theorem 7: sigma(S_hat) >= the minibatch prox-SDCA rate; Theorem 8: interpretation as Iterative Hessian Sketch. Cost per iteration: solving a tau x tau system (O(tau^3)) plus O(tau d) for forming it.
relevance: B1 (alternative route to curvature): instead of a global metric P, SDNA uses exact curvature of the sampled block in the dual; its rate constant sigma_tau quantifies how much curvature a block of tau examples carries, which is related to leverage-type quantities of the data (large gains when examples are correlated). Useful for the project's discussion of what 'preconditioning' means for finite sums and as a contrast to SAGA in the primal (B1), and as another method whose constants are data-dependent (B2).

title: SAPPHIRE: Preconditioned Stochastic Variance Reduction for Faster Large-Scale Statistical Learning
authors: Jingruo Sun, Zachary Frangella, Madeleine Udell
venue: arXiv preprint 2501.15941 (Jan. 2025); no journal/conference version found on Crossref as of Nov. 2026
summary: Extends PROMISE-type sketch-based preconditioned variance reduction to composite problems with non-smooth regularizers (lasso, elastic net) via a scaled proximal mapping in the preconditioned metric. Proves linear convergence whose rate does not depend on the condition number (under a local assumption), and reports about 20x faster convergence than Catalyst, SAGA and SVRG on lasso and logistic regression, robust to infrequent preconditioner updates and to nonconvexity.
main_result: Abstract-level statement (full text not mined): a variance-reduced (SVRG-type) method with a sketched Hessian preconditioner P (cost O(r p) per step) and the scaled proximal map prox^P of the regularizer achieves condition-number-free linear convergence to the optimum under a local (quadratic-regularity-type) assumption, with batch size scaling with a local quantity rather than kappa; experiments on lasso and l1/l2 logistic regression; the advantage persists for non-convex objectives and infrequent preconditioner updates.
relevance: B1: shows that the P-metric SVRG analysis extends to composite objectives with prox^P (the counterpart of Bach's proximal SAGA remark) and that the fixed-P rate is governed by local curvature constants (B2). A4: a modern baseline for the preconditioned version of the empirical exponent experiments.

title: Bregman Stochastic Proximal Point Algorithm with Variance Reduction
authors: Cheik Traore, Peter Ochs
venue: arXiv preprint 2510.16655 (v1 Oct. 2025, v2 Jan. 2026); no journal/conference version found on Crossref
summary: Introduces SAGA-like and SVRG-like variance reduction for the Bregman stochastic proximal point algorithm (BSPPA) in non-Euclidean geometry, obtaining improved stability with constant step sizes and better rates with vanishing step sizes than vanilla BSPPA; the same variance-reduction techniques are recovered for Bregman SGD within a unified framework.
main_result: Abstract-level statement (full text not mined): for convex finite sums on a closed convex set with nonempty interior, with Bregman distance D_h, the variance-reduced BSPPA variants (SAGA- and SVRG-type) are stable under constant step sizes (convergence to the exact minimizer instead of a noise ball) and achieve improved convergence rates with vanishing step sizes compared with vanilla BSPPA; the analysis also covers Bregman SGD, recovering the same variance-reduction techniques; rates depend on relative smoothness/convexity constants w.r.t. h.
relevance: B1: most recent development of Bregman (P-metric and beyond) variance reduction, complementing Dragomir-Even-Hendrikx 2021; useful as a pointer for the 'non-quadratic P' discussion and for the proximal-point (implicit) counterpart of the preconditioned SAGA step.

title: Finite-sum optimization: Adaptivity to smoothness and loopless variance reduction
authors: Bastien Batardiere, Joon Kwon
venue: arXiv preprint 2307.12615 (v1 July 2023, v2 April 2024); no journal/conference version found on Crossref
summary: AdaLVR combines AdaGrad-type adaptive (diagonal/scalar) step sizes with loopless variance-reduced estimators (SAGA or L-SVRG). For convex L-smooth finite sums it attains O(n + (L + sqrt(nL))/eps) gradient complexity without knowledge of L; experiments also show that RMSprop/Adam-type scalings combined with VR estimators converge fast.
main_result: Theorem 1 (Algorithm 1 with p = 1/n, convex L-smooth f_i): a convergence rate of O((L + sqrt(nL))/T) in function value for AdaLVR (AdaGrad step with SAGA or L-SVRG gradient estimator), i.e. gradient complexity O(n + (L + sqrt(n L))/eps) to reach eps-suboptimality, adaptively (no knowledge of L), matching the known convex VR rates up to the sqrt(nL) term; diagonal scaling costs O(d) per step.
relevance: B1/B2: a SAGA/L-SVRG analysis with an adaptive (data-dependent, Mahalanobis-type diagonal) step, showing which VR proof steps tolerate a changing metric (the loopless SAGA/L-SVRG Lyapunov argument) in the convex case; a cheap diagonal-preconditioning baseline for (B3).

title: Stochastic Gradient Methods with Online Scaling
authors: Wanyu Zhang, Wenzhi Gao, Yinyu Ye, Madeleine Udell
venue: arXiv preprint 2609.11751 (v1 10 Sept. 2026, v2 11 Sept. 2026)
summary: Extends the online-scaled gradient framework (learning a preconditioner online by regret minimization) to stochastic optimization: SOSGM is analysed with large batches or with variance reduction, works with diagonal and low-rank preconditioners and heavy-ball momentum at Adam-like cost, and substantially outperforms adaptive first-order methods on statistical learning tasks; the introduction explicitly motivates the method by the poor behaviour of SVRG/SAGA/Katyusha on ill-conditioned data and by the cost of low-rank (SketchySGD/PROMISE) preconditioners on sparse data.
main_result: Abstract-level statement (full text not mined): under standard smoothness/convexity assumptions, SOSGM with either large batch sizes or variance reduction converges at rates that depend on the best preconditioner in the chosen family (diagonal or low-rank) in hindsight, with memory and computation comparable to Adam.
relevance: B1/B2: the most recent framework for choosing the metric P adaptively inside variance-reduced methods, with guarantees relative to the best fixed P in hindsight - a direct way to assess, on the project's instances, how far a fixed P is from the best fixed P (B3).

title: Utilizing Second Order Information in Minibatch Stochastic Variance Reduced Proximal Iterations
authors: Jialei Wang, Tong Zhang
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 20(42):1-56 (2019); preprint arXiv 1706.07001 (v2 Oct. 2017) under the title 'Improved Optimization of Finite Sums with Minibatch Stochastic Variance Reduced Proximal Iterations'
summary: Minibatch methods for ERM of linear predictors that combine variance-reduced first-order information with sub-sampled higher-order (Hessian) information inside proximal iterations (plus acceleration), with improved iteration complexity over the state of the art; global fast convergence for quadratic objectives and local fast convergence for general convex objectives. The analysis works in a preconditioned space where the relevant quantities are the effective dimension and the statistical leverage at the regularization level.
main_result: Definition 5 (effective dimension d_lambda of the Hessian H_0(w) = (1/n) sum_i l''(w^T x_i) x_i x_i^T at level lambda) and Definition 6 (statistical leverage at lambda: the leverage scores of the data matrix w.r.t. H(w) = H_0(w) + lambda I are bounded by a constant chi); Theorem 10 (L-smooth, lambda-strongly convex components): iteration complexity of the minibatch stochastic variance-reduced proximal iteration with sub-sampled Hessian preconditioning in terms of the minibatch size, d_lambda and chi; Theorem 12 (ill-conditioned problems, L/lambda >= n^{3/2}): choice of the regularization/sub-sampling parameters giving the improved complexity; Theorem 13: rate of the accelerated variant IMBA-SVRG; the sub-sampling size and the condition number of the preconditioned problem are controlled by the effective dimension and the statistical leverage (bounded leverage holds e.g. for sub-Gaussian designs). (Statement at the level of the theorem headings and definitions; exact expressions not transcribed.)
relevance: B1 and leverage scores/effective dimension: an early reference tying the minibatch size and the preconditioned condition number of VR methods to ridge leverage scores and d_eff; complements Gonen et al. and PROMISE for the quadratic case.

title: Accelerating SVRG via second-order information
authors: Ritesh Kolte, Murat Erdogdu, Ayfer Ozgur
venue: OPT 2015: 8th NIPS Workshop on Optimization for Machine Learning (Montreal, Dec. 2015), workshop paper (listed on the workshop's accepted-papers page opt-ml.org/oldopt/opt15/papers.html); PDF hosted at cs.toronto.edu/~erdogdu/papers/asvrg-opt.pdf
summary: Proposes two ways to precondition SVRG while keeping O(p)-type per-iteration cost: SVRG+I uses, per epoch, a subsampled Hessian whose spectrum is truncated after the top r singular values (H^{-1} = Q(Sigma_r^{-1} - sigma_{r+1}^{-1} I) Q^T + sigma_{r+1}^{-1} I, applied in O(rp)), and SVRG+II uses L-BFGS built from full-gradient differences at epoch boundaries (metric fixed within an epoch). Experiments on l2-regularized logistic regression (mnist, covtype, ...) show SVRG+II is by far the fastest.
main_result: Each epoch of SVRG+I is vanilla SVRG applied to the transformed functions psi_i(H^{-1/2} w), so linear convergence follows with step O(1/L') and epoch length Omega(L'/lambda') where L' and lambda' are the smoothness and strong-convexity constants in the H-metric; Lemma 1 (matrix Hoeffding on the subsampled Hessian with |S| samples): L' <= L_H + O(L sqrt(log p/|S|)) and lambda' >= lambda_H - O(lambda sqrt(log p/|S|)) (constants of the thresholded Hessian metric), so the preconditioned condition number is controlled by the subsample size; for SVRG+II the proof of Moritz et al. applies with little change; per-step cost O(rp) (SVRG+I) or O(Mp) (SVRG+II), plus O(rp^2) per epoch for the truncated SVD.
relevance: B1: the earliest explicit 'SVRG in a fixed metric per epoch' with the change-of-variables argument (preconditioned SVRG = SVRG on P^{-1/2}-transformed functions) that the project can reuse for SAGA, and a cheap low-rank-plus-identity P with O(rp) application cost; its empirical observation that a fixed per-epoch L-BFGS metric with exact gradient differences works best is relevant to (B3).

title: RSN: Randomized Subspace Newton
authors: Robert M. Gower, Dmitry Kovalev, Felix Lieder, Peter Richtarik
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (NeurIPS 2019); arXiv 1905.10874
summary: A sketched Newton method x_{k+1} = x_k - (1/L_hat) S_k (S_k^T grad^2 f(x_k) S_k)^+ S_k^T grad f(x_k) with a random sketch S_k in R^{d x s}, analysed under 'relative smoothness and relative convexity' of f with respect to its own Hessian (constants L_hat >= mu_hat > 0), a condition weaker than c-stability and satisfied by generalized linear models. Gives global linear convergence with a rate that is the relative condition number L_hat/mu_hat times a sketch-quality factor, and recovers Newton's method for S = I.
main_result: Assumption 1 (relative smoothness/convexity w.r.t. the Hessian H(y) = grad^2 f(y)): mu_hat/2 ||x - y||^2_{H(y)} <= f(x) - f(y) - <grad f(y), x - y> <= L_hat/2 ||x - y||^2_{H(y)} for all x, y (eqs. (3)-(4)); Assumption 2: grad f(x) in Range(H(x)). Theorem 2: with G(x) = E_S[S (S^T H(x) S)^+ S^T] and rho = min_x lambda_min^+ of H(x)^{1/2} G(x) H(x)^{1/2} on Range(H(x)) (rho in (0, 1], rho = 1 for S = I), E[f(x_k)] - f* <= (1 - rho mu_hat/L_hat)^k (f(x_0) - f*), hence k >= (L_hat/(rho mu_hat)) log((f(x_0) - f*)/eps) iterations suffice (eq. (16)); Theorem 3 (mu_hat = 0): E[f(x_k)] - f* <= 2 L_hat R^2/(rho k). Lemma 8: formula for L_hat and mu_hat as extreme values of ratios of Bregman divergences of f to Hessian-weighted squared distances; c-stable functions have L_hat <= c and mu_hat >= 1/c; Proposition 1: generalized linear models with 0 < u <= phi_i'' <= ... satisfy Assumption 1 with explicit constants. Cost per iteration: s Hessian-vector products (or an s x s sketched Hessian) and an s x s solve, O(s^2 d + s^3).
relevance: B1/B2: Assumption 1 is exactly the pair of constants (gamma_u, gamma_l 'quadratic regularity') that PROMISE and SketchySGD build on (they cite this paper for the notion): with P = grad^2 F(w_0) (Hessian preconditioning) the constants replacing R^2 and mu in Bach's Prop. 5.9 are L_hat and mu_hat, whose ratio is 1 for quadratics and tends to 1 locally - the cleanest explanation of why a Hessian-type P removes kappa from the rate and of what remains (the sketch factor rho, the batch/dissimilarity factor of PROMISE). L_hat/mu_hat measured along the trajectory is a natural 'trajectory-dependent constant' for (B2).

title: Weighted SGD for l_p Regression with Randomized Preconditioning
authors: Jiyan Yang, Yin-Lam Chow, Christopher Re, Michael W. Mahoney
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 18(211):1-43 (2018); conference version in Proceedings of the ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA 2016); arXiv 1502.03571
summary: pwSGD for l_1 and l_2 regression min ||Ax - b||_p: first compute, by randomized sketching, a preconditioner R such that U = A R^{-1} is a well-conditioned basis (condition number kappa_bar_p(U) = poly(d), independent of n and of kappa(A)), then run SGD on the preconditioned problem with rows sampled proportionally to (approximate) leverage scores ||U_i||_p. The number of SGD iterations then depends only on d, and the total time is O(log n * nnz(A) + poly(d) ...), competitive with the best randomized linear algebra solvers.
main_result: Definitions 1-2: (alpha, beta, p)-well-conditioned bases and l_p leverage scores lambda_i = ||U_i||_p^p; Proposition 4: the preconditioned basis U = A R^{-1} from sketching has condition number kappa_bar_p(U) = poly(d). Proposition 6 (l_2, F = R^{-1}): with a suitable step size, after T = c_1 kappa_bar_2^2(U) log(c_2 kappa_bar_2^2(U)/eps) (1 + kappa_bar_2^2(U)/eps)-type iterations (gamma the leverage-score approximation factor enters c_1), pwSGD returns x_T with E||A(x_T - x*)||^2/||A x*||^2 <= eps; Proposition 5: the analogous l_1 result with kappa_bar_1(U)/eps^2 dependence; Proposition 7 (total complexity): time(R) + O(log n * nnz(A) + d^3 log(1/eps)/eps) for unconstrained l_2 regression and time(R) + O(log n * nnz(A) + d^3 kappa_bar_1(U)/eps^2) for l_1, i.e. O(log n * nnz(A) + poly(d)/eps^2)-type overall with sparse preconditioners; the rate is robust to crude leverage-score approximations (e.g. gamma = 0.5). Without the preconditioner the SGD iteration count depends on kappa(A) and on the leverage-score distribution of A (Section 3.3 example).
relevance: B1 + leverage scores: the clearest statement that 'preconditioning plus leverage-score sampling' turns the condition number of a least-squares finite sum into a function of d only (well-conditioned basis), i.e. after whitening the sampling difficulty is entirely captured by the leverage scores; it is the SGD counterpart of Gonen et al.'s preconditioned SVRG and is the 'weighted and preconditioned SGD' that Derezinski's SVRN cites for its leverage-score result. For the project (B3/A4) it motivates measuring leverage scores of the (whitened) design on the anisotropic logistic/ridge instances and explains the role of coherence after preconditioning.

title: A Stochastic Quasi-Newton Method for Large-Scale Optimization
authors: Richard H. Byrd, S. L. Hansen, Jorge Nocedal, Yoram Singer
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization 26(2):1008-1031 (2016); arXiv 1401.7020
summary: SQN: stochastic gradient steps w_{k+1} = w_k - alpha_k H_k grad F_S(w_k) with an L-BFGS inverse-Hessian approximation H_k whose curvature pairs (s, y) are formed every L iterations from subsampled Hessian-vector products (batch b_H) at averaged iterates, rather than from noisy gradient differences; this is the stochastic quasi-Newton metric later combined with variance reduction by Moritz et al. (SLBFGS), Gower et al. (block BFGS) and Kolte et al.
main_result: Lemma 3.1: under Assumption 1 (the subsampled Hessians satisfy lambda I <= grad^2 F_S <= Lambda I), the limited-memory BFGS matrices generated by Algorithm 1 satisfy mu_1 I <= H_t <= mu_2 I for some 0 < mu_1 <= mu_2 (eq. (3.4)), with explicit constants from the trace/determinant bounds on the direct approximations B_t. Theorem 3.2 (strongly convex F, bounded gradient variance, Assumptions 2): for the Newton-like iteration w_{k+1} = w_k - alpha_k H_k grad f(w_k, xi_k) with mu_1 I <= H_k <= mu_2 I and alpha_k = beta/k, beta > 1/(2 mu_1), E[F(w_k) - F*] <= Q(beta)/k for all k, with Q(beta) = max{L mu_2^2 beta^2 sigma^2/(2(2 mu_1 beta - 1)), F(w_1) - F*}-type (eqs. (3.16)-(3.17)), i.e. the usual O(1/k) SGD rate with the step scaled by the eigenvalue bounds of the metric. Cost per iteration: b gradient samples plus 4Md for the two-loop recursion and, every L iterations, b_H Hessian-vector products (about 3 b_H n flops for logistic regression), so the overhead of curvature pairs is (2 b_H/L)/b relative to the gradient cost.
relevance: B1: the origin of the quasi-Newton metric used by SLBFGS, Stochastic Block BFGS and VITE (all in this list), and of the analysis style that only exploits mu_1 I <= H <= mu_2 I; it therefore shows, already without variance reduction, that the proof pays mu_2/mu_1-type factors because it never uses the fact that H approximates the Hessian - the same 'loose step' that B1 asks the project to identify for preconditioned SAGA. Also the template for a cheap P refreshed every L steps with Hessian-vector products (O(b_H d)) that can be plugged into the project's SAGA runs.

title: Communication Complexity of Distributed Convex Learning and Optimization
authors: Yossi Arjevani, Ohad Shamir
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28 (NIPS 2015); arXiv 1506.01900
summary: Lower bounds on the number of communication rounds needed to minimize an average F = (1/m) sum_i F_i of local functions held by m machines, for a broad class of algorithms (Assumption 1: iterates built from spans of local gradients/Hessian-vector products, with unlimited local computation), both when the local functions are unrelated and when they are delta-related (||grad^2 F_i - grad^2 F_j|| <= delta, Definition 1), the latter modelling statistically similar data; this is the lower bound against which DANE, AIDE, DiSCO, SPAG and Kovalev et al. are measured.
main_result: Theorem 1: for any even m, lambda in [0,1) and delta in (0,1), there exist 1-smooth, lambda-strongly convex, delta-related quadratics on R^d (d large enough) such that any algorithm satisfying Assumption 1 needs Omega(sqrt(delta/lambda) log(||w*||^2/eps)) communication rounds to reach F(w_hat) - F* <= eps (an Omega(sqrt(delta/eps))-type bound when lambda = 0); with delta = Theta(1) (unrelated functions) this is the Omega(sqrt(1/lambda) log(1/eps)) and Omega(sqrt(1/eps)) rounds matched by a distributed implementation of accelerated gradient descent, so unbounded local computation does not help in the unrelated case. Theorem 2: polynomial-in-1/eps lower bounds for non-smooth Lipschitz local functions (strongly convex and merely convex). Theorem 3: an assumption-free lower bound for one-round algorithms communicating at most d^2/128 bits (suboptimality at least c delta^2 for delta-related strongly convex quadratics). The sqrt(delta/lambda) log(1/eps) bound is matched up to constants and logs for quadratics by DiSCO (Zhang-Xiao 2015) and, as shown later, by AIDE and by Kovalev et al.'s sliding for general strongly convex smooth functions.
relevance: A1/B1: the preconditioned analogue of the project's lower bound (A1): under Hessian similarity delta (the regime of statistical preconditioning by a local Hessian), no span-based scheme beats sqrt(delta/lambda) log(1/eps) rounds, i.e. the square root of the relative condition number 1 + delta/lambda is the right target for accelerated preconditioned methods (SPAG, AIDE, DiSCO, Kovalev et al.), and Lin et al. (2023) extend the construction to the stochastic finite-sum setting (n^{3/4} sqrt(delta/mu)). It also shares the 'span' assumption with the A1 argument, which clarifies what the project's lower bound does and does not cover once a non-Euclidean metric is allowed.

title: Performance of first-order methods for smooth convex minimization: a novel approach
authors: Yoel Drori, Marc Teboulle
venue: Mathematical Programming 145(1-2):451-482
summary: Founding paper of the Performance Estimation Problem (PEP): the worst-case behaviour of a black-box first-order method over L-smooth convex functions after N steps is itself an optimization problem over functions and initial conditions, relaxed to a convex semidefinite program. Applied to the gradient method, to a class containing heavy-ball and fast-gradient schemes, and to step-size selection.
main_result: Theorem 3.1 (confirmed in the text): for the fixed-step gradient method x_{k+1} = x_k - (h/L) f'(x_k) on L-smooth convex f with ||x_0 - x*|| <= R, f(x_N) - f* <= L R^2/(4 N h + 2) for h in (0,1], attained by a Huber-type one-dimensional function; Conjecture 3.1 (gradient method, h in (1,2)) and Conjecture 4.1 (fast gradient method, numerically supported bounds about a factor 2 better than 2 L R^2/(N+1)^2) are left as conjectures; the SDP is also used to compute optimal step sizes.
relevance: Pipeline/B3: the SDP dual multipliers of a PEP say exactly which inequalities (cocoercivity, convexity, strong convexity) are active in the worst case, the theoretical counterpart of the 'tightness ratio per inequality' of B3; a step with zero multiplier is provably not the bottleneck. Foundation for all computer-aided analyses of SAGA/SVRG listed below.

title: Smooth strongly convex interpolation and exact worst-case performance of first-order methods
authors: Adrien B. Taylor, Julien M. Hendrickx, François Glineur
venue: Mathematical Programming 161(1-2):307-345
summary: Gives closed-form necessary and sufficient conditions for a finite set of (point, gradient, value) triples to be interpolable by an L-smooth mu-strongly convex function, which makes the PEP of any fixed-step first-order method an exact, dimension-independent SDP (no relaxation). Worst-case functions are recovered constructively from the SDP solution.
main_result: Theorem 4 (F_{mu,L}-interpolability, confirmed): {(x_i, g_i, f_i)} is F_{mu,L}-interpolable iff for all i,j: f_i >= f_j + <g_j, x_i - x_j> + (1/(2(1 - mu/L))) [ (1/L)||g_i - g_j||^2 + mu ||x_i - x_j||^2 - (2 mu/L) <g_j - g_i, x_j - x_i> ]. Corollary 3: the exact worst case of any fixed-step method on F_{mu,L} is the value of a finite SDP. Section 4 (confirmed): gradient method with step h/L: ||x_N - x*|| <= kappa^N ||x_0 - x*|| with kappa = max{|1 - h mu/L|, |1 - h|}, and f(x_N) - f* <= L R^2 max(kappa_1^{2N}, kappa_2^{2N}) up to the stated constants; several function-value bounds are stated as numerically supported conjectures.
relevance: B3: the inequalities instrumented in the project (cocoercivity of each f_i, strong convexity of F) are special cases of these interpolation inequalities; because they are necessary AND sufficient, any proof using only them can be checked for slack by an SDP, which gives the reference 'tight' rate against which measured tightness ratios can be compared. B1: with a preconditioner P the Euclidean interpolation inequalities must be combined with linear-operator interpolation (see bousselmi2024interpolation).

title: Analysis and design of optimization algorithms via integral quadratic constraints
authors: Laurent Lessard, Benjamin Recht, Andrew Packard
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization 26(1):57-95
summary: Imports Integral Quadratic Constraints from robust control: an iterative method is a linear system in feedback with the gradient nonlinearity; properties of F_{mu,L} are encoded as quadratic constraints (sector/one-point condition at x*, and a 'weighted off-by-one' IQC derived from cocoercivity) and a small LMI certifies a linear rate. Applied to gradient, heavy-ball and Nesterov methods, including a design use.
main_result: Object: x_{k+1} = A x_k + B u_k, u_k = f'(C x_k) with f in F_{mu,L} (or the one-point sector class S(mu,L)); certificate: feasibility of the LMI [A^T P A - rho^2 P, A^T P B; B^T P A, B^T P B] + lambda M(mu,L) <= 0 with P > 0 gives ||x_k - x*|| <= sqrt(cond(P)) rho^k ||x_0 - x*||. Rates: gradient method with step 2/(L+mu): rho = (kappa-1)/(kappa+1) (tight); Nesterov's method: numerically computed rates that are 'slightly sharper bounds than Nesterov's' (the arXiv v7 note corrects an earlier misquoted textbook rate); heavy-ball (Section 4.6, Appendix B, confirmed): an explicit one-dimensional strongly convex function with condition ratio 25 on which heavy-ball with Polyak's quadratic-optimal parameters converges to a limit cycle, i.e. does not converge.
relevance: A2: generic warning that momentum tuned for quadratics (naive acceleration) can diverge outside quadratics, so an explicit Lyapunov certificate is needed (A3). B2: the sector IQC is a one-point condition at x* (the same type as mu_eff(t) >= mu), so IQC rates are naturally stated with trajectory-type constants. B3: the LMI multipliers lambda identify which constraint binds, the SDP analogue of the per-inequality tightness ratio.

title: Lyapunov functions for first-order methods: tight automated convergence guarantees
authors: Adrien Taylor, Bryan Van Scoy, Laurent Lessard
summary: Merges PEP interpolation inequalities with the IQC/Lyapunov viewpoint: for a method with a given state (e.g. x_k, x_{k-1}, f'(x_{k-1})), a small SDP returns the fastest linear rate that can be certified by a quadratic Lyapunov function (plus function-value term) with that state. Applied to gradient, heavy-ball, Nesterov and triple-momentum methods.
main_result: Theorem 5 (main result): for a fixed-step first-order method on F_{mu,L} with state xi_k = (x_k, g_k, f_k), the existence of a quadratic Lyapunov function V(xi_k) = (xi_k - xi*)^T P (xi_k - xi*) + p (f(x_k) - f*) with V(xi_{k+1}) <= rho^2 V(xi_k) for ALL f in the class is equivalent to the feasibility of a small SDP built from interpolation inequalities (necessary and sufficient within that Lyapunov class); bisection on rho gives the best certifiable rate; the method recovers known tight rates (gradient descent, triple momentum rho = 1 - 1/sqrt(kappa)) and shows when a Lyapunov of a given structure provably cannot certify a desired rate, in which case one must enlarge the state.
relevance: B3/pipeline: gives a precise meaning to 'the Lyapunov analysis of Prop. 5.9 is tight': compare the measured one-step contraction of V_t to the best rho certifiable with the structure (||theta - eta*||^2 + Delta sum ||z_i - f_i'(eta*)||^2). B1: a preconditioned step changes only the (A,B) matrices, so the same SDP quantifies which inequality becomes loose.

title: Stochastic first-order methods: non-asymptotic and computer-aided analyses via potential functions
authors: Adrien Taylor, Francis Bach
summary: Computer-aided design of potential (Lyapunov) functions for deterministic and stochastic first-order methods: verifying one potential inequality phi_{k+1} <= phi_k + e_k over a function class is an SDP, so sequences of potentials (hence sublinear rates) can be designed and checked numerically, then proved analytically. Covers gradient/proximal/accelerated methods, SGD under a unified variance model, SGD with averaging, over-parametrized (interpolation) models and bounded variance at x*, and randomized block-coordinate descent. CHECKED in the full text: Table 1 lists the 'Finite sums' setting (f_i in F_L, G(x;i) = grad f_i(x)) as '(not presented)', and the conclusion only says 'minor adaptations allow studying algorithms specifically designed for finite sums problems' (citing SAG, SVRG, SAGA).
main_result: Proposition 1: a tuple (phi_{k+1}, phi_k, e_k) is a valid potential inequality for all f in the class and all admissible oracles iff a sup-problem (an SDP for quadratic potentials, Remark 2) is nonpositive, so the approach fails only if no potential with the chosen structure exists ('tightness relative to the potential structure'). Settings treated (Table 1): no noise (Sec. 3.2.1), unified variance model E_i||G||^2 <= sigma^2 + 2 delta L (f - f*) + ... (Sec. 3.2.2), over-parametrized models f_i'(x*) = 0 (Sec. 4) generalized to variance sigma^2 at x* (App. H), block-coordinate descent (App. I, Theorems 16-17 for f in F_L and F_{mu,L}); finite sums are not presented.
relevance: Pipeline/A3: this is exactly the 'Lyapunov style of Bach's notes' automated; the project can reproduce the SAGA/L-Katyusha potential inequalities as one-step SDPs (the finite-sum extension the paper leaves open, done in PEPit's SAGA example). B3: the SDP value is the theoretical tightness bound of the whole chain for the chosen V_t, to be compared with empirical tightness ratios.

title: A unified analysis of stochastic optimization methods using jump system theory and quadratic constraints
authors: Bin Hu, Peter Seiler, Anders Rantzer
venue: COLT 2017, PMLR 65:1157-1189 (COLT, not ICML; confirmed on the PMLR page and in the arXiv comment)
summary: Models SAGA, SAG, Finito and SDCA as Markov jump linear systems xi^{k+1} = A_{i_k} xi^k + B_{i_k} w^k with w^k = [grad f_1(v^k); ...; grad f_n(v^k)] and i_k i.i.d. uniform; combines jump-system Lyapunov theory with quadratic constraints on each f_i to get LMI certificates whose size, after exploiting symmetry (Table 2), is at most 3x3. Analytical rates for SAGA, Finito, SDCA with and without individual convexity are read off feasible LMI points; numerics show the LMI can certify sharper rates than the analytical ones; the basic LMI does not recover the known rate of SAG (whose proof needs function-value coupling).
main_result: Classes: F(m,L) = m-strongly convex L-smooth; S(m,L) = functions with a unique minimizer satisfying the one-point sector constraint at x* (no convexity needed; F(m,L) subset of S(m,L)); each f_i satisfies a quadratic constraint with parameter gamma = -m (f_i in F(m,L)), 0 (convex), L (only smooth). Lyapunov: E[||x^k - x*||^2 + (p_1/p_2) sum_i ||y_i^k - grad f_i(x*)||^2] <= rho^{2k} R^0 (same structure as Bach's V_t). Corollary 3 (SAGA, g in S(m,L), confirmed in the text): (i) f_i in F(m,L), 0 < alpha <= 1/(2L): rate 1 - min{(2 L alpha - 1)/((L alpha - 1) n), 2 m alpha - alpha m^2/((1 - L alpha) L)} (eq. 39), plus a second bound (40) for alpha <= 4/(9L); the paper notes that (39) 'works better under the big data condition while (40) is less conservative with large condition number L/m'; (ii) f_i in F(0,L), alpha <= 1/(2L), b in [2 L alpha, 1]: rate 1 - min{(2 L alpha - b)/((L alpha - b) n), 2(1-b) m alpha - m^2 alpha (1-b)^2/((2 - b - L alpha) L)} (eq. 41); at alpha = 1/(3L), b = 5/6: 1 - min{1/(3n), m/(10L)} (eq. 42) with R^0 = ||x^0 - x*||^2 + (5/(18 L^2)) sum ||y_i^0 - grad f_i(x*)||^2; (iii) f_i only L-smooth (possibly nonconvex), alpha = m/(8L^2): 1 - min{1/(2n), 3 m^2/(32 L^2)} (eq. 44), and alpha = m/(4(m^2 n + L^2)) gives 1 - m^2/(8(m^2 n + L^2)) (eq. 45), i.e. complexity O~((L^2/m^2 + n) log(1/eps)). Corollary 3 also gives analytical rates for Finito (under a big data condition) and SDCA without duality. Appendix B (confirmed quotes): 'one may get sharper rate bounds for SAGA using our proposed LMI' and 'the numerical results obtained by the proposed semidefinite programs actually inspire our analytical proofs'. Compare Bach Prop. 5.9: gamma = 1/(4R^2), rate 1 - min{1/(3n), 3 mu/(16 R^2)}.
relevance: B3 (central): identical Lyapunov structure to Bach's V_t with weight p_1/p_2 playing the role of Delta; solving the 3x3 LMI gives the best rate for that structure, and the multipliers expose which of the square-norm/cocoercivity/strong-convexity steps are slack per (n, kappa) regime. B2: the whole analysis only needs g in S(m,L), a one-point curvature condition at x*, so m can be replaced by the trajectory constant mu_eff; also shows rates differ with 'individual convexity' of the f_i (relevant to the cocoercivity step). B1: a preconditioner P^{-1} enters the (A,B) matrices; the Kronecker reduction requires P to act identically on all memory slots.

title: Analysis of biased stochastic gradient descent using sequential semidefinite programs
authors: Bin Hu, Peter Seiler, Laurent Lessard
venue: Mathematical Programming 187(1-2):383-408 (online 2020)
summary: Convergence analysis of biased SGD x_{k+1} = x_k - alpha_k (u_k + e_k), u_k = grad f_{i_k}(x_k), with an error model unifying relative and absolute errors, via stochastic quadratic constraints yielding a small LMI; a sequential minimization of SDPs handles arbitrary time-varying step sizes and maps the trade-offs between step size, linear rate, final accuracy and robustness, with closed-form bounds under several assumptions on the f_i (strongly convex, one-point conditions).
main_result: Error model (1.4): ||e_k||^2 <= delta^2 ||u_k||^2 + c^2 (delta = relative, c = absolute error; delta = c = 0 is standard SGD). An LMI in (rho^2, multipliers) certifies E||x_k - x*||^2 <= rho^{2k} ||x_0 - x*||^2 + H (bounds of the form (1.7)); solved numerically (sequential SDP for time-varying alpha_k) and analytically: for constant step size rho^2 = 1 - (m^2 - delta^2 M~) alpha + O(alpha^2) and H = (c^2 + 2 delta^2 G^2)/(m^2 - delta^2 M~) + O(alpha), where M~ and G^2 are constants fixed by the assumptions on the f_i; the limiting error (c^2 + 2 delta^2 G^2)/(m^2 - delta^2 M~) is 'uncontrollable' (cannot be shrunk by the step size). Note: PEPit's SGD example credits its one-step bound to the PESTO code (Taylor-Hendrickx-Glineur 2017) and cites this paper only for the SDP methodology.
relevance: B3: the 'variance <= second moment' step of Prop. 5.9 is a stochastic quadratic constraint; this paper shows how such constraints are kept tight inside an LMI and how a bias term propagates to a floor. B2: closed forms under one-point conditions at x* (mu_eff-type).

title: Potential-function proofs for first-order methods
authors: Nikhil Bansal, Anupam Gupta
venue: Theory of Computing 15(4):1-32
summary: Expository note giving unified potential-function (Lyapunov) proofs of the standard rates of gradient descent (smooth, strongly convex, non-smooth), mirror descent and Nesterov-type accelerated methods: in each case a scalar potential Phi_k = A_k (f(x_k) - f*) + (L/2)||z_k - x*||^2 (or a Bregman analogue) is shown to be non-increasing, which yields the rate from the growth of A_k. No stochastic or finite-sum methods (the paper itself notes that Taylor and Bach 2019 followed up on its preprint for stochastic methods).
main_result: Gradient descent, L-smooth convex, step 1/L: Phi_k = k (f(x_k) - f*) + (L/2)||x_k - x*||^2 is non-increasing, hence f(x_k) - f* <= L||x_0 - x*||^2/(2k); strongly convex: ||x_k - x*||^2 contracts by (1 - mu/L); accelerated gradient: with A_k ~ k^2/4 and an auxiliary sequence z_k, Phi_k = A_k (f(x_k) - f*) + (L/2)||z_k - x*||^2 is non-increasing, hence O(L||x_0 - x*||^2/k^2); mirror descent via Bregman potentials.
relevance: Pipeline/A3: the pedagogical template for the Lyapunov proof style of Bach's notes used to reproduce the L-Katyusha argument (A3) in the same style; shows that acceleration = coupling a function-value term with a distance term with growing weights, which is what the negative-momentum term makes possible with a stochastic estimator.

title: Automated tight Lyapunov analysis for first-order methods
authors: Manu Upadhyaya, Sebastian Banert, Adrien B. Taylor, Pontus Giselsson
venue: Mathematical Programming 209(1-2):133-170 (online 2024; print volume 2025)
summary: For first-order methods written as linear state-space systems in feedback with the subdifferentials of the components of a finite-sum convex problem (components possibly strongly convex and/or smooth), gives a necessary and sufficient condition, checkable by a small SDP, for the existence of a quadratic Lyapunov inequality in a predefined class. Deterministic methods only (no sampling, confirmed in the abstract and method list); application extends the parameter region for duality-gap convergence of Chambolle-Pock with identity operator.
main_result: Abstract/Section 2 (confirmed): a quadratic Lyapunov inequality (quadratic in the state plus linear in function values, with a residual term) holds for all problem instances in the class iff a small-sized SDP built from interpolation inequalities is feasible, so the obtained rates are tight with respect to the Lyapunov class ('automated tight Lyapunov analysis'); illustrated on gradient, accelerated and primal-dual methods (Section 2.5.5 Chambolle-Pock); for Chambolle-Pock with identity operator the parameter region for duality-gap convergence is significantly extended.
relevance: Pipeline/B3: the formal 'tightness w.r.t. Lyapunov class' statement for finite-sum structure (deterministic analogues of SAGA steps); B1: preconditioned deterministic updates fit the linear state-space model, so which inequality becomes loose with P can be diagnosed by SDP before experiments.

title: PEPit: computer-assisted worst-case analyses of first-order optimization methods in Python
authors: Baptiste Goujaud, Céline Moucer, François Glineur, Julien M. Hendrickx, Adrien B. Taylor, Aymeric Dieuleveut
venue: Mathematical Programming Computation 16(3):337-367 (arXiv 2022)
summary: Python package that turns the description of a first-order method (gradient, proximal, projection, linear-optimization oracles, Bregman/approximate variants) into the PEP SDP and solves it. The paper showcases point-SAGA (Section 5.3); the package's documented examples include SGD (bounded variance at x*, over-parametrized), SAGA, point-SAGA and randomized coordinate descent, each checking a one-step Lyapunov contraction against the published bound.
main_result: Example wc_saga (confirmed in the source file): Lyapunov V^(t) = (1/n) sum_i [f_i(phi_i^(t)) - f_i(x*) - <grad f_i(x*), phi_i^(t) - x*>] + (1/(2 n gamma (1 - mu gamma))) ||x^(t) - x*||^2 with gamma = 1/(2 (mu n + L)); for L = 1, mu = 0.1, n = 5 PEPit returns worst-case E[V^(1)] <= 0.966667 V^(0), equal to the theoretical 1 - gamma mu = 0.966667, i.e. Defazio et al. (2014, Thm 1) is tight for this Lyapunov. Example wc_point_saga (confirmed): V = (1/(L mu)) (1/n) sum_i ||grad f_i(x) - grad f_i(x*)||^2 + ||x - x*||^2, gamma = sqrt((n-1)^2 + 4 n L/mu)/(2 L n) - (1 - 1/n)/(2L); for L = 1, mu = 0.01, n = 10 PEPit gives 0.971405 vs the bound 1/(1 + mu gamma) = 0.973292 (Defazio 2016, Thm 5), slightly loose. Example wc_sgd (confirmed): one-step bound (gamma (L - mu) R/2 + sqrt((1 - gamma (L + mu)/2)^2 R^2 + gamma^2 v^2))^2, 'empirically tight', credited to the PESTO code of Taylor-Hendrickx-Glineur (2017).
relevance: B3 (tool): plug Bach's V_t (Delta = 3 gamma^2, gamma = 1/(4R^2)) into PEPit to get the exact one-step worst-case contraction and compare it with 1 - min{1/(3n), 3 mu/(16 R^2)}; the SDP dual gives the theoretical tightness ratio of each inequality, to be set against the empirical ratios on logistic regression. A3: same for the L-Katyusha potential. Note the SAGA example uses the function-value Lyapunov (Defazio) rather than the gradient-memory Lyapunov of Bach's notes; both can be encoded.

title: The AutoLyap software suite for computer-assisted Lyapunov analyses of first-order methods
authors: Manu Upadhyaya, Shuvomoy Das Gupta, Adrien B. Taylor, Sebastian Banert, Pontus Giselsson
venue: arXiv preprint 2506.24076 (v2, March 2026)
summary: Python/Julia software implementing the automated-Lyapunov methodology of Upadhyaya et al. (2024): checks, via an SDP, whether a Lyapunov analysis exists for a wide class of first-order methods on structured optimization and inclusion problems, and is used to verify and extend several convergence results.
