The abstract and the full text do not mention stochastic or variance-reduced methods (SAGA/SVRG absent).
main_result: Software result (abstract, confirmed): the user specifies (i) the problem class, (ii) the method and (iii) the type of Lyapunov analysis; AutoLyap builds and solves the SDP that decides existence of such a Lyapunov analysis; the suite reproduces and extends known rates (deterministic/operator-splitting setting).
relevance: Pipeline: candidate tool, alongside PEPit, for the computer-aided part of B3/B1 for the deterministic skeleton of SAGA-type updates (expected-step analyses); stochastic support not provided per the opened text.

title: Interpolation conditions for linear operators and applications to performance estimation problems
authors: Nizar Bousselmi, Julien M. Hendrickx, François Glineur
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization 34(3):3033-3063
summary: Extends PEP to methods involving linear operators by deriving necessary and sufficient interpolation conditions for two classes: matrices with bounded singular values and symmetric matrices with eigenvalues in a given interval. Applied to the gradient method on h(Mx), to Chambolle-Pock (exact primal-dual gap rate), and to last-iterate primal accuracy.
main_result: For a finite list (x_i, y_i), existence of M in the class (e.g. symmetric with spectrum in [mu_M, L_M]) with M x_i = y_i is characterized by explicit Gram-matrix conditions, so worst-case bounds over all such operators become SDPs; (abstract, confirmed) the exact worst case of the gradient method on the composed objective h o M 'always corresponds to M being a scaling operator'; exact convergence rate of the primal-dual gap for Chambolle-Pock on f + g o M.
relevance: B1 (direct): theta_t = theta_{t-1} - gamma P^{-1} g_t involves the symmetric operator P^{-1} with spectrum in [1/lambda_max(P), 1/lambda_min(P)]; these interpolation conditions let one compute the exact worst-case contraction of preconditioned SAGA over all admissible P (not just a fixed one) and identify which proof step (cocoercivity in the Euclidean vs P-norm) becomes loose.

title: New optimisation methods for machine learning
authors: Aaron Defazio
venue: PhD thesis, The Australian National University (2014); arXiv 1510.02533 (2015), 205 pages
summary: Defazio's thesis covering finite-sum optimization (Finito and Prox-Finito in Chapter 3, SAGA and other primal incremental methods in Chapter 4, with full proofs; properties of the finite-sum class in Chapter 5) and graph-structured objectives (Gaussian graphical models, Chapters 7-9). Confirmed from the full text: Definition 2.1 is the 'big data condition' n >= beta L/mu; Section 4.8 analyses SAGA under the step sizes 1/(2(mu n + L)) and 1/(3L) (strongly convex) and 1/(3L) (non-strongly convex).
main_result: Finito: fast linear rate for strongly convex problems under the big data condition, with the remark that when the condition fails 'we conjecture that the step size must be reduced proportionally to the violation' and that 'in practice, the most effective step size can be found by testing a number of step sizes, as is usually done with other stochastic optimisation methods'; SAGA: the Lyapunov analysis of Defazio et al. (2014) for the three step-size regimes of Section 4.8; the thesis also states that SVRG's inner-loop length set 'conservatively as m = n ... does not give anywhere near the best practical performance', and that having one parameter instead of two is a practical advantage of SAGA.
relevance: Background for A4/B3 (extended SAGA/Finito proofs and discussion of the big-data condition, i.e. the n versus L/mu regimes of the min-of-two-rates) and documented evidence that practical step sizes are chosen by testing rather than from the theory (theory-practice gap).

title: SGD: general analysis and improved rates
authors: Robert M. Gower, Nicolas Loizou, Xun Qian, Alibek Sailanbayev, Egor Shulgin, Peter Richtárik
summary: Single convergence theorem for SGD under arbitrary sampling, based on expected smoothness instead of a uniform variance bound and on quasi-strong convexity (a one-point condition at x*); exact step-size formulas as functions of the mini-batch size, optimal mini-batch size, and rules for switching to decreasing steps.
main_result: Assumption 2.1 (expected smoothness): E||grad f_v(x) - grad f_v(x*)||^2 <= 2 L_cal (f(x) - f*), and gradient noise sigma^2 = E||grad f_v(x*)||^2; f mu-quasi-strongly convex. Theorem 3.1 (confirmed): for constant gamma in (0, 1/(2 L_cal)], E||x^k - x*||^2 <= (1 - gamma mu)^k ||x^0 - x*||^2 + 2 gamma sigma^2/mu; Theorem 3.2: switching to decreasing steps after 4 ceil(L_cal/mu) iterations; closed-form L_cal(b) for sampling with replacement and independent sampling; optimal mini-batch size increases with sigma^2 and equals 1 when sigma^2 = 0.
relevance: B3: the inequality E||f_i'(theta) - f_i'(eta*)||^2 <= 2 L_cal (F(theta) - F(eta*)) is the exact data-dependent replacement of the cocoercivity-with-R^2 step of Prop. 5.9 (L_cal <= L_max, often much smaller under anisotropy); B2: only a one-point (quasi) strong convexity at eta* is needed, the same object as mu_eff(t).

title: Stochastic gradient descent, weighted sampling, and the randomized Kaczmarz algorithm
authors: Deanna Needell, Nathan Srebro, Rachel Ward (NIPS 2014 version: Needell, Ward, Srebro)
venue: Mathematical Programming 155(1-2):549-573 (online 2015; conference version NIPS 2014)
summary: Finite-sample analysis of constant-step SGD for smooth strongly convex objectives whose dependence on conditioning is linear in L/mu (instead of quadratic), with the worst-case component smoothness sup_i L_i replaced by the average L_bar = E L_i under (partially biased) importance sampling; randomized Kaczmarz is an instance.
main_result: Theorem 2.1 (confirmed): each f_i convex with Lipschitz gradient L_i <= sup L, F mu-strongly convex, sigma^2 = E||grad f_i(x*)||^2, step gamma < 1/sup L: E||x_k - x*||^2 <= [1 - 2 gamma mu (1 - gamma sup L)]^k ||x_0 - x*||^2 + gamma sigma^2/(mu (1 - gamma sup L)). Corollary 3.1 (confirmed): with partially biased sampling (weights (3.10), a mixture of uniform and p_i proportional to L_i) and step gamma = mu/(4(mu L_bar + sigma^2/eps)), after k = 4 log(2 eps_0/eps) (L_bar/mu + sigma^2/(mu^2 eps)) iterations E||x_k - x*||^2 <= eps, i.e. the conditioning enters through L_bar = E L_i and the residual term is only doubled; Kaczmarz with partially biased sampling converges to the unweighted least-squares solution.
relevance: B3: the hierarchy L(F) <= L_bar <= L_max quantifies the slack of the 'cocoercivity of each f_i' step; on logistic regression with anisotropic features the per-sample L_i = ||x_i||^2/4 vary widely. B1: importance sampling acts as a diagonal preconditioning of the sampling distribution.

title: Self-concordant analysis for logistic regression
authors: Francis Bach
venue: Electronic Journal of Statistics 4:384-414
summary: Shows that the logistic loss is generalized self-concordant (|phi'''| <= phi''), which controls how fast the Hessian of the empirical logistic risk can vary, and uses it to transfer least-squares results (non-asymptotic bounds for l2- and l1-regularized estimators) to logistic regression with the Hessian at the optimum playing the role of the design covariance.
main_result: Proposition 1 (Taylor expansions, confirmed, eq. (3)-(6)): for a generalized self-concordant F with constant R, F(w+v) is sandwiched between F(w) + v^T F'(w) + v^T F''(w) v (e^{-R||v||} + R||v|| - 1)/(R^2||v||^2) and the analogous bound with e^{R||v||}, and the Hessians satisfy e^{-R||v||} F''(w) <= F''(w+v) <= e^{R||v||} F''(w); consequently the logistic objective is locally strongly convex around the optimum with constant ~ lambda_min(F''(eta*)) in a ball of radius ~ 1/R, and non-asymptotic bounds for regularized logistic regression follow from the least-squares ones with Sigma replaced by the Hessian at the optimum.
relevance: B2 (central): rigorous basis for a trajectory-dependent curvature: once ||theta_t - eta*|| <~ 1/R the effective strong convexity is lambda_min(H(eta*)) + lambda, usually far above the regularization lambda used in the bounds; B3: motivates reporting mu_eff(t) against lambda_min(H(eta*)). | (B2): quantifies how fast the local curvature can change along a trajectory: within ||theta_t - eta*|| <= 1/R the Hessian (hence mu_eff) varies by at most a factor e; outside, the global constant lambda is the only guarantee, explaining a theory-practice gap that shrinks as iterates localize. (B3): identifies the cocoercivity step (which uses R^2) as the one that is loose relative to the local Hessian. Pipeline: gives the region nu <= lambda^{1/2}/(2R) of guaranteed quadratic Newton convergence for computing eta* to high precision.

title: Adaptivity of averaged stochastic gradient descent to local strong convexity for logistic regression
authors: Francis Bach
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 15(19):595-627
summary: Averaged SGD with constant step proportional to 1/(R^2 sqrt(N)) on logistic regression (single pass) always achieves O(1/sqrt N) and automatically achieves O(R^2/(mu N)) when mu, the lowest eigenvalue of the Hessian at the global optimum, is large enough, without knowing mu; proof via generalized self-concordance; extends to generalized linear models with bounded features.
main_result: Abstract (confirmed): with step size proportional to 1/(R^2 sqrt N), R the maximum norm of the observations, the convergence rate is always O(1/sqrt N) and improves to O(R^2/(mu N)) where mu is the lowest eigenvalue of the Hessian at the global optimum, 'without any exponentially increasing constant'; the algorithm 'can adapt to the local strong-convexity constant' without requiring to know it.
relevance: B2 (central precedent): the clearest statement that the relevant constant is local curvature at eta* rather than the global mu; the project's mu_eff(t) is the SAGA analogue. A4: interpretation of measured exponents when lambda is tiny (rates governed by lambda_min(H(eta*)) rather than lambda). | (B2): formalizes 'effective curvature at the optimum' (lambda_min of the local Hessian, typically >> lambda) as the quantity that governs rates for logistic regression, the exact idea behind mu_eff(t); motivates measuring lambda_min(H(eta*)) and the Rayleigh quotient along the SAGA trajectory. Pipeline: tells the experimenter that mu_eff depends on the data distribution (norm of theta*, anisotropy), not on lambda alone.

title: Fast global convergence of gradient methods for high-dimensional statistical recovery
authors: Alekh Agarwal, Sahand N. Negahban, Martin J. Wainwright
venue: The Annals of Statistics 40(5):2452-2482
summary: Introduces restricted strong convexity (RSC) and restricted smoothness (RSM) for regularized M-estimators in high dimensions, where global strong convexity fails, and proves that projected/composite gradient methods converge geometrically up to the statistical precision, with constants holding w.h.p. for Lasso, group Lasso, log-linear models, low-rank recovery.
main_result: Definition 1 (RSC): L(theta') - L(theta) - <grad L(theta), theta' - theta> >= (gamma_l/2)||theta' - theta||^2 - tau_l (tolerance in the regularizer norm), and the analogous RSM with (gamma_u, tau_u); then the gradient iterates satisfy ||theta^t - theta_hat||^2 <= kappa^t ||theta^0 - theta_hat||^2 + O(statistical precision) with contraction kappa < 1 depending on gamma_l/gamma_u (not on the global condition number), until the error reaches the statistical precision ||theta_hat - theta*||.
relevance: B2: effective curvature need only hold on the directions actually visited (a cone of near-sparse directions here); for anisotropic logistic regression the analogue is curvature along the SAGA trajectory, i.e. mu_eff(t); also the template for 'linear convergence up to a floor' arguments.

title: Linear convergence of SVRG in statistical estimation
authors: Chao Qu, Yan Li, Huan Xu
venue: arXiv preprint 1611.01957 (v3, 2017); no peer-reviewed version found on Crossref
summary: Shows that SVRG converges linearly, up to statistical precision, for a class of M-estimators (Lasso, group Lasso, logistic regression, corrected Lasso, SCAD) using restricted strong convexity instead of strong convexity, even without convexity.
main_result: Under RSC (in the sense of Agarwal-Negahban-Wainwright/Loh-Wainwright) with a 'modified restricted strongly convex parameter' and L-smooth components (Theorems 1-2), Prox-SVRG iterates satisfy a geometric decrease of E[F(x_s) - F(x_hat)] with a contraction depending on the restricted constants, down to the fundamental statistical precision of the estimator; no global strong convexity or convexity required.
relevance: B2: variance-reduced methods inherit 'effective' restricted curvature constants, supporting the hypothesis that SAGA's practical rate is governed by local/restricted curvature; complements agarwal2012fast for the SVRG family.

title: Gradient methods for convex minimization: better rates under weaker conditions
authors: Hui Zhang, Wotao Yin
venue: arXiv preprint 1303.4645 (UCLA CAM report 13-17)
summary: Relaxes Lipschitz-gradient and strong convexity to hold only along specific segments and introduces the (restricted) secant inequality <grad f(x), x - x*> >= nu ||x - x*||^2 (x* = projection on the solution set); shows the classical gradient and accelerated-gradient complexities persist under these weaker, larger-nu/smaller-R conditions, hence are tighter.
main_result: Abstract (confirmed): under a Lipschitz constant R restricted to the segments joining x and x - (1/R) grad f(x): O(R/eps) for gradient descent and O(sqrt(R/eps)) for accelerated gradient; adding the secant inequality with constant nu: O((R/nu) log(1/eps)) and O(sqrt(R/nu) log(1/eps)); 'the secant condition is also shown to be necessary for the geometric decay of solution error'.
relevance: B2 (definition): the project's mu_eff(t) = (theta_t - eta*)^T F'(theta_t)/||theta_t - eta*||^2 is exactly the secant-inequality (RSI) constant evaluated along the trajectory; this is the paper that introduced it as a sufficient condition for linear rates.

title: Linear convergence of gradient and proximal-gradient methods under the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition
authors: Hamed Karimi, Julie Nutini, Mark Schmidt
venue: ECML PKDD 2016, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 9851:795-811
summary: Organizes the conditions used to prove linear rates without strong convexity (essential/weak strong convexity, restricted secant inequality, error bound, PL, quadratic growth), proves the implication chain, and derives simple linear rates for gradient, coordinate, sign-based, stochastic and variance-reduced (SVRG) methods under PL, plus a proximal-PL extension; covers least squares, logistic regression, boosting, l1, SVM, SDCA.
main_result: Theorem 2 (confirmed): for f with Lipschitz gradient, (SC) => (ESC) => (WSC) => (RSI) => (EB) <=> (PL) => (QG), and under convexity (RSI) <=> (EB) <=> (PL) <=> (QG) (arXiv v4 fixes a constant in the PL => QG proof); Theorem 1: gradient descent under mu-PL (||grad f||^2 >= 2 mu (f - f*)) with step 1/L gives f(x_k) - f* <= (1 - mu/L)^k (f(x_0) - f*); Appendix D (confirmed): SVRG with convex L-smooth f_i and PL/QG f keeps the Johnson-Zhang form E[f(x_s) - f*] <= (1/(1 - 2 L eta)) (1/(m mu eta) + 2 L eta) E[f(x_{s-1}) - f*]; logistic regression (confirmed): strictly convex only, but 'the PL inequality will still be satisfied over any compact set'.
relevance: B2: dictionary relating mu_eff (RSI) to PL/EB/QG constants, with the exact loss factors; A4: unregularized logistic regression satisfies PL on compact sets, explaining linear rates with an effective mu unrelated to lambda.

title: Linear convergence of first order methods for non-strongly convex optimization
authors: Ion Necoara, Yurii Nesterov, François Glineur
venue: Mathematical Programming 175(1-2):69-107 (online 2018)
summary: Defines four relaxations of strong convexity relative to the projection x_bar onto the solution set (quasi-strong convexity, quadratic under-approximation, quadratic gradient growth, quadratic functional growth), proves their ordering and derives linear rates for projected gradient, fast gradient (with restart) and feasible descent methods under each, with examples (least squares, LP, duals of linearly constrained problems).
main_result: Definitions (x_bar = projection of x on X*): qSC: f* >= f(x) + <grad f(x), x_bar - x> + (kappa_f/2)||x - x_bar||^2; QUA: f(x) >= f* + <grad f(x_bar), x - x_bar> + (kappa_f/2)||x - x_bar||^2; QGG: <grad f(x) - grad f(x_bar), x - x_bar> >= kappa_f ||x - x_bar||^2; QFG: f(x) - f* >= (kappa_f/2)||x - x_bar||^2. Theorem 4 (arXiv numbering, confirmed): SC => qSC => QGG => QUA => QFG (nested classes S, qS, G, U, F); Theorem 7: QFG implies the error bound ||g(x)|| >= c ||x - x_bar|| with a reduced constant. Projected gradient with step 1/L_f and kappa_f = sigma_f/L_f (confirmed): under qSC (Theorem 11) ||x^k - x_bar^k||^2 <= ((1 - kappa_f)/(1 + kappa_f))^k ||x^0 - x_bar^0||^2; under QFG (Theorem 12) ||x^k - x_bar^k||^2 <= (1/(1 + kappa_f))^k ||x^0 - x_bar^0||^2.
relevance: B2: QGG at x_bar = eta* is exactly mu_eff; gives the gradient-descent rates one should expect when mu is replaced by mu_eff, i.e. the reference for interpreting measured mu_eff(t) against observed SAGA contraction.

title: Gradient descent is optimal under lower restricted secant inequality and upper error bound
authors: Charles Guille-Escuret, Adam Ibrahim, Baptiste Goujaud, Ioannis Mitliagkas
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022), pp. 24893-24904
summary: Studies the function class RSI-(mu) ∩ EB+(L) defined by a lower restricted secant inequality <grad f(x), x - x*> >= mu ||x - x*||^2 and an upper error bound ||grad f(x)|| <= L ||x - x*|| (which includes non-convex functions and avoids the pathological discontinuity of L/mu); derives interpolation conditions for the class (Theorem 1), a lower bound on the rate of any first-order method, and shows gradient descent is exactly optimal on this class.
main_result: Proposition 1 (confirmed): on RSI-(mu) ∩ EB+(L), gradient descent with step gamma = mu/L^2 satisfies ||x_i - x*||^2 <= (1 - mu^2/L^2)^i ||x_0 - x*||^2 (per-step contraction of the squared distance 1 - 2 gamma mu + gamma^2 L^2, optimized at gamma = mu/L^2; complexity O((L/mu)^2 log(1/eps))); Theorem 2 (confirmed): for any first-order algorithm and any x_0 there is a function in the class with ||x_i - x*||^2 >= (1 - mu^2/L^2)^i ||x_0 - x*||^2 for i <= d - 1, so gradient descent is optimal and acceleration is impossible under these one-point conditions alone; Section 6 uses the interpolation conditions in a PEP to compute worst-case rates of heavy-ball on the class (best at zero momentum).
relevance: B2 (caveat): conditions of the mu_eff type (one-point at eta*) do not by themselves allow acceleration, so an A3-type speed-up with mu replaced by mu_eff needs more (convexity of the f_i); B3: shows the class in which 'tightness' of a gradient-type analysis is provable by PEP.

title: A study of condition numbers for first-order optimization
authors: Charles Guille-Escuret, Baptiste Goujaud, Manuela Girotti, Ioannis Mitliagkas (order of the PMLR PDF and arXiv; the PMLR HTML metadata list Girotti second)
summary: Shows that smoothness and strong convexity (hence kappa = L/mu) are discontinuous under arbitrarily small perturbations of the function, which can produce overly conservative tunings; studies alternative continuous metrics (one-point/restricted conditions at the optimum such as RSI/EB-type constants), proves their continuity and relations, and derives guaranteed gradient-descent rates when tuned with them.
main_result: The map f -> (L, mu) is not continuous in the relevant topology (small perturbations can send mu to 0 or L to infinity), whereas the alternative metrics are continuous; gradient descent tuned with those metrics has guaranteed linear rates in terms of them.
relevance: B2/B3: argues for reporting effective condition numbers (mu_eff, EB constants along the trajectory) rather than L/mu in the experimental diagnosis.

title: Adaptive restart of accelerated gradient methods under local quadratic growth condition
authors: Olivier Fercoq, Zheng Qu
venue: IMA Journal of Numerical Analysis 39(4):2069-2095
summary: Under a local quadratic growth condition F(x) - F* >= (mu/2) dist(x, X*)^2 (mu unknown), restarted accelerated proximal gradient is globally linearly convergent for any restart frequency, and a rule that adapts the frequency from the observed decrease of the gradient-mapping norm estimates the growth constant online; tested on Lasso and l2-regularized logistic regression.
main_result: Abstract (confirmed): 'restarting these algorithms at any frequency gives a globally linearly convergent algorithm' (previously known only for long enough frequencies); since the rate depends on the match between the frequency and the quadratic error bound, the adaptive scheme 'automatically adapt[s] the frequency of restart from the observed decrease of the norm of the gradient mapping' and 'has a better theoretical bound than previously proposed methods for the adaptation to the quadratic error bound'.
relevance: B2: a practical online estimator of the local growth constant along the trajectory (a mu_eff surrogate) and A3: restart-based acceleration as the deterministic analogue of negative momentum; useful for reporting mu_eff(t) in B3.

title: Sharpness, restart, and acceleration
authors: Vincent Roulet, Alexandre d'Aspremont
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization 30(1):262-289 (short version NIPS 2017)
summary: Uses the Łojasiewicz/sharpness inequality f(x) - f* >= mu dist(x, X*)^r, which holds generically, to design optimal restart schedules for accelerated methods; shows the schedules are robust so a log-scale grid search suffices although the sharpness constants are unobservable; concludes restart generically accelerates.
main_result: Proposition 2.2 (confirmed; smooth case s = 2, tau = 1 - 2/r, kappa = L/mu^{2/r}): scheduled restarts of the accelerated gradient method with geometrically increasing cycle lengths t_k = C e^{alpha k} give f(x_hat) - f* <= exp(-2 e^{-1} (c kappa)^{-1/2} N) (f(x_0) - f*) when tau = 0 (r = 2: linear rate, complexity O(sqrt(kappa) log(1/eps)) matching the strongly convex case) and f(x_hat) - f* = O(N^{-2/tau}) when tau > 0, i.e. complexity O(sqrt(L/mu^{2/r}) eps^{-(1/2)(1 - 2/r)}) for r > 2, faster than the eps^{-1/2} of plain accelerated methods; the schedule is robust to misestimation of (mu, r), so a log-scale grid search suffices.
relevance: B2: local sharpness exponent/constant as trajectory-dependent quantities that can be estimated from runs (r = 2 corresponds to QG/mu_eff); A3 alternative to momentum correction.

title: Local convergence properties of SAGA/Prox-SVRG and acceleration
authors: Clarice Poon, Jingwei Liang, Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb
summary: For composite problems whose non-smooth part is partly smooth relative to a manifold, SAGA and Prox-SVRG identify the active manifold in finitely many iterations and then enter a local linear convergence regime governed by local parameters; proposes exploiting this by adapting to the better local constants and by higher-order (super-linear) acceleration.
main_result: Abstract (confirmed): (i) finite activity identification: SAGA/Prox-SVRG iterates identify the smooth manifold in a finite number of iterations; (ii) the sequence then enters a local linear convergence regime whose rate is determined by the restricted (manifold) problem, i.e. a local condition number smaller than the global one; discussion of acceleration schemes (including higher-order methods with super-linear local convergence) on machine-learning examples.
relevance: B2 (direct): explains better-than-bound SAGA rates by a trajectory-dependent local regime; B1: local Newton/preconditioned acceleration once the manifold is identified.

title: Acceleration through spectral density estimation (arXiv title: Average-case acceleration through spectral density estimation)
authors: Fabian Pedregosa, Damien Scieur
summary: Average-case analysis of first-order methods on random quadratic problems: the expected error after k steps depends on the whole expected spectral density of the Hessian, not just its extreme eigenvalues; derives average-case-optimal momentum methods for Marchenko-Pastur, uniform and exponential spectra, with parameters not requiring the smallest eigenvalue, and shows regimes (quadratic and logistic regression) where they beat worst-case accelerated methods.
main_result: Theorem 2.1 (confirmed): for gradient-based methods with residual polynomial P_k, x_k - x* = P_k(H)(x_0 - x*) and E||x_k - x*||^2 = integral of P_k(lambda)^2 d mu(lambda) over the expected spectral distribution mu of the Hessian (Definition 3); the average-case optimal method is given by the orthogonal polynomials of mu (explicit momentum schemes for Marchenko-Pastur, uniform and exponential spectra); worst-case bounds (functions of kappa only) can be far from typical behaviour.
relevance: B2/B3 (alternative explanation of the theory-practice gap): typical rates on anisotropic logistic regression depend on the feature-covariance spectrum (the anisotropy knob of B3), not on kappa alone; suggests reporting spectral densities alongside tightness ratios.

title: On fundamental proof structures in first-order optimization
authors: Baptiste Goujaud, Aymeric Dieuleveut, Adrien Taylor
venue: 62nd IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2023), pp. 3023-3030
summary: Tutorial-style paper on the structure of worst-case convergence proofs of first-order methods: function classes described implicitly by interpolation inequalities (Section 2), algorithms as linear combinations of oracle outputs (Section 3), a systematic approach to obtain and verify worst-case certificates as nonnegative combinations of interpolation inequalities and how this structure can be exploited to extend guarantees and build algorithms (Section 4), and a natural approach for discovering Lyapunov sequences from PEPs (Section 6).
main_result: Any worst-case guarantee P(f, (x_t)) <= tau for a first-order method over a class described by interpolation inequalities can be certified by a weighted sum of those inequalities with nonnegative multipliers (the dual of the PEP SDP), and the multipliers reveal which inequalities are active; Lyapunov (potential) sequences are obtained by the same mechanism applied to one iteration with a quadratic ansatz (Section 6).
relevance: B3 (methodological backbone): makes explicit that a proof such as Prop. 5.9 is a nonnegative combination of per-step inequalities, so the 'tightness ratio per inequality' measured empirically has an exact theoretical counterpart (the dual multipliers) and the bottleneck step is the one with the largest multiplier that is also loose on the data; also explains how to search for a better Lyapunov weight Delta.

title: Beyond Least-Squares: Fast Rates for Regularized Empirical Risk Minimization through Self-Concordance
authors: Ulysse Marteau-Ferey, Dmitrii Ostrovskii, Francis Bach, Alessandro Rudi
venue: Proceedings of the 32nd Conference on Learning Theory (COLT 2019), PMLR vol. 99, pp. 2294-2340
summary: Studies regularized ERM with a squared Hilbertian norm for generalized self-concordant losses (logistic, softmax). Obtains a bias-variance decomposition driven by the Hessian at the population optimum and an effective dimension (degrees of freedom), and shows that source and capacity conditions give the same fast rates as for least squares.
main_result: Verified from the PDF. Assumption (generalized self-concordance): |nabla^3 ell_z(theta)[k,h,h]| <= sup_{g in phi(z)} |k.g| nabla^2 ell_z(theta)[h,h], with sup ||g|| <= R; for the logistic loss phi(z) = {y Phi(x)}. Define H(theta) = E nabla^2 ell_Z(theta), H_lambda = H + lambda I, Bias_lambda = ||H_lambda(theta*)^{-1/2} nabla L_lambda(theta*)|| = lambda ||H_lambda(theta*)^{-1/2} theta*||, and the degrees of freedom df_lambda = E||H_lambda(theta*)^{-1/2} nabla ell_Z(theta*)||^2 (eq. 5), which equals Tr(H_lambda(theta*)^{-1} H(theta*)) under the Bartlett identities (well-specified case) and Tr(C C_lambda^{-1}) in the least-squares-like case. Theorem 4 (general bound): for 0 < lambda <= B_2 and delta in (0,1/2], if n >= c_1 (B_2^2/lambda) log(c B_2^2/(lambda delta)) and n >= c_2 (df_lambda v (Q*)^2)/r_lambda(theta*)^2 log(2/delta) (r_lambda = Dikin-ellipsoid radius, (Q*)^2 = B_1^2/B_2), then with probability >= 1 - 2 delta: L(theta_hat_lambda) - L(theta*) <= C_bias Bias_lambda^2 + C_var (df_lambda v (Q*)^2) log(2/delta)/n, with universal constants (C_bias, C_var, c_1 <= 414, c_2 <= 5184) when Bias_lambda <= r_lambda(theta*)/2 and constants of order e^{O(R||theta*||)} otherwise. Corollaries: lambda ~ 1/sqrt(n) gives O(1/sqrt(n)); source condition theta* = H(theta*)^r v (r in (0,1/2]) gives rate n^{-(1+2r)/(2+2r)}; adding the capacity condition df_lambda <= Q lambda^{-1/alpha} (Assumption 7) with lambda = (C_0/n)^{alpha/(1+alpha(1+2r))} gives the minimax-type rate n^{-alpha(1+2r)/(1+alpha(1+2r))} (Corollary 3, verified).
relevance: Pipeline: the statistically meaningful range of lambda is n^{-1/2} down to about n^{-1} (fast rates), i.e. kappa = R^2/lambda between sqrt(n) and n; therefore kappa >> n (needed for (A3)/(A4)) is an optimization-driven regime and should be presented as such. Defines the effective dimension d_eff(lambda) = tr(H(H+lambda)^{-1}) used in the project and links it to the spectrum decay (capacity condition). (B2): everything is governed by the Hessian at theta*, not by global constants.

title: Finite-sample analysis of M-estimators using self-concordance
authors: Dmitrii M. Ostrovskii, Francis Bach
venue: Electronic Journal of Statistics, vol. 15, no. 1, pp. 326-391
summary: Non-asymptotic localization theory for M-estimators with (pseudo) self-concordant losses, including logistic regression. Introduces an effective dimension accounting for misspecification, a Dikin ellipsoid around theta*, and a curvature parameter rho comparing the data covariance with the Hessian; proves chi-square-type excess-risk bounds once n exceeds a critical sample size.
main_result: Verified from the PDF. Pseudo self-concordance (logistic, Bach 2010): |ell'''(y,eta)| <= ell''(y,eta); canonical (Nesterov-Nemirovski): |ell'''| <= 2 (ell'')^{3/2}. With H = nabla^2 L(theta*), G = E[nabla ell_Z(theta*) nabla ell_Z(theta*)^T], d_eff := Tr(H^{-1} G) (= d when well specified). Dikin ellipsoid Theta_r(theta*) = {theta : ||theta - theta*||_H <= r}. Curvature parameter rho: smallest constant with Sigma = E[XX^T] <= rho H (generic bound rho <= (inf ell'')^{-1}, vacuous for the logistic loss). Theorem 1.1 (simplified form of Theorems 3.1-3.2): L(theta_hat_n) - L(theta*) <~ ||theta_hat_n - theta*||_H^2 <~ d_eff log(e/delta)/n with probability >= 1 - delta, once n >~ d_eff d log(ed/delta) for canonically self-concordant losses, and once n >~ rho d_eff d log(ed/delta) for pseudo self-concordant losses; improved critical sample sizes under subgaussianity uniform over the Dikin ellipsoid. Logistic regression with Gaussian design X ~ N(0, Sigma) (Proposition D.1, verified): rho <~ 1 + ||theta*||_Sigma^3; K_2 <~ (1 + log(1 + ||theta*||_Sigma)) sqrt(1 + ||theta*||_Sigma); in the well-specified case K_1 <~ (1 + ||theta*||_Sigma)^{3/2}.
relevance: (B2): rho = sup Sigma/H is exactly the ratio between the covariance geometry that fixes L (through ||x_i||^2/4) and the local Hessian geometry that fixes mu_eff; for Gaussian designs rho grows like 1 + ||theta*||_Sigma^3, so stronger signals (larger-margin optima) make the Hessian flatter relative to Sigma/4 and widen the theory-practice gap. Pipeline: when generating synthetic logistic data, the norm ||theta*||_Sigma is the knob that controls local curvature independently of lambda and of the covariance spectrum.

title: Random Design Analysis of Ridge Regression
authors: Daniel Hsu, Sham M. Kakade, Tong Zhang
venue: Foundations of Computational Mathematics, vol. 14, no. 3, pp. 569-600
summary: Sharp random-design analysis of OLS and ridge regression. Expresses sample-size requirements and variance through effective dimensions d_{1,lambda}, d_{2,lambda} of the covariance, and shows that the empirical regularized covariance is spectrally close to the population one once n exceeds d_{1,lambda} log d_{1,lambda}.
main_result: Verified from the PDF. With lambda_j the eigenvalues of Sigma = E[x x^T], d_{p,lambda} := sum_j (lambda_j/(lambda_j + lambda))^p, p in {1,2}; Condition 1 (bounded statistical leverage): ||(Sigma + lambda I)^{-1/2} x|| / sqrt(E||(Sigma + lambda I)^{-1/2} x||^2) <= rho_lambda almost surely, where E||(Sigma + lambda I)^{-1/2} x||^2 = d_{1,lambda}. Theorem 2 (ridge): if n >= 6 rho_lambda^2 d_{1,lambda} (log d~_{1,lambda} + t) (d~_{1,lambda} a closely related quantity, eq. 6), then with probability >= 1 - 4e^{-t}: (i) ||(Sigma+lambda I)^{1/2}(Sigma_hat+lambda I)^{-1}(Sigma+lambda I)^{1/2}|| <= (1 - delta_s)^{-1} with delta_s = sqrt(4 rho_lambda^2 d_{1,lambda}(log d~_{1,lambda}+t)/n) + 2 rho_lambda^2 d_{1,lambda}(log d~_{1,lambda}+t)/(3n) <= 0.93; (ii) ||beta_hat_lambda - beta||_Sigma^2 <= 3(eps_rg + eps_bs + eps_vr) with eps_rg = ||beta_lambda - beta||_Sigma^2 <= sum_j lambda_j beta_j^2/(lambda_j/lambda + 1)^2 and eps_vr <~ sigma^2 (d_{2,lambda} + sqrt(d_{1,lambda} d_{2,lambda}) delta_f)/(n (1 - delta_s)^2). Simplified: ||beta_hat_lambda - beta||_Sigma^2 <= ||beta_lambda - beta||_Sigma^2 + O((rho_lambda^2 d_{1,lambda} E[approx_lambda(x)^2] + ||beta_lambda - beta||_Sigma^2 + sigma^2 d_{2,lambda})/n); at lambda = 0, d_{p,0} = d and the variance is sigma^2 d/n.
relevance: Pipeline: for synthetic designs the empirical regularized Hessian (Sigma_hat + lambda I, or its logistic weighted version) is a (1 +/- delta_s)-accurate copy of the population one as soon as n >~ d_{1,lambda} log d_{1,lambda}, so one can prescribe the condition number and d_eff by choosing the population spectrum. Supplies the standard definition d_eff(lambda) = d_{1,lambda} = tr Sigma(Sigma + lambda I)^{-1} and its variance counterpart d_{2,lambda}.

title: Distribution of eigenvalues for some sets of random matrices
authors: Vladimir A. Marchenko (Marcenko), Leonid A. Pastur
venue: Mathematics of the USSR-Sbornik, vol. 1, no. 4, pp. 457-483
summary: Original derivation of the limiting eigenvalue distribution of large sample covariance matrices (and more general random matrices) when dimension and sample size grow proportionally. It is the base case for every Hessian-spectrum statement about Gaussian-feature regression.
main_result: Let X in R^{n x d} have i.i.d. centered entries with unit variance and d/n -> c in (0, infinity). The empirical spectral distribution of Sigma_hat = (1/n) X^T X converges to the Marchenko-Pastur law with density f_c(x) = sqrt((b - x)(x - a))/(2 pi c x) on [a, b] = [(1 - sqrt c)^2, (1 + sqrt c)^2], plus an atom of mass 1 - 1/c at 0 when c > 1. Consequently lambda_max(Sigma_hat) -> (1 + sqrt c)^2, lambda_min(Sigma_hat) -> (1 - sqrt c)^2 (c < 1), and the condition number of Sigma_hat tends to ((1 + sqrt c)/(1 - sqrt c))^2. With features x_i ~ N(0, I_d), the logistic Hessian at theta = 0 is Sigma_hat/4 + lambda I, so kappa(0) ~ ((1 + sqrt c)^2/4 + lambda)/((1 - sqrt c)^2/4 + lambda).
relevance: Pipeline/(A4): the aspect ratio c = d/n is a hidden source of ill-conditioning in Gaussian synthetic problems; to make kappa controlled by lambda alone (so that kappa ~ R^2/(4 lambda) and the lambda-sweep of (A4) is clean) one needs c small (e.g. d/n <= 1/10), otherwise the Hessian is intrinsically ill-conditioned (singular as c -> 1) even for lambda = 0. (B2): the bulk of the Hessian gives the typical curvature vs lambda_min.

title: Strong Convergence of the Empirical Distribution of Eigenvalues of Large Dimensional Random Matrices
authors: Jack W. Silverstein
venue: Journal of Multivariate Analysis, vol. 55, no. 2, pp. 331-339
summary: Proves almost-sure convergence of the empirical spectral distribution of sample covariance matrices with a general (anisotropic) population covariance, characterized by the Marchenko-Pastur-Silverstein fixed-point equation. This is the tool for anisotropic Gaussian features and for weighted sample covariances such as the logistic Hessian.
main_result: Let B_n = (1/n) T^{1/2} X X^* T^{1/2} with X having i.i.d. standardized entries, T Hermitian nonnegative with empirical spectral distribution converging to nu~, and d/n -> c > 0. Then the ESD of B_n converges a.s. to a deterministic F whose Stieltjes transform m(z) is the unique solution in C^+ of m(z) = integral d nu~(t) / ( t (1 - c - c z m(z)) - z ). The same equation (with T on the other side) describes weighted sample covariances (1/n) sum_i tau_i x_i x_i^T. Edges of the support and hence lambda_max, lambda_min of the empirical Hessian follow from nu~ (the population spectrum, e.g. power law lambda_j ~ j^{-alpha}) and c.
relevance: Pipeline: gives the map (population spectrum of Sigma, c = d/n) -> (lambda_max, lambda_min, d_eff) of the empirical Hessian for anisotropic designs, which is what (B3) needs to control 'feature-covariance anisotropy' deterministically; the logistic Hessian (1/n) X^T D X + lambda I is a weighted sample covariance of this type.

title: Hessian Eigenspectra of More Realistic Nonlinear Models
authors: Zhenyu Liao, Michael W. Mahoney
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (NeurIPS 2021), pp. 20104-20117
summary: Uses deterministic-equivalent random-matrix techniques to characterize the Hessian spectrum of generalized GLMs (logistic regression included) with Gaussian features of arbitrary mean and covariance, at any parameter w. Shows the spectrum can have bounded or unbounded support, one or several bulks, and isolated eigenvalues on either side of the bulk, depending on data, response model and loss.
main_result: Verified from the PDF (Theorem 1, Corollary 1 qualitative content). Model: y_i ~ f(y | w*^T x_i), x_i ~ N(mu, C) i.i.d., Hessian H = (1/n) sum_i ell''(y_i, w^T x_i) x_i x_i^T = (1/n) X D X^T; n, p -> infinity with p/n -> c, ||w||, ||w*||, ||mu||, ||C|| = O(1). Theorem 1: the ESD of H converges a.s. to the law with Stieltjes transform m(z) = (1/p) tr Q_bar(z), Q_bar(z) = ( E[g C /(1 + g delta(z))] - z I_p )^{-1}, delta(z) = (1/n) tr(C Q_bar(z)), where g = d^2 ell(y,h)/dh^2 and h = w^T x ~ N(w^T mu, w^T C w); constant g gives Marchenko-Pastur. Logistic loss: g <= 1/4 so the support is bounded (the exponential loss gives unbounded support); the support is compact iff both the law of g and the spectrum of C are compactly supported; heterogeneous C produces multi-bulk spectra (Fig. 3). Corollary 1 (logistic model, w = w* = 0, C = I): the limit is exactly the Marchenko-Pastur law rescaled by 1/4; a nonzero mean mu (rho = lim ||mu||^2) creates a single isolated eigenvalue to the right of the bulk once rho exceeds a threshold of order sqrt(c), with a BBP-type eigengap/eigenvector-alignment transition (explicit location (1/4)(1 + rho + c(rho + 1)/rho) and alignment (rho^2 - c)/(rho^2 + c rho) as reported by the search agent; these two closed forms were not re-extractable from the PDF text). Corollary 2: at most one isolated eigenvalue due to the model parameter w, which can lie to the left of the bulk.
relevance: (B2)/(B3): exact description of the logistic Hessian spectrum under controlled anisotropy: the bulk is a deformed MP law shrunk by the weights g_i = sigma(m_i)sigma(-m_i) < 1/4 (so local curvature falls below the Sigma/4 bound as the iterates move away from 0 and classify confidently), while a mean shift mu or the signal w creates a few isolated eigenvalues that set L without raising mu_eff. Pipeline: tells which synthetic knobs (||mu||, ||w*||, spectrum of C, c = d/n) generate single-bulk, multi-bulk or spiked Hessians, i.e. qualitatively different geometries for the bottleneck-step diagnosis of (B3).

title: Eigenvalues and Condition Numbers of Random Matrices
authors: Alan Edelman
venue: SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications, vol. 9, no. 4, pp. 543-560
summary: Derives exact eigenvalue densities of Wishart matrices and the asymptotic distribution of the 2-norm condition number of Gaussian random matrices. Establishes that square Gaussian matrices are ill-conditioned with condition number of order n.
main_result: Abstract verified via Crossref: for real or complex n x n matrices with i.i.d. standard normal entries, E log kappa_2(A) is asymptotic to log n, more precisely about log n + 1.537 for real and log n + 0.982 for complex matrices as n -> infinity; the paper also describes the limiting distributions of the condition number (square and rectangular cases), gives exact distributions for 2 x n matrices, and studies the largest/smallest Wishart eigenvalues (exact distributions in some cases, expected characteristic polynomial). Consequence: kappa(A^T A) is of order n^2 for square Gaussian matrices; for rectangular n x d matrices with d/n -> c < 1 the extreme singular values scale like sqrt(n)(1 -/+ sqrt c), so kappa(A^T A/n) stays bounded, consistent with the Marchenko-Pastur edges.
relevance: Pipeline: warns that 'random Gaussian design with d close to n' produces Hessians with kappa ~ n^2 independently of lambda; for the lambda-sweep experiments of (A4) and for the anisotropy study of (B3), keep d/n well below 1 (or use explicit spectra) so that the measured kappa is the intended one.

title: Acceleration through Spectral Density Estimation
authors: Fabian Pedregosa, Damien Scieur
venue: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2020), PMLR vol. 119, pp. 7553-7562 (arXiv version titled 'Average-case Acceleration Through Spectral Density Estimation')
summary: Develops an average-case analysis of first-order methods on random quadratic problems whose Hessian eigenvalues follow a prescribed density, and derives momentum methods that are optimal on average for uniform, Marchenko-Pastur and exponential spectral densities. Benchmarks on quadratic and logistic regression show regimes where they beat worst-case accelerated methods.
main_result: Abstract verified (PMLR page). For quadratics f(x) = (1/2)(x - x*)^T H (x - x*) with H random and expected spectral density rho (e.g. Marchenko-Pastur with ratio r = d/n, edges (1 +/- sqrt r)^2), the average-case optimal method minimizes E||x_t - x*||^2 over polynomial-based (momentum) methods; explicit algorithms are derived for the uniform, Marchenko-Pastur and exponential densities, with simple momentum-like updates using only the current gradient and the previous two iterates; the momentum and step-size parameters can be estimated without knowledge of the Hessian's smallest singular value, unlike Nesterov acceleration and Polyak momentum. Empirical benchmarks on quadratic and logistic regression identify regimes where these methods improve over classical (worst-case) accelerated methods.
relevance: Pipeline: a ready-made recipe for 'random quadratics with controlled Marchenko-Pastur spectrum' benchmarks, and a reminder that the whole spectral density, not only kappa, drives first-order methods, so (A4) exponents should be measured at fixed spectral shape. (B1): preconditioning/momentum tuned to the spectrum is the deterministic counterpart of the P^{-1} modification of SAGA.

title: Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger Convergence Rates for Least-Squares Regression
authors: Aymeric Dieuleveut, Nicolas Flammarion, Francis Bach
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research, vol. 18, no. 101, pp. 1-51
summary: Averaged accelerated regularized SGD for least squares with optimal bias O(1/n^2) and variance O(d/n) rates, with finer dimension-free bounds under source and capacity conditions on the covariance spectrum. Its synthetic experiments are a template for power-law-spectrum ill-conditioned problems.
main_result: Synthetic protocol (Section 7, verified from the PDF): d = 25, normally distributed inputs with a random covariance Sigma whose eigenvalues are 1/i^3 (i = 1..d), random optimum theta* and starting point theta_0 with ||theta_0 - theta*|| = 1, outputs from a linear function with homoscedastic noise with unit signal-to-noise ratio (sigma^2 = 1), R^2 = tr Sigma ('the average radius of the data'), step gamma = 1/R^2, lambda = 0, additive-noise oracle, results averaged over 10 replications; Fig. 1 shows bias and variance panels. Theory: capacity condition tr(Sigma^b) < infinity, i.e. eigenvalues decaying at least as (tr Sigma^b)^{1/b}/i^{1/b}, b in [0,1]; source condition ||Sigma^{r/2} theta*|| < infinity, r in [-1,1]; rates: bias O(1/n^2), variance O(d/n), with dimension-free refinements under the two conditions. Under lambda_j ~ j^{-alpha}: kappa(Sigma + lambda I) ~ (1 + lambda)/(d^{-alpha} + lambda) and d_eff(lambda) ~ lambda^{-1/alpha}.
relevance: Pipeline: concrete generator for ill-conditioned least-squares/logistic designs with power-law spectra (eigenvalues i^{-alpha}, R^2 = tr Sigma, step 1/R^2) that the (B3) anisotropy study can reuse; shows how alpha and d jointly fix kappa and d_eff, so that 'same kappa, different spectrum' comparisons are possible.

title: On the existence of maximum likelihood estimates in logistic regression models
authors: Adelin Albert, John A. Anderson
venue: Biometrika, vol. 71, no. 1, pp. 1-10
summary: Classical characterization of when the (unregularized) logistic-regression MLE exists. Introduces the trichotomy complete separation / quasi-complete separation / overlap and shows that the MLE exists and is unique exactly in the overlap case.
main_result: Data (x_i, y_i), y_i in {-1,+1}. Complete separation: there is b with y_i x_i^T b > 0 for all i; quasi-complete separation: y_i x_i^T b >= 0 for all i with equality for some i (and not all zero); overlap: neither. Theorem: the logistic MLE exists (finite) and is unique iff the data overlap; under complete or quasi-complete separation the likelihood supremum is approached only as ||b|| -> infinity, so the MLE does not exist. Consequence for optimization: with lambda = 0 the empirical logistic risk F has inf F not attained, its Hessian weights sigma(m_i)sigma(-m_i) -> 0 along maximizing sequences, and the problem is not strongly convex; with lambda > 0 the regularized optimum exists but ||theta*_lambda|| grows like log(1/lambda) on separable data.
relevance: Pipeline: explains why unregularized or nearly unregularized synthetic logistic problems are ill-posed and why Newton/IRLS or GD reference solutions can diverge; mandates checking for (quasi-)separation (an LP feasibility test) before running the lambda -> 0 sweeps of (A4). (B2): on nearly separable data mu_eff(t) collapses toward lambda while L_eff collapses below R^2/4, so nominal kappa = R^2/lambda misrepresents the geometry.

title: Geometrical and Statistical Properties of Systems of Linear Inequalities with Applications in Pattern Recognition
authors: Thomas M. Cover
venue: IEEE Transactions on Electronic Computers, vol. EC-14, no. 3, pp. 326-334
summary: Function-counting theorem: counts the dichotomies of n points in general position in R^d that are linearly separable, giving the probability that random labels are separable and the sharp n = 2d threshold ('capacity' of a linear classifier).
main_result: For n points in general position in R^d, the number of homogeneously linearly separable dichotomies is C(n, d) = 2 sum_{k=0}^{d-1} binom(n-1, k). Hence, for uniformly random labels, P(separable) = 2^{1-n} sum_{k=0}^{d-1} binom(n-1, k): equal to 1 for n <= d, equal to 1/2 at n = 2d, and tending to 0 for n/d > 2 (sharp transition at n = 2d as d -> infinity). In the proportional regime p/n -> kappa this is the kappa = 1/2 threshold at zero signal recovered by Candes and Sur (2020).
relevance: Pipeline: minimal design rule for synthetic logistic problems, n >= 2d is necessary but not sufficient (random labels), and with informative labels the separability threshold moves to smaller d/n; in practice choose n >> 2d or keep lambda > 0 to avoid the degeneracy of Albert-Anderson.

title: The phase transition for the existence of the maximum likelihood estimate in high-dimensional logistic regression
authors: Emmanuel J. Candès, Pragya Sur
venue: Annals of Statistics, vol. 48, no. 1, pp. 27-42
summary: Shows that, for Gaussian covariates in the proportional regime p/n -> kappa, the existence of the logistic MLE (equivalently, absence of complete/quasi-complete separation) undergoes a sharp phase transition at an explicit boundary curve depending on the signal strength. Generalizes Cover's 1/2 threshold to informative labels.
main_result: Verified from the PDF. x_i ~ N(0, Sigma) i.i.d. (Sigma nonsingular), P(y_i = 1 | x_i) = sigma(beta_0 + x_i^T beta), p/n -> kappa, Var(x_i^T beta) -> gamma_0^2. Let X, Z ~ N(0,1) independent, (Y, V) =_d (Y, Y X) with P(Y = 1 | X) = sigma(beta_0 + gamma_0 X). Define h_MLE(beta_0, gamma_0) = min_{t_0, t_1 in R} E (t_0 Y + t_1 V - Z)_+^2 (eq. 6). Theorem 1: if kappa > h_MLE then P(MLE exists) -> 0; if kappa < h_MLE then P(MLE exists) -> 1; the transition occurs in an interval of width O(n^{-1/2}). Special case: h_MLE(0,0) = 1/2 (Cover 1965); h_MLE decreases as the signal strength increases. 'MLE does not exist' = the data are completely or quasi-completely separated in the sense of Albert and Anderson.
relevance: Pipeline: for Gaussian synthetic logistic designs with signal, separation (hence an ill-posed lambda = 0 limit and a lambda-dependent optimum norm) occurs already at d/n well below 1/2; choose d/n below h_MLE(signal) or accept that the small-lambda regime of (A4) is a regime where ||eta*|| and the local curvature are themselves set by lambda. (B2): quantifies when local curvature becomes degenerate.

title: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data
authors: Daniel Soudry, Elad Hoffer, Mor Shpigel Nacson, Suriya Gunasekar, Nathan Srebro
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research, vol. 19, no. 70, pp. 1-57
summary: On linearly separable data, gradient descent on unregularized logistic (or any exponential-tailed) loss diverges in norm but converges in direction to the hard-margin SVM solution, extremely slowly (logarithmically), while the loss itself decays as 1/t.
main_result: Verified from the PDF. Assume linearly separable data, a positive, decreasing, beta-smooth loss with exponential tail (logistic, exp), step size eta < 2 beta^{-1} sigma_max^{-2}(X), arbitrary initialization. Theorem 3: the GD iterates satisfy w(t) = w_hat log t + rho(t), where w_hat = argmin ||w|| s.t. w^T x_n >= 1 for all n (hard-margin SVM) and ||rho(t)|| = O(log log t); Theorem 4: for almost every data set rho(t) stays bounded. Theorem 5 (any separable data set): || w(t)/||w(t)|| - w_hat/||w_hat|| || = O(log log t / log t) and 1 - cos(angle) = O((log log t / log t)^2), improving to O(1/log t) and O(1/log^2 t) for almost every data set; margin gap 1/||w_hat|| - min_n x_n^T w(t)/||w(t)|| = O(1/log t); loss L(w(t)) = O(1/t).
relevance: Pipeline: explains what a near-unregularized run looks like (loss O(1/t), iterate norm growing like log t) and why a GD-computed 'reference optimum' on nearly separable data is unreliable, supporting Newton-based reference solutions with lambda > 0. (B2): along such trajectories the effective curvature decays continuously, the extreme case of a trajectory-dependent mu_eff(t).

title: Fast Rates for Regularized Objectives
authors: Karthik Sridharan, Shai Shalev-Shwartz, Nathan Srebro
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 21 (NIPS 2008), pp. 1545-1552 (pages as commonly cited)
summary: Shows that for strongly convex regularized objectives whose stochastic part is linear (e.g. SVM / regularized ERM with Lipschitz loss), the empirical minimizer converges to the population minimizer of the regularized objective at rate O(1/n) instead of O(1/sqrt n), which yields tight oracle inequalities and the standard scaling of the regularization parameter with n.
main_result: Abstract verified: the empirical minimizer of a stochastic strongly convex objective whose stochastic component is linear converges to the population minimizer at rate O(1/n); this applies to the SVM objective, gives O(1/n) convergence of the SVM objective to its infinite-data limit, is essential for tight oracle inequalities for SVMs, and extends to strong convexity with respect to other l_p norms. For objectives (lambda/2)||w||^2 + E ell(w; z) with ell convex and L-Lipschitz the bound takes the form O(L^2/(lambda n)) (up to logarithmic/confidence factors). Combined with the approximation term lambda ||w_0||^2/2 this gives oracle inequalities whose optimization of lambda yields lambda of order L/(||w_0|| sqrt n) in general (kappa = R^2/lambda of order sqrt(n)), and lambda down to order 1/n in favorable (low-noise) regimes.
relevance: Pipeline/(A1)/(A4): the statistically sensible range of lambda is between ~1/sqrt(n) and ~1/n, i.e. kappa between sqrt(n) and n; Bach's lambda = R^2/n is thus the most ill-conditioned statistically motivated choice, and the kappa >> n regime where acceleration pays (A3/A4) must be presented as an optimization regime, not a learning one; also guides the test-error panels of the experiments.

title: Convex Optimization
authors: Stephen Boyd, Lieven Vandenberghe
venue: Cambridge University Press
summary: Standard reference for Newton's method with backtracking line search, including the two-phase (damped / quadratically convergent) analysis under strong convexity and Lipschitz Hessian, and the affine-invariant self-concordant analysis with the Newton decrement as an optimality certificate.
main_result: Newton's method x+ = x - t nabla^2 f(x)^{-1} nabla f(x) with backtracking (alpha in (0, 1/2), beta in (0,1)). For f m-strongly convex with L-Lipschitz Hessian there exist eta in (0, m^2/L] and gamma > 0 such that: damped phase, if ||nabla f(x)||_2 >= eta then f(x+) - f(x) <= -gamma; quadratic phase, if ||nabla f(x)||_2 < eta then t = 1 and (L/(2m^2))||nabla f(x+)||_2 <= ((L/(2m^2))||nabla f(x)||_2)^2; total iterations <= (f(x_0) - p*)/gamma + log_2 log_2(eps_0/eps) (Section 9.5.3). Self-concordant case (verified from the book PDF): iterations <= (20 - 8 alpha)/(alpha beta (1 - 2 alpha)^2) (f(x_0) - p*) + log_2 log_2(1/eps) (eq. 9.56), and the Newton decrement lambda(x)^2 = nabla f^T nabla^2 f^{-1} nabla f certifies f(x) - p* <= lambda(x)^2 for lambda(x) <= 0.68 (eq. 9.50). For l2-logistic regression the Hessian is (1/n) X^T D X + lambda I with D_ii = sigma(m_i) sigma(-m_i), m_i = y_i x_i^T theta, cost O(n d^2 + d^3) per step (or Hessian-vector products O(nd) with CG).
relevance: Pipeline: the recommended way to compute eta* to ~1e-15 relative accuracy for the suboptimality curves (quadratic convergence from the Dikin-type region given by Bach 2010's Proposition 2), with the Newton decrement as a certified bound on F(theta) - F*, far better than 'run GD for many epochs'.

title: Trust Region Newton Method for Logistic Regression
authors: Chih-Jen Lin, Ruby C. Weng, S. Sathiya Keerthi
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research, vol. 9, no. 22, pp. 627-650 (conference version ICML 2007, pp. 561-568)
summary: Introduces TRON, a trust-region Newton method with conjugate-gradient inner solves for large-scale l2-regularized logistic regression, using only Hessian-vector products. It takes approximate Newton steps early and converges quadratically at the end, beating quasi-Newton (L-BFGS) on large sparse data; it is the solver behind LIBLINEAR's primal logistic regression.
main_result: Abstract verified (JMLR page): a trust region Newton method is applied to maximize the log-likelihood of the logistic regression model; it uses only approximate Newton steps in the beginning but achieves fast convergence in the end; experiments show it is faster than the commonly used quasi-Newton approach; the method is also extended to large-scale L2-loss linear SVMs. Objective f(w) = (1/2) w^T w + C sum_i log(1 + exp(-y_i w^T x_i)) (equivalently lambda = 1/(nC) in the (lambda/2)||w||^2 + (1/n) sum formulation); gradient nabla f = w - C sum_i (1 - sigma(y_i w^T x_i)) y_i x_i, Hessian nabla^2 f = I + C X^T D X with D_ii = sigma(y_i w^T x_i)(1 - sigma(y_i w^T x_i)); Hessian-vector products cost O(nnz(X)) so the trust-region subproblem is solved matrix-free by CG; globally convergent and locally quadratically convergent.
relevance: Pipeline: reference solver for high-accuracy optima on the canonical LIBSVM datasets (ijcnn1, covtype, w8a, a9a, rcv1, mushrooms) when d is too large for dense Newton; also provides the conversion C = 1/(n lambda) between LIBLINEAR's parametrization and the project's lambda.

title: LIBLINEAR: A Library for Large Linear Classification
authors: Rong-En Fan, Kai-Wei Chang, Cho-Jui Hsieh, Xiang-Rui Wang, Chih-Jen Lin
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research, vol. 9, no. 61, pp. 1871-1874
summary: Open-source library for large-scale linear classification (logistic regression and linear SVM) with primal trust-region Newton and dual coordinate-descent solvers; the standard tool for computing accurate logistic-regression optima on LIBSVM data.
main_result: Solves min_w (1/2) w^T w + C sum_i xi(w; x_i, y_i) with xi the logistic, L1- or L2-SVM loss; primal L2-regularized logistic regression (-s 0) uses the trust-region Newton method of Lin, Weng and Keerthi (2008); the tolerance parameter -e controls the stopping rule on the gradient norm (its default 0.01 for -s 0 is far too loose for reference optima and must be lowered to ~1e-10 or less); matching the project's objective (lambda/2)||w||^2 + (1/n) sum ell_i requires C = 1/(n lambda) and, if a bias is used, a regularized or unregularized intercept must be handled consistently (-B option).
relevance: Pipeline (optional real-data follow-up): practical path to eta* on the canonical datasets and to the exact per-sample constants L_i = ||x_i||^2/4 + lambda after the usual feature scaling.

title: Proximal Newton-Type Methods for Minimizing Composite Functions
authors: Jason D. Lee, Yuekai Sun, Michael A. Saunders
venue: SIAM Journal on Optimization, vol. 24, no. 3, pp. 1420-1443
summary: Generalizes Newton-type methods to composite objectives g + h (g smooth convex, h convex with cheap proximal map): the search direction minimizes a quadratic model of g plus h, with backtracking; proves global convergence, local quadratic convergence for exact Hessians, superlinear for quasi-Newton, and robustness to inexact subproblem solves.
main_result: Iteration x_{k+1} = x_k + t_k Delta x_k with Delta x_k = argmin_d nabla g(x_k)^T d + (1/2) d^T H_k d + h(x_k + d) and t_k from a backtracking line search on the composite objective; if H_k = nabla^2 g(x_k), g strongly convex with Lipschitz Hessian, then unit steps are eventually accepted and ||x_{k+1} - x*|| <= C ||x_k - x*||^2 (quadratic convergence); with Dennis-More-type quasi-Newton H_k the rate is superlinear; the subproblems may be solved inexactly with adaptive forcing terms while keeping these rates. For h = 0 and H_k = P (fixed s.p.d. matrix) the method reduces to preconditioned gradient descent.
relevance: Pipeline: high-precision optima for composite variants (l1 + logistic, proximal SAGA/Katyusha comparisons) and for the l2 case when a prox-friendly regularizer is kept outside the smooth part. (B1): the fixed-metric case H_k = P is the deterministic analogue of theta_t = theta_{t-1} - gamma P^{-1} g_t and shows which quantities (P-norms, P-relative smoothness L_P = lambda_max(P^{-1/2} H P^{-1/2})) replace L and mu.

title: A comparison of numerical optimizers for logistic regression
authors: Thomas P. Minka
venue: Technical note, Microsoft Research (2003; revised 10/21/2003); earlier version: 'Algorithms for maximum-likelihood logistic regression', CMU Statistics Dept. Tech. Report 758 (2001; revised 9/19/2003)
summary: Derives and compares eight optimizers for MAP (l2-regularized) logistic regression, including Newton/IRLS, conjugate gradient, quasi-Newton, coordinate-wise and iterative-scaling methods, on synthetic data of varying size. Concludes that conjugate gradient and quasi-Newton methods are fastest at scale, far outperforming iterative scaling, with Newton-type methods best when d is small.
main_result: Verified from the author's page: the note compares eight algorithms for computing the MAP parameter estimate with full derivations (including new derivations of Iterative Scaling and of the Modified Iterative Scaling of Collins et al.); all algorithms are compared in computational complexity by experiments on large synthetic data sets; 'the fastest algorithms turn out to be conjugate gradient ascent and quasi-Newton algorithms, which far outstrip Iterative Scaling and its variants'; the earlier CMU version (seven algorithms, maximum likelihood) found line-search and Newton-type algorithms to be the best performers; the author notes that later real-data studies reached the same conclusions. Per-iteration costs: Newton/IRLS O(n d^2 + d^3) with quadratic convergence, CG and quasi-Newton (BFGS) O(nd) per iteration, coordinate ascent and iterative scaling O(nd) but many more iterations.
relevance: Pipeline: practical guidance for choosing the reference solver (dense Newton for d up to a few thousand, CG/L-BFGS or TRON beyond) and a reminder that the Newton Hessian (1/n) X^T D X + lambda I is also the object whose spectrum the (B2)/(B3) diagnostics need.

title: LIBSVM: A library for support vector machines
authors: Chih-Chung Chang, Chih-Jen Lin
venue: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology, vol. 2, no. 3, article 27, pp. 1-27
summary: Reference for the LIBSVM software and its dataset repository, which hosts the binary-classification datasets used in essentially all variance-reduction papers (SVRG, SAGA, SAG, Katyusha, L-Katyusha). The repository page documents sizes, feature counts and sources.
main_result: Canonical binary datasets (verified on the LIBSVM binary-datasets page; training / test, features): a9a 32,561 / 16,281, d = 123 (UCI Adult); w8a 49,749 / 14,951, d = 300; ijcnn1 49,990 / 91,701, d = 22; covtype.binary 581,012, d = 54; rcv1.binary 20,242 / 677,399, d = 47,236; mushrooms 8,124, d = 112; phishing 11,055, d = 68 (unit-length rows); real-sim 72,309, d = 20,958; news20.binary 19,996, d = 1,355,191 (unit-length rows). With features scaled to [0,1] (or rows normalized to unit norm) the per-sample constants are L_i = ||x_i||^2/4 + lambda, L_max = max_i ||x_i||^2/4 + lambda, and the dataset-dependent ratio L_max / lambda_max((1/4n) X^T X) measures the slack between Bach's R^2-based kappa and L/mu.
relevance: Pipeline (optional real-data follow-up): fixes n, d and hence the kappa = L/lambda range reachable by lambda in {1/n, 1/(10 n), ...} for each dataset, and the conventions used in the VR literature (SVRG: rcv1/covtype/protein; SAGA: ijcnn1/covtype/MNIST; L-Katyusha: a9a/w8a/mushrooms/phishing/cod-rna; Katyusha: a9a/w8a/mnist/rcv1/covtype/sensit).

title: Introductory Lectures on Convex Optimization: A Basic Course
authors: Yurii Nesterov
venue: Springer US / Kluwer Academic Publishers, Applied Optimization vol. 87
summary: Source of the 'chain' (tridiagonal) quadratic worst-case functions for first-order methods, in both the smooth convex and smooth strongly convex settings, which are the building blocks of all finite-sum hard instances and the simplest synthetic problems with exactly known condition number and optimum.
main_result: Smooth case (Section 2.1.2): f_k(x) = (L/4) [ (1/2)( x_1^2 + sum_{i=1}^{k-1} (x_i - x_{i+1})^2 + x_k^2 ) - x_1 ], Hessian (L/4) A_k with A_k tridiagonal (2 on the diagonal, -1 off), eigenvalues in [0, L]; Theorem 2.1.7: any method with x_t in x_0 + Lin{nabla f(x_0), ..., nabla f(x_{t-1})} satisfies f(x_t) - f* >= 3L||x_0 - x*||^2 / (32 (t+1)^2) and ||x_t - x*||^2 >= (1/8)||x_0 - x*||^2 for t <= (k-1)/2. Strongly convex case (Theorem 2.1.13, Q_f = L/mu): f_{mu,L}(x) = (mu(Q_f - 1)/8) [ x_1^2 + sum_{i>=1} (x_i - x_{i+1})^2 - 2 x_1 ] + (mu/2)||x||^2 gives ||x_t - x*|| >= ((sqrt Q_f - 1)/(sqrt Q_f + 1))^t ||x_0 - x*|| and f(x_t) - f* >= (mu/2) ((sqrt Q_f - 1)/(sqrt Q_f + 1))^{2t} ||x_0 - x*||^2 for every first-order (span) method. (Textbook-standard statements; book metadata verified via Crossref, constants not re-checked against the printed book.)
relevance: (A1)/(A4)/pipeline: the chain quadratic is the canonical controlled-kappa synthetic problem (kappa = Q_f exactly, x* in closed form, geometric decay of the solution along the chain), and the atom of the Lan-Zhou and Woodworth-Srebro finite-sum instances; (B1): a block/tridiagonal preconditioner P solves the chain in one step, illustrating which inequalities of the SAGA proof become loose under P^{-1}-scaled steps.

title: Condition Number Analysis of Logistic Regression, and its Implications for Standard First-Order Solution Methods
authors: Robert M. Freund, Paul Grigas, Rahul Mazumder
venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:1810.08727 (math.OC), October 2018; also Optimization Online 6870 (no journal version found on Crossref)
summary: Introduces two condition numbers for binary-classification data: the degree of non-separability DegNSEP (for non-separable data) and the degree of separability DegSEP (the margin, for separable data), and shows how they govern the existence, norm and local curvature of the logistic-regression optimum and the convergence guarantees of steepest descent and SGD, including linear convergence without strong convexity (extending Bach's self-concordance analysis) and approximate-max-margin guarantees in the separable case.
main_result: Verified from the arXiv PDF (abstract, Section 2, theorem headings). Unregularized logistic regression L_n(beta) = (1/n) sum_i log(1 + exp(-y_i beta^T x_i)) with a given norm on R^p. DegNSEP := min_{||beta|| = 1} (1/n) sum_i [y_i beta^T x_i]_- (eq. 4), the smallest average misclassification 'error' over normalized models; DegNSEP > 0 iff the data are strictly non-separable, and L_n(beta) >= DegNSEP ||beta|| for all beta. Proposition 2.1: if DegNSEP > 0 then the ML problem has a unique optimal solution beta*, H(beta*) = nabla^2 L_n(beta*) is positive definite, and the optimum satisfies norm bounds of the form ||beta*|| <= ln(2)/DegNSEP (level sets {L_n(beta) <= L_n(beta_0)} have radius <= (ln 2 + L_n(beta_0))/DegNSEP). Proposition 2.2: lambda_min(H(beta*)) >= (1/(4n)) lambda_min(X^T X) exp(-ln(2) ||X|| / DegNSEP) > 0, with H(beta) = (1/n) X^T G X, G_ii = sigma(m_i) sigma(-m_i), i.e. a strictly positive local curvature at the optimum without any regularizer, degrading exponentially as DegNSEP -> 0. For separable data DegSEP := max_{||beta|| = 1} min_i y_i beta^T x_i (the margin, eq. 9). Theorem 3.2: sublinear guarantees for steepest descent (any norm) on logistic regression whose constants scale with 1/DegNSEP; Theorem 3.3: linear convergence of steepest descent in the non-separable case without strong convexity, at a rate governed by DegNSEP and the data (expanding Bach 2010); SGD obtains adaptive guarantees in which DegNSEP enters similarly. Theorem 3.4 (separable case): l2 steepest descent and SGD deliver approximate-maximum-margin solutions with computational guarantees depending on DegSEP, although the ML solution does not exist. Both condition numbers are interpreted as distances to separability/non-separability under data perturbations.
relevance: (B2)/(B3): gives a data-dependent, regularization-free lower bound on the curvature at the optimum, lambda_min(H(beta*)) >= (lambda_min(X^T X)/(4n)) e^{-ln 2 ||X||/DegNSEP}, i.e. mu_eff at eta* is controlled by how non-separable the data are, which is exactly the quantity to compute (an LP/convex program) on synthetic and LIBSVM data to explain the gap between the nominal mu = lambda and the observed effective curvature, and a linear-rate analysis without strong convexity to contrast with SAGA's lambda-based rate. Pipeline: compute DegNSEP/DegSEP to certify (non-)separability before the lambda -> 0 sweeps of (A4) and to choose the signal strength of synthetic generators.

title: Generalized self-concordant functions: a recipe for Newton-type methods
authors: Tianxiao Sun, Quoc Tran-Dinh
venue: Mathematical Programming, vol. 178, no. 1-2, pp. 145-213 (online May 2018)
summary: Unifies standard self-concordance (Nesterov-Nemirovski) and Bach's logistic-type condition into the class of (M_f, nu)-generalized self-concordant functions, establishes the key local estimates (Hessian sandwich bounds, Taylor bounds in the local norm), and uses them to design damped-step Newton and proximal-Newton methods with explicit step sizes, global convergence without line search, and local quadratic convergence without a Lipschitz-Hessian assumption; regularized logistic regression is a running example.
main_result: Verified from the arXiv PDF (Section 2, Definition 2, Examples; Example 4; Section 6.1). Definition 2: a C^3 convex f is (M_f, nu)-generalized self-concordant (M_f >= 0, nu > 0) if its third derivative satisfies |<nabla^3 f(x)[v] u, u>| <= M_f ||u||_x^2 ||v||_x^{nu - 2} ||v||_2^{3 - nu} (for nu in [2, 3]; ||.||_x the local Hessian norm); in one dimension |phi'''(t)| <= M phi''(t)^{nu/2}: nu = 3 is standard self-concordance, nu = 2 is Bach's condition |phi'''| <= M phi''. The logistic loss phi(t) = log(1 + e^{-t}) is generalized self-concordant with M = 1 and nu = 2, and finite sums f(x) = (1/n) sum_i phi(a_i^T x) + (gamma/2)||x||^2 are (M_f, 2)-generalized self-concordant with M_f = max_i ||a_i||_2 (Example 4), with alternative nu = 3-type characterizations after scaling. Key estimates: for nu = 2, e^{-M_f ||y - x||_2} nabla^2 f(x) <= nabla^2 f(y) <= e^{M_f ||y - x||_2} nabla^2 f(x) (Loewner order) and matching Taylor bounds, generalizing Bach's Proposition 1; for nu in (2, 3] analogous bounds in the local norm. Algorithms: damped-step Newton x+ = x - t nabla^2 f(x)^{-1} nabla f(x) with an explicit step size t = t(M_f, nu, lambda(x)) (lambda(x) the Newton decrement) that guarantees a global decrease without line search, a quadratic-convergence region in terms of lambda(x), and proximal-Newton extensions for composite problems; Section 6.1 shows better step sizes than Zhang-Lin for regularized logistic regression.
relevance: (B2): the formal local-curvature calculus for the logistic finite sum: the Hessian, hence mu_eff(t) = lambda_min-type quantities, changes by at most e^{+/- R ||theta_t - theta_s||} between two iterates (R = max ||x_i||), which bounds how fast the effective curvature can drift along a SAGA trajectory and over one step of length gamma ||g_t||. Pipeline: damped Newton with explicit step size and certified quadratic region for computing eta* without line search. (B1): the generalized self-concordant framework is the natural setting for analyzing a Hessian-preconditioned (P = nabla^2 F) variant of SAGA.

title: The Impact of Regularization on High-dimensional Logistic Regression
authors: Fariborz Salehi, Ehsan Abbasi, Babak Hassibi
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (NeurIPS 2019), pp. 12005-12015
summary: Precise asymptotics (via the Convex Gaussian Min-max Theorem) of regularized logistic regression in the proportional regime n/p -> delta with Gaussian features: the performance of the regularized estimator is characterized by a system of six nonlinear equations, generalizing the Sur-Candes MLE theory (recovered at zero regularization); detailed study of l2^2- and l1-regularized logistic regression, including the regularization weights that optimize given metrics, and the observation that regularization allows parameter recovery even when the MLE does not exist.
main_result: Verified from the NeurIPS/arXiv PDF (abstract, Theorems 1-2, Section 4.1). Model: x_i i.i.d. N(0, I_p/p), y_i ~ Bernoulli(sigma(x_i^T beta)), beta with i.i.d. entries from a distribution Pi, n/p -> delta > 0, signal strength kappa = ||beta||/sqrt(p); RLR estimate beta_hat = argmin_w { (1/n) sum_i [log(1 + e^{x_i^T w}) - y_i x_i^T w] + (lambda/n) f(w) } with a separable convex regularizer f. Theorem 1: as p -> infinity, for every locally Lipschitz Psi, (1/p) sum_j Psi(beta_hat_j, beta_j) -> E Psi(Gamma(...), Beta) where the limit is determined by the unique solution (alpha, sigma, gamma, theta, tau, r) of a system of six nonlinear equations (first-order conditions of a six-variable scalar min-max problem obtained from the CGMT); hence any performance metric (mean, MSE, support recovery probability) is computable. Theorem 2 (l2^2 regularizer): the centered estimate beta_hat - alpha beta becomes decorrelated from beta with entries approaching N(0, sigma^2), where (alpha, sigma) solve a reduced system involving the proximal map of the logistic loss; increasing lambda reduces the correlation factor alpha and the variance sigma^2, and there is an MSE-optimal lambda_opt(delta, kappa). With lambda = 0 the equations reduce to the three Sur-Candes equations (biased MLE with alpha > 1 and inflated variance). Regularization yields a well-defined estimate even when the unconstrained MLE does not exist (separable regime).
relevance: Pipeline/(B2): in the proportional regime d/n = 1/delta the norm of the l2-regularized optimum (alpha kappa sqrt(p)) and therefore the Hessian weights sigma(m_i)sigma(-m_i) at eta* are explicit functions of (delta, kappa, lambda): as lambda -> 0 the optimum inflates (alpha > 1) and the local curvature collapses, and below the Candes-Sur boundary only lambda > 0 keeps eta* finite; this is the quantitative version of the 'lambda sets the local geometry' effect the project must control when sweeping lambda on Gaussian synthetic data, and it provides a statistically motivated lambda_opt(delta, kappa) to contrast with the optimization-driven lambda << R^2/n regime of (A4).

title: A Large Scale Analysis of Logistic Regression: Asymptotic Performance and New Insights
authors: Xiaoyi Mai, Zhenyu Liao, Romain Couillet
venue: ICASSP 2019 - IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing, pp. 3357-3361
summary: Random-matrix analysis of Tikhonov (l2) regularized logistic regression for a two-class Gaussian mixture with arbitrary covariance when p and n are both large: the estimated coefficient vector is asymptotically Gaussian with explicit mean and covariance given by a three-scalar fixed-point system, which yields the asymptotic classification error, reveals a bias of the separating hyperplane for non-identity covariance, and shows that for identity covariance the best test performance is reached as the regularization weight tends to infinity.
main_result: Verified from the authors' PDF (abstract, Assumption 1, Theorem 1, Corollary 1). Model: two-class Gaussian mixture x_i ~ N((-1)^a mu_p, C_p) (class a in {1,2}), labels y_i = +/-1, p/n -> c > 0 (Assumption 1), and the regularized logistic classifier beta = argmin (1/n) sum_i rho(y_i x_i^T beta) + (gamma/2)||beta||^2 with rho(t) = ln(1 + e^{-t}) and Tikhonov weight gamma > 0 (gamma = 0 being the ML estimate when it exists). Theorem 1 (distribution of beta): ||beta - beta_bar|| -> 0 where (I_p + gamma' C_p) beta_bar ~ N(eta mu_p, zeta C_p / n), the three scalars (eta, zeta, gamma') being the unique solution of a fixed-point system of three equations (eq. 3) involving expectations of the logistic proximal operator under r ~ N(m, sigma^2), with m and sigma^2 explicit in mu_p^T (I_p + gamma' C_p)^{-1} mu_p and tr((I_p + gamma' C_p)^{-1} C_p)/n. Corollary 1: explicit asymptotic misclassification rate. Insights: the unregularized ML solution is biased (its scale is inflated, consistent with Sur-Candes for N(0, I_p) features) and the separating hyperplane is biased in direction when C_p is not proportional to the identity; regularized solutions are 'even more biased' yet generalize better; for identity covariance the optimal generalization performance is attained as gamma -> infinity (the direction tends to the class-mean direction); the theory predicts the optimal gamma from (mu_p, C_p, c).
relevance: (B2)/(B3): closed-form asymptotics of the l2-regularized logistic optimum under anisotropic covariance C_p, the exact setting of the project's feature-covariance-anisotropy experiments: the optimum is an (I + gamma' C_p)^{-1}-shrunk Gaussian vector, so the Hessian at eta* is a weighted covariance whose weights are driven by r ~ N(m, sigma^2), giving the map (spectrum of C_p, c = p/n, gamma, ||mu_p||) -> local curvature at the optimum that Liao-Mahoney provide only at a fixed w. Pipeline: a two-class Gaussian-mixture generator (mu_p, C_p, c) with theoretically known test error and optimum statistics, including the degenerate c above the separability threshold where only gamma > 0 is meaningful.
